thereof at chambers upon the filing of the appeal bond with the clerk of said Court or on proof that it has been filed with the Justice, and being satisfied of the legality and sufficiency of the same, may order a stay of any execution which may have been issued by the Justice, until the said Court or Judge shall make further order, a rule to which effect shall be entered in the minutes of the said Court, and a copy thereof certified by the clerk, shall be served on the constable in whose hands the execution may be. 

83. The Court of Common Pleas may permit the appellant to substitute a new appeal bond in the place of the appeal bond filed and sent up by the Justice. 

84. The Courts of Common Pleas shall hear and determine all such appeals in a summary way and give judgment and award execution thereon with costs, either on the affirmance or reversal of the judgment so appealed. 

85. Upon the trial of any appeal either party may produce any witness not produced or sworn in the Court below, or any documentary evidence not offered or admitted in the Court below, if otherwise legal and competent, without notice to the opposite party. 

86. If the judgment appealed from shall have been rendered upon the report of referees, the Court to which such appeal shall be made shall have power to inquire into such report of referees, and the judgment thereupon, and either to affirm or set aside the same for the same causes and upon the same principles as reports of referees are set aside in such Court in other cases, and to award a trial before the Court, if need be, in the same manner as in other cases. 

87. After the trial of an appeal in the Court of Common Pleas a new trial may be granted by such Court. 

88. Judgments of the Court of Common Pleas upon appeals from 

The Small Cause Courts shall not affect or bind any lands, unless a rule shall be entered in the minutes of the Court of Common Pleas in which said judgment shall be rendered, for recording such judgment, which rule shall be a rule of course, and may be entered at any time without notice. 

89. The clerk of the Court of Common Pleas, upon the entry of such rule, shall record any such judgment in the book of judgments of said Court, and index the same, as now required by law respecting the judgments of said Court, in suits originally commenced therein, which record shall be a transcript from the minutes of the said Court on said judgment, and for this service the clerk shall be entitled to receive twenty-five cents; and such judgment shall, from the time of entering such rule, affect and bind all lands within the county where such Court of Common Pleas is held, belonging to any person against whom such judgment may be; and executions against the goods and lands of such person may be issued out of such Court thereupon, immediately upon the entry of such rule. 

90. All appeals to the Court of Common Pleas shall be put on the list by the appellant for trial at the next term after the same shall be appealed, if sufficient time to notice the same, for ten days, remain between the perfecting of the appeal and the first day of the next term; either party may give such notice and place said appeal on the list for trial; in default of such notice the Court, unless good cause be shown, shall dismiss the appeal.

X. CERTIORARI 

91.

No judgment, order or proceeding, to be had or made by vir-

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

tue of this Act, shall be removed by writ of error, but by certiorari to the Supreme Court or Circuit Court. 

92. All judgments, orders and proceedings in The Small Cause 

Courts and in the Courts of Common Pleas upon appeals from said Courts may be removed into the Circuit Court of the same county by writ of certiorari, allowed by any Judge of such Court in the same manner and upon like terms as such writs are issuable out of the 

Supreme Court. 

93. Where The Small Cause Court has jurisdiction, no judgment from which an appeal is given by this Act shall be removed into the Supreme or Circuit Court by certiorari or otherwise, for the correction of any supposed error therein; but the party thinking himself aggrieved shall have relief by appeal only, and that both as to matter of law and matter of fact. 

94. No Justice of the Supreme Court or Judge of a Circuit Court shall grant or allow any certiorari to remove any judgment, order or proceeding, to be had by virtue of this Act to the Supreme or Circuit Court, unless the party applying for such certiorari shall present to the said Justice or Judge the reasons therefor, drawn up in writing and subscribed by himself or some attorney-at-law, and the same be deemed by the said Justice or Judge to contain a probable cause for allowing such certiorari; nor unless such applicant shall enter into bond to the other party in double the amount of the judgment with one or more good surety or sureties, conditioned that such applicant shall prosecute the said certiorari in the Supreme or Circuit Court, as the case may be, and shall pay the sum recovered in the Court below, with interests and costs, if the judgment be affirmed and shall in all things stand to and abide the judgment of the said Supreme or Circuit Court respecting the judgment, order or proceeding given or made by the Court below; which said bond shall be tendered to the Justice or 

Judge granting such certiorari, to be by him filed with the clerk of the Court out of which said writ shall issue for the benefit of the obligee therein named, and on failure thereof no certiorari shall be allowed. 

95. Such certiorari shall be prosecuted before the Supreme or Circuit Court, at the first term after the due return thereof shall be made, or be dismissed with costs, unless the Court for good cause shall otherwise direct; a motion to dismiss for such default to prosecute shall be a matter of course, and no notice thereof shall be required. 

96. If any judgment, to be given by virtue of this Act, shall, on removal by certiorari, be affirmed, the plaintiff in certiorari shall pay to the defendant all costs arising on such suit in the Supreme or Circuit Court, for which the party entitled to such costs may have execution, to be issued out of said Supreme or Circuit Court; but if such judgment be reversed, then the plaintiff in certiorari shall not be entitled to costs except the Court so order. 

97. No judgment of a Small Cause Court, removed by certiorari to the Supreme or Circuit Court, shall be reversed in the whole for any error or mistake by the Justice by whom such judgment may have been rendered, in the entering the same or calculating the amount thereof or for error in the awarding of the costs of suits, but such judgment shall be corrected or revised in so far as respects such error or mistake only; nor for an irregularity in the proceedings of such 

Court, unless such irregularity tends to defeat or impair the substantial right or interest of the party in certiorari praying for such reversal; nor for any error made by a constable in the proper return of a summons as to its service if it appear the defendant was in fact duly and legally served.

98. In case any judgment be so affirmed in part and reversed in part, neither party shall pay costs in certiorari to the other, unless upon express order of the Court therefor. 

99. If in any cause or proceedings removed by certiorari it shall appear equitable and just that a re-hearing thereof be had before The Small Cause Court, the Supreme or Circuit Court may order that such re-hearing be had upon such terms and conditions as are reasonable, and The Small Cause Court shall thereupon proceed to re-hear said cause or proceeding and give judgment as in other cases.

102. When the plaintiff in any action on Contract shall demand a jury of twelve men, and the jury shall find a sum in favor of the plaintiff, not exceeding fifty dollars, then the plaintiff shall pay one-half of the costs of the jury. 

103. No constable or other officer, authorized to serve a subpoena, summons or other mesne process issued out of The Small Cause

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Court, shall be required to serve such process until his legal fees and mileage for so doing shall have been paid to him. 

104. No appeal from the judgment of a Justice shall be allowed until the party applying for the same shall, in addition to the matters now required by law, pay to said Justice all costs incurred by him except such as shall be adjudged to the prevailing party. 

105. The fee of the Court for hearing the appeal, and the fees of the clerk for entering the action and filing the bond and transcript, shall be paid in the first instance by the appellant; if he refuses to pay the same before the hearing, the Court shall, on application of the clerk, refuse to hear such appellant, and the appellee, if he will pay the same, may move the Court to make, and the Court may thereupon make, such disposition of the case as if the appellant failed to appear and prosecute his appeal. 

1. AMENDMENT 

106. When judgment shall have been rendered upon the verdict of a jury, the Court of Common Pleas, to which an appeal shall be made, shall, before proceeding to hear and determine the same, amend the process, proceeding, verdict and judgment in all things which by the Act entitled "An Act respecting amendments and jeofails," are amendable on writs of error after verdict in other Courts; and if it should be inconvenient actually to make such amendments, then everything so amendable shall be taken and considered as amended, and proceeding shall be had thereupon, as if the same had been actually done. 

107. If the constable's return to any summons or warrant be defective, and such constable has, in point of fact, complied with all the requirements of this Act in serving such writ, whether the defendant appears or not and whether he objects or not, such constable may amend his return in such manner as to make it conform to the fact; provided, he do so on or before the trial of the cause. 

2. REFERENCES 

108. In every suit instituted in The Small Cause Court, and in every appeal to the Court of Common Pleas, the Justice of the Peace, or Court of Common Pleas as the case may be, with the assent and at the request of the parties, shall enter a rule of reference of the matters in difference to such person or persons as shall be nominated and agreed upon by and between the parties; and the reference so made shall be conducted in the same manner as directed in the case of references by the rule of Court, in and by the Act entitled "An Act for regulating references, and determining controversies by arbitration,' and the report of the said referee or referees, or the major part of them, whether in favor of the plaintiff or defendant, appellant or appellee, shall be final and conclusive to the parties, judgment shall be entered thereon with costs, and execution issued accordingly. 

3. DEPOSITIONS 

109. If a material witness in an action instituted in The Small 

Cause Court is in the State, but is infirm or sick, or is about to go out of the State, the deposition of such witness may, at the option of either party, be taken before a Justice of the Peace; the party at whose request the deposition is to be taken shall cause two days' notice to be given to the adverse party of the time, place and the person before whom the deposition will be taken, or such shorter notice as the cause in the opinion of the Justice may require, to attend at the taking there-

of, and cross-examine, if he shall think fit; and a deposition so taken and offered in evidence shall be subject to the same rules and exception that the witness would be if personally present. 

110. Every person so deposing shall be sworn or affirmed, and shall subscribe the testimony by him given, after the same shall be reduced to writing, which shall be done only by the Justice taking the deposition, or by the deponent or other person in his presence, and the deposition, so taken, shall be retained by such Justice until he deliver the same, with his own hand, into the Court for which it was taken, or shall be by said Justice sealed up, directed and transmitted to such Court, and remain under his seal until opened in Court, and when so opened the same shall be deposited in the office of the Justice before whom the action shall be brought, there to remain on record, and either of the parties in the said action may, at his cost, take copies of such deposition as soon as it is so deposited. 

111. The provisions of the Act entitled "An Act concerning evi dence" (Revision of 1900), so far as the same can be applied, are hereby extended to The Small Cause Courts. 

4. JUSTICES, THEIR DUTIES AND DOCKETS 

112. Every Justice of the Peace, before whom any suit shall be instituted, shall enter in a book to be kept for that purpose, the names of the plaintiff and defendant, the style and nature of the action, the sum demanded or penalty sued for, the time of issuing process, and when returnable, the return made thereto by the constable, when the copy of the account, or state of the demand, or set-off, was delivered by the parties or either of them, the time of taking the recognizance, of making or filing any order, the adjournment, the rule of reference, and report of referees, the jury, when and by whom demanded, the venire, when issued and how returned, the time of trial, the names of the jurors and witnesses, the admission of evidence objected to, the rejection of evidence offered, a description of each paper offered in evidence, the verdict and judgment and when given, the execution or executions, when issued, the endorsement thereon, and how returned by the constable, the appeal, when and by whom demanded, the date of receiving notice thereof, and all the proceedings before him had, touching the said suit; such Justice shall grant to either party, when required, a certified copy of such entries, which copy may be used as evidence in any Court in this State; no imperfection or irregularity in the book so kept shall invalidate any proceedings or judgment, but the same may be corrected to conform to the fact at any time, under rule by the Court to certify or otherwise. 

113. The Justice before whom any judgment is rendered shall make out and enter in his docket a full bill of costs in the case, speci fying each item and the fees for the same, and the amount paid him by each party. 

114. Every Justice of the Peace whose term of office has expired, or who has resigned, shall, when required so to do, make out transcripts from his docket or dockets, under his hand and seal, and certify them as "late Justice of the Peace;" which said transcripts shall have the same force and effect and be liable to the like legal objections as though the said Justice was still in commission. 

115. The book in which such proceedings shall be entered by any 

Justice of the Peace, shall, within one year after the death of the said Justice, be deposited in the office of the clerk of the county wherein the said Justice held his commission, to be there kept as a public record; if any Justice of the Peace shall be removed from his office by

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

impeachment, or if either before or after the expiration of his term of office, he shall be about to remove from the county in which he was commissioned, the docket or dockets of the said Justice shall be forthwith deposited in the clerk's office of his county; every Justice of the Peace and his legal representatives shall at all times, after the said docket or dockets are so deposited, have free access to the same without payment of any fees to the clerk therefor, to enable them to recover any costs which may be due the said Justice thereon. 

116. If any Justice of the Peace or his executor or administrator shall neglect or refuse to deposit his docket or dockets in the clerk's office, at the time and in the manner by this Act directed, he shall forfeit and pay the sum of fifty dollars, to be recovered by action on Contract, with costs, in any Court of competent jurisdiction, and to be sued for and recovered by the collector of the county, for the use of the county. 

117. The transcript of the record of any case entered in any docket, deposited in the clerk's office as aforesaid, certified to be a true transcript by said clerk, shall be received in evidence in any Court of this State, and be as good, effectual, and available in law, as if the deposited docket were then and there produced. 

118. No Justice of the Peace, unless duly licensed as an attorneyat-law of this State, or constable shall appear and prosecute or defend any action brought in The Small Cause Court unless such Justice or constable shall be one of the parties on record in the cause; and any 

Justice or constable who shall offend against this provision shall forfeit the sum of fifty dollars, to be recovered by action on Contract, with costs of suit, in any Court having cognizance thereof, in the name and for the use of any person who shall prosecute for the same. 

5. CONSTABLES, THEIR DUTIES 

119. The constables of the several wards and townships in any county shall be the ministerial officers of the said Courts, and said constables shall execute within the county all precepts, summons, warrants, writs, and all other process, issuing out of the said Court, and to them or any of them directed and delivered and make return thereof, and to perform all matters, acts, and things appertaining to their offices aforesaid. 

Approved April 8, 1903.

SUPPLEMENT SEAL OF COURT 

(Supplement, April 27, 1911; Laws, p. 544; C. S. Supp., p. 1667). 

1. Every Justice of the Peace shall use a seal, which shall bear the inscription in circular form "The Small Cause Court of the County of -, New Jersey," and the name of the Justice and State, ward or township from which he is elected, and every Justice of the Peace shall, on or before the first day of July, one thousand nine hundred and eleven, file a certificate with the county clerk of his county, with an impression of his seal thereon. 

2. Every summons, subpoena, commitment, warrant and transcript of every judgment entered in the docket in said Small Cause Court shall bear the impression of said seal, and no process issued by any Justice of said Small Cause Court shall be valid without the impression of said seal. 

3. Every Justice of the Peace hereafter elected shall, before entering upon his duties, file with the county clerk of the county of which he is elected a certificate bearing an impression of his seal, described in section one of this Act.

JUSTICES OF THE PEACE AND THEIR CIVIL JURISDICTION 39 Justices of the Peace and Their Civil Jurisdiction I. THE OFFICE OF JUSTICE 

Origin of the office

The origin of the office of Justice of the Peace is involved in some obscurity, because it is so ancient. As a civil officer, having power to try civil actions, in what is now known as The Small Cause Court, his functions are probably traceable to the Courts of Conscience, or Requests, first inaugurated in London in the reign of Henry VIII (1509-1547). But the office of "Conservator of the Peace," subsequently changed to "Justice of the Peace," was created in England in the time of Edward III (1327). Prior to that date there were itinerant magistrates, dating from the time of William the Conqueror (1027-1087).

In 1675 the first civil Court under the jurisdiction of a Justice of the Peace was established in East New Jersey and called a "Monthly Court of Small Causes." Subsequently a similar 

Court was established in West New Jersey. After various alterations, an Act of March, 1798, comprised the general law of to day regulating  (Penn. Treatise, 2nd 

Ed., pp. 9-12; Leam. & Spicer 99, 229, 270, 271, 304; see Wright v. Moran, 14 Vr. 49).

Office of Justice a constitutional one The office of Justice of the Peace in New Jersey is a constitutional one, and cannot be abolished by the Legislature. (Const. 

of N. J., Art VI., Sec. VII., par. 1; Art. VII., Sec. II., par. 8). 

Number of Justices to be elected

The Constitution of the State provides for the number of Justices who may be in commission at any one time in any township or ward, as follows: "When a township or ward contains two thousand inhabitants or less, it may have two Justices; when it contains more than two thousand inhabitants and not more than four thousand it may have four Justices; and when it contains more than four thousand inhabitants it may have five Justices; provided, that whenever any township not voting in wards contains more than seven thousand inhabitants, such township may have an additional Justice for each additional three thousand inhabitants above four thousand." (Const. of N. J., Art. VI., Sec. VII., par. 1.).

The number of inhabitants is determined by the last preceding census, whether of the State or of the United States. (C. S. 

3017, § 1).

Women may now be Justices of the Peace in this State. (P. 

L. 1921, p. 866; N. J. Cum. Supp. 4055, § 12).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Method of their election, commission, etc. "Justices of the Peace shall be elected by ballot at the annual meetings of the township in the several counties of the State, and of the wards in the cities that may vote in wards, in such manner and under such regulations as may be hereafter provided by law. They shall be commissioned for the county, and their commissions shall bear date and take effect on the first day of May next after their election. They shall hold their offices for five years; but, when elected to fill vacancies, they shall hold for the unexpired term only; provided, that the commission of any 

Justice of the Peace shall become vacant upon his ceasing to reside in the township in which he was elected." (Const. of N. J., Art. VII., Sec. II., par. 8). 

If a Justice is elected in the legal manner, but there are already a sufficient number in commission to meet the constitutional requirement, he will not be commissioned to act, and the election will be a nullity. Although at the expiration of another year a new vacancy may arise, by death, expiration of office, or otherwise, the previous election is still a nullity as to the person elected. He must again be elected before he can serve. 

The county clerk will notify the Justice on or before April first after an election of his lawful election. (C. S. 3018, § 11).

If he has been convicted of a misdemeanor or higher crime he cannot qualify. The cost of qualifying is $5 for use of the State and $1.50 for use of the county. The office is to date from May 

1st. (See Laws 1931, p. 224). 

Bond of the Justice "Every person elected to the office of Justice of the Peace in any of the counties of this State and eligible to qualify therefor shall give bond to the State of New Jersey in such sum as the Judge of the Court of Common Pleas of such county may deem sufficient, not less than five hundred nor more than three thousand dollars, with good freehold security, to be approved by such Judge, conditioned for the payment, on demand, to the person entitled or authorized to receive the same, of all moneys that may come into his hands as such Justice of the Peace during his continuance in office; such bonds shall be filed in the office of the clerk of the county, and shall be for the benefit of any person concerned or aggrieved; and the Court of the Common Pleas of the county may, from time to time, upon application in writing by any person concerned or aggrieved, order a prosecution of the bond to be conducted at the expense of the applicant." (C. S. 

3017, § 3; am. by Laws 1931, p. 225). The bond may be filed on or before May 1. (Ibid, § 11). 

To attempt to execute the office of Justice before filing such

JUSTICES OF THe Peace and THEIR CIVIL JURISDICTION 41 

bond or taking the official oath, is punishable by a fine of one hundred dollars. (Ibid, § 4).

The bond is for the benefit of any party aggrieved, and if such party shall make application in writing to the Governor, stating his ground for being aggrieved by the neglect or misconduct of the Justice, the Governor may order prosecution to be commenced upon the bond; the same to be instituted in the Supreme 

Court. (C. S. 3786, §§ 16, 17). 

The bond must be sued on within ten years after its date, or it will not affect the sureties. (C. S. 3168, § 15). 

Oath of office

The oath of office is to be taken before the county clerk, and will include the Federal and State oath of allegiance. (C. S. 

3018, § 11; P. L. 1931, p. 224). This oath is usually taken when the bond is approved by the Judge and filed. 

If bond is filed and oath taken before the county clerk on or before May 1st, the Justice may perform the duties of his office on and after May 1st, regardless of receiving his commission, which comes from the Governor. (Ibid).

When a Justice is reëlected the same oath is to be again taken and a new bond filed; the proceedings differing none from those at his first qualification. 

General qualifications of a Justice

No qualifications as to property or learning are now required for a Justice of the Peace in New Jersey. He need not be a freeholder, nor be subjected to any examination in the law. But he must reside within the county and municipality wherein he is elected, and exercise no office or vocation incompatible with it. 

Thus, he cannot at the same time hold the office of Justice of the Peace and of a county clerk, or sheriff, or sit in the State Senate or House of Assembly, or be a member of Congress. If he, while Justice, is called to hold and accepts any of the above offices, it will be a virtual surrender of his commission. (See N. J. 

Cum. Supp. 3783). 

Justice as a county official

Although the Justice is elected in a township, or ward, etc., both his civil and criminal jurisdiction is co-extensive with the limits of the county. In other words he is a township, ward, or borough official by election only; his real jurisdictional field is the county, limited only by express statutes, as where there are District Courts, etc., (as to which see infra). The language of The 

Small Cause Act is that "his writs, precepts and processes. shall run in and through such county, and he may in causes pending before him award writs of subpoena for witnesses into other

J-3

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE counties of this State." (S. C. A., § 9; Gage v. Clark, 22 Vr. 

97). 

Penalty for misconduct in office 

If a Justice of the Peace "shall at any time presume to let, farm out or transfer such office, or any part thereof, to any person or persons whatsoever, he shall for such offense forfeit the sum of fifteen hundred dollars, to be recovered with full costs of suit, by any person who will sue for the same, one-half to the prosecutor, and the other half to the treasurer, for the use of the State." 

(C. S. 3783, § 1). 

It will also be a misdemeanor for him to take a bribe, or wilfully refuse or neglect to perform, within the time required by law, any duty imposed upon him by law; or to take from a complainant, witness or other person, directly or indirectly, any fee or reward for the performance of any service in any criminal case. 

(C. S. 1750, §§ 22, 23). 

The Justice, and also all other civil officers in this State, "shall be liable to impeachment for misdemeanor in office during their continuance in office and for two years thereafter." (Const. 

of N. J., Art. V., par. 11). 

But judgment in impeachment "shall not extend farther than to removal from office, and to disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, profit or trust under this State." If impeached, the officer "shall be suspended from exercising his office until his acquittal." The House of Assembly has the sole power of impeachment, and all impeachments are to be tried by the Sen ate. (Ibid, Art. VI., Sec. III). 

It is not misconduct in office so that one can maintain an action against a Justice, that he decides a point of law erroneously or uses his official power arbitrarily. But if he acts maliciously, it is misconduct, and then the remedy is not by an action but by impeachment. (Taylor v. Doremus, 1 Harr. 473; Loftus v. 

Fraz, 14 Vr. 667). 

Jurisdiction protects the Justice from actions for damages to recover any supposed wrong his judgments do to the parties to an action. (Mangold v. Thorpe, 4 Vr. 134). Thus, where a

Justice issued a summons, but adjourned the case before the return day, and neither he nor the Justice appeared on the return day, but the defendant did, and on another day, without defendant's knowledge or consent, the Justice entered up a judgment, an action for damages was not sustained. (Frichnicht v. Hulsaidt, 6 N. J. L. J. 57).

Where he has no judicial cognizance of a cause by the stat-

JUSTICES OF THE PEACE AND THEIR CIVIL JURISDICTION 43 

ute; or where having such cognizance, he has not acquired jurisdiction over the party, by bringing or having him in Court, through regular process or otherwise, his acts, while of a judicial character, are void, and he and all persons concerned in executing his judgment or award will be trespassers. (Taylor v. Doremus, 1 

Harr. 476).

Expiration of office does not deprive a Justice of jurisdiction over undetermined causes A Justice of the Peace, whose term of office has expired or who has resigned, may proceed to the final determination of any cause then undetermined; may grant an appeal from any judgment by him rendered; and make return to all writs, orders or rules to him directed issuing out of any Court. Also, when required so to do, he must issue writs of scire facias to revive any judgment remaining unsatisfied upon his docket; issue any final process of execution upon such judgment or any other judgment remaining unsatisfied; and such writs and process shall be returnable before him and have the same force and effect and be liable to the same legal objections as though he were still in commission. But to issue such writs he must have his docket lawfully in possession. (S. C. A., §§ 7, 8). If he has parted with his docket he cannot issue such writs. 

Justice monthly to report fines for use of county "Every Justice of the Peace shall report monthly, during his term of office, on the first of each month, to the collector of his county, the amount of fines imposed and received by him during the preceding month, and shall at the same time pay over all fines so by him imposed and received, the said fines to be received and held by the county collector for the use of the county." But this provision only applies to such fines as are declared to be for the use of the county. And "if any Justice shall fail to report and make payment as above directed for thirty days after notice in writing from the county collector so to do, such Justice shall be deemed guilty of a misdemeanor." (C. S. 3017, §§ 5, 6). 

Justice may resign his office "When any Justice of the Peace shall be desirous of resigning his office, he shall send or deliver his resignation in writing to the Governor or person administering the government, and deliver a copy of such resignation forthwith to the clerk of the municipality within which such Justice shall have been elected, to be by him filed, and thereupon his said office shall be considered vacant." (Ibid, § 2).

Courts which a Justice may hold by statute A Justice of the Peace has power in New Jersey to hold: 

1. The Small Cause Court, (civil), under the Act of 1903 (see more fully infra). 

2. A magistrate's Court for the summary hearing and determination of certain actions for penalties, the enforcement of which are summary and incompatible with the design and scope of The Small Cause Court Act. The nature of this Court appears to be semi-civil and semi-criminal. (See under general topic "Penalties and Fines"). In such cases he acts only as a magistrate and must not designate the action in the Small Cause Court, but "Before L. B., Justice of the Peace." 

3. A magistrate's Court to have criminals arrested and held to bail. (See under general title "Criminal Procedure").

Strictly speaking what is termed above "a magistrate's Court" is not a Court, his only "Court" being  (See Dept. of Health v. Monheit, 101 Atl. Rep. 413). Still it is in common practice called a "Court," and we use here the term for that reason.

Besides the commitment of criminals, a Justice of the Peace, acting as a magistrate, is given jurisdiction to apprehend, convict and imprison disorderly persons; commit tramps; enforce the acts concerning vice and immorality, acts relating to cruelty to children and automobile cases; hear cases of forcible entry and detainer, landlord and tenant, etc. (See these various subjects under their respective heads). Statutes from time to time add to these classes. 

4. In connection with one or more other Justices to hold a Court under certain provisions of the Landlord and Tenant Act (C. S. 3069, § 10); but not where the District Court has exclusive jurisdiction, and wherever otherwise the statute may confer authority on two or three Justices to act.

II. CIVIL JURISDICTION The Small Cause Court and its jurisdiction 

This Court was formerly known as the "Court for the Trial of Small Causes," but since the Act of 1903 it is known as 

"The Small Cause Court." (S. C. A., § 1). 

The jurisdiction of The Small Cause Court is wholly civil, and concerns only those matters which are embraced in The Small Cause Act, or in other statutes conferring jurisdiction upon this Court directly or by clear implication. 

The primary jurisdiction of the Court is thus explicitly stated in the Act itself:

JUSTICES OF THE Peace and THEIR CIVIL JURISDICTION 45 

"Every suit of a civil nature at law, where the matter in dispute does not exceed, exclusive of costs, the sum of two hundred dollars, shall be cognizable before any Justice of the Peace of any county, who is hereby authorized to hold a Court within such county, to hear, try and determine the same according to law, although the cause of action did not arise in said county; which Court shall be known as "The Small Cause Court' and shall be a Court of record and vested for the purpose aforesaid with all such power as is usual in Courts of record of this State; the Small Cause Court shall also have jurisdiction in proceedings between landlords and tenants and in actions of forcible entry and detainer; provided, this Act shall not extend to any action of replevin, slander, trespass for assault, battery or imprisonment nor to any action wherein the title to lands shall come in question; provided further, the said Court shall not have jurisdiction over any cause or proceeding cognizable before a District Court, where any defendant resides within a municipality wherein a District Court is established." (S. C. A., § 1, as amended by P. L. 1923, p. 462).

The Small Cause Court has jurisdiction in attachment for any sum not exceeding_two hundred dollars (C. S. 148, § 37), except where District Courts have exclusive jurisdiction. 

The territorial jurisdiction of The Small Cause Court is, as a rule, co-extensive with the limits of the county, but there is an exception made in municipalities where District Courts are established. The exception is thus stated in three different Acts: "The said Court shall not have jurisdiction over any cause or proceeding cognizable before a District Court, where any defendant resides within a municipality wherein a District Court is established." (S. C. A., § 1). "No Justice of the Peace resident within the limits of any city where a District Court is or may be established shall exercise any civil jurisdiction whatever." (C. S. 3018, § 8). "No Justice of the Peace, or Small Cause Court, shall have jurisdiction over any cause or proceedings cognizable before a District Court, where the defendant or defendants reside within any city or judicial district where a District Court is established, nor shall any Justice of the peace resident within the limits of any city or judicial district, where a District Court is or may be established, exercise any civil jurisdiction whatever. Provided, however, that in judicial districts that are or may be created in counties of this State bordering on the Atlantic ocean, the Justice of the Peace or Small Cause Court shall have jurisdiction in every such District Court district in every suit of a civil nature where the debt, balance, damages or other matter in dispute does not exceed, exclusive of costs, the sum of fifty dollars as if there were

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

no judicial district in said county." (C. S. 1963, § 31, as amend. by P. L. 1921, p. 689; N. J. Cum. Supp. 963; Hankins v. Berrian, 33 Vr. 180; Thompson v. Walker, Ibid, 637).

These Acts do not prevent a defendant, residing in a judicial district wherein a District Court is established, from being sued in another county where process is served upon him, and he appears and makes defense, as thereby he waives his personal privilege as to jurisdiction, if he has any. (Edwards v. Currie, 49 Vr. 566).

Here, it will be noticed, it was not determined that he had a personal privilege to be sued only where he resided, and we doubt any such privilege, as it is a general rule that wherever process can be served on a defendant there and then jurisdiction is obtained over him.

In 1909 it was enacted that where a District Court is established "Justices of the Peace residing within any such judicial district are hereby empowered and given jurisdiction over all civil matters in which the process for appearance shall actually have been issued prior to the formation of such judicial district, such jurisdiction extending to the right to hear and try such actions, give judgment therein, issue and execute executions and executory processes, grant and perfect appeals and issue transcripts for docketing judgments in the Court of Common Pleas.' 

1963, § 31a). (C. S. 

These different Acts make it clear that a Justice of the Peace, resident within a judicial district within which a District Court is established, is without any civil jurisdiction except: 1. Where a process has been issued before the District Court was established, when he may continue the cause to a conclusion. 2. Where some later Act than that of. 1898 again and specifically confers jurisdiction, as to which examples appear under their appropriate heads in this work. 3. In counties bordering on the Atlantic ocean he has civil jurisdiction everywhere over the county to the extent of $50, exclusive of costs.

It is not to be overlooked, however, that a judicial district of a District Court may be less than a whole county, and hence a Justice resident in that part of the county not within the judicial district does have usual civil jurisdiction and can hold a Small Cause Court. So if a city has no District Court The Small Cause 

Court has jurisdiction over civil actions between residents thereof. (104 N. J. L. 465). 

Other rules as to jurisdiction

To give jurisdiction to The Small Cause Court, the amount in dispute must not exceed two hundred dollars, and the action must not be one of replevin, slander, or trespass for assault, bat-

JUSTICES OF THE Peace and THEIR CIVIL JURISDICTION 47 

tery or imprisonment, or wherein the title to land comes in ques

Sometimes a Justice of the Peace has jurisdiction at the commencement of an action, but loses it by the subsequent act of himself, or of the parties, or of the Legislature. In such case a judgment entered up after such loss of jurisdiction will not be a void judgment, but voidable only. It will be erroneous and liable to be set aside.

Jurisdiction is never given by implication to a Justice of the Peace. His office being wholly statutory as to his civil authority he can acquire jurisdiction over civil causes only by express terms in the law. The Justice ought to be assured of his jurisdiction, as nearly as may be, before he issues a process; as the dismissal of the suit must necessarily follow the discovery of a want of jurisdiction. Consent of the parties will not give jurisdiction if the statute does not. (School Trustees v. Stocker, 13 Vr. 117).

A Justice has no jurisdiction over an abstract question of right, though the parties agree to enter the action before him. 

The demand in a civil cause must be for some sum due and his judgment also for a sum certain.

The residence of plaintiff or defendant does not determine jurisdiction. It does not matter where the residence of plaintiff may be, within or without the county or State; he can bring his action, provided he can have the defendant served by process within the county.

The Justice obtains jurisdiction over the matter so far as the plaintiff is concerned by the plaintiff's act, in asking the Justice to issue process; and over the defendant when the latter is "in

Court," by either legal service of process, or his voluntary appearance. 

Application of the $200 limitation in the statute in the matter of jurisdiction

The statute says that where "the matter in dispute does not exceed, exclusive of costs, the sum of two hundred dollars," it is cognizable in  But it also provides that "where the amount really due or claimed exceeds, exclusive of costs, the sum or value of two hundred dollars, the plaintiff may elect to sue in said Court for a sum not exceeding two hundred dollars and costs; and judgment on the merits in such suit shall bar any other suit on the same claim in any other Court." (S. C. 

A., §§ 1, 3); which means that the plaintiff, to bring suit on a claim of over two hundred dollars must, practically, waive any further claim to any sum above two hundred dollars, and does so if there is "a judgment on the merits in such suit"; while if the action does not go to a judgment on the merits, the suit may be

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

renewed again, even in the higher Courts and for a sum exceeding two hundred dollars.

The penalty in a bond, bill, note or other contract in writing may exceed two hundred dollars, but if the amount really due or recoverable does not exceed, exclusive of costs, that sum, The 

Small Cause Court has jurisdiction. (Ibid, § 2). 

The jurisdiction of The Small Cause Court is not exclusive, even where the amount sought to be recovered is less than two hundred dollars. A party may bring an action in a higher Court, but in that case he will usually recover no costs. (But to this rule as to costs in the higher Courts there are exceptions). 

Where a summons is issued for two hundred dollars, but the demand filed calls or appears to call for a greater amount, the case must be dismissed, as the Justice has no jurisdiction, unless the demand is amended, or there is a distinct waiver of any claim beyond two hundred dollars. 

When a Justice is disqualified to exercise jurisdiction

The Justice or any other Magistrate or Judge may not have jurisdiction in a cause of action when he is disqualified to act. 

Disqualification for a Judge in New Jersey (and this is held to be applicable to Justices of the Peace) exists in the following cases: 

1. When related in the third degree to any of the parties to an action pending in the same Court. Such is the statute; under the common law rule he was disqualified if related to either party in the ninth degree. (C. S. 4121, § 224; see Vanauker v. Beemer, 1 South. 364; Stevenson v. Stiles, 1 Penn. 740). 

2. When he is interested in the event of the action. (Ibid). 

3. When he, as an attorney-at-law, has been attorney of record, or counsel, for any party to the action. (Ibid). 

4. When he has acted as an agent or attorney-in-fact for another; that is to say, he cannot issue any process in behalf of any persons for whom he is agent or attorney-in-fact, nor take any fee or reward for such service. But he may write out or prepare, or assist in preparing or writing out, any state of demand or other paper necessary or proper to be made use of in the progress of any suit, or proceeding in any Court, not charging for the same in excess of fifty cents, which, however, is not to be put into the bill of costs. If a Justice of the Peace violates this provision he is liable to a penalty of fifty dollars, which can be recovered by any person aggrieved who may sue for the same. (S. C. 

A., § 10).

Under this head it is to be noted that a Justice as a private person may receive for collection and collect by solicitation an account sent to him, but he cannot sue upon it. He could give

JUSTICES OF THE PEACE AND THEIR CIVIL JURISDICTION 49 

it to another Justice to sue, but he could not legally collect a charge therefor as he cannot act as an attorney. 

5. When he has given his opinion upon the matter in question in such action. (C. S. 4121, § 224). That is to say, it must have been an opinion or judgment rendered in his own Court on the same point and in the same action. It does not mean that if a cause has been sent back to him by a higher Court upon certiorari that he may not re-hear the cause. Some of the disqualifications named above are to be construed in the light of the proviso to the Act already referred to: "Provided, nothing herein shall be construed to prevent any Judge from sitting on the trial or argument of any point in controversy in an action because he may have given his opinion in another action wherein the same matter in controversy shall have come in question, or because he may have given his opinion on any question in controversy in the same action in the course of the previous proceedings therein, or because the board of chosen freeholders of any county, or any township or municipality, in which he is an inhabitant or liable to be taxed, are or may be parties to the record or otherwise interested." 

6. When he is a necessary witness in the cause. But to oust jurisdiction upon this ground, an affidavit of his materiality as a witness, and in what particulars his testimony is requisite, must be made and presented to the Justice, who will either himself determine the sufficiency of the objection, or appoint triors. 

7. That he is not in commission as Justice, having removed from the township where he was elected, or not having been elected to office and qualified, or his term having expired (but, if his term has expired he may proceed with a cause begun previously). 

Where the Justice or a Judge is disqualified by reason of any of the foregoing reasons, the Supreme Court, on certiorari, will set his judgment in the action aside. At common law an injunction may be obtained preventing one who is disqualified from sitting in a cause, from acting in the capacity of a Judge therein. 

Challenges for disqualification 39 The usual method of challenging for a disqualification is by the oral statement, "I challenge the Court, upon the ground that," etc. Thereupon: 

1. The Justice, Magistrate or Judge may himself try the challenge. If there appears good ground, upon facts personally known to him-as relationship to the parties, previous adjudication of the same cause, etc.-he should dismiss the action without further proceedings. If the facts are not known to him, or there

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

is doubt of the soundness of the ground of challenge, he should require affidavits, or oral testimony. 

2. Or he may appoint three indifferent triors, according to the statute, which is the better way in cases of doubt. The statute says: "All challenges to a Judge for the causes aforesaid shall be made previous to the trial or argument, and the Court may try such challenges or appoint three indifferent persons triors for that purpose at the discretion of the Court, and the finding of a majority of such triors shall be received as the determination of such triors." (C. S. 4122, § 225).

He must select men unrelated to the parties and uninterested, from among the by-standers, if such are present, to whom the following oath should be administered: "You do solemnly swear that you shall well and truly try and determine this issue of challenge joined in the cause in which A. 

B. is plaintiff, and C. D. defendant, and a true report to make. 

So help you God."

The witnesses examined by the triors are also to be sworn. 

The examination is to proceed at once, without delay, and the triors are to report thereon as soon as the examination is concluded. The majority of the triors may deliver a finding (that the cause for challenge is "true" or "not true"), and it ought to be in writing, signed by them. Their determination of the facts is conclusive. (Davis v. Mahany, 9 Vr. 104).

The Justice may lose jurisdiction after acquiring it The Justice may lose his jurisdiction although he had previously acquired it: 

1. By removal from the township or ward wherein he was elected to office. But not if township or ward lines are altered during his term of office (State v. Dilloway, 2 Vr. 42). 

2. By granting an appeal, and filing the record in the office of the Clerk of Common Pleas. 

3. When the record is transmitted to a higher Court upon certiorari; although, if the cause is remanded to the Justice for a retrial, his jurisdiction is again complete over the subject matter. 

4. By the act of one or both of the parties to the action, as in the withdrawal of a suit, a settlement, etc.: 

5. By the act of the Justice himself, as in adjourning the cause in the absence of both parties, and without their consent, or in some other manner which serves so to adjourn the cause illegally that jurisdiction is lost. 

6. By the act of God; as where the Justice becomes insane, or is sick for a period longer than the law permits an adjournment, or shall die.

JUSTICES OF THE PEACE AND THEIR CIVIL JURISDICTION 51 

7. By title to land suddenly coming into question after he has begun the hearing. 

Actions not cognizable before the Justice

The Small Cause Act expressly excepts five classes of actions from the jurisdiction of The Small Cause Court (S. C. A., § 1): 

I. Of Replevin. This is an action for the wrongful and unlawful taking or detention of goods or chattels, in which the articles themselves are taken into the possession of the officer having the writ, for delivery to the plaintiff, upon the officer receiving security from the plaintiff to prosecute the action. But replevin may be waived and the plaintiff may sue in Tort to recover the value of the articles. 

II. Of Slander. This consists in the utterance of false, malicious and defamatory words, tending to the damage and derogation of another.

III. Of Trespass for assault and battery or imprisonment. 

The distinction must be made between a civil action for an assault, or assault and battery which is not cognizable before a Justice, or an action simply growing incidentally out of the assault, which is cognizable in  (See Carman v. 

Smock, 1 Penn. 112; Bates v. Adams, 2 Penn. 718; Marentille v. Oliver, 1 Penn. 379; Jeffers v. Brookfield, Coxe 38; Sordayo v. Lunetta, 82 N. J. L. 338.

IV. Wherein the title to land shall come in question. It is not always easy to distinguish when the title to land properly comes in question. The mere possession of land does not necessarily make the title come in question in every action against the possessor. Under the decisions of the Supreme Court it has been held that The Small Cause Court has no jurisdiction in an action for mesne profits after a recovery in ejectment; nor for damages by rain from the roof of the kitchen, which stood upon property in the peaceable possession of the defendant, which property plaintiff claimed to be his own; nor where defendant started fire on his land, which spread to the land of plaintiff and injured his timber, the latter being a tenant by curtesy; nor for obstructing a by-road, which involved the plaintiff's right to use the road as a right of way without obstruction; nor wherein the right to a pew in church came in question, that being a hereditament; nor for fishing on plaintiff's land, if defendant claims title. 

But it has been held that there was jurisdiction where damages were sought for overflowing the plaintiff's land by a dam, the possession only and not the title coming into question; also where the defendant broke into the plaintiff's close and cut down

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

grass, the defendant not setting up title; also for cutting down, and removing growing grain; also against an overseer of the highway for removing a fence, stones, etc., from plaintiff's land. A special statute known as the Timber Act gives the Justice jurisdiction of suits for penalties for cutting growing timber. 

Mr. Justice Depue in an important case once laid down the rule to be observed as to when or when not the Justice had jurisdiction in cases concerning land actions in the following language: "The jurisdiction of a Justice of the Peace extends no further than to enable him to try the fact of possession. He has no jurisdiction to inquire into the title to land, or into the right of possession. He can only take cognizance of possession as a question of fact. Where the plaintiff can maintain his right to sue in Trespass" [now Tort] "by proof of actual possession, which the Justice may determine upon evidence of facts, without any inquiry into title, the action is cognizable in a Justice's Court; but if the possession be merely constructive, and can be shown only by proof of title, the Justice has no jurisdiction." (Jeffery v. Owen, 12 Vr. 262). This decision, of course does not prevent jurisdiction in ordinary landlord and tenant cases if the law gives such jurisdiction. (See general head, "Landlord and Tenant").

Where Justice may hold The Small Cause Court 

The Justice, like a Police Justice or Recorder, must hold his Court only in his "regular and customary office;" otherwise it is a misdemeanor. (P. L. 1926, p. 136).

Justice of the Peace not to practice in The Small Cause Court "No Justice of the Peace, unless duly licensed as an attorneyat-law of this State, or constable shall appear and prosecute or defend any action brought in The Small Cause Court unless such Justice or constable shall be one of the parties on record in the cause," under penalty of $50. (S. C. A., § 118). 

Justice's powers to preserve order in his Court

A Justice of the Peace sitting in The Small Cause Court, may not commit for contempt, but he may vindicate his authority in the manner laid down in the leading case in this State, wherein 

Mr. Justice Depue said: "For abusive and reproachable words spoken to a Justice of the Peace relative to his judicial conduct, the Justice has power to cause his arrest and require bail for his appearance to answer to an indictment and for good behavior until the next Sessions. (Richmond v. Dayton, 10 J. R. 393; Albright v. Rapp, 26 Penn. 

St. 99). . A Justice of the Peace or coroner, when in

JUSTICES OF THE PEACE AND THEIR CIVIL JURISDICTION 53 

the exercise of his judicial functions, has the power to cause a bystander, whose conduct or presence in the Court room is prejudicial to the interests of the Justice, to be removed from the room; and such an order, if made in the exercise of a sound judicial discretion, will be a justification in an action of trespass; and, if resisted, will subject the offender to indictment for resisting the officer in discharge of his duty. (Garnett v. Ferraud, 6 

B. & C. 611; State v. Capp, 15 N. Hamp. 212). The power to remove persons who, by disorderly conduct, interfere with the business of the Court, is a power essential to the very existence of the Court, and is implied from the creation of the Court. . In the present case the Justice might have caused the plaintiff to be removed from his Court room. He might have required of him bail for his appearance at Court to answer to a criminal charge, and as security for good behavior. He might have committed the plaintiff into custody until the cause on trial was concluded, before he gave him a hearing; and if the plaintiff refused or was unable to give bail, he might have committed him to jail in default of bail." (See Rhinehart v. Lentz, 14 Vr. 311).

Justice acting in The Small Cause Court must use an official seal 

By Act of April 27, 1911, (P. L., p. 544; N. J. Cum. Supp. 

1667), every Justice of the Peace must use a seal in The Small Cause Court, without which no process issued by him in said Court shall be valid. The Act is an important one and is as follows: "Every Justice of the Peace shall use a seal, which shall bear the inscription in circular form "The Small Cause Court of the County of New Jersey,' and the name of the Justice and State, ward or township from which he is elected. Every summons, subpoena, commitment, warrant, and transcript of every judgment entered in the docket in said Small Cause Court shall bear the impression of said seal, and no process issued by any Justice of said Small Cause Court shall be valid without the impression of said seal. Every Justice of the Peace hereafter elected shall, before entering upon his duties, file with the county clerk of the county of which he is elected a certificate bearing an impression of his seal."

This Act does not apply to process issued or other proceedings when he acts as a magistrate and not in  This distinction must be kept clear, as the only seal to be used in such criminal, penal or other summary actions as are not in The Small Cause Court is the usual sign of a seal, viz., [L. S.], or a wafer.

When a process is issued, therefore, in The Small Cause Court (i. e., a summons, warrant, writ of attachment, execution,

Justices, as such, cannot take acknowledgments Acknowledgments or proofs of written instruments cannot be taken before a Justice of the Peace. If he is a Master in 

Chancery, a notary, or a commissioner of deeds, he may acknowledge as such official. The legal fee therefor is $1.00. (P. L. 

1920, p. 412; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1240). 

Who may take acknowledgments (or proofs)

In New Jersey an acknowledgment or proof of a written instrument (as a deed, mortgage, etc.) to be recorded in New 

Jersey, can be taken before any of the following officials: Chancellor, Justice of the Supreme Court, Master in Chancery, attor-

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS 

55 ney-at-law of this State, notary public, Judge of the Common Pleas, commissioner of deeds, clerk of the Court of Common Pleas, deputy county clerk, surrogate, deputy county surrogate, or register of deeds. (P. L. 1916, p. 299; N. J. Cum. Supp. 628, § 22).

Every written instrument to be recorded in the county clerk's, register's or secretary of state's office needs, as a rule, to be acknowledged or proved.

It is not necessary that the person acknowledging shall reside where the acknowledgment is taken, nor that he reside in this State. If he "happen" to come before any acknowledging officer in this State, the latter may take the acknowledgment. Nor need the official taking the acknowledgment reside in the county where the lands concerned are, or where the acknowledgment is taken. 

As to acknowledgment of deeds, etc., where the acknowledgor resides out of this State, see P. L. 1919, p. 38; N. J. Cum. 

Supp. 629, § 23.

Difference between acknowledgment and proof An acknowledgment of an instrument is where one person formally declares before an officer, authorized to take an acknowledgment, that an instrument executed by him is his act and deed. 

A proof of an instrument means that, instead of the person or persons executing the paper acknowledging the execution in person, the subscribing witness makes the acknowledgment and certifies under oath to the authenticity of the execution. It is commonly used where the person executing the paper is dead or cannot be found, or, as in case of a corporation, where it may not be convenient to have all the officers who execute an instrument present. 

Married woman's acknowledgment 

A married woman, if twenty-one years of age, need no longer, as formerly, acknowledge a written instrument privately, apart from her husband, and declare "that she signs, seals and delivers the same as her voluntary act and deed, freely, without any fear, threats or compulsion of her husband. (P. L. 1916, p. 

321; N. J. Cum. Supp. 628, § 21a). But only "that she signs, seals and delivers the same as her voluntary act and deed." (P. L. 

1918, p. 120; N. J. Cum. Supp. 632). In other words she may acknowledge without her husband leaving the room of the person taking the acknowledgment (as was the custom) and just as if she were a feme sole. In this connection we might state that a married woman may now convey real estate directly to her husband or he directly to her. (P. L. 1919, p. 95; N. J. Cum. Supp. 

632, § 39).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Acknowledgment by infants

Infants may not convey lands or execute acknowledgments, nor may idiots, lunatics, or persons who do not understand the nature of what they are doing. Even if married an infant may not acknowledge. (Ross v. Adams, 1 Vr. 506).

Acknowledgment by corporations A corporation may acknowledge an instrument through its 

President, Vice-President or other presiding officer, or any Secretary, Assistant Secretary or other recording officer. (Laws 1912, p. 208; N. J. Cum. Supp. 646).

Miscellaneous 

In all cases the identity of the acknowledgor must be established to the satisfaction of the officer. In other words, no one can in the discharge of his duty take an acknowledgment from an entire stranger without first being certain he is the proper acknowledgor.

If the grantor is an old and ignorant person, it is not enough to read formally the instrument to him and ask if he acknowledges it: there must always be a certainty that the grantor understands it.
