Actions and Defenses to Actions I. ACTIONS 

Actions not cognizable by Justice 

The statute expressly excepts the following classes of actions (suits at law), from the jurisdiction of the Justice of the Peace holding The Small Cause Court: replevin, slander, trespass for assault, battery or imprisonment, and that wherein the title to lands shall come in question; also any cause cognizable before a 

District Court, where defendant resides within a municipality wherein a District Court is established. But in counties bordering on the Atlantic ocean there is jurisdiction over the defendant up to $50, exclusive of costs, notwithstanding he resides within the limits of a District Court. (S. C. A., § 1; P. L. 1921, p. 689.

As to these exceptions, see general title "Justices of the Peace and their Civil Jurisdiction").

J-4

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Bringing of actions

An action is a claim of right to be prosecuted in a Court having jurisdiction over, first, the subject matter, and, second, the defendant, or as in attachment-the defendant's property. It is to be brought in the party's own proper name, and not in the name of a third person who has no right in himself, or as a legal representative, to sue. Where one man maintains an action in another's name, it must be by one authorized by law to sue for another, as an executor, administrator, guardian, trustee, assignee, receiver, etc.

Whether a party shall bring an action or not rests entirely with himself, the peril-usually-being of costs only, if not sustained. There is no law to prevent his bringing the action, if he wills it; no punishment afterwards, unless there is not only not probable cause but malice, in which he may be sued for malicious prosecution and damages recovered. 

Who may sue or be sued

As a rule any person of full age and sound memory may bring an action in his or her own proper person, and by his or her own name.

Infants must bring suit by their guardian or next friend; and when suit is brought against them, although the summons is against the infant, the Justice must appoint a guardian to attend to the cause before it can be tried. (Foulks v. Young, 1 Zab. 

438. See general title "Infancy"). sons.

Attorneys-at-law may sue or be sued the same as other per- Any politic or corporate body of this or any other State may sue or be sued in  (S. Č. A., § 6). 

Officers having quasi corporate powers may sue and be sued in The Small Cause Court; such as county collectors, overseers of the poor, trustees of school districts, etc. But in such case their official titles are to be employed, for example: "A. B., overseer of the poor of the township of D.," etc. 

The maker and indorsers of a check or promissory note may be included in one action as defendants, the same as if they were joint contractors. But in such action the plaintiff shall follow the statute as to the state of demand, etc. (S. C. A., §§ 41-46).

Executors and administrators of a decedent's estate may sue and be sued.

A married woman may sue and be sued without joining her husband, unless he would be a necessary party if he were not her husband. (P. L. 1912, p. 416; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1838, § 17).

This also holds in actions in Tort for damages to her person or property. (C. S. 3237, § 12b).

ACTIONS AND DEFENSES TO ACTIONS 

59 Partners are to sue and be sued in their partnership name. 

If a debtor dies intestate, seized of real estate, his creditor may maintain an action against his heirs or devisees. (C. S. 

2739, § 1).

Drunkards and lunatics may sue and be sued; and they must be sued in their own name as well after they have had a statutory guardian appointed by order of Court as before. 

Actions to recover physician's fees

No person who is not qualified to practice medicine or surgery according to the laws of this State, can sue and collect any fees for medical or surgical services. (C. S. 3327, § 21). It is not necessary, however, for such physician or surgeon to prove before the Justice that he is properly licensed by the State authorities in advance of the issuing of process. The Justice ordinarily will presume that a physician has complied with the law for the purposes of bringing an action. But if the Justice believes otherwise, or the defendant objects to a judgment on the ground that the physician is not licensed, the burden of proof will rest upon the plaintiff. 

Actions by veterinary surgeons

No person who is not qualified to practice veterinary medicine or surgery according to the laws of this State, can sue and collect for veterinary, medical or surgical services. (C. S. 5711, § 18). The same rule governs his bringing an action and proving that he is qualified, if such proof be required, as in the case of physicians. 

Actions against United States' officials

The President of the United States may be sued in a State Court. He may be plaintiff also, in his individual capacity, in any 

Court. All right to sue or proceed against ambassadors, or other public ministers, or their domestics or domestic servants, or against consuls or vice-consuls, is vested in the Federal Courts; but they may bring actions in any Court. 

Actions without process

A defendant may appear without process and consent to the Justice entering a suit against him, providing the Justice has jurisdiction. But no consent will give jurisdiction where the law does not give it. (S. C. A., § 5; Bayles v. Newton, 22 Vr. 

553; School Trustees v. Stocker, 13 Vr. 117). 

Joinder of parties

All persons jointly indebted to any person or persons upon

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

any joint contract or matter are answerable to their creditors separately for such debts. If the creditor brings suit against such joint debtors, but only some be served by process, such of them so served and brought into Court shall answer to the plaintiff, and the judgment shall pass against the other joint debtors named in the process the same as if all had been served. (The general Act upon joint debtors in actions upon obligations will be found in C. S. 3776).

Generally speaking, all the persons with whom a contract is made should join as plaintiffs in an action brought upon such contract. There cannot be separate actions with separate bills of costs.

It is not an infrequent mistake that parties are misjoined in actions both on Contract and in Tort, or that they are not joined when they should be. For instance: A trespasses upon the lands of B and also upon the lands of C. In their ignorance of the law B and C jointly sue A in one action to recover damages for the trespass. Such a joint action cannot be sustained. 

In actions in Tort, one, or any, or all of several joint wrongdoers may be sued. Every person who joins in committing a tort is separately liable for it, and cannot escape liability by showing that another person is liable also. And when there are several defendants, each defendant, if judgment goes against him, is liable for all the damages incurred; he cannot require a division to be made and a share apportioned to him, nor that his co-partners in inflicting the injury shall contribute to him their share of the damage.

In actions in Tort, plaintiffs who have a separate interest and sustain a separate damage should sue separately. Those who have a separate interest but sustain a joint damage, may sue either separately or jointly.

Where one of two or more persons who should be joint parties to an action dies, the suit may be maintained by or against the survivors only.

Where several persons are joint debtors, and it happens that, in consequence of an acknowledgment or part payment of the debt by one or more of them, the effect of the statute of limitations (which would otherwise wholly bar the claim) is avoided as regards such but not as regards others; those only can be legally sued against whom the claim is not barred. 

Designation of parties to action

The person bringing suit in Court is called the "plaintiff," and the party against whom suit is brought is called the "defendant." The usual form of expressing it is, "J. D. versus R. R.” or, in the docket, "J. D., Plaintiff, v. R. R., Defendant."

ACTIONS AND Defenses to ACTIONS 

61 

Forms of actions 

There are usually two forms of action only in The Small 

Cause Court: 1. On Contract; 2. In Tort. The statute reads: 

"All suits in The Small Cause Court for debt or damages arising from breach of contract, or the non-performance of duties arising from contract, shall be styled actions on Contract; all other actions in said Court shall be styled actions in Tort." (S. 

C. A., § 23).

As will be seen below, there are also other occasional forms of action.

Actions on Contract 

Every action, upon any bond, note of hand, check, book account, judgment, or other debt, whether in writing or not and under seal or not, and all actions for injuries arising from breaches of contract or for the non-performance of duties arising from contract, must now be styled "on Contract." 

Actions in Tort

Every action to recover damages for the wrongful use of force and injuries to personal or real property, must be styled “in Tort." These actions, therefore, would be actions in Tort: for wrongfully taking one's personal property; for wounding, disabling, or killing one's animals, or by one's being injured by a dog if the owner is present and consenting; for an injury done by the cattle of another, breaking into an enclosure; for criminal conversation and seduction; for cutting and breaking nets, working a horse distrained, or injuring him by negligent driving on the highway; for entering a house, lands, etc., in another's possession; for hunting, or other trespassing on one's grounds without permission; for breaking into one's close and damaging fences, banks, hedges, etc. (in the latter three cases the damages are to one's lands, and, if their title comes in question, the Justice, of course, will have no jurisdiction). 

Certain other forms of action

There are actions which are to be in other forms because expressly directed so to be brought by other statutes since 1903, or not properly embraced in the Act. For example:

If a suit is brought for a usual statutory penalty, there the penalty is not of the nature of a contract, and the action is to be brought "in Debt," unless otherwise directed by the statute itself. (See chapter on Penalties). Sometimes a law provides for an action "in Trespass."

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE II. DEFENSES TO ACTIONS 

Classification of them

The defenses to suits at law are numerous. We note the usual ones, in alphabetical order, and state their meaning in law: 

Abatement: Any matter of defense which only suspends the right to sue, or defeats the particular proceedings instituted, is termed in abatement. 

Accord and satisfaction: 

That there has been a settlement of the claim by an agreement which has been, or is to be executed. 

Account stated: That accounts have been rendered by both sides and balances struck, which have been received and held without objection. 

Action pending: That another and prior suit at law is pending involving precisely the same claim. 

Against public policy: That it is contrary to public policy to enforce the contract. 

Alteration of instrument: That the instrument of writing has been altered without consent of both parties. efit. 

Another's benefit: That the contract was for another's ben- 

Bankruptcy: If one has been discharged by bankruptcy, it is a defense as to all claims barred by such discharge. 

Compromise: That the claim has already been compromised and settled either by the defendant or his joint-debtor. 

Contributory negligence: That in action in Tort the plaintiff has himself contributed to the injury. 

Death of party: That the action is strictly personal and has been abated by death. 

Demand not made: That, in an action in the nature of

Trover, if the defendant is in lawful possession of goods and chattels he may set up that no demand was made for them before suit brought.

Duress: That the contract was entered into by means of undue restraint. 

Failure of consideration: A total or partial failure of consideration in the execution of negotiable instruments-the action being between the original parties.

Former judgment: That the claim has already been put into judgment. 

Fraud: Fraud always vitiates a contract. Even as to contracts under seal, the statute says: "In every action upon a sealed instrument, and where a set-off is founded upon a sealed

ACTIONS AND Defenses to ACTIONS 

63 instrument, any party may plead and set up as a defense thereto fraud in the consideration of the contract upon which recovery is sought, or the want or failure of consideration, the same as if such instrument were not sealed." (C. S. 2225, § 15).

General denial: That the alleged statement of facts by plaintiff is not true.

Giving time to principal: A surety upon a written agreement (a promissory note, for instance), may be discharged by a new agreement between the creditor and the principal, in which the surety has no part. 

Impossibility: Because of the act of God, (as fires, floods, etc.); or a new statute, which renders the action illegal; or physical impossibility. tract. 

Infancy: That the defendant was lawfully unable to con- 

Insolvency: That the defendant has been discharged by a court of bankruptcy, or through the claim being proven before a general assignee.

Intoxication: That the defendant was too intoxicated to enter into a contract intelligently. 

Judicial proceedings: A magistrate, constable or other officer may plead his privilege in action against him arising from acts done in his official capacity. 

Jurisdiction wanting: That Court has no jurisdiction, 1. 

Of the subject; or, 2. Of the parties.

License: In cases for trespass on lands, license (or leave) to enter the premises, etc., may be shown in defense. 

Lunacy or idiocy: That the person, being a lunatic, or idiot, was incapable of contracting. (See general title "Idiots and Lunatics").

Martial law: That the country, being in a state of war, is under the reign of martial law, which overrides the civil law. 

Merger: That the particular debt is extinguished by its having merged into another obligation. 

Misjoinder and non-joinder: That wrong parties are joined in the action or that all the right parties are not joined. 

Mistake: That an error was made in an account, etc. 

Necessity: That the act complained of was absolutely necessary for preservation of life or property. 

Not due: That the contract is not yet fully executed, and therefore the amount sought to be recovered is not due. 

Payment: That the claim has been fully paid. 

Performance: That the contract has been fully performed.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Possession: In actions in Tort for injuries to lands, the defendant, if he has possession, if he does not have title, may plead possession.

Receipt and release: This is practically the same as payment, although one may give a receipt and release without payment being made and, if given without undue influence, will bar recovery in a future action.

Recoupment: This defense usually admits the original justice of the claim, but seeks an equitable set-off in damages. (See general title, "Set-off and Recoupment").

Rescission: That the contract has been mutually rescinded. 

Set-off: That the defendant has a legal set-off. (See general title "Set-off and Recoupment"). 

Sunday contract: Sunday contracts are usually void. (See general title "Sunday"). 

Statute of frauds: That the statute of frauds and perjuries prevents recovery. 

Statute of limitations: That the time for recovery of judgment has passed and the Statute of Limitations has practically extinguished the debt. 

Statutory permission or inhibition: For example, actions for a wager are prohibited; or certain franchises are granted by the 

Legislature, which rule out damages to private parties; or brokers suing for commissions without complying with statute, etc. 

Tender: As this is an important defense and terms of tender need to be fully understood, we note that every tender of money for a debt due must be of the exact sum due. Such money must be tendered as the laws of the land have made legal tender. 

Tender must be by the person owing the debt, to his proper creditor, upon a day other than Sunday, and upon the very day the debt is due. It must be unequivocal, unconditional and to pay the entire demand. In case of a contract, the tender of willingness to perform it at the time and manner named is sufficient. There can be no tender where damages are unliquidated. Where a debt is past due, lawful interest is to be added.

Title: A plea, usually to be set up in writing. 

Usury: Usury is the excess over legal interest charged to a borrower for the use of money. In this State the legal rate is six per cent. The defense of usury is one which does not go to the whole debt as a debt, but to the interest. The recovery can be had for the amount actually lent, without interest or costs of suit, and no more. (C. S. 5705, § 2).

A contract having its inception and completion in another

ADJOURNMENT 

65 State is governed by the laws of that State relating to usury and not by the laws of New Jersey.

The usury must arise from and belong to a contract in violation of the statute; hence an agreement subsequent to the instrument for the forbearance of the debt upon the payment of illegal interest is not usury.

If the contract be usurious it is not necessary that illegal interest be actually taken. It is the contract which affects and taints plaintiff's right to recover. 

Corporations may not plead usury to recover damages, or enforce a remedy. (Ibid, § 7). 

Defenses not to be in writing

Except in the case of plea of title to land, or of set-off, or where recoupment is demanded, or of usury, the defendant need not file a plea in writing in  But in these cases the pleas must set up the facts. (See under general titles "Title to Land," "Set-off and Recoupment," in this volume). 

The statute Adjournment

For statute concerning adjournments, see Small Cause Act, §§ 29-32. What is stated below applies specifically to The Small 

Cause Court and not to Justices acting as magistrates.

The first adjournment 

To prevent the usual adjournment on the return day of the summons, except upon "reasonable cause" shown by affidavit, the statute permits copies of the state of demand to be served with the summons, so as to apprise defendant of the particulars of the claim. In such case the hearing should proceed on the return day, and no adjournment given on application of the defendant, unless for the "reasonable cause," as stated, and upon his filing an affidavit showing effectually such "reasonable cause." The plaintiff, however, may ask for an adjournment, and secure it, without an affidavit, provided the Justice is satisfied there is "reasonable cause."

If no state of demand be served on the defendant with the summons, as a matter of course the defendant should be given one adjournment, if he desires it, in order to prepare for his defense.

A motion for an adjournment cannot be granted before the return of the summons or warrant.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

In case of entry of suit without process, the motion may be made at any time before the hearing. 

In uncontested suits, and when the defendant does not appear upon the return day, it is not customary to adjourn, unless the plaintiff is not ready with his proof, when his motion should be granted as of course. It is his cause and he should control the time of hearing if such control does not interfere with the rights of the defendant. 

Further adjournments

As to motions for subsequent adjournment of a cause, the Justice is to consider the rights of both parties to the action, rather than his own convenience. He is only limited as to the time by the statute, which says, "to any time not exceeding thirty days from the return day of the summons,' or the return of the warrant, unless where the statute permits the time to be extended to three months. 

The Justice may adjourn for his own convenience, but not beyond the thirty days from the return day of the summons. 

However, the consent of both parties will make valid an adjournment beyond the thirty days. But consent by the defendant will not be presumed from mere attendance of the defendant on the trial day if he takes no part. (White v. Lippincott, 1 Penn. 266).

The following statement on this subject by the Supreme Court of this State deserves to be quoted here: "It seems to be a prevalent opinion among the magistrates, that when a day has been prefixed, by summons or adjournment, for a meeting of the parties before him, and he afterwards foresees that sickness or some imperious necessity will prevent his attendance on that day, he may lawfully, in the absence of both parties, adjourn the cause to another day, and send them notice of the adjournment. 

It is, however, a mistake; for, though a Justice is empowered to do some official acts when both parties are not present; such as to receive an application for a jury, to award a venire to a constable, and to grant subpoenas for witnesses, there is no express or implied authority to alter the day appointed for a meeting, before it arrives. If sickness or other imperious obstacle should prevent the Justice from attending at the day prefixed, the plaintiff has no other way than to sue out a new summons. 

It seems to many magistrates much more reasonable, in order to save such a waste of cost, time and expenses, to adjourn and send notices of it, and its reasonableness has led many into a belief that it is lawful; not considering that where there is a written statute, and a day fixed according to it, that it overcomes all reasoning from expediency about it.' (Taylor v. Doremus, 1 Harr. 480). 

---

ADJOURNMENT 

67 

Hour of adjournment

Except by consent of both parties to the action, the statute explicitly fixes the time to which a cause may be adjourned as between nine o'clock A. M., and three o'clock P. M. The exact hour must be fixed.

Some decisions on adjournment If a Justice refuses an adjournment, to which a party is legally entitled, relief may be had on appeal to the Court of Common Pleas. (Gould v. Brown, 4 Hal. 165).

If the defendant or plaintiff is not present on the return day, or first day of adjournment, and the cause is postponed by the Justice, the party not present must be notified. And such adjournment must be made at the regular time and place for the hearing, not by the Justice before or afterwards, or at some other place. (Edwards v. Hance, 7 Hal. 108; Halsey v. Whitlock, 2 

Penn. 869; Brannin v. Voorhees, 2 Green, 590; Nicholson v. 

Wright, 1 Harr. 232; Lloyd v. Hance, 1 Harr. 127).

An adjournment cannot be made after the trial has been commenced by going into evidence on the merits, unless by consent, or for the most important reasons; but after nonsuit refused a motion to adjourn is not illegal. (Stretch v. Forsyth, 2 Penn. 

713; Potter v. Carman, 2 Penn. 521; Parker v. Mercantile Safe 

Co., 34 Vr. 505).

If a defendant has prepared for trial but is unable to attend on the day because in prison, the cause must be adjourned. (Truax v. Roberts, 1 South. 288).

If defendant appears before the Justice, before the return day of the summons, and craves adjournment, and does not appear on the day of adjournment, the Justice may proceed and try the cause. (M'Collister v. Richman, 1 Penn. 208).

If the Justice adjourns the cause in the absence of the defendant, the summons not having been duly served, and gives him no notice of the adjournment, but tries the cause in his absence, judgment will be reversed. (Camman v. Perrine, 4 Hal. 253).

If a defendant in a cause pending, and in which he has a defense, is led into a mistake with regard to the time to which the cause is adjourned, and the trial is had in his absence and without his knowledge, the Court above will reverse the judgment. (Probasco v. Hartough, 5 Hal. 55).

If a cause be adjourned without fixing a day, but to such a date as counsel shall agree upon, and the defendant's counsel refuses to agree to a day, the Justice cannot fix a day and give notice thereof to the defendant; the cause is out of Court and must be commenced anew. (Woodworth v. Wolverton, 4 Zab. 419).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Notice to the attorneys, who on the trial represent the parties, of the time and place of adjournment, is sufficient. (Day v. 

Hall, 7 Hal. 203).

If a party does not attend on the return of the process or the day to which the cause has been regularly adjourned in the presence of the parties, and with the knowledge of the defendant, and a further adjournment becomes necessary, the Justice is not bound to send after the defendant and give him notice of such adjournment. (Neighbour v. Trimmer, 1 Harr. 58; Slaght v. 

Robbins, 1 Green 340).

If plaintiff does not appear on the day adjourned to by his own consent, the defendant is entitled to a nonsuit; and if under arrest on a warrant, to his discharge. (Dunham v. Solomon, 1 

Harr. 50).

The Justice having adjourned a cause for thirty days, namely, to the 27th day of the next month, and having then, by error, entered the 24th day in his docket, on which day plaintiff appeared, and judgment was given in the absence of defendant, who appeared on the 27th, the judgment was set aside on certiorari, for want of jurisdiction. (Ritter v. Kunkle, 10 Vr. 259).

A suit having been discontinued before the time to which the case had been adjourned, the defendant assenting thereto and leaving the room, and a subsequent order made to take up the case, on a future day, when it was decided in the absence of the plaintiff, held irregular. (Drake v. Berry, 13 Vr. 62).

When a cause has been adjourned to a particular time and place, and the Justice fails to attend, but at another place, in the absence of the parties and without the consent of the defendant, adjourns the cause to another day, he cannot on that day proceed to trial and judgment, although notice of the adjournment has been given to the defendant. Such an adjournment operates as a discontinuance of the suit. (Allen v. Summit Board of Health, 17 Vr. 99).

Where a Justice takes time to decide a cause (fixing no date), he must notify both parties of the time he will render judgment, or he loses jurisdiction. (Holland v. Chester, 35 Vr. 535).

Where a Justice is absent on the day and place to which a cause is adjourned he loses jurisdiction, even if the attorneys consent. (McKenna v. Murphy, 39 Vr. 522; Chalmers v. Wildwood 

Water Works Co., 55 Vr. 573).

Where the adjournment is for more than thirty days, without affidavit and without consent, jurisdiction is lost. (Ibid).

Affidavits and Oaths 

What an affidavit is

An affidavit is an oath in writing, sworn to before some person who has authority to administer such oath. It may or may not be connected with a legal action or suit. There is no such thing as an unwritten affidavit. The ordinary form of an affidavit begins and ends as stated in Forms below. 

A Justice of the Peace is authorized to take affidavits. They may also be taken before the Chief Justice, Chancellor, Vice- 

Chancellor, or Judge of a Court; Master in Chancery; mayor, recorder or alderman of any city, town or borough; Supreme Court commissioner; city clerk; clerk or surrogate of any county, or deputy clerk or surrogate; clerk of any Court of record; notary public, commissioner of deeds, or attorney-at-law. Oaths of office to officials are excepted as they are not affidavits in the usual sense and are to be taken as statutes direct. There are also ex-

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

cepted affidavits in cases where the procuring party must give notice to any interested person. 

There is no law forbidding the Justice taking an affidavit in another county than that in which he resides. 

Some points concerning affidavits

Several persons may swear to and sign the same statement of facts in a single affidavit. 

An insane person cannot make an affidavit; nor an infant who has not attained to the age of discretion.

Where one states that he is conscientiously scrupulous of taking an oath, he is to be affirmed, or may declare. (G. S. 2332, § 26; Clarke v. Collins, 3 Green 473). 

To swear, affirm or declare falsely, if done wilfully, is perjury.

In making oath to an affidavit it is not necessary for the person making it to kiss the Bible, but the hand may be held upon the book. (C. S. 3775, § 39); or it may be by uplifted hand. (Ibid, § 24).

The customary way is for the affiant first to sign the affidavit, and then for the person administering the oath to say: "You do solemnly swear" [or, if he affirms, "solemnly, sincerely and truly declare and affirm"] "that the affidavit to which you have affixed your name is true to the best of your knowledge and belief, so help you God." The affiant then says: "I do." 

If the person conscientiously scrupulous of taking an oath does not affirm, but desires to declare, the oath is to be: "You do declare, in the presence of Almighty God, the witness of the truth of what you say in this affidavit." (C. S. 3772, § 26).

If the oath is by uplifted hand, the person administering the oath should say: "You do solemnly swear (or solemnly, sincerely and truly declare and affirm), by the ever-living God, that the affidavit to which you have affixed your name is true to the best of your knowledge and belief." (Ibid, § 24).

Amendments 

Amendments permitted

The following sections from the Practice Act apply to The Small Cause Court: 

"If at the trial of an action there appears variance between any pleading and the proof thereunder which would not mislead the adverse party to his prejudice, the Court may order an immediate amendment of the pleading to avoid such variance; if the variance be one that might mislead the adverse party, the Court may order the pleading to be amended upon terms. "In order to prevent the failure of justice by reason of mistakes and objections of form, the Court or a Judge at all times may amend all defects and errors in any proceeding in civil actions, whether there is anything in the writing to amend by or not, and whether the defect or error be that of the party applying to amend or not, and all such amendments may be made with or without costs and upon terms; and all such amendments as may be necessary for the purpose of determining in the existing action the real question in controversy between the parties shall be so made." (C. S. 4091, §§ 125, 126).

This allows the amendment of a summons by the Justice after it has been served. (Abrahams v. Jacoby, 40 Vr. 178).

Independent of this Act, it is allowable, or enjoined, to amend in the following instances: 

1. Where the parties both agree to the amendment. 

2. Where the higher Court directs an amendment to be made in the Justices's return (in case of appeal, or return to a mandamus or certiorari) so as to conform to the facts. (Levy v. 

Stern, 52 Vr. 318). 

3. Where the constable has made an error in his return to a writ. In such case the statute says: "If the constable's return to any summons or warrant be defective, and such constable has, in point of fact, complied with all the requirements of this Act in serving such writ, whether the defendant appears or not and whether he objects or not, such constable may amend his return

AMENDMENTS 

73 in such manner as to make it conform to the fact; provided, he do so on or before the trial of the cause. (S. C. A., § 107). 

4. Where a jury of twelve men renders a verdict in "lack of form, touching false English," etc. (C. S. 43, § 9). 

5. Generally speaking, any amendment to the usual proceedings in ordinary suits in The Small Cause Court, which does not alter the rights of the parties, and is not to their prejudice but simply corrects an inadvertence, may be permitted. 

Amendments to be in open Court

Usually amendments are to be made upon motion and in open Court, because both parties must be apprised of what is to be amended, so that either party in interest may object, if he desires to do so.

Should the Justice see faults in the papers, he may state them, and thus give the party who made the errors an opportunity to move to amend. But if so he should state them publicly, not privately, as he is not the counsel for either party. Therewith his duty ends. 

Mr. Justice Southard once pertinently remarked: “After a state of demand, or other paper, is filed in the office of the Justice, the party has no longer any power over it. It is a record of the Court, and as such beyond his control; he may not touch it, or amend it, but by the express permission of the Court; much less may he alter it against the will of the Court. If he do alter or amend it, he takes upon himself the consequence, and has no right to complain, if his cause be dismissed. The law requires the pleadings to be filed on the return day of the summons. If a party may afterwards alter his plea, or state of demand, the law is nugatory. Its object, which was thus early to apprise the opposite party of what was objected against him, is defeated. În truth, a paper thus altered is no longer the same. It ought to be regarded as withdrawn, and the plaintiff, if it be his state of demand, ought to be nonsuited. It is no answer to this objection, to say that the alteration could do no injury to the other party. It is not for one party to say that no injury will be done to the other by his unlawful act; and, besides, if one alteration may legally be made, I see not why another may not." (Blackwell v. Leslie, 1 

South. 113). 

Improper amendments may be contempt

For a Justice to amend his own docket after he has transmitted a copy of the record to a higher Court, is not only irregular, but may be a contempt of that Court, unless that Court has directed such amendment. He should do nothing in the way of J-5

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

amendment or alteration of the record of any cause after the cause has passed out of his jurisdiction. 

Amendment of affidavit for warrant to hold to bail not permitted

There can be no amendment of an affidavit for a civil warrant to hold to bail, after the issue of such warrant; the proceedings in such case are of a wholly technical nature and the statute on amendments does not apply. 

Amending execution

An execution can be amended in order to conform to the facts; not to a new state of facts arising after its issuance. 

Amendment in attachment proceedings

Amendments may generally be made in attachment proceedings the same as in ordinary civil causes, provided it does not injure the defendant. (Wright v. Moran, 14 Vr. 49. But see

Abrahams v. Jacoby, 40 Vr. 178, where it is held a defendant's fictitious name is not amendable; and Garrison v. Seckendorf, 50

Vr. 203, where it is held that substituting one Christian name for another after judgment entered is not amendable). 

The State Society 

Animals, Cruelty to 

The New Jersey Society for the "Prevention of Cruelty to

Animals," through its members, agents and officers, is given large powers respecting offenses against animals by Act of 1880 (Č. 

S. 55, with amendments).

By the 1880 Act, as amended in Section 13 in 1929 (Laws, p. 312), it is provided: "13. That any person or persons who shall overdrive, overload, drive when overloaded, overwork, torture, torment, deprive of necessary sustenance, or cruelly beat or otherwise abuse or needlessly mutilate, or kill, or who shall by their agents, servants, employees or otherwise, cause or procure to be overdriven, overloaded, driven when overloaded, overworked, tortured, tormented, deprived of necessary sustenance, or to be unnecessarily or cruelly beaten, or otherwise abused or needlessly mutilated and killed, any living animal or creature and any person having the charge or custody of any living animal or creature either as owner or otherwise who inflicts unnecessary cruelty upon the same, or unnecessarily fails to provide the same with proper food, drink, shelter or

protection from the weather and any person who shall keep or use, or in any way be connected with or interested in the management of, or who shall receive money or other consideration for the admission of any person to any place kept or used for the purpose of fighting or baiting any bull, bear, dog, cock, bird or other living animal or creature and every person who shall be present and witness, encourage, aid, or assist therein or who shall permit or suffer any place owned or controlled by him to be so kept or used, and any person who shall carry or cause to be carried in or upon any vehicle or otherwise, any living animal or creature in a cruel or inhuman manner, and any person who shall hereafter use any dog or dogs for the purpose of drawing or helping to draw any cart, carriage, truck, barrow or other vehicle for business purposes, and any person who shall impound or confine or cause to be impounded or confined in any pound or other place any living animal or creature and shall fail or neglect to supply to the same during such confinement a sufficient quantity of good and wholesome food and water, and any person who shall abandon to die in any public place any maimed, sick, infirm or disabled animal or creature shall forfeit and pay such sum not to exceed one hundred dollars ($100), together with costs, as the Court shall determine." 

By a supplement of 1931 (Laws, page 44), to crop off the ears or part ears of a dog, other than certified as necessary by a registered veterinarian, will be subject to a penalty of not over $250. 

Method of procedure

By the same section the statute says the penalty (above named) is "To be sued for and recovered in an action of Debt with costs of suit, by any person or persons in the name of the New Jersey 

Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, in any Criminal

District Court of the county where the defendant resides or in which the offense was committed, or, if no such Court, before any Justice of the Peace, Recorder or Police Magistrate of the municipality wherein the defendant resides or where the offense or offenses were committed, or before any District Court in cases where the defendant resides in or where the offense or offenses were committed in any municipality in which there is located a District Court; where the offense or offenses were committed in a municipality having no Justice of the Peace, Recorder, Police Magistrate or District Court, then such person or persons shall be tried either before a Justice of the Peace, Recorder or Police Magistrate in the municipality wherein the defendant resides or before any Justice of the Peace, Recorder or Police Magistrate within the county where the offense or offenses were committed.

In cases where the defendant resides in or where the offense or offenses were committed in a municipality in which there is located a District Court, the jurisdiction of such District Court shall not be exclusive but shall be concurrent with the jurisdiction of the Recorders or Police Magistrates of such municipality." Complaints are amendable, whether before a Magistrate, Court, or on appeal (Laws 1929, page 317). 

The magistrate or Court may proceed as follows: "I. By summons: When the defendant or defendants are resident within the jurisdiction of the Court. "II. By warrant: When the defendant or defendants are temporarily within the jurisdiction of said Justice, Court or magistrate, but not residing therein; or when the said person or persons is or are likely to evade judgment by removal therefrom; or when the name or names and residence or residences of said person or persons is or are unknown. 

"III. By attachment: When said Justice, Court or magis trate is satisfied by affidavit that the owner or owners of any animal which has been or is being cruelly treated within the provisions of section thirteen of this Act, is the party chargeable with such offense under said section, and that said owner or owners reside out of the local jurisdiction of such Justice, Court or magistrate, the said Justice, Court or magistrate shall order and enforce the same by summary attachment against the animal so cruelly treated, and the vehicle, truck, cart, barrow or wagon to which said animal is or may be fastened, yoked, hitched or harnessed at the time of said offense, together with the appurtenances. "IV. By summary arrest: In all cases where any person or persons are arrested without warrant for violating any of the provisions of this Act in the presence of the officer making the arrest, as hereinafter provided, the procedure shall be the same as that provided in section eleven of this Act in cases of violation of that section of this Act. In all cases where such defendant is a nonresident of the county in which the alleged offense was committed, or where such defendant desires an adjournment or continuance of the hearing, the Justice, Court or magistrate before whom such complaint shall have been made, may, in his discretion, require such defendant to furnish security in an amount not exceeding two hundred and fifty dollars ($250) for his appearance at the hearing."

When proceeding before Justice in The Small Cause Court If the proceeding brought is an action for a penalty under section 13 of the Act of 1880 (as quoted above), it is in The Small Cause Court, and a jury trial is allowed. (Rosen v. N. J.

Summary proceeding where animals are baited, etc.

Any sheriff, constable, police officer, or agent of the New Jersey Society, may enter a place where there is the fighting or baiting of an animal, and, without warrant, arrest all persons there present, taking possession of the animals and implements. 

The persons arrested shall be taken to the nearest Police Judge, or Recorder (if any in the municipality; otherwise to nearest Justice of the Peace). Thereupon, a written complaint shall be made and a warrant issued returnable immediately. The parties being in custody the magistrate shall proceed to determine their guilt. 

This he must do upon the usual sworn proof. If found guilty, he may adjudge that each of them shall forfeit and pay a sum not to exceed one hundred dollars, together with costs, and thereupon issue a process that they be imprisoned and kept in custody until the amount and costs are paid. (C. S. 59, § 33). These proceedings, as stated, are, when before the Justice, to be before him as a magistrate and not in  But the arrest is to be summary and then the complaint is to be made. 

Selling seized property

In the case of fighting or baiting animals, where animals or implements are seized, the person who makes the seizure shall make application in writing to the proper magistrate within twenty-four hours to have the same forfeited and sold, specifying the articles seized, the place and the reason; thereupon the magistrate shall advertise such seizure and appoint a time and place from five to ten days distant to hear the application. The advertisement shall be in a newspaper circulating in the neighborhood at least three times, if a daily, or one time if a weekly. At the hearing, he may adjudge the property forfeited and order a sale. (C. S. 56, § 27).

Searching buildings When complaint is made in any cruelty to animals' case, on

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

oath or affirmation, before the proper official, that the complainant believes and has reasonable cause to believe that the law, in relation to cruelty to animals, has been or is being violated, such magistrate, if satisfied, shall issue a search warrant, but, unless specially authorized upon satisfactory cause shown, the search must be made between six A. M. and six P. M. (Ibid, § 31).

Unlawful to receive or offer for sale a disabled horse To receive or offer for sale any horse which by reason of debility, disease or lameness, or for any other cause, could not be worked in this State without violating the law is unlawful. The penalty is a fine of $10 to $100, or imprisonment not exceeding six months. (P. L. 1923, p. 164; N. J. Cum. Supp. 59).

So if horse has glanders, offering it for sale is a misdemeanor. (Ibid). 

Bulls running at large

A person may not suffer a bull of the age of one year or over to run at large out of the inclosed ground of owner or keeper under a penalty of $25, recoverable by any person who sues for the same. (P. L. 1920, p. 95; N. J. Cum. Supp. 77). 

Plea of guilty

Where suit for a penalty is brought under certain sections of the general Act the defendant may plead guilty, upon which the magistrate may immediately impose the penalty, and, if forthwith paid with costs, the proceedings will cease; otherwise judgment is to be entered and then execution, which may be against the body or goods of defendant. (C. S. 63, § 41). 

Abandoned animal

Where an animal is found to be abandoned in a maimed or disabled condition, any proper magistrate (Police Justice or Recorder, if any, otherwise a Justice of the Peace), sheriff, or agent of the New Jersey Society may appoint a suitable person to destroy the animal if unfit for further use, or, if fit for further use, may advertise and sell it in such manner as the Justice or Society's agent may direct. (C. S. 56, § 26). 

Fees and costs; to whom paid (See under general title "Fees and Costs"). But all fines and penalties imposed and collected are to be paid by the Justice, Court, magistrate or Clerk of Court receiving the same within 30 days to the District Society S. P. C. A. of the county, or, if no

such Society, to the New Jersey Society. (Laws 1929, p. 318, § 15).

Miscellaneous 

Provisions are made by the statute for the seizure and sale of vehicles in which living animals are carried in a cruel manner, in case the necessary expenses of arrest, etc., are not paid; providing that corporations, as well as individuals, may be held to be guilty of the misdemeanors named; that indictments of persons under the Act shall not relieve them from the ordinary penalties; and that the Act shall not prohibit the shooting of pigeons from a trap upon the ground of any shooting or athletic club. 

If a defendant in any cruelty to animals case is a non-resident of the county the magistrate may require him, when first appearing, to furnish security not exceeding $250 for his appearance at the hearing. (C. S. Sup., 17). Appeals

Appeals are allowed in all cruelty to animals cases to the Common Pleas, in the same manner as other appeals allowed in the Court trying the cause. (C. S. Sup., 17).

Other Penalties 

There are various other penalties concerning animals which cannot be detailed here.

Suits before Justice

Animals-Estrays 

The only manner in which the law as to estray cattle, horses or sheep concerns Justices of the Peace is in the bringing of actions for penalties.

If any person, who shall have any such estrays upon his improved lands or in his possession between November 1 and April

ANIMALS SHEEP, POULTRY, Etc. 

85 1 of any year, shall not acquaint the owner thereof, or give the notice which the Act prescribes within twenty days after his discovery of the estray, he shall lose any demand he may have of the owner for keeping and feeding the estray, and, in addition, shall forfeit the sum of six dollars for every such stray cattle or horse, and fifty cents for each sheep, to be recovered by action. of Debt before any Justice, with costs. If the owner does not prosecute, within twenty days after the first day of April, the overseer of the poor, upon notice, is required to prosecute, and to apply the penalties recovered to the use of the poor. (C. S. 85, § 141). 

Animals Sheep, Poultry, Etc. 

Suits before Justice 

Where a dog is found killing, worrying or wounding any sheep, lamb, domestic animal or poultry, and the owner or person harboring the dog, being informed, shall neglect or refuse to kill him within twenty-four hours from the time of receiving such information, such owner or person shall forfeit and pay to any person who shall sue for the same the sum of ten dollars, with costs, by an action of Debt before any Justice of the Peace, or District Court, of the county. If damages have been done, he shall also pay triple damages. And any person may kill any dog found chasing, worrying or wounding such sheep, lamb, poultry, or domestic animal (not poultry). (P. L. 1922, p. 261, § 3; 

N. J. Cum. Supp. 63; see also Laws 1927, p. 338).

The money so collected shall be paid over to the municipality and kept by it as a separate fund to make good any loss sustained in the municipality by the destruction, etc., of sheep, lambs, domestic animals or poultry. (P. L. 1931, p. 505).

In addition, the owner, possessor, or harborer of any dog who destroys sheep, etc., is responsible to the person who sustains injury in damages, the action to be an action of Trespass.

In such action it will not be necessary to prove that the dog was accustomed to commit such an injury. If, however, the injured person present a claim for damages to the municipality, that shall be a waiver of the right to sue the owner of the dog for damages. (Ibid, §§ 6, 7). In presenting such claim against a township, town, borough or village, there must be an appraisement according to the directions of the Act. (N. J. Cum. Supp. 65, § 5).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Who and when to appeal Appeal

Either party to a judgment (except a confessed judgment) in The Small Cause Court may appeal his cause to the Common Pleas, within twenty days after judgment rendered. (S. C. A., § 80).

This right of appeal to the Pleas is not taken away by the fact that the Justice acted without having jurisdiction, and that his judgment was practically a nullity; if it is a judgment it is appealable (Williamson v. Middlesex Pleas, 13 Vr. 386), and in such case there may be either appeal or certiorari taken, but not both. (Furnam v. Motley, 38 Vr. 174).

Where a judgment has been obtained against two or more defendants any one of the defendants may appeal, without order of severance, etc. (S. C. A., § 80a). 

Method of appeal, bond, etc.

If the judgment appealed from is one entered against the party demanding the appeal, or if there be in the action a set-off against his demand, then the applicant shall file with the Justice a bond to the other party, with at least one sufficient security, being a freeholder in the county, and in double the amount of such judgment or set-off, "conditioned that the appellant shall appear and prosecute the said appeal in the Court of Common Pleas, shall stand to and abide the judgment of the said Court, and pay such costs as shall be taxed against him if the judgment be affirmed." (S. C. A., § 80).

But if the judgment appealed from is in favor of the party demanding the appeal and there be no offset in the action against his demand, then no appeal bond is required, but the appeal shall be taken by a notice in writing, signed by or on behalf of the appellant, briefly describing the judgment, and stating that the party appeals therefrom to the Court of Common Pleas. (Ibid).

It will be perceived that under the Act the party appealing must file a notice of appeal with the Justice within twenty days after judgment. It is also requisite that the appellant shall pay to the Justice "all costs by him except such as shall be adjudged to the prevailing party," or the appeal cannot be granted. (Ibid, § 104).

In granting or refusing to grant an appeal, the Justice acts judicially, and is to adjudge, and be satisfied, (1) whether it is a case in which appeal lies; (2) whether the application being in writing is made in due time; (3) whether the bond, if one is required, is in due and legal form in the matter of penalty, and in the terms of its condition; (4) whether the surety named in the

APPEAL 

87 bond is a freeholder in the county, and otherwise sufficient; (5) whether the bond has been executed in due form of law, so as to be a valid and actual security to the opposite party. (Tichenor v. Hewson, 2 Gr. 26). Also (6) the appellant must pay his costs.

To have any of these defective (unless amended in time) or not to file the bond in season, will be to deprive the party of his right to appeal. The mere fact that his bond is good will not make the appellant's appeal good if the bond is not in time. (Park v. Hunt, 7 Hal. 87; see also 116 Atl. Rep. 688).

The Justice cannot refuse to grant an appeal, if the notice is in time, the bond sufficient, etc.; but otherwise should refuse the appeal.

If the appeal is perfected before the Justice in time, and the papers not sent up, a rule can be obtained in the Pleas upon the Justice requiring his immediate return of the proceedings. 

Even if the Justice has resigned, or his term has expired, he may grant an appeal. (S. C. A., § 7).

If the party intending to appeal endeavors, in reasonable time, good faith and with proper diligence, to see the Justice and demand an appeal, but is not able to do so through the absence of the Justice or some other sufficient cause, an appeal made later than required by the Act may, perhaps be sustained. Or, if the appeal bond should be left at the house of the Justice in his absence on the proper day, but he does not receive it until the next day, it has been held to be a good delivery and at the correct time. (Lacy v. Cox, 3 Green 469).

An appeal bond executed by a minor (against whom a judgment has been rendered) and by a substantial freeholder, is sufficient to sustain an appeal, although the guardian who was appointed by The Small Cause Court to defend the suit did not join in the bond. (Andruss v. Stewart, 5 Hal. 160).

The bond must be free of erasures, or at least there must be a certainty that it has not been altered since its execution, or the 

Pleas will not receive it. (Bell v. Quick, 1 Gr. 312). 

Sending up the record

The Justice who grants an appeal must send a transcript of the proceedings and judgment under his hand and seal, together with the bond, to the clerk of the Common Pleas within ten days after he receives notice of the appeal. (Ibid, § 81). This provision must be construed, of course, with other provisions, for, if a bond be required but none is filed, or it is insufficient, or if costs are not paid, the Justice will refuse the appeal and, then, he will not send up any transcript.

The transcript to be sent up is to be a literal and exact copy

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

of the record in the case as entered in Justice's docket. This is what a transcript means- -an actual copy of the record. The actual bond filed, if any, is to be attached to the record (not a copy of the bond), and so should be all the papers filed in the case (state of demand, note, copy of book account, etc.). 

If the transcript is incorrect then the Common Pleas may enter a rule directing the Justice to correct its errors, or to certify to facts which he should have entered on his dockets, but did (Lazarus v. Martling, 44 Vr. 84). 

Stay of execution in case of appeal

If an execution has been issued by the Justice prior to the granting of an appeal, it may be stayed by the Common Pleas, or its Judge, if the Court, upon filing of the appeal bond with the clerk, is satisfied with the legality and sufficiency of such bond; the stay to operate until the Court or Judge shall make some further order thereon. A rule to such an effect will be entered in the minutes of the Court, and a copy, certified by the clerk, served on the constable in whose hands the execution is. (S. C. A., § 82).

The copy of the rule for a stay should be served both upon the Justice and constable; the former in order that the entry of it may be made in his docket, the latter because the writ is in his hands for execution. Upon its receipt the constable will at once desist from doing anything further with the writ, as the stay of it will void the lien acquired by the levy made under the execution. For, after the appeal taken the verdict and judgment below are superseded, and any subsequent proceeding as to the judgment before the Justice is absolutely void. He may not issue an execution on the judgment after appeal granted.

But the judgment itself in The Small Cause Court is not void, nor even vacated, because of an appeal; it remains until a new judgment of some sort is rendered above. (Thompson v. 

Thompson, Coxe 159; Stader v. Chosen Freeholders of Sussex, 3 Gr. 433; Vannoy v. Givens, 3 Zab. 201; Ten Eyck v. Farlee, 1 

Harr. 269; Lum. v. Price, 1 Harr. 195). 

When appeal to be heard

The appeal must be put by the clerk upon the list for trial at the next term of the Common Pleas after the cause is appealed, provided the appeal has been taken, (that is, demanded of, and perfected before the Justice and papers sent to the clerk) so that ten days' notice may be given before the first day of the next term. Either party may give such ten days' notice to the other party. In the computation of such ten days, one of the days is to be excluded, not both. In default of such notice the Court,

APPEAL 

89 unless good cause be shown, shall dismiss the appeal. (C. S. A., § 90; Gaskill v. Miller, 42 Vr. 103).

In the Pleas certain fees of Court and clerk must be first paid by the appellant, or he will not be heard. (Ibid, § 105).

The appeals are to be heard by the Judge without a jury unless a demand for a jury is made in writing and filed with the clerk of the Court at least five days before the day for which it is noticed for trial. (Ibid, § 80).

Upon the trial of an appeal neither party to the cause is bound to call only such witnesses as were heard below, nor is he confined to the same documentary evidence. (Ib., § 85). 

In case the judgment appealed from is one rendered by the Justice upon the report of referees (see general title "References"), the Common Pleas has power to inquire into such report and the judgment, and affirm or set the same aside as in other causes before the Court. (Ibid, § 86). 

For costs on appeal, see S. C. A., § 101. 

Appeals from city ordinances to be by certiorari

In case of proceedings for violation of city ordinances, or ordinances of city boards of health, the proper manner of review is by certiorari. (C. S. 255, § 16; see Plainfield v. Russell, 4 N. 

J. Misc. R. 246). 

When to Quarter Sessions

In cases of disagreements between master and servant, employer and apprentice or clerk, where three Justices have jurisdiction, an appeal from their judgment is allowed to the Quarter 

Sessions. (C. S. 100, § 5.)

It is also allowed in bastardy cases. (C. S. 187, § 12). 

Also in proceedings under the Vice and Immorality Act. (C. 

S. 5719, § 19).

Also under the Disorderly Persons Act, relating to family desertion. (C. S. 1933, § 21). 

There may be other statutes giving appeal to the Quarter

Sessions and, if so, they are to be consulted.

Apprentices, Servants and Clerks 

Proceedings by or against apprentices, servants or clerks

If any master, to whom a clerk, apprentice or servant is regularly bound by written indenture, is guilty of misusage, refusal of necessary provision or clothing, unreasonable correction, cruelty, or other ill-treatment, or if the clerk, apprentice or servant shall absent himself from the service of his master, or be guilty of any ill-behavior, the party aggrieved may complain to the Justice of the Peace of the county where the master dwells, who shall make such order as the equity of the case shall require. 

If such Justice, however, is unable to effect a settlement in the matter between the parties, he shall call to his assistance two other Justices of the Peace of the same county, unconnected with either of the parties. These three Justices, when met shall

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

constitute a Court for the hearing of the matters in difference. 

They should hear the witnesses in the usual manner, and then make an order under their hands and seals. This order may discharge the clerk, apprentice, or servant from his service, and may order such part of the money as shall have been paid or contracted for in relation to such clerk, etc., to be refunded to the person who paid the same; or, if the default is that of the clerk, etc., the Court shall cause such due punishment to be administered as is just and reasonable. An appeal will be allowed from such order to the next Court of General Quarter Sessions in the county, the person bringing the appeal giving six days' notice of his intention, and of the cause and matter of the appeal to the adverse party, and entering into a bond, within three days after such notice, before some Justice of the Peace of the county, with sufficient surety, conditioned to try the appeal, etc., (C. S. 100, § 5).

Any person who shall persuade any clerk, apprentice, or servant, to run away or absent himself from service, shall forfeit and pay the sum of $30, to be sued for in action of Debt with costs. 

Every person harboring or concealing any clerk, etc., who is a fugitive, shall forfeit one dollar for every day of such harboring, or concealment, to be sued for in action of Debt. (§§ 6, 7). He may also be sued in damages. (Gould v. Trandt, 15 N. J. L. J. 28).

Should a male servant above the age of twenty-one years, or a female servant above the age of eighteen years, abscond from service, such servant when apprehended may be taken by the master before three Justices of the Peace of the county where the master resides, who, upon hearing of the whole matter, shall adjudge the servant to serve any term not exceeding double the time he absented himself, besides paying or serving for all damages and costs. (§ 8).

A clerk, apprentice, or servant, under the ages heretofore mentioned, absenting himself without leave, or running away, may be sued by an action on the case, [now to be on Contract, under S. C. A., § 23], and such action shall be brought within six years after such clerk, etc., shall arrive at full age. (§ 9).

It is the evident intention of the Act to apply to clerks and servants only when they are regularly indentured for a specific term of service. Formerly such indentures were common; now they are rare except in the case of some classes of foreigners. 

Hence the following forms are likely to be seldom used.

What an arbitration is Arbitration

An arbitration is the submission of a controversy between parties to individuals chosen by themselves, who hear and decide the matter by authority derived from that consent. The difference between an arbitration and a reference is that the former is brought about wholly by the parties concerned in a dispute, whereas a reference is the submission of a controversy to the decision

ARBITRATION 

95 of a referee by rule or order of Court. A Small Cause Court has no power to appoint arbitrators. The subject is noticed here only because the Justice, who may sometimes be a peacemaker, should know how a dispute may be settled by arbitration. (For Acts see C. S. 103-109). 

Submission to abitrators

All persons having a controversy with another for which there is no ready remedy except by suit, may agree in writing to submit their controversy to the award of any person or persons, or may enter into bond to such effect. This applies to boards of education in disputes arising where the school law does not require some other specific manner of settlement. (See P. L. 1922, p. 391, § 1; N. J. Cum. Supp. 3179). Such an agreement may be made a rule of any of the (higher) Courts of records of this State that the parties may choose. The agreement should be witnessed. Upon one or more of the witnesses making an affidavit as to the signatures to the agreement, which affidavit shall be read and may be filed in any Court of which the same is agreed to be made a rule, the agreement may be entered of record and a rule made by the Court that the parties shall be finally concluded by the arbitration.

Although The Small Cause Court is in a restricted sense a Court of record in this State, it has not been held that this arbitration Act applies to said Court. 

Justices of the Peace, within the county wherein an arbitration issues, may make out subpoenas for witnesses to appear before the arbitrators. (C. S. 106, § 7). They may also administer the oath to the arbitrators, which should be written and signed in order that they may make up a record. 

The new Arbitration Act 

In 1923 (P. L., p. 291; N. J. Cum. Supp. 86), a new Arbitration Act was enacted, providing for arbitration when a written contract provides that a controversy be so settled. Its enforcement is applicable to the higher Courts, not before a Justice of the Peace.

Assignment for the Benefit of Creditors 

Usual proceedings

This matter of an assignment for the benefit of creditors does not come within the regular jurisdiction of a Justice of the Peace, but is noted here because a Justice is frequently called upon in small places to prepare the necessary first papers, or to give advice to persons unable to employ an attorney; yet it is always better to refer the debtor to a responsible lawyer. The substance of the Assignment Act is as follows: 

Any debtor may assign his estate in trust to an assignee or assignees for the benefit of his creditors, but it must be of his entire estate and for the equal benefit of his creditors in proportion to their several demands, and without preferences. The debtor thereby releases all control of the estate. 

Partners may assign, and also any corporation organized under the laws of this State. In the case of partnership property the assignment may include only the partnership property, or also the several estates of the parties; or any of the parties, after the general assignment of the partnership property, may make a separate general assignment of his individual estate. In case of a general assignment including both partnership and an individual estate, the same is to be kept separate in all proceedings, notices and accounts relating thereto.

The assignment must be acknowledged or proved the same as a deed, and recorded in the office of the county clerk. There must be annexed to the assignment an inventory, under the debtor's oath, of the debtor's estate, real and personal, together with a list of his or its creditors and the amount of their respective claims, according to the best of his knowledge. But if any of the

ASSIGNMENT FOR THE BENEFIT OF CREDITORS 

97 debtor's property is omitted in the inventory it will pass to the assignee the same as if designated.

After the assignee has received and recorded the assignment in the county where the assignor resides, or in any other counties where he deems it necessary to record it, he must give forthwith public notice by advertising, at least once a week, for four weeks successively, in one of the newspapers printed in this State circulating in the neighborhood where the creditors reside, making known that the assignment has been made, and when made, and setting forth a general description of the business carried on by the assignor, and the place where the same was so carried on, and that all claims of creditors against the estate must be presented, under oath or affirmation, to the assignee within three months from the date of the assignment, or the same will be barred from coming in for a dividend of the estate. Within thirty days after the date of the assignment the assignee must mail a copy of such notice, with postage prepaid, to every creditor of the assignor, addressed to the creditor at his usual post office address, so far as the same can be ascertained.

The assignee is also "forthwith" to exhibit to the surrogate of the county, under oath, the true inventory and valuation of the estate, and also enter into bond to the Ordinary of the State in such amount and with such sufficient security as the Orphans' Court of the county, or any Judge thereof, may approve for the faithful performance of his trust, which bond is to be filed with the surrogate. Until such inventory, valuation and bond are filed, the assignee may not proceed to the discharge of his trust except for the preservation of the estate, unless the Orphans' Court, or its Judge, shall, by order, authorize the assignee to perform certain duties in relation to the trust.

At the expiration of three months from the date of filing the assignee must file with the surrogate a true list, sworn to, of all such creditors as have proved their claims, with a true statement of such claims, and proof of publication and mailing of the notice. (As to other proceedings consult the Act, C. S. 114-125, with Amendments by Chap. 234, Laws of 1928).
