The nature of writ Attachment

When a debtor who owes a debt, or has incurred a penalty, (not exceeding two hundred dollars) absconds from his creditors, and is non-resident in this State, the statute prescribes a summary proceeding whereby, upon the application of the creditor and affidavit filed before the Justice, his personal property may be seized and taken into the possession of the law. (C. S. 148, § 37).

The first process in the action is the writ of attachment, which is an extraordinary writ issued against the property to compel the defendant to appear to the suit, or to make that property answerable for the judgment ultimately recovered.

The proceedings are in The Small Cause Court, but necessarily such Court must have jurisdiction, i. e., not excluded from it because of any exclusive jurisdiction of a District Court. 

When proper

It can be used only when the ordinary process of summons or warrant cannot be served. As the particular purpose of the 

Act is, by the seizure of the property of a debtor, to answer the demand of the plaintiff when, from non-residence or flight, he is beyond the reach of judicial process, it must be in its very nature an extraordinary, not an ordinary writ, and hence to be used only on the extraordinary occasion stated. (City Bank v. Merrit, 1 

Gr. 131).

The idea is sometimes prevalent that it is only necessary to make affidavit of a proper cause of action against a non-resident, or absconding defendant in order to secure a writ of attachment. 

Whereas, if the cause of action is founded upon a trespass or damages to one's person or property, or is for damages upon a covenant broken, or is in any other respect unliquidated (that is, uncertain, not fixed) it will be error to issue the writ. A debtor is one who owes a debt, and damages do not constitute debt in law until liquidated. (Day v. Bennett, 3 Harr. 288).

If a sum is payable on conditions or contingencies, those must be performed or happen before it becomes such a certain debt as

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

that plaintiff can make the required oath. (Barber v. Robeson, 3 Green 18).

The writ may also be employed when the non-resident defendant has incurred a penalty under the statute, which penalty and statute shall be specified in the affidavit. 

The exact language of the statute as to when the writ may be employed is as follows: (1) Where the plaintiff, his agent or attorney, shall make affidavit that he verily believes the debtor absconds from his creditors and is not, to deponent's knowledge or belief, resident in this State at the time, and that he owes to the plaintiff a debt, specifying as nearly as practicable the amount thereof, or has incurred a penalty under a statute, which penalty and statute shall be specified. (2) Where the plaintiff, his agent, or attorney, shall make affidavit that the debtor is not to deponent's knowledge or belief resident in this State at the time, and that he owes to the plaintiff a debt, specifying, as nearly as practicable, the amount thereof, or has incurred a penalty under a statute, which penalty and statute shall be specified." (C. S. 133, § 1).

But the Act makes exceptions which must be carefully noted, viz: Wages for labor due to a non-resident employee, from a nonresident creditor, and debts due from a non-resident when the property to be attached is exempt by the law of the State of which debtor and creditor are residents. (Ibid).

Otherwise than as excepted the writ may be sued out by any creditor whether resident in or out of the State. 

A corporation created by a law of this State may sue out a writ. (Trenton Bank v. Haverstick, 6 Hal. 171).

A separate creditor of one partner may attach that partner's interest in partnership property.

If the Justice causes a writ of attachment to issue when the Justice has no jurisdiction, the plaintiff who causes the debtor's goods to be seized becomes a trespasser. (McFadden v. Whitney, 22 Vr. 391).

The writ, as stated, can be against either absconding or nonresident debtors, and hence is designated as 1. a Domestic; or 2. a 

Foreign attachment.

As stated, the jurisdiction of the Justice is limited in attachment, as in ordinary suits, to causes involving not exceeding two hundred dollars. 

Who is an absconding debtor

An absconding debtor is one who, with intent to defeat or delay the demands of his creditors, conceals or withdraws himself from his usual place of residence beyond the reach of civil process; and it does not matter that he is within or without the

ATTACHMENT 

101 State, or even if he be concealed within his own house. (State, Stafford, v. Miller, 28 Vr. 574).

Mere temporary absence from the State upon business or pleasure with the intention of returning is not sufficient ground upon which to found an attachment, although the absence may be subsequently so prolonged as to render his property liable to attachment as that of an absconding debtor. (Ibid).

If the plaintiff made his oath in good faith and verily believes that the defendant absconds, etc., being led thereto by the debtor's conduct, the writ must stand: for in this class of attachments (domestic, against absconding debtors) it is only when the plaintiff acts in bad faith and abuses the process of the Court, that the writ will be quashed on the review of a higher Court. (Walker v. Anderson, 3 Harr. 217; Weber v. Weitling, 3 C. E. Gr. 441; 

Depue, J., in Lesage v. Schmidt, Essex Circuit, 10 N. J. L. J. 10). 

Who is a non-resident debtor

A non-resident, or absent debtor, is one who has his abode out of the State; and mere presence in the State at the time of the issuing of the writ will not invalidate it, as that does not make a residence here. Thus where a man's wife is boarding in this 

State, and he visits her, the process of attachment against him may be proper. (Hackettstown Bank v. Mitchell, 4 Dutch. 516).

To constitute a residence in this State within the Attachment Act it must be the debtor's home, where he then is, or to which if he be absent he has the intention of returning, and where, in his absence, he is represented by some member of the family, or some one who can answer for him and communicate with him. 

The practical test, as to non-residence, is whether a legal service of a summons can be made on a debtor at his dwelling house, or usual place of abode in this State. If it can, the extraordinary writ of attachment cannot be used. (Leonard v. Stout, 1 Vr. 370).

While this case was reversed, (8 Vr. 492), its general principles were not disturbed. (See also Brundred ads. Del Hoyo, Spen. 328).

Some cases where attachment will and will not lie Executors, administrators, trustees, heirs and devisees may also be attached "in all cases in which the writ might have issued against such debtor immediately prior to his decease, and all real estate descended from or devised by him to the heir or devisee may be attached; and his personal estate in the hands of the executor, administrator, trustee or other person may be attached, and the executor, administrator, trustee, heir and devisee, and such other person, or any or all of them, may be joined as defendants in the same action; provided, that in the distribution of the

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

proceeds of any attachment so issued against the executor, administrator, trustee, heir or devisee, the plaintiff shall not be preferred but shall share ratably with the applying creditors; a legacy or distributive share of an estate in the hands of the executor, administrator, or trustee, may be attached in an action against the legatee or next of kin for his debt." (C. S. 136, § 5).

It will lie against a foreign corporation, not created or recognized by the laws of this State, and also a joint stock association; not where either has a place of business in this State and officers upon whom an ordinary process may be served. (Ibid, § 4; Phillipsburg Bank v. Del. & Lack. R. R. Co., 3 Dutch. 206). 

It may issue against females, whether married or not. (§ 4).

It may issue "against the separate and joint estate of joint debtors or any of them, either by their names or the names of the partnership or by whatsoever name they may be generally distinguished, or against the heirs, executors or administrators of them, or any of them; and the estate so attached, whether separate or joint, may be sold or assigned for the payment of the joint debt." 

(§ 3). 

It may issue by one partner against his interest in the copartnership. (Brown v. Bissett, 1 Zab. 46). But not if one or more of the defendants reside within this State. (Hollingshead v. Curtis, 2 Gr. 402; Barber v. Robeson, 3 Gr. 17). And it must issue against both of two joint debtors and not one only. (Bright v. Hand, 1 Harr. 273).

It may issue against the estate of a non-resident lunatic. (Weber v. Weitling, 3 C. E. Gr. 441).

It will not lie against a tenant removing goods, after he has completed his tenancy and is about to leave, because he can be served with process. (Kugler v. Shreve, 4 Dutch. 129).

It will not lie against the uniforms, equipments, etc., of the 

National Guard of the State, or its members. (P. L. 1918, p. 

794; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1939). 

The affidavit

No writ can issue without an affidavit, to be made by the plaintiff himself, or by the plaintiff's agent or attorney. 

The affidavit, in case of domestic attachment, must set forth in the exact language of the statute that the plaintiff "verily believes the debtor absconds from his creditors, and is not, to deponent's knowledge or belief, resident in this State at the time; and that he owes to the plaintiff a debt," specifying, as nearly as practicable, the amount thereof; or that he has incurred a penalty under a statute, which penalty and statute shall be specified; or, in case of a foreign attachment, that the debtor "is not, to deponent's knowledge or belief, resident in this State at the time, and

ATTACHMENT 

103 that he owes to the plaintiff a debt," specifying, as nearly as practicable, the amount thereof. This is to be filed before the Justice, and the writ will then be issued. He is required to issue the same, but, as stated, it must not be to exceed two hundred dollars. (C. S. 148, § 37).

The cause of action need not be set forth in detail in such affidavit, as in a state of demand. But the form of the affidavit must follow the statute. To make oath that the defendant absents himself from his creditors, or that the debtor absconds, without stating that he is indebted to the party for whom the writ is asked, is not sufficient. So an affidavit by an agent that the defendant owes him is defective. 

Form of writ 

The names of parties writ, as in the affidavit; surname must be used. be quashed. (State v. 

Ibid 68). must be stated with certainty in the and to do this the Christian name and When initials only are used the writ will 

Leon, 13 Vr. 540; Elbertson v. Richards,

The writ must be directed to a constable, as a private citizen cannot serve it. (Orenstine v. Schaffer, 29 Vr. 344).

The writ should be intituled in The Small Cause Court and the record of proceedings entered in the usual civil docket. 

How writ is executed

The statute directs how the writ is to be executed. "The officer to whom a writ of attachment is directed shall execute the same by going to the house or lands of the defendant, or to the person or house of the person having custody or possession of the defendant's property and estate, and then and there declare in the presence of one credible person at the least, that he attaches the rights and credits, moneys and effects, goods and chattels, lands and tenements, of the defendant at the suit of the plaintiff." 

To enable the constable fully to execute the writ of attachment he is "empowered and required (having first made demand and being refused) to break open any house, chamber, room, shop, doors, chest, trunks, or other place or thing, where he shall be informed or have reason to believe any money, goods, books of account, bonds, bills, notes, papers or writings of the defendant may be deposited, secreted, had, or found." (C. S. 139, § 10).

After attaching the effects of defendant, such constable shall, with the assistance of one discreet and impartial freeholder, make a just and true inventory and appraisement of all the personal property and estate of the defendant, so by him attached, which inventory and appraisement, dated and signed by himself and said

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

freeholder, shall be annexed to and returned with the writ. The officer must endorse on the writ the true time of executing it, and sign his name thereto. (Ibid, § 7).

Observe (1) that there must be one credible witness present when the writ is executed; (2) that the constable must say, that "he attaches the rights and credits, moneys and effects, goods and chattels, lands and tenements," of the defendant at the suit of plaintiff: (3) That an inventory must be made, to be signed by himself and one freeholder; and (4) that the time of these proceedings must be endorsed on the writ.

The return of the attachment is to be immediately after the execution of the writ.

The return must show a substantial service; but if defective it may be amended. The officer cannot recover of the plaintiff in attachment the costs of a suit brought against him for improperly executing the writ.

If the constable does not return that he has attached anything, the Justice cannot appoint a day for the hearing, and there can be no further proceeding upon such writ. (Lentz v. Callin, 2 Dutch. 218).

The inventory need not be made the same day the goods are attached, but should be as speedily as possible. 

Where a garnishee declines to make known what moneys he has of the defendant, or what rights and credits are within his control, that fact should be certified to by the constable and the freeholder and will be sufficient, if they can ascertain no further facts, to make the garnishee responsible for whatever is in his hands at the time.

It has been decided in this State that the following may be attached as "rights and credits:" money in the sheriff's hands; a debt due the defendant on negotiable paper before maturity; the proceeds of an execution in the hands of a constable; the equity of the redemption in mortgaged chattels; a legacy charged upon real estate. But not a penalty intended to secure unliquidated damages; nor the liability of an officer for negligence; nor the equitable interest of the husband in the proceeds of his wife's land.

It has also been decided that as "moneys and effects" there may be attached, money, whether in specie or bank notes, if capable of identification as defendant's property; surplus money in the hands of a sheriff arising from sale under mortgage of land held in trust; an heir's share of the proceeds of an executor's sale of lands under a will. But not money due on a judgment recovered in a Court of record and still in the hands of the defendant in the judgment, when the attachment is against the plaintiff therein; nor salary due to a public officer in the hands of the

ATTACHMENT 

105 State treasurer; nor a husband's interest in his wife's personal property in the executor's hands.

As "goods and chattels," shares of stock cannot be attached if the certificate is delivered, or stock transferred on company's books, unless fraudulent. Goods in transitu through the State may be. 

The advertisements

Immediately after the issuing of the writ of attachment it is made the duty of the plaintiff "to advertise in three of the most public places in the county, that an attachment has been taken out from such Justice against such absconding or absent debtor, in order that any person having a greater demand against such debtor than is cognizable before a Justice of the Peace may have an opportunity to take out an attachment for the recovery of the same.' (C. S. 149, § 38). If the advertisements are not put up in "three of the most public places," the attachment will be void. 99 The plaintiff should himself sign these notices, and see that they are properly posted; and the Justice in his docket should record, not generally that he "was satisfied with the putting up of the advertisements," which may have been based upon hearsay or conjecture, but that it was "proved" before him. (Conover v. 

Conover, 2 Harr. 187). 

Proceedings on the return day

Upon the return of the attachment, the Justice must appoint a day for the hearing of the cause, not less than twenty days from the issuing of the writ. Before he does this he must satisfy himself by proof as to the advertisements having been set up, and the due and proper execution of the writ by the constable, as appears by the return; and also that there was property attached, as without the latter no further proceedings can be had. (Ibid, § 

37; Dodge v. Butler, 13 Vr. 37). 

The hearing

On or before the day fixed for the hearing, the plaintiff must file a copy of his account, or state of demand. 

If there is some clerical error only in a writ it may then be amended, provided it does not injure the defendant. (Wright v. 

Moran, 14 Vr. 49). But generally speaking proceedings in attachment are not amendable as in other cases (Elberson v. Richards, 13 Vr. 69).

Supposing the defendant not to have given bond (as stated below) so as to dissolve the attachment, the hearing may proceed on the day appointed, at which time the creditor shall make J-7

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

sufficient proof of the debt due to him. This means the usual proof upon competent sworn evidence by himself or others as witnesses. (C. S. 148, § 37). 

The defendant may give bond

On or before the day appointed for the hearing, the defendant may "file with the Justice a bond to plaintiff, executed by one or more sufficient sureties, being freeholders and resident in the county in which such attachment shall issue, in double the amount of the claim of the plaintiff, as set forth in the affidavit filed with said Justice conditioned for the due and safe return of the goods and chattels, rights and credits, moneys and effects seized and taken by virtue of such writ of attachment, in case judgment shall be rendered for the plaintiff; which said bond shall be approved by said Justice, and filed by him for the use and benefit of the plaintiff; and thereupon the property attached shall be restored to the defendant and released from the lien of said attachment." (Ibid, § 40).

After filing said bond, the defendant shall file his plea, copy of account, or set-off, if any he have; and the cause thereafter is to be conducted as in other causes commenced by summons in The Small Cause Court, and this includes the right of adjournment and of either party to appeal. Even after judgment defendant may give bond, if he failed to do so before filing his plea, and then may appeal. (§ 41). 

Quashing the writ

The writ may be set aside and quashed upon an affidavit of or on behalf of the defendant, setting forth facts which if uncontradicted would render it illegal or void. Thereupon the Justice tries the facts set forth in this affidavit, without requiring defendant to file a bond. (§ 43).

The burden of proof is on the plaintiff, and he must tender lawful evidence; and affidavit of the plaintiff cannot be used as evidence. He must produce witnesses who can be cross-examined. (State, Morris v. Quick, 16 Vr. 308).

If the writ is quashed, the proceeding ends; and defendant will have his costs of the plaintiff. (Kennedy ads. Chumar, 2 

Dutch. 305). 

Judgment and execution

Upon the day of hearing (or, later, if the cause be adjourned) if the creditor has made sufficient proof of the debt due to him, the Justice shall give judgment to the plaintiff and award his execution to the constable against the effects of the defendant thereon taken. But such effects shall not be sold in less than three months

ATTACHMENT 

107 (unless the same are perishable), to the end that the debtor or his friend may redeem the same, and in the meantime the same shall be inventoried and safely kept in such manner as the Justice shall direct. (C. S. 148, § 37). Appeal

An appeal will lie to the Common Pleas from a judgment in attachment in the same manner as in any other cause in The Small 

Cause Court. (Ibid, § 41). Should the Justice refuse an appeal when a proper bond is presented, a mandamus will lie. (Breunecke v. Denyse, 33 Vr. 148). 

Proceedings against garnishee

The peculiar operation of the process, by which such rights, credits, etc., of the defendant as cannot be seized and taken into custody, may still be rendered liable for the payment of his debts, has received the designation of "garnishment," or warning. The person in whose hands such effects are attached is styled the "garnishee," because of his being garnished or warned not to pay the money or deliver the property of the defendant in his hands to such defendant, but to appear and answer the plaintiff's suit. 

When the garnishee gives up the defendant's property, no proceedings against him are necessary. It is only when he denies having it in his possession or refuses to give it up that he is proceeded against, (which must be within sixty days from the date of the garnishment, C. S. 149, § 39a); and this may be by summons, or, in case of a fraud duly proved, by a capias ad respondendum. In either case the plaintiff must make oath that he believes the garnishee has moneys, goods, chattels or effects of the defendant in his custody or possession, or that the garnishee is indebted to the defendant in attachment, and is in fear of his absconding. 

This he must file with the Justice, who will thereupon issue a summons against the garnishee, (or capias, if fraud is proven); and plaintiff will declare in Tort as for trover and conversion in his demand, if the garnishee has property of defendant in possession; otherwise on Contract. But this action will not be tried until after the first action. Then, if nothing is found due from the defendant to the plaintiff, the garnishee will have judgment of costs against the plaintiff. So the garnishee will have costs if the plaintiff in the suit against him is nonsuited, or discontinues, or otherwise loses his cause. (Ibid, §§ 29, 30, 31, 39).

The trial of the action against the garnishee will be by the Justice, and if he finds for the plaintiff upon legal proof he must give judgment to him and execution will issue against the garnishee.

If suit is not brought against the garnishee before judgment

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

is obtained against the defendant, the Justice must issue a scire facias summoning him to appear and show cause why the plaintiff should not have execution against the property of defendant in the hands of the garnishee, or of the money due from garnishee to defendant. This he may do if the judgment is in his Court, against a garnishee residing within the limits of a city where there is a District Court. The writ must be directed from the Court where the judgment is. (N. Y., L. E. and W. R. R. v. Cookson, 16 Vr. 302).

Should the term of a Justice expire, before whom a judgment in attachment has been obtained, proceedings against a garnishee may be had before any other Justice having jurisdiction. (C. S. 

151, § 44).

In case of judgment for or against a garnishee, either party may appeal to the Common Pleas, the same as in ordinary causes decided in  (§ 42). 

Claim to property

If property, seized by a writ of attachment, is claimed by another, the method of trying the right is not as set forth in the Attachment Act, (§ 11), which applies to the higher Courts; but by application to a Justice for a jury, precisely as in case of a claim under an execution. (S. C. A., § 62; Stryker v. Skillman, 2 Gr. 189).

To notify the constable in writing of a claim and demand him to summon a jury, is not a proper application; nor will a written agreement to abide by the finding of such a verdict by the jury make it legal. The application is to be to the Justice who issued the writ. (Lindaur v. Teeter, 2 N. J. L. J. 28). 

The debtor's exemption "Household goods and furniture not exceeding in value two hundred dollars of a debtor having a family residing in this State, and against whom an attachment has issued, are reserved and exempted for the use of the family and shall not be attached, except for a debt incurred in the purchase of the same; if the officer deem that such goods and furniture exceed the value of two hundred dollars, he may attach the same and the family entitled to the exemption shall forthwith on demand of the officer select from the inventory and appraisement, goods and furniture to the value of two hundred dollars; and failing to do so shall be deemed to waive the exemption." (C. S. 148, § 36; see also C. S. 2245, § 10).

The proceedings for ascertaining the value of the property attached and setting aside the part exempted, will be the same as under an ordinary execution (see under general title, "Execu-

ATTACHMENT 

109 tion"), except, of course, the order in the execution is not to be "forthwith." (See Form below). 

Liability of officer

It has been stated that the officer should take the personal property attached into possession, where it is possible. If, on judgment in attachment and execution, the constable does not have the property of defendant on hand, it will be a legal excuse that, although when he returned that he had attached certain property he believed it to be defendant's, he had subsequently ascertained that it was not; but he must prove that fact, if charged with neglect of duty.

If the property is taken away from him, by stealth or otherwise, it will not excuse him, nor the fact that the execution was delivered to another constable, nor that it perished, nor that he left it where he found it, and being exposed to the weather, it was thereby damaged, nor that the expense of keeping it would be great, nor that the plaintiff's judgment was erroneous.

If by consent of the parties, or statutory authority, the constable has sold the property attached before judgment, he is bound to keep the proceeds of the sale to answer the execution, and the delivery of the execution to him authorizes him to apply the money in his hands to its satisfaction. The defendant has no right of action against the officer until the attachment is dissolved, whether the goods are safely kept or not. Until the adjudication of plaintiff's claim, the plaintiff's right is paramount. But after redelivery of property of the defendant, and attachment dissolved, any improper care of the property while in the officer's hands may be the foundation for a recovery by the defendant. 

Acceptance of bond

The Justice cannot be too careful in accepting the bond given by the defendant, since the object of giving it is to secure the release of his property, and he may frequently endeavor to give a "straw" bond. The statute requires it to be given "by one or more sufficient sureties, being freeholders and residents in the county in which such attachment shall issue, in double the amount of the claim of the plaintiff, conditioned," etc. It is to be indorsed "approved" by the Justice and filed "for the use and benefit of the plaintiff." (C. S. 150, § 40). He is to be satisfied it is a good bond, as to its form and the responsibility of the sureties, and he is safely to keep it.

If there are two different attachments against the same defendant by different plaintiffs, one bond will not do for both suits, but there should be separate ones given, and until they are, the property should not be given up to the defendant's control. (Hanness v. Smith, 2 Zab. 332).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Lien of an attachment As every attachment in The Small Cause Court is a separate and distinct proceeding, writs have priority, when several are issued, in the order in which they are actually served or executed. 

Their effect in that respect is similar to different executions, though there is not the same binding force in a seizure under a writ of attachment as under an execution, because the former is not a final proceeding.

But it is not the plaintiff who is considered as having a lien upon the goods attached; they are in custody of the law. It is true the defendant cannot recover their control and possession without satisfying or securing the plaintiff; but this is not because the plaintiff has a lien, but because the statute has impounded the goods for the double purpose of compelling an appearance by the defendant, and, ultimately, satisfying the plaintiff, if anything is due him. Hence it is not the officer's duty to put the plaintiff or any other person in possession of the goods, but to keep them safely himself until the sale under judgment and execution. (Austin v. Wade, 2 Penn. 997; Melville v. Brown, 1 Harr. 364; Cummins v. Blair, 3 Harr. 152).

The lien of the writ from The Small Cause Court is superior to a later one from a higher Court, the sheriff of which cannot dispossess the constable of his possession of the property under the former writ. (Woodward v. Lishman, 51 Vr. 586). 

Sale of the property

Except the property is perishable the effects of the defendant attached shall not be sold notwithstanding a judgment for plaintiff, in less than three months after seizure, to the end that the debtor or his friend may redeem them, and in the meantime they shall be inventoried and safely kept in such manner as the Justice shall direct. (C. S. 148, § 37).

Should the result of the suit be that the plaintiff's demand is not sustained, the attachment will be dissolved and the property released.

In case (after judgment) the property be perishable, the plaintiff, his agent or attorney, should make and file with the Justice an affidavit to that effect, whereupon the Justice should make an order for the sale forthwith, without waiting for the three months to elapse. 

Proceedings on the bond

In case the debtor appears, gives bond, etc., and judgment subsequently is given for the plaintiff, the property released from the attachment cannot be seized in that same proceeding by an officer and sold; but the remedy of the plaintiff, if the defendant

ATTACHMENT 

111 does not return the goods, is by action upon the bond. Judgment being recovered upon the bond, and execution issued, then such property, or any other belonging to the original debtor, or any of his security on the bond, can be levied upon in the usual way. (Vreeland v. Bruen, 1 Zab. 214).

The amount of judgment in a suit upon the bond will not be the penalty, but the amount of the plaintiff's judgment recovered in the former suit. The bond is, of course, forever discharged in case the plaintiff in the attachment suit fails to recover judgment against his alleged debtor. No third party can claim a recourse to that same bond. (Schuyler v. Silvester, 4 Dutch. 487).

Attorneys-at-Law 

Attorneys in all Courts "No person except in his own case or in the case of an infant shall be permitted to appear and prosecute or defend an action in any Court, unless he is a licensed attorney-at-law of the Supreme Court of this State, who shall be under the direction of the Court in which he acts." (C. S. 4055, §§ 17, 256).

Practicing law without a license is both a contempt of Court and an offense against the Crimes Act. (N. J. Photo Eng. Co. v. 

Schonert, 122 Atl. 307).

An attorney will be as responsible to his client for gross ignorance or gross carelessness in his conduct of the suit before the Justice's Court as before any other Court, or even in his office practice. If he is licensed to practice in the regular way the law will require that he bring to the exercise of his profession a reasonable degree of skill and care. Mere erroneous views will not render him liable to any action; but if he is grossly negligent, or acts in bad faith, he may be sued for damages; and in that case while he is sued in his own name, the fact that he is an attorneyat-law should be set out in the demand. 

Attorneys-at-law may sue and be sued in ordinary actions in all Courts, in like manner as other citizens. They have no special privileges as parties to actions. And all actions brought by them for another must be in the name of the principal and not in the name of an attorney. (Brackney v. Shreve, Coxe 33).

An attorney may not become surety on a bond given as security for costs, nor replevin bond, nor certiorari bond. (C. S. 

4054, § 10).

An attorney may sue and recover for services rendered his client in the manner stated in an Act of 1911. (P. L. 1911, p. 

412; C. S. 4034, § 9, as amend. by laws 1911, p. 412; N. J. Cum. 

Supp. 2793; see Truitt v. Darnell, 26 N. J. L. J. 309).

The attorney is presumed to have authority to bring suit in the manner in which he prosecutes; his want of authority, if disputed afterward, must be shown. (Norris v. Douglass, 2 South. 817). 

If he appears without authority, he is answerable in damages

BASTARDY 

115 to the party whom he professed to represent. (Field v. Gibbs, 1 

Peters C. C. 155).

He is a competent witness himself to prove his authority. 

It is not a proper practice to allow both an attorney and the party he represents to try a cause, as a man cannot well act for himself and by another at the same time; and it would also lead to confusion and irregularity of proceedings.

The Justice may restrict the time to be occupied by an attorney in summing up a cause.

Attorneys are usually privileged from service on juries, but are not ineligible.

Communications between attorneys and their clients are privileged and cannot be given in evidence. 

Women may become attorneys. (See P. L. 1923, p. 266; N. 

J. Cum. Supp. 2794). Bastardy 

The offense and proceedings

A bastard is one who is begotten and born out of lawful wedlock. Bastardy is the designation given to the crime of begetting the bastard, which is visited upon the male parent, to ascertain whom the statute directs: "If any woman shall be delivered of a bastard child, which shall be chargeable or likely to become chargeable to any township; or shall declare herself to be pregnant of a child likely to be born a bastard, and to become chargeable to any township, any overseer of the poor of the township where such woman may be, or of the township wherein the legal settlement of such woman may be, may apply to a magistrate of the same county wherein such woman may be, to make inquiry into the facts and circumstances of the case." (C. S. 184, § 1). The parentage, however, must be undisputed. (104 N. J. L. 51).

The term "township" is construed by the statute to comprehend city, town corporate, borough, village, precinct and ward respectively. (§ 25).

The term magistrate is construed by the statute to mean all 

Justices of the Peace, Judges of city Criminal Courts, Police Jus tices, Recorders, and all other officers having powers of a committing magistrate. But in cities having Police Courts, Criminal

Courts or a Recorder's Court, the proceedings shall be had therein and Justices of the Peace have not jurisdiction. (§§ 28, 30). In counties where a Juvenile Court is established, that Court also has jurisdiction in bastardy cases. (P. L. 1922, p. 299).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

The proceedings not being in The Small Cause Court (although a civil and not criminal case) should not be so entitled on the papers when the case is before a Justice, but as "Before 

Justice of the Peace." (State, Lynch, v. Pott, 29 Vr. 253). (Note as to the record to be kept, what is said below under "Justice's Record"). 

When natural parents (not married) marry their children previously born are to be recognized as such, and will enjoy all the privileges of legitimate children. (P. L. 1915, p. 333; N. J. Cum. 

Supp. 136). 

The complaint

The complaint that a child has been (or is about to be) born a bastard, must be made by the overseer of the poor (or Director of Welfare of the county where it applies; see P. L. 1933, Chap. 

181), where the woman is, or where she has a legal settlement. If mother and child are non-residents, notwithstanding the child was begotten within the State no complaint can be made, as the sole object is to provide for the child's support and to protect the public against its becoming a charge upon it. 

The complaint ought to be in writing, for convenience, though it is not required by the law. (State v. Overseer, 4 Zab. 533); and it should be filed by the Justice.

In County Juvenile Courts, which have now concurrent jurisdiction with other Courts and magistrates complaint may be made by the mother. There is also a provision that it may be made by two disinterested citizens without intervention of the overseer of the poor, but this has been declared unconstitutional. (P. L. 

1922, p. 299; N. J. Cum. Supp. 921. See 6 Misc. N. J. Rep. 586). 

Preliminary examination

The affidavit of the mother should be taken, and there may be other sworn testimony, if offered. Her statement under oath must be voluntary, and, in most cases, it will be advisable for the magistrate to caution her of the penalties of perjury. He is to ascertain, by such examination, the probable father. It is not necessary that a woman be a single woman in order that proceedings for support may be had. (State v. Overseer, supra). 

The warrant

After such preliminary examination a warrant shall issue, directed to any constable or police officer of the county, commanding him forthwith to apprehend the reputed father and to bring him before the magistrate who issued the warrant. In case such reputed father resides or is in any other county, the magistrate shall indorse upon the warrant the sum in which bail may be given. The officer will then proceed to such county and have

BASTARDY 

117 some magistrate therein, on proof made of the handwriting of the magistrate issuing the warrant, indorse his name thereon, with authority to arrest in such county. (C. S. 184, §§ 2, 3). 

The warrant is to be served like any other warrant; and it may be issued and served, and also indorsed, on Sunday as well as on other days. (§ 26). 

The preliminary bond

If the reputed father is arrested in another county than that wherein the warrant was issued, he may be taken before the magistrate who indorsed the warrant, or some other magistrate, (this also is allowed upon Sunday), who may take from such person a bond to the State with sufficient sureties in the sum directed on the warrant, for his appearance at the time stated in the warrant, and thereafter as directed. Thereupon the person arrested shall be discharged. Such magistrate (if other than the same magistrate who issued the warrant) shall certify the facts on the warrant and deliver warrant and bond to the officer, who shall deliver them to the original magistrate; the latter will then act as if the bond had been taken by him. If no bond be given, the officer will take his prisoner to the original magistrate. (§ 4).

In all cases where a bond is given, whether to appear, or on appeal, or on an order of filiation, the bond must be filed at once by the magistrate with the county clerk for record; and the party offering the bond is to be required to pay the legal fees for such record. (P. L. 1912, p. 147; N. J. Cum. Supp. 134. See under head below, "Bond of Filiation," as to the cost). 

Marriage will dissolve proceedings

If the reputed father is willing to marry the mother of the child, he may secure a marriage license in the usual way (See title "Marriages") and the marriage may then be performed at once -but not by a Justice of the Peace as he cannot perform marriages. On proof of such marriage, the proceedings should be dismissed. The effect of such marriage will also be to legitimate the child, which will be entitled to all the rights of one born in lawful wedlock. (P. L. 1915, p. 333; N. J. Cum. Supp. 136). 

The hearing

In case the reputed father is brought before the magistrate who issued the warrant (whether arrested in the same or another county) the latter will give a hearing without unnecessary delay.

Of course he may adjourn it to suit the convenience of complainant, or even defendant, and especially in order that the proper witnesses may be present; but the trial should be speedy. The limit of adjournment is six weeks. In the meantime the defend-

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

ant must give bond for his appearance at the hearing (with sufficient sureties), or be committed to jail. (C. S. 185, §§ 5, 7).

A jury trial may be demanded; but, supposing no jury to be demanded, the mother is to be examined on oath in the presence of the person charged, and any legal proof heard that may be offered. Subpoenas may be issued as in other cases. (§ 5).

If the mother refuses to disclose the name of the father of the child at the original examination or at the hearing, the magistrate or Court shall commit her to jail as for contempt of Court, but not until she is sufficiently recovered from her confinement. 

(§ 21). 

Trial by jury

If before the hearing is begun the reputed father denies his guilt and demands a trial by jury, the magistrate shall issue a venire for a twelve-men jury, and the summoning, return, challenging and swearing in of the jury, the hearing of witnesses before them, etc., shall be as in usual actions. But before issuing the venire the person demanding the jury shall pay to the magistrate the fees or costs for its issuance and the costs of the jury. 

(§ 6). 

It is not error to allow the bastard child to be exhibited to the jury to permit them to determine as to resemblance of the child to the alleged father. (State v. Smith, 6 N. W. Rep. 153).

If the jury disagree and is discharged, a new venire may issue and a new jury hear the case. (State, Lynch, v. Pott, 29 Vr. 253). 

Order of filiation

If the verdict of the Justice (or jury) be that the person charged is not the father of the bastard, or child likely to be born a bastard, he is to be forthwith discharged. Otherwise the magistrate shall make an "order of filiation,”—often called an order for a bond of indemnity-in which shall be specified the sum to be paid weekly, or otherwise, by the putative father for the support of the bastard, and if necessary, a sum for the sustenance of the mother during her confinement. At the same time he shall certify to the reasonable expense of apprehending the father and of the trial and order, and shall reduce his proceedings to writing and sign the same. (C. S. 186, § 8). 

Bond of filiation

Upon the making of such order, the father shall immediately pay the costs certified and enter into bond to the State to obey the order of filiation and indemnify every township of the State for expenses incurred or to be incurred for support of bastard and

BASTARDY 

119 confinement of mother. Thereupon he will be discharged. But if he does not execute such bond, he is to be committed to jail. 

In all cases the penalty of the bond shall be such as to insure full indemnity to all townships interested. (§§ 9, 11, 11C). 

The usual sum for the bond is one thousand dollars, and it may include an order to educate the child. (State v. Such, 24 

Vr. 353). The bond is not to be of the father alone, but with "sufficient surety or sureties."

If the bond be not given, and the father be committed to jail, he can later enter into the bond and be discharged. (C. S. 187, § 10).

The bond of filiation must also be sent at once by the magistrate to the clerk of the county, the magistrate requiring the father to pay the lawful fee (fifteen cents per 100 words for recording, add to which 8 cents for filing). 

Appeal to the Sessions

The putative father, or any township interested, aggrieved by the finding of magistrate, or jury, or the order of filiation, may, within five days after the order, give written notice to the magistrate of appeal to the Quarter Sessions. In such case the magistrate shall send any bond taken and all the papers in the case immediately to the clerk of that Court, and the case may be brought to a hearing on ten days' notice to the other side. (§§ 12, 13). 

If the appeal papers are not promptly sent up the Sessions will grant a rule requiring it to be done. (State, Taylor v. Cassidy, 9 Vr. 437). 

Seizure of estate of father or mother

Whenever a putative father or mother, having sufficient real or personal estate to support the bastard child, etc., absconds from the township or county, leaving the child a charge upon the township where it was born or legally settled, the overseer of the poor of such township may apply to any magistrate in the county where the estate, or any part thereof, is, for a warrant; and such magistrate is required to issue a warrant or warrants, under his hand and seal, commanding the overseer to seize the goods and chattels of such parent, and to let out and receive the annual rents and profits of the lands towards the sustenance, bringing up and education of the child. The seizure must be confirmed by the Quarter Sessions, after which the goods and chattels may be sold to the highest bidder at public vendue. (§ 22). 

Birth of bastard in poorhouse

If the bastard be born in a poorhouse, or be removed to it

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

before proceedings had, the officer or keeper of the poorhouse may take the same proceedings as previously directed for overseers of the poor. (§ 23). 

Fees and costs

Jurymen, magistrates and officers shall receive the same fees as in The Small Cause Court and witnesses as other witnesses. 

(§ 24). 

The record

The record of the proceedings kept by the magistrate is not the usual one of an entry in his civil docket. The action is neither civil nor criminal, and hence he must keep a separate record of his proceedings. (State, Lynch v. Pott, 29 Vr. 253). This record should not be in a book but on sheets of paper, which can be sent up to the Court above in case of appeal or certiorari. At the same time he should make and keep such minutes of the proceedings as that, if papers sent up are lost, he could certify to what did transpire.

Bicycles, Tricycles, Etc. 

Bicycles, etc., may be deposited in lieu of bond

Any person arrested charged with violation of any ordinance of any municipality of this State, providing for the regulation and use of bicycles, tricycles and similar vehicles propelled by foot or physical power on the public streets within the limits of said municipalities, "shall have the right in lieu of giving bonds or entering into recognizance for his, her or their appearance or examination under such charge, to deposit and leave as such security with the magistrate or authority causing such arrest to be made, his, her or their bicycle or other vehicle, provided such person or persons shall make oath to the ownership of such bicycle or other vehicle, which oath shall be in writing and duly signed by such person or persons so arrested, and any person or persons who shall make false oath as to such ownership shall be liable to the penalties now provided by law for perjury." (C. S. 206, § 9). 

Other matters concerning lights, sidewalk riding, carrying children, etc., will be found in the Road Traffic Act of 1915 with its amendments. (See general subject, Road Traffic). 

Nature of the Act 

Bottle Act 

There is in New Jersey what is known as "The New Jersey

Bottle Act," of 1933, taking the place of earlier ones, which Act may be so cited and referred to in all processes and proceedings taken under it. (P. L. 1933, Chap. 366).

Persons or corporations engaged in manufacturing, bottling or selling soda waters, aerated waters, porter, ale, beer, cider, ginger

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

ale, ice cream, milk, cream, medicines, perfumery, or mixtures, etc., in bottles, boxes, siphons, tins, kegs, or other articles, having his or its name or other marks or devices branded, stamped, etc., on such articles, may file in the county clerk's office of the county where the principal place of business is situated, or if the manufacturer manufactures out of the State, then in any county where he or it transacts business, and also in the office of the secretary of state, a description of the names, marks, etc., giving two weeks' publication of the same.

When this is done, it is unlawful for other persons to use similar mixtures in the bottles, etc., so marked, or to remove such marks from bottles, etc., or to traffic in them, without the written consent of the owners, under a penalty of imprisonment of from ten days to one year for the first offense or a fine for each bottle, etc. 

Who has jurisdiction 

Any criminal Court or Police Justice in any city of the first class, or any Recorder, police magistrate, or Justice of the Peace in any other city, or municipality, has jurisdiction to try the offense. (C. S. 294, § 5, as amend. by P. L. 1920, p. 351).

The proceedings are not in The Small Cause Court, but are summary and before the magistrate as magistrate, and must be so intitled. That is to say, the papers should be headed: "Before L. 

M., Justice of the Peace," or "Recorder," etc. 

Method of procedure

The first proceeding is for some person to complain on oath or affirmation to the magistrate. This should be in writing, filed with him. Thereupon the magistrate shall issue process at the suit of the State of New Jersey, with the name of the complainant as prosecutor, which process may be either a summons or a warrant. If a warrant, it is returnable forthwith. If a summons, it is returnable in not less than two nor more than ten days, and shall be served at least one day before its return. The process shall state generally the violation of the Act. The summons may be served when not upon a corporation either personally or by leaving a copy at the defendant's dwelling house or usual place of abode; and upon a corporation by delivering a copy of the summons to any officer or employee of such corporation who may be found in this State.

On the return day, or at any time to which the trial of the case shall be adjourned, the magistrate shall proceed in a summary way to hear the testimony, and give judgment without the filing of any pleadings.

It is not necessary to take or keep any records of the exact

BOTTLE ACT 

129 evidence taken on the trial, but the usual record on separate sheets of paper, naming witnesses, etc. Of course the customary record should be kept in the Complaint Docket. 

The Act does not permit of a jury trial. 

Search warrant may issue

If the person who makes complaint shall make oath that the articles named are being unlawfully used and are secreted in any place, the magistrate shall issue a search warrant. In such case the constable will bring before the magistrate the person in whose possession the articles may be found, and upon judgment the magistrate shall also award possession of the property so taken. 

Miscellaneous provisions 

Fines and costs in cities of the first class shall be paid into the city treasury, and those collected in any other city, or any borough or township, shall be disposed of "as now provided by law." (See under general title "Penalties and Fines," subhead, "Disposition of Fines").

The use by any person or corporation other than the owners of such bottles, etc., without the written consent of the owners, or the having them in possession by any dealer in second-hand articles, is declared to be presumptive evidence of their unlawful use. (§ 11).

The Act does not affect the Acts concerning producers and shippers of milk in milk cans.

Act of 1917 

Buildings, Scaffolding, Etc. 

By an Act of 1917 (P. L., p. 497; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1730), if a complaint is made to the State Commissioner of Labor, or to any mayor, superintendent of police, or other persons in charge of the police force in any city, town, borough or township, that the scaffolding, hangers, blocks, pulleys, ladder, etc., used in the construction of, or any work on any building is likely to prove dangerous to life or limb, such official is to cause an inspection by a representative of the Commissioner of Labor, or a building department, or a competent architect or builder; if found unsafe said official may prohibit the use thereof and serve a written notice on the person responsible. The Act has specific provisions as to lawful scaffolding, etc.

The punishment for non-compliance, destroying the notice, etc., is a fine of from $10 to $100, and is to be enforced by an action of Debt "in any District Court of a city, Recorder's Court of cities, or before any Justice of the Peace having due jurisdiction" (which means where the District Court does not possess exclu-

CEMETERIES 

131 sive civil jurisdiction, so far as The Small Cause Court is concerned). (N. J. Cum. Supp. 1732). When before a Justice the proceedings are to be, we think, in The Small Cause Court, and to be entered in the docket of that Court. 

The proceeding for the fine The Act provides that the complaint is to be made by and in the name of the Commissioner of Labor, or mayor or chief of police of any city or borough, or the clerk or chief of police of any township or village in which the offense is committed. First process shall be a summons returnable in from 5 to 10 days; and if the owner or person responsible is in the county it is to be served upon him, otherwise upon the superintendent or person in charge; if a corporation is the defendant, upon the president, vice-president or any director, or, if neither is in the county, upon the person in charge. If the owner is outside the county it may be made upon the agent in charge, or, if none, by affixing a copy to the main outer door ten days before the return. The finding is to be that the defendant has or has not incurred the fine claimed in the demand. Execution on the judgment, if returned unsatisfied, may follow (on the Court's awarding it by an order)' against the body. If imprisoned, the Court may discharge the defendant when satisfied further confinement will not result in payment of the judgment and costs.

The fine collected is to be paid to the State Treasurer when the Commissioner of Labor conducts the prosecution; otherwise to the municipality concerned. (For proceedings in general concerning penalties and fines, see general title "Penalties and Fines"). Cemeteries

Penalties by municipal authorities 

Municipal authorities have the power to pass or to repeal ordinances to regulate interments and disinterments in any cemetery in a city, town, or township, and to prescribe the penalty by fine not exceeding fifty dollars, or imprisonment in the county jail not exceeding ten days or both; and any Recorder, Police 

Justice, or Justice of the Peace (when the latter has jurisdiction) is empowered to proceed against offenders. (C. S. 378, §§ 19, 20).

The proceedings are to be begun by "oath, affirmation or affidavit," that any person has been guilty of a violation of such ordinance. Thereupon a process shall issue, either summons or a

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

warrant, as to the magistrate shall seem most advisable. The process if a warrant shall be returnable forthwith; if a summons, in five entire days. The process shall state what ordinance defendant has violated and in what manner. 

The proceedings, it would seem, are to be in The Small Cause Court when before the Justice, or Recorder's Small Cause Court when before the Recorder and he has that Court. 

On return of the process, or at the time to which the case is adjourned, the magistrate shall hear and determine the matter. 

If judgment be given for the plaintiff, execution shall forthwith issue against the goods, chattels, and person of the defendant, (that is to say, the execution shall issue against the body, as well as the goods and chattels of the defendant). Penalties recovered are to be paid to the treasurer of the local municipality. But the municipal authorities may remit any penalties so adjudged. (Ibid, § 20).

There may be a trial by jury where the penalties shall exceed ten dollars, or the punishment may be by imprisonment; such trial to be conducted as in jury trials in

Owners of such may be fined $2.

Lien on monuments 

By an Act of 1912 (P. L., p. 104; C. S. Sup., p. 897, § 71), a person, firm or corporation furnishing or placing in a cemetery or burial-ground a monument, gravestone, inclosure or other structure, may have a lien thereon for the agreed price, or balance due, with interest. To enforce his right the first step is to serve, at any time after the completion of the work, but at most within one year after the agreed price is due, a notice of lien with the superintendent or person in charge of the burial-ground, signed and verified. Within ten days thereafter the lienor shall serve a copy, personally or by mail, upon the one with whom the agreement is made, and the owner of the lot, if his name and residence can be ascertained.

But the monument, etc., cannot be removed or altered after notice of lien, except pursuant to terms of a judgment, which is to be obtained in "an action to recover the amount of the debt," and is the second step to enforce the rights of the lienor. The 

Act then provides: "If such lienor succeeds in establishing his lien, the judgment recovered may authorize him to remove such monuments," etc., "from the burial-ground or cemetery, and to sell the same at public auction," etc. The action is to be brought in any Court having jurisdiction over the amount involved, but the method of enforcing the judgment, when rendered, is not made clear. Presumably the action is to be in Debt, and the

CERTIORARI 

133 judgment should be a special one, reciting the facts and adjudging that the monument, etc., be levied upon, taken and removed, and sold, after proper notice, etc. The writ of execution must then follow the wording of the judgment.

This Act is a peculiar one in that it does not state before whom or what Court "an action to recover the amount of the debt" is to be instituted. If before a Justice of the Peace, we judge the action must be begun in  If so, it would permit of a jury trial and an appeal.

The writ

The writ of certiorari is a writ issuing out of a superior, directed to an inferior Court, commanding its Judge, or, if to The

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Small Cause Court or the Justice as a magistrate, the Justice of the Peace, to certify and return the record of proceedings of some cause depending, or which has been tried before such inferior Court for the purpose of a judicial review of its action. In New 

Jersey it must issue out of the Supreme Court, although sections 92, etc., of The Small Cause Court act also give power to a Judge of the Circuit Court to grant a writ. But it has been decided that only the Supreme Court has power to issue such certiorari. 

Service of and return to the writ

The writ directs the Justice or Judge to whom directed, to certify, under his hand and seal, and send the judgment and all proceedings had before him in the cause to the Supreme Court within a time fixed by the writ. It must be served upon the Justice personally, before the return day, otherwise it loses its vitality and cannot be revived even by rule of Court. (State, Van Cleef, v. New Burnswick, 8 Vr. 394; State v. Kennedy, 3 Harr. 22).

Any person may serve the writ; it need not be done by an officer. (State v. Dwyer, 12 Vr. 93).

The Justice or judge must return the writ with an exact transcript (copy) of his docket, the summons, the warrant, or other original process, the copy of account, or state of demand filed by the plaintiff, the plea and the copy of account, or state of demand filed by the defendant by way of set-off, the venire, jury panel, and return thereto, and all papers filed in the cause. These are to be attached to the writ by a piece of tape, or other ligature, closed with his seal and neatly folded into the writ; and the Justice must indorse his return on the writ, and seal it with his seal. (Rules Sup. Ct., No. 163).

He is not to send up notes of testimony taken if that be not ordered in the rule allowing the certiorari. (Lloyd v. Richman, 28 Vr. 385).

The party applying for the writ should call upon the Justice for the return and transmit it to the Court to which the case is taken up. The Justice will have done his duty if he has the papers ready when called for.

The return to a certiorari, directed to a Justice of the Peace, where the Justice has left the State, may be by the party taking from the docket of the Justice a true copy of the record, annexing it to the writ of certiorari, returning it to the Court and proving by competent evidence that it is a copy of the record. But if the Justice has followed the directions of the statute and deposited his docket with the county clerk, the latter should certify a transcript. (S. C. A., § 117; Ball v. Van Houten, 1 

South. 31).

CERTIORARI 

135 If the Justice has his docket in possession but is out of office, he is to certify as "late Justice of the Peace." (S. C. A., § 114).

A return that the demand and plea filed in the cause cannot be found is sufficient for reversal of judgment. (Power v. Seeley, 1 Harr. 216). 

Effect of the writ

The effect of the writ upon the proceedings before the Justice is that of a complete stay of proceedings. All subsequent proceedings by him, except making the return, will be void. He is to send up the papers and record, and there his duty ends, unless and until they are returned with directions to rehear the case. (McQuaid v. Emmons, 9 Vr. 397).

If execution has been issued before the certiorari is served, an application to a Judge at chambers will enable the appellant to obtain a supersedeas, which will be an order directing the constable to desist from executing a writ. Without such supersedeas, or directions to the contrary from the Justice, the constable might execute his writ and would not be in contempt of Court; but the 

Justice who issues process after certiorari served upon him will be in contempt. (Ibid).

Where it appears by a proper record in a Justice's docket that the amount of the claim or judgment has been paid to the Justice or constable, and the party paying the same, having judgment in certiorari in his favor, finds it necessary, he may obtain a writ of restitution from the higher Court, and so obtain back the money. (McChesney v. Rogers, 3 Hal. 179). 

Rehearing after certiorari proceedings

If the Supreme Court thinks it is equitable and just that a re-hearing shall be had before The Small Cause Court, it may so order, "upon terms and conditions that are reasonable." When such order is served upon the Justice, he is required to re-hear and determine the matter anew. (S. C. A., § 99). 

Certiorari to Justice as a magistrate

What has been said above applies to a Justice sitting in The 

Small Cause Court. If the Justice's proceedings are not in that

Court, but before him as magistrate, section 9 of the general Certiorari Act applies, as concerns the recognizance to be entered into by the party applying for a certiorari. (C. S. 405, § 9). A distinction is thus properly made between a bond in a certiorari to the Supreme Court and recognizance to be given in a criminal or semi-criminal case. Section 9 specifies that in certiorari to a magistrate a $150 recognizance be entered into before an allowance of the writ, and both the recognizance and certiorari must

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

be delivered to the magistrate to be effectual; otherwise the magistrate is to proceed as if certiorari had not been allowed, unless there is an order dispensing with the recognizance. 

Violations of ordinances 

All judgments or other judicial proceedings of any city Judge,

Police Court, or other inferior Court, on account of violations of city ordinances, or of city boards of health, are reviewable by certiorari to the Supreme Court (or by application to the Common Pleas within thirty days after judgment rendered, which Court may grant an order to certify the proceedings to the 

Court). (P. L., 1915, p. 413; N. J. Cum. Supp. 255).

Chattel Mortgage 

What a chattel mortgage is

A chattel mortgage is a transfer of personal property as security for a debt or obligation, and the mortgagor agrees to pay the debt at a certain time, or, if he does not, the title of the personal property shall vest in the mortgagee, so that he may sell the goods to make himself whole and pay the balance over to the mortgagor.

The mortgage, unless immediately followed by possession and so continued, must be immediately recorded in the county clerk's, or register's office, or it will not affect claims of creditors prior to the recording. Of course it must be regularly acknowledged and have proper affidavit annexed. (C. S. 463, § 4; P. L., 1928, p. 131).

Children, Cruelty to 

Penalties for cruelty to children

There are various Acts concerning injuries to or abuse of children. The following is more clear in their provisions than others:

CHILDREN, CRUELTY TO 

141 

Cruelty under Act of 1915

An Act concerning cruelty, etc., to children, (P. L., 1915, p. 

441; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1563, as amended by Laws 1928, p. 229 and Laws 1932, p. 598) is that under which proceedings for their welfare are now usually taken. It is termed "An Act concern. ing the welfare of children." It defines at length what is abuse of children, what is abandonment, what is cruelty and what is neglect, the definitions being full enough to cover every case of cruelty, neglect, etc. Any parent, guardian or person having the care, custody or control of a child, who infringes this law, if found guilty of "cruelty and neglect of children," is to be fined not to exceed $100 or imprisoned in a workhouse or penitentiary or in a common jail for not exceeding one year, or both, at the discretion of the convicting magistrate; and if it is for the best interest of the child it may be placed temporarily in the custody of a Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, and sentence may be postponed and defendant placed on probation, and ordered to pay a stated sum for the child's maintenance. (Ibid, § 2, as amend. by P. L. 1918, p. 217; N. J. Cum. Sup. 1564).

Magistrates acting under this Act should be careful to read and follow its provisions.

Complaints under this Act may be made "to any Justice of the Peace, or to any police magistrate of any municipality, or a Judge of the Court of Common Pleas, or Criminal District Court in any county or the Judges of the Juvenile or Domestic Relations'

Court in every county of the State." (§ 3, also amended by P. 

L. 1918, p. 218; and P. L. 1932, p. 598).

If a person is convicted and furnishes a bond with one sufficient surety to any S. P. C. C. in $500 (for each child), conditioned to pay a certain weekly amount for the child's care, support and education during its minority (or a shorter time), sentence may be postponed. In this matter the magistrate is given discretion to accept such bond or not. If the bond be accepted and sentence postponed, and the bond condition is not fulfilled, the magistrate must issue a warrant for defendant's arrest and sentence him. (Ibid).

Fines go to the S. P. C. A., if existing; otherwise to the overseer of the poor of the municipality. (§ 8).

Still another order may be made by the magistrate, which is to commit the child to the care of the New Jersey State Board of Guardians, to become the ward of that Board. (§ 6, also amend. by P. L. 1918, p. 219; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1565; P. L. 1932, p. 599).

When any person complains under oath that he believes the 

Act has been violated, the magistrate must forthwith issue a warrant to an authorized officer to enter the place, or house, and

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

investigate, and arrest all offenders and bring them before the magistrate for a hearing. (§ 10).

The two Forms given below are prepared under the Act of 1915. Other Forms must necessarily follow the directions of the statute.

Laws concerning 

Clams and Oysters

The laws for the preservation of clams and oysters are so multifarious and are amended and supplemented so constantly that only a careful examination of the statutes will indicate what they are. They occupy 80 pages of the "Compiled Statutes," and many more in the Pamphlet Laws since. 

Generally speaking the various statutes relating to natural seed oysters and clams are to be enforced by summary proceedings, in the name of the State, but it is said to be more usual in South Jersey to proceed by indictment, which abates offenses more effectually. The Department of Shell Fisheries of the State may always be applied to, to assist in prosecutions. 

Because of the complexity and variety of these laws we do not undertake to digest their provisions, which consist chiefly of penalties, nor prescribe Forms.

Summary procedure 

By Act of 1920 (P. L., p. 514; N. J. Cum. Supp. 602), Justices of the Peace and police magistrates are given summary power to hear and dispose of complaints under all clam and oyster laws. 

Justices may act in cities notwithstanding District Courts may be there. This particular Act should be consulted in all proceedings, but does not apply to misdemeanors. (See § 2). 

Who they are 

Commissioners of Deeds

Commissioners of deeds are appointed by the Senate and General Assembly in Joint Meeting. Their number is not re-

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

stricted, but are to be "as many as they [the Senate and General Assembly] may deem necessary for each of the counties." They may be of either sex. When so appointed they are commissioned by the Governor, and hold office for five years. (C. S. 

1544, § 26, as amend. by N. J. Cum. Supp. 630).

In case any commissioner removes out of the county in which he resides at the time of his appointment his commission becomes void; or the Governor may remove him for malconduct. 

He may resign his office by sending his resignation to the Governor if the Legislature is not in session. (Ibid). 

While commissions bear date on the date of appointment by the Joint Meeting, the term of office begins on the first day of May next following, on or before which day the commissioner must take and subscribe the official oath (that he will perform well and faithfully the duties required of him by law as such commissioner) before the clerk of the Court of Common Pleas of the county, paying to said clerk a fee of $1.50. (C. S. 1545, § 27). But all applications to be a commissioner must have $10 enclosed with it, which goes to the State if granted; otherwise is returned. (P. L. 1919, p. 42; N. J. Cum. Supp. 631).

Commissioners of deeds are empowered to take the acknowledgment or proof of deeds, mortgages and other instruments requiring to be acknowledged or proved as a prerequisite to recording, and may also take oaths, affirmations and affidavits of the usual lawful character. They cannot, however, take the official oaths of the officers of the State, nor those required to be made in open Court, nor where it is necessary for the party making or procuring the oath to give notice to any person interested. 

It is not necessary to the validity of an affidavit made before a commissioner of deeds of this State that the same be certified by him under his official seal, but for many reasons it should be; and it should be used in acknowledgments and all instruments to be recorded. (See C. S. 3774, § 34).

A Justice of the Peace is not ineligible for appointment to the office of commissioner of deeds. 

Ministerial officers Constables

Constables are the ministerial officers of magistrates and Courts, to whom (or to sheriffs), as a rule, all writs are directed for service, and who are given by statute, other duties to per form. The General Act is in C. S. 1527.

CONSTABLES 

145 

Election 

Constables are elected by the governing bodies of the various municipalities, and usually may equal the number of Justices of the Peace to which a township is entitled. (§ 11). 

In incorporated cities, boroughs and towns, the number is sometimes fixed by the charter (in the case of boroughs, no number is fixed), but, if not, each ward in cities and towns elects as many as will equal the number of Justices of the Peace to which such ward is entitled. (§§ 17-19). 

In boroughs, the marshals have all the power of constables (C. S. 234, § 14), and often they and policemen have the same power of arrest and serving process, in cities. 

The term is for three years, beginning on the first day of January next ensuing the election. No constable shall hold over in office after the expiration of his term. (C. S. 3488, § 125 et seq.). 

Bond and oath

Constables shall give and renew bonds to the municipality wherein they are elected annually. Failure to do so within thirty days after expiration of each yearly term will cause the office to become vacant. (P. L. 1917, Art. XII). It must be approved by the governing body, which will fix the amount. The form is prescribed by the statute. (C. S. 1527, § 1; see also C. S. 1530, 13).

All constables in every municipality shall, between the date of his election and the first day of January, or, if appointed to fill a vacancy, within ten days after such appointment, file with the municipal clerk an oath prescribed by the statute. (Ibid, 1531, § 15; see "Form" below). 

Constable not to be personated

Any person holding himself out to be a constable without authority is guilty of a misdemeanor. (C. S. 1757, § 36).

Under special provisions, however, authority is sometimes given private persons to act as constable to arrest, when crimes are committed in their presence. 

Vacancy in office 

Where, by reason of resignation, removal or death the office of constable becomes vacant, the board of aldermen, common council, township committee or other governing body of the municipality may fill the vacancy for the unexpired term. (C. S. 

1530, § 14).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Constable's civil and criminal jurisdiction The jurisdiction of the constable civilly does not extend only to the ward or township wherein he was elected, but he shall "execute within the county all precepts, summons, warrants, writs, and all other process, issuing out of the said [Small Cause] Court, and to them or any of them directed and delivered and make return thereof, and to perform all matters, acts, and things appertaining" to his office. (S. C. A., § 119). In criminal matters he may serve warrants, etc., in any part of the State, and is to receive mileage therefor. (C. S. 1851, § 99).

As to the manner of serving writs, subpoenas, warrants, executions, etc., see under proper heads elsewhere in this volume. 

Constable may not fill up blank process 

The Justice may not sign his name to a blank summons or warrant, nor the constable (nor any other person) fill up the same "without the special direction of said Justice." Every such process shall be void. (S. C. A., § 12).

Constable to receive and pay over moneys Whenever a summons or warrant is issued by a Justice of the Peace the sum demanded is to be entered therein and it is also to be indorsed thereon with costs; and the defendant may pay the amount to the constable; "and if any constable shall not pay the money so by him received, to the Justice issuing such process, or to the plaintiff in the said process or his legal representative, within fifteen days after he shall receive the same, then such constable shall be liable to pay to such plaintiff or his legal representative, the amount thereof, with interest, to be recovered by action on contract, with double costs." (S. C. A., § 18).

So, too, when he has received an execution, but fails to perform his duty, the statute provides for prosecution. (Ibid, § 71). 

Constable may require prepayment of fee "No constable or other officer, authorized to serve a subpoena, summons or other mesne process issued out of The Small Cause Court, shall be required to serve such process until his legal fees and mileage for so doing shall have been paid to him." (Ibid, § 103).

This, of course, does not apply to an execution, but to processes issued prior to final judgment. Nor does it apply to criminal proceedings. (See, further, general title "Fees and Costs"). 

General duties in preserving peace

It is the duty of all constables to apprehend all persons committing a breach of the peace in their presence and take them

CONSTABLES 

147 before a Justice of the Peace or other magistrate. Where not performed in their presence, they must, as a general rule, first obtain a warrant from a magistrate. (See under general title "Criminal Procedure"). 

Prosecution of constables' bonds

All suits for the prosecution of constables' bonds are to be brought in a higher Court. The Small Cause Court has no jurisdiction of such prosecutions. 

If constable absconds

If a constable absconds, or becomes insolvent or incapable of performing his duties, the Common Pleas, on application, may authorize his sureties to demand and recover any moneys the constable might demand or levy by virtue of any execution in his hands. Such sureties, when an execution or process in such a case is unexecuted wholly or in part, may apply to any Justice of the Peace in the county for a summons upon the judgment on which such execution is founded, in the name of the plaintiff in the original process against the defendant therein, and recover judgment thereon in the usual way, founding the demand, however, upon the transcript of the original judgment. (C. S. 1529, 

§§ 7, 8). 

Death of constable

Upon the death of a constable, his executors or administrators have full power to collect and settle up all unsettled executions and processes in the same manner as that described for the sureties above. (Ibid, § 9).

Immunity in executing writs A constable cannot be held to answer in damages for executing a writ issued by a Justice, or Court having the authority to issue it, and directed to him. (Mangold v. Thorpe, 4 Vr. 138, and cases there cited).

But if the Justice has no jurisdiction the constable and Justice also are liable in damages. (Nelfi v. Maguire, 22 N. J. L. 

J. 275).

Special duties 

Besides the usual authority of constables to serve process and writs and make arrests, statutes sometime confer special authority, or permit it to be conferred, by official boards, or by city and borough councils, etc.; for example: to act as policemen, or truant officers; to collect liens upon vessels; to serve subpoenas for

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

courtmartials under the National Guard Act, etc. In these cases, however, his only authority comes from statutes or by municipal ordinances, etc.

As to his general duties, see further under general titles "Summons," "Warrant," "Execution," "Criminal Procedure,” etc., in this volume.
