CONVEYANCES 

149 

What are conveyances Conveyances

Conveyances are transfers of property. Strictly they are transfers of real property by a sealed writing. They include deeds, mortgages, leases, etc. 

A warranty deed warrants (guarantees) the title; a quitclaim deed does not do this, but simply transfers the right and title of the guarantor. 

Forms of conveyances

The usual forms of conveyances heretofore used, which, as in the case of deeds especially, are unseemingly lengthy, do not have to be followed in New Jersey. Short forms are permitted. 

The statute gives a short form of deed (C. S. 1570, § 99), and mortgages and leases may also be in briefer form than that usually employed. (That even the short form of deed, however, should embrace the words "heirs and assigns," see 22 N. J. L. J. 

225). A general short warranty is declared in the statute to have the same effect as the longer one in former use. (C. S. 1570, § 104).

All deeds must be acknowledged to be recorded. (See general title "Acknowledgments"). 

Sealing of conveyances

It is necessary that a conveyance be sealed, but in this State either a seal, or a scroll, or any device in place thereof may be used. (C. S. 1540, § 20). The instrument should declare it to be sealed, usual form being "Signed, Sealed and Delivered in presence of."

Miscellaneous 

A minor may witness a deed (if of sufficient understanding), but may not make it.

As to married women executing deeds, see general title "Married Women." 

To be recorded, deeds must be written in English.

We do not give the long form of a deed below, as, if used, a printed blank is always obtained.

When Justice may act as coroner

A Justice of the Peace is authorized to act (but only when a coroner "cannot be had in due time"), in taking inquests of deaths in prison, or any violent, sudden, or casual deaths within his county. (C. S. 1585, § 4).

This provision has thus been construed by the Courts: "If the condition of a dead body, when found, should be such that it would be manifestly improper, in the judgment of ordinary men, to defer its burial long enough to notify a coroner, in such case a Justice would unquestionably be authorized to act, and, upon presenting satisfactory proof of the circumstances which rendered it necessary for him to do so, would be entitled to have his costs taxed by the clerk. But the fact that a Justice may be more conveniently notified than a coroner; that he has received the first notice; that he has, in good faith, performed the first official act, believing that a coroner could not be had in due time-no one of these facts, nor all of them together, will be sufficient to authorize a Justice to act where it plainly appears that a coroner might

CORONERS 

151 have been had in due time in the sense just stated. Even in the case supposed, where the condition of the body plainly required almost immediate burial, and the Justice has taken charge of it for that purpose, a coroner, appearing before it has been finally disposed of, may, at his option, assume control of it, in which case he, and not the Justice, would be entitled to have the costs taxed, and to receive them from the treasurer.' (The State treasurer in case of shipwreck; otherwise the county collector). "All that the Justice would be entitled to in such case, would be to receive from the coroner a reasonable compensation for the services rendered by him before the coroner arrived." (Chadwick v. Errickson, 11 Vr. 159). 

Since the foregoing decision, it has been made the duty of the county physician in all cases of death in prison and all violent, sudden or casual deaths in his county, to first take a view of the body and make all proper inquiry respecting the cause and manner of death, for the purpose of ascertaining whether an inquest should be held. If, upon such view and inquiry, he shall be of opinion that there is cause to suspect that the person came to his death by murder or manslaughter, or by the misconduct of any person, then it is made his duty to call upon a coroner of the county, or, if he cannot be had, upon a Justice of the Peace, and request him in writing to issue the precept for the summoning of a jury of inquisition, (now to consist of six men) and to hold an inquest. (C. S. 1704, § 2; N. J. Cum. Supp., 1586, §§ 7 and 

7a). 

The proceedings in case of inquest

It will be noted from the foregoing, therefore, that a coroner is not called first, but where there is a county physician, he is first to be summoned to view the body in cases of sudden or violent death. In case there be no county physician, duly qualified and acting, the coroner, or, in his absence, a Justice of the Peace, is to act. In case, however, a county physician is sick or unable to attend to the matter, he may appoint in writing any other licensed physician of the county to perform the specific service required, and such physician shall possess all the powers of said county physician. (C. S. 1704, § 4). 

If the county physician's presence cannot be obtained within six hours after written notice given to him (or left at his usual place of abode, by the coroner) of the discovery of the death, the coroner (or Justice of the Peace acting when no can be obtained) may proceed to view the body, etc. (§ 6). coroner

The county physician, where there is one, and the coroner (or the Justice, if a Justice be acting) shall take charge of the remains of any unknown person found dead in the county, and

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

his effects, and, after using such of the clothing as may be necessary in the burial of the body, he shall deliver the effects and unused clothing to the county collector within ten days after the burial. An inventory of the effects, sworn to, he shall file with the clerk of the board of chosen freeholders. (§ 7). 

If an inquest is ordered by the county physician it is to be required (as stated above), in writing, whereupon the coroner (or a Justice of the Peace when a coroner "cannot be had" in due time) must issue his precept as stated for a six men jury, and it must be in statutory form (as below). 

The constable shall forthwith execute the precept and make return of it at the time mentioned in the precept. (C. S. 1586, § 8).

Should any constable or person summoned as juror neglect or refuse to obey the precept, the coroner (or Justice if acting) shall certify the fact to the next Court of General Jail Delivery in the county that he may be fined. (§ 9).

The statute directs the oath to be administered to the foreman of the jury and the other jurors, and also the charge to be given to the jurors as soon as they are sworn. (§§ 10, 11). 

Subpoenas may be issued for witnesses and the statute directs the form of oath. (§ 12).

The coroner (or Justice, if acting) shall put in writing the effect of so much of the evidence given to the jury as shall be material. (§ 14).

The inquisition is to be returned to the Court of Oyer and Terminer; usually is given to the Prosecutor of the Pleas for that purpose.

Persons who declare anything material to prove the murder or manslaughter, or that any persons are accessories to the murder, shall be bound over by recognizance to appear at the next Court of Oyer and Terminer of the county, then and there to give their evidence.

Such recognizances, with the evidence and the inquisition, are all to be certified to the higher Court. 

In case the coroner (or Justice) is remiss and fails to carry out the directions of the statute, he may be fined by the Oyer and 

Terminer not exceeding five hundred dollars. (§ 22). (For other provisions see the Acts referred to). 

Coroners or Justices also act in case of dead bodies being found from shipwrecks. (See general title "Shipwrecks"). 

Fees and costs of 1927

A statute directs what fees shall be allowed to the coroner, or person acting as coroner. (See under general title "Fees and Costs").

Some general definitions Crimes or

A crime, in its legal significance, is an act committed omitted in violation of a public law either forbidding or commanding it. At common law there are three classes of public crimes Treason, Felonies and Misdemeanors.

Treason consists only in levying war against the government of the State, or in adhering to its enemies, giving them aid and comfort.

Felonies at common law were every species of crime which occasioned a forfeiture of lands or goods. They consist, whenever the term is now used in New Jersey, of treason, murder, manslaughter, arson, burglary, robbery, rape, sodomy, mayhem, and forgery. These are the unbailable offenses. (C. S. 1828, § 23).

Misdemeanors are every species of indictable offenses lower than felonies. Our statute says that "assaults, batteries, false imprisonments, affrays, riots, routs, unlawful assemblies, nuisances, cheats, deceits, and all other offenses of an indictable nature at common law, and not provided for in or by this or some other Act of the Legislature, shall be misdemeanors and be punished accordingly." (C. S. 1811, § 215).

In New Jersey the law quite ignores the distinction between felonies and misdemeanors and divides crime into two classes: high misdemeanors and misdemeanors. (Jackson v. State, 20 Vr. 

255; State v. Wilson, 50 Vr. 241). So that whatever is declared

CRIMES 

157 to be a high misdemeanor is really a felony and an unbailable crime. 

Common law crimes

It has been laid down in this country as a general principle that whatever is (1) productive of a disturbance of the public peace; or (2) of malicious injury; or (3) of a nuisance or scandal to the community; or (4) partakes of the character of personal lewdness; or (5) incites to the commission of any specific crime, is indictable as a common law misdemeanor, although our own statutes may be silent about it. 

Specific definitions of crimes

In many cases the statute, in other cases the common law only, defines what constitutes ordinary crimes. We give below some definitions of some crimes of grave importance, but there are hundreds of other statutory crimes of minor importance. (For reference to nearly all the statutory crimes, see the Appendix to this volume).

Abortions: The statute defines the crime to be the administering or prescribing to or advising or directing a woman, pregnant with child, to take any poison, drug, medicine or noxious thing with intent to cause or procure miscarriage. It must be done without lawful justification. If done to save the mother's life, by a regular physician, it will be no crime. 

Adultery: Adultery is the criminal intercourse between a man and a married woman. Consent must be obtained, of course; otherwise it will be rape. 

Affray: An affray is the fighting of two or more persons in a public place to the terror of the citizens. The parties engaged may be complained of for assault and battery or an affray, or both; the affray being a greater offense, because it not only includes the breaking of the peace by an assault, but the terrifying and alarming the neighborhood.

Arson: This crime consists of the malicious and wilful burning of the dwelling house, barn, stable, store, church, vessels, etc., etc., of another. The offense is consummated by the least burning, and it does not matter how soon the fire is extinguished. 

The offense it not bailable. 

Assault and Battery: An assault is an attempt or offer with force or violence to do injury to the person of another; and it must be coupled with the present ability to do it. Thus, presenting a loaded gun, or striking with a weapon, or holding up one's fist in an angry, threatening manner is an assault. A battery is an injury following the assault, and consists in the doing of an 1

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

actual injury, however inconsiderable. Thus, violently jostling another, or spitting in his face, if done with malice, is a battery. 

The usual charge against the defendant is of assault alone, or assault and battery, as the battery must always of necessity be accompanied by an assault.

Bigamy: This offense consists in having two wives, or two husbands living at the same time.

Blasphemy: Christianity is a part of the common law of the land and maliciously to revile it is an indictable offense. It does not matter whether the words are spoken, or printed, or written. 

Our statute makes it a misdemeanor to "wilfully blaspheme the name of God, by denying, cursing or contumeliously reproaching His being or providence, or by cursing or contumeliously reproaching Jesus Christ, or by profane scoffing at, or exposing them or either of them to contempt or ridicule." 

Bribery: Bribery is any attempt to influence an officer in his official conduct by a reward, pecuniary or otherwise. The offense is complete when the offer is made, whether it is accepted or not, or whether within the officer's jurisdiction or not.

Barretry: This is the stirring up or incitement to suits and quarrels. Both common barretors and common scolds are also public nuisances and punishable as such. 

Burglary: Burglary is the breaking and entering into a dwelling house by night with the intent to commit a crime. Our statute has extended it to certain other houses, and buildings, besides dwelling houses, viz: to any "church, meeting house, dwelling house, shop, warehouse, storehouse, mill, barn, stable, outhouse, railway car, canal boat, ship, vessel, or other building whatever," but limits the crime intended to be committed to the following: murder, robbery, theft, rape, mayhem or battery. The offense of burglary is not bailable. 

Compounding Crime: Compounding a crime is committed by agreeing to conceal a crime known to have been committed. 

The mere taking back of one's goods is no offense unless it be shown that some favor was extended or agreed to be extended to the thief. To receive a note signed by a person guilty of larceny, as a consideration for not presenting him, is to compound a felony. By our statute a reward or promise of reward must be given before the offense of compounding a crime is effectuated. 

Conspiracy: "Any two or more persons who shall combine, unite, confederate, conspire or bind themselves by oath, covenant, agreement or other alliance to commit any crime, or falsely and maliciously to indict another for any crime, or to procure another to be charged or arrested for any crime, or falsely to move and

CRIMES 

159 maintain any suit, or to cheat and defraud any person of any property by any means which are in themselves criminal, or to cheat and defraud any person of any property by any means which, if executed, would amount to a cheat, or to obtain money by false pretenses, or to conceal or spread any contagious disease, or to commit any act for the perversion or obstruction of justice or the due administration of the laws, shall, on conviction, be deemed guilty of a conspiracy, and be liable to the same penalty as persons convicted of a misdemeanor; but no agreement to commit any crime other than arson, burglary, manslaughter, murder, rape, robbery or sodomy shall be deemed a conspiracy unless some act in execution of such agreement be done to effect the object thereof by one or more of the parties to such agreement." (P. L. 1899, p. 214).

Disorderly Houses: A disorderly house is a house so kept as to be a nuisance to the neighborhood. Violence and noise are not necessary constituents of it. Where there is an unlawful sale of liquor and it is the practice of the house to make such sales, it will be disorderly. Any house kept in violation of law to the detriment of public morals is disorderly, and any person who keeps or causes to be kept, or rents out any building for the unlawful purpose named, commits a misdemeanor. The statutes also name other cases where houses are to be considered disorderly. 

Embezzlement: This crime is a species of larceny, generally of money, committed by clerks, servants or agents. A public officer may embezzle, and officers and clerks of private corporations; also trustees, executors, administrators, guardians, etc. The crime is now so broadened by the statute that it applies to nearly every intentional concealment or conversion of personal property to the use of one not the owner.

Extortion: Extortion is the unlawful taking by a public officer, through color of his office, of any money, or thing of value not due to him. There must be an intent to take the unlawful fee or reward; a guilty knowledge.

Embracery: This is the offense of proffering to jurors money, entertainment, entreaties, promises or threats to influence their verdict; or, as the statute defines it, of "attempts to corrupt or influence a jury, or any juror, or any way to incline such jury or any juror to be more favorable to the one side than to the other by promises, persuasions, entreaties, threats, letters, money, entertainments or other sinister means," etc. 

False Pretenses: To knowingly and designedly by any false pretense obtain from any person money, wares, merchandise, goods, chattels, or any other valuable thing, or to induce any such per-

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

son to execute, accept or destroy any instrument, with intent to cheat or defraud such person or any body corporate, is a misdemeanor in law. That the party restores such property afterward is no defense to the crime. 

Forgery: Forgery at common law is the false making or alteration of a writing for the purpose of fraud. The offense is consummated by the false making of the instrument with intent to defraud, without any uttering of it. The crime may be committed by an agent, the principal himself being present and directing. An alteration of a genuine instrument in a material part is a forgery of the whole; such, for instance, as adding a cipher to ten dollars in a note and making it one hundred dollars, or erasing a genuine endorsement and inserting another. The statutory definition simply expresses in great detail what the comprehensive definition first above given includes. The offense is not bailable. 

Fornication: This crime consists in the intercourse of two unmarried persons, or of one married man with an unmarried woman.

Homicide: The crime consists in the killing of any human creature, and is either felonious, excusable or justifiable. A killing of a reasonable being with malice aforethought is felonious, and constitutes murder. A killing without malice (as in cases of negligence), if felonious, is manslaughter. Excusable homicide is by misadventure (accident) or in self-defense. Justifiable homicide is when the act was unavoidable and without malice, expressed or implied; as, for instance, where an officer executes a criminal according to a judicial sentence; where an officer kills a person who resists his authority and does it because he could not help it, as it were; and where it is by any one in prevention of a forcible and atrocious crime. All homicides are presumed to be with malice aforethought, and, to excuse it, it must appear to have been by misadventure, or of necessity. Murder and manslaughter are unbailable.

Incest: This crime consists in carnal knowledge between persons related within the degree prohibited by the statute relating to marriages. When parties who are within the prohibited degrees are divorced and then cohabit again, they will be guilty of incest.

Larceny: Larceny is divided into two kinds, grand and petit. 

The former consists in stealing the money, or personal goods and chattels of another, of a greater value than twenty dollars, and is a high misdemeanor, punishable by imprisonment in the State prison. The latter consists in stealing personal property of a value not greater than twenty dollars, and is a misdemeanor. 

Our statute states with much detail what shall constitute the crime

CRIMES 

161 of larceny. (As to distinctions beween larceny, burglary and robbery, see "Robbery," infra).

Libel: A libel is a malicious publication, expressed either in printing or writing, or by signs or pictures, tending either to injure society generally, or to blacken the memory of one dead, or the reputation of one living, and expose him to public hatred, contempt or ridicule. The malice of the publication is the essence of the offense. A person is guilty of libel who gives an owner, editor, etc., of a publication, for publication, a libellous statement. 

Lotteries: A lottery is a scheme for the distribution of prizes by chance, among buyers of the chances. All lotteries in this State are declared to be misdemeanors. 

Malicious Mischief: Any malicious or mischievous injury to the rights of another, or to those of the public in general, is a crime at common law. Thus to destroy another's horse or cow; to be guilty of wanton cruelty to animals in general; to cast the carcass of an animal in a well in daily use; to poison chickens; to maliciously break windows; to girdle trees; are instances which the common law declares to be misdemeanors. The statute also defines malicious mischief and affixes specific penalties in a great variety of instances: as removing piles from any sea, river or canal wall, etc., or obstructing navigation; injuring any public bridge, or viaduct, or dam; breaking or firing any buildings, grain, fences, etc.; killing animals; injury to tenant houses by tenants; cruelly torturing animals; cutting timber without owner's leave; appropriating driftwood; injuring railroads, telegraphs, water or gas pipes, steam engines, machinery, books, works of art, instruments of writing, landmarks, etc.; desecrating graves, etc., etc.

Mayhem: This was originally the violent deprivation of the use of another's members (as an arm, or leg), rendering him less able to defend himself. The statutory offense is to "cut out and disable the tongue, put out an eye, cut off or slit a lip, cut off, slit, or destroy a nose or ear, or cut off or disable any limb or member of another." 

Murder: (See "Homicide").

Nuisance: A public nuisance is that which is injurious to a large class in the community. Pursuing a trade noxious to the public health, or offensive to the senses, is a nuisance, if carried on in the midst of a populated place. A swine yard in a city, polluting the waters of a river which supplies a city with water, leaving a dead animal where it becomes offensive, etc., may be nuisances. So the keeping of a disorderly house, open lewdness, being publicly drunk, obstructing the highway, keeping a gambling house, etc., may be nuisances. Every public nuisance is a

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

misdemeanor and indictable. In our State it is also laid down that "any place of public resort in which illegal practices are habitually carried on, or when it becomes the habitual resort of thieves, drunkards, prostitutes, or other idle, vicious and disorderly persons, who gather together there for the purposes of gratifying their own depraved appetites, or to make it a rendezvous where plans may be concocted for depredations upon society and to disturb either its peace or its rights of property, is a public nuisance."

Perjury: Perjury is committed where a person, who takes a lawful oath in some judicial proceeding, swears wilfully false in a matter material to the issue. The matter must have been material in the suit, and it must have been in a legal proceeding before a Court, or an officer of the Court, and the oath must have been false to the knowledge of the affiant, or, at least, it must have been made as to the facts which he did not know were true or false. 

Rape: This crime consists in carnal knowledge of a woman forcibly against her will. If the woman is under sixteen years of age, our statute says there cannot be consent and in such a case consent is not a defense which may legally be set up. Rape being one of the most detestable of crimes, shocking to the moral sense, and ruinous to female character for life, the Justice should be well assured of the truth of the charge before he issues his warrant, and then he must hold the defendant without bail. 

Robbery: The difference between larceny, burglary and robbery is very clear. The first is a simple stealing of personal property; the second a stealing by night through a breaking and entering, or it may be the breaking and entering alone, without stealing, yet with evident intent to steal; while robbery is taking of personal property from one's person or presence, by violence, against the party's will and by putting him in fear. If not in the person's presence it is larceny or burglary; it cannot be robbery. 

As graded, robbery is the highest crime, burglarly the next higher and larceny the least. Where one honestly believes the property is his own, and obtains it by menaces, it is not robbery, as he had no felonious intent. To put a man in fear and drive off his cattle is robbery. So, where a man, fleeing from a robber, drops his hat, which the robber steals. The essence of robbery, it will be seen, is not in the theft but in the violence and putting in fear.

The offense of robbery or burglary is not bailable, but that of larceny is bailable.

Seduction: Seduction at common law is illicit intercourse with any female of good repute under twenty-one years of age under promise of marriage. The statute broadens the scope of the offense, but puts the age of the woman as "under sixteen years." (C. S. 1784, § 117).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

163 

Sodomy: The "infamous crime against nature" committed with man or beast. Not bailable. (P. L. 1898, p. 806, § 44; C. 

S. 1759).

Treason: This is thus defined by the Constitution of our 

State: "Treason against the State shall consist only in levying war against it, or in adhering to its enemies, giving them aid and comfort." An infant may commit treason. The offense is not bailable. "Misprision of treason" is being cognizant of treason, without informing of it, and is a high misdemeanor. (C. S. 1745). 

Criminal Procedure 

The Justice as magistrate

It is the duty of a Justice of the Peace under the common law, as of other magistrates under the statute, to preserve the peace, and to do this he is empowered to arrest offenders guilty of breaches of the peace committed in his presence, without warrant; or, when complaints have been made to him that the criminal law of the State has been broken, to issue warrants of arrest. 

His jurisdiction as magistrate is not that of a Justice as a civil officer in  He acts solely as a magistrate; as a Justice of the Peace; and all his recorded proceedings, writs, etc., should be entitled "Before A. B., Justice of the 

Peace," and not "The Small Cause Court before A. B., Justice of the Peace." His two functions as criminal magistrate and as civil Judge must not be confounded. 

Criminal docket of Justice

The Justice, and every magistrate must keep a criminal complaint docket in writing. (See under general title "Dockets and 

Record of Justice"; subhead, "Criminal Complaint Docket".)

But this is an office record, and he must also write out in full his judgment of conviction on a separate paper, if, as in rare instances, he is authorized to try and convict. 

Limitation of prosecutions for crimes

By our statutes the following are the limitations of time within which a person may be indicted by the grand jury for crimes; the time to run from the date when the crime was committed: 

1. For treason, three years. 

2. For any offense not punishable with death, two years, except as to-

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

3. Forgery or embezzlement committed by a person holding any employment, whether elective or appointive, committed while in such employment; then the limitation is five years. None of the above limitations apply, however, when the criminal is a fugitive from justice. (C. S. 1870, § 152). 

No person shall, after acquittal, be tried for the same offense.

(Const. of N. J., Art. I, § 10). 

Nor can he again be restrained of liberty on the same criminal charge when he has been discharged by the order of a superior Court or Justice thereof, upon habeas corpus, unless: (a.) He shall have been discharged from a commitment upon a criminal charge and be afterward committed for the same offense by the legal order of the Court wherein he is bound by recognizance to appear, or be there indicted and convicted for the same offense; or (b.) After a discharge for defect of proof or in the commitment, he be again arrested on sufficient proof and committed by legal process; or, (c.) Having been discharged, shall be recommitted on a reversal of the order of discharge by a Court of review. (C. S. 

2647, § 34).

To imprison a person twice for the same alleged crime except as stated is not only punishable by a forfeiture of fourteen hundred dollars, but the magistrate knowingly issuing the warrant shall be guilty of a misdemeanor. (Ibid, § 35). 

Duties of a magistrate

The statute makes it the duty of all magistrates to "apprehend and cause to come before them and imprison and punish all persons offending against" the criminal laws of this "State. (P. L. 1915, p. 399; N. J. Cum. Supp. 880, § 16). This is to be construed in connection with other Acts which make exceptions as to the imprisonment and punishment feature. For example, most crimes cannot be punished by a Justice, but the persons must be held to bail, or committed, to await the action of the grand jury. 

Again under Acts relating to certain classes of cities all the Justice can do, where the offense is bailable, is to admit the offender to bail to appear before the nearest Recorder, or Police Justice, or

Criminal Court or, failing to give bail, to commit him to jail (as stated later).

Summary arrest by Justice 

To carry out the general mandate of the Legislature magistrates may arrest without warrant all persons guilty of public offenses in their presence, and, if necessary, command the assistance of other persons. It is their duty to interpose to prevent

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

165 a breach of the peace, and to arrest any person about to engage in an affray. They may even pursue and arrest felons, and call out any number of men to aid them. (4 Black. Com. 292; Chitty 

Crim. Law 25).

But summary arrests by the magistrate himself are to be made only when the crime is committed within his view and presence. There would be an exception to this rule if a man were running away, and the magistrate is informed, or has every ground to believe, that he has committed a crime and is fleeing from justice. This same exception would apply to a constable, or other officer, or even to a private citizen. 

Where the arrest is summary, no previous complaint is re quired. If the offense is bailable, bail may be given; otherwise the magistrate must commit the offender to jail by written commitment, and, in default of an officer to execute the writ, he himself may convey the offender to jail. A magistrate may be thus judge, jury and constable, if it be necessary "to insure the domestic peace of the State." There is frequently no time for delay or formalities, when a crime is being committed, and the law requires none.

Summary arrest by other officers The same remarks apply to all magistrates, Judges, sheriffs, coroners and constables. They are equally conservators of the peace by their personal power, as well as by process of law. A constable, or other peace officer, may arrest without warrant a person whom he sees commit a grave crime, but not if he does not see it. (State v. Schmitt, 21 N. J. L. J. 123).

By special statutes officers are authorized to arrest summarily in cases not of grave crimes. For example, constables or police officers where persons hawk, peddle or sell in municipalities without first procuring a license (if a license be required); marshals of pursuing societies for any crime committed in their county; police officers in townships governed by commissioners where breaches of the peace are committed; special constables appointed by stud-farm exhibitors at times of exhibition; license inspectors in cities who may arrest draymen, etc., who are unlicensed, etc., etc.

Summary arrest by private persons Private persons may summarily arrest offenders guilty in their presence of crimes amounting in the common law to felonies (murder, manslaughter, arson, burglary, robbery, rape, sodomy, mayhem and larceny), or of attempting to commit them. But they must be quite certain of the facts, as, if innocent, they will be liable to an action for false imprisonment. The rule is that,

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

if the actual crime was not viewed by them in its commission, there must be probable or reasonable ground upon the information of a by-stander to fairly suspect the person to be guilty. (Reuck v. McGregor, 3 Vr. 70).

Any person who hears the call of an officer for assistance in the arrest of a fleeing criminal may respond to that call and aid in the arrest, without waiting for information as to the offense charged. (State v. Bertchey, 48 Vr. 640). 

What to do with offenders summarily arrested

Persons summarily arrested without warrant are to be taken before a magistrate as soon as practicable, unless the arrest is by the magistrate himself. He may be either a Justice of the Peace, or Judge of the Common Pleas, or, in municipalities where the law creates such an office, the Police Justice, Law Judge, Recorder, or whoever has authority in the premises.

If the person making the arrest saw the crime, he should make a sworn complaint. At all events, some one, whether he or another, should make oath to the facts, or suspicions, that the magistrate may have a lawful basis for his proceedings. The latter must not act without due caution and authorization. When the magistrate himself saw the crime, and made the arrest, he may act without the affidavit or complaint, but his record must show those facts. 

Making a complaint

The usual mode of inaugurating criminal proceedings is by a written complaint, sworn to by the party making it. This is generally made out prior to the arrest, although, as above stated, it may be subsequent to an arrest, if the arrest be made at the time the crime is committed.

The complaint is an affidavit by some person that a crime has been committed, or that he suspects one has been committed. 

It should be made before the magistrate who is asked to issue the warrant.

The complaint need not be drawn by an attorney, or be technical in its language; but it must set forth a crime, and be sworn to before the magistrate and filed with him. In cases of important crimes, the Prosecutor of the Pleas of the county should always be consulted. 

Complaint in case of suspicion

When a crime has been committed and the party who makes complaint only suspects the perpetrator, he should not be allowed to make the affidavit of suspicion until cautioned by the magistrate of the risk run if it be unfounded, particularly if he is an

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

167 ignorant man. The magistrate is also to be intelligently satisfied that there is reasonable ground for the suspicion. "The causes of suspicion," said a text-book in general use at the beginning of this century, and which is yet good common-law authority, "that are generally agreed to justify the arrest of an innocent person for felony," (and held to be a good defense in case of suit for damages by a person arrested on suspicion, but who was innocent) are: "1. The common fame of the country; but it seems that it ought to appear upon evidence, in an action brought for such arrest, that such fame had some probable ground. "2. The being found in such circumstances as induce a strong presumption of guilt; as coming out of a house wherein murder has been committed, with a bloody knife in one's hand; or being found in possession of any part of goods stolen, without being able to give a probable account of coming honestly by them. "3. The behaving one's self in such manner as betrays a consciousness of guilt; as when a man accused of felony, on hearing that a warrant is taken out against him, doth abscond. "4. The being in company with one known to be an offender, at the time of the offense, or generally at other times keeping company with persons of scandalous reputation. "5. The living an idle, vagrant and disorderly life, without having any visible means to support it. "6. The being pushed by hue and cry." (Conductor Generalis; see 4 Blacks. Com. 292, 293). 

Complaints in first-class cities

Justices of the Peace in cities of the first-class in this State are required to take complaints in criminal proceedings under a special Act of 1898. (C. S. 1894). But in such cases the defendant's recognizance is to be to appear "at the earliest possible day before the nearest Criminal Court or Police Justice holding Court in such city," or, failing to give bail (or the offense not being bailable) the Justice of the Peace shall commit him to the common jail of the county. In all cases he shall send up the complaint and papers to the nearest Criminal Court or Police Justice of the city. Unless the defendant is convicted in such Court, however, the Justice will not be allowed fees.

For a Justice of the Peace not to comply with this Act is to be guilty of a misdemeanor. 

Complaints in second-class cities of over 30,000

By an Act of 1916 (P. L., p. 143, amend. by P. L. 1919, p. 

351; Ñ. J. Cum. Supp. 2713), relative to second-class cities of over 30,000 population, Recorders, Police Judges, etc., may try all

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

cases of assault, simple assault and battery, malicious mischief, larceny or embezzlement where the value of property taken is under $50, obtaining property under false pretenses, or receiving stolen property of value under $50, and all other criminal offenses where the penalty does not exceed $100, or imprisonment for sixmonths; but always provided the defendant waives indictment and trial by jury. If such hearing be waived, or the offender is held, he is to be admitted to bail (if the offense is bailable). Where the population of such city is over 50,000, Justices of the Peace may take complaints and admit the offender to bail for his appearance at "the earliest possible day before the nearest Recorder, Police Justice, or other official presiding over any Recorder's Court, Police Court, or municipal Court having jurisdiction over criminal offenses and power of committal;" if bail is not given he is to be committed to the common jail, and the magistrate is to send the complaint and recognizance, with a list of names and addresses of all witnesses for the State, in a "properly closed and sealed-in envelope," to the nearest Recorder or Police Justice of a Criminal Court in the municipality. To neglect this duty under the Act will make the Justice guilty of a misdemeanor. (P. L. 

1916, pp. 144-146; N. J. Cum. Supp. 2714). (As to the fees and costs of Justice and constable, see under general title "Fees and Costs"). 

Complaints in other classes of cities

Substantially the same provisions as in the case of the abovenamed second-class cities are embodied in an Act of 1916 (P. L., p. 453; N. J. Cum. Supp. 2718, § 189), and in cities of the fourthclass, Justices of the Peace may take complaints. (P. L. 1933, ch. 160).

There may be other statutes specially applying to certain classes of municipalities, especially as referring to Recorder's or Police Courts. In all cases the Act conferring jurisdiction to try complaints must be strictly followed. 

Complaints against infants

When infants under 16 are complained against (except for murder or manslaughter), and there is a Juvenile Court in the county, the complaint may be made directly before it. If made to a Justice he should send it under a writ to the Juvenile Court. 

The criminal warrant

The ordinary criminal warrant is a process to compel the defendant to appear in person to answer the complaint made against him. It is to be under the hand and seal of the Justice (not the seal of The Small Cause Court, but the usual [L. S.] of the mag-

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

169 istrate), and set forth the time and place of making it, and the cause for which it is made; not necessarily in the complainant's language, but so as to describe the offense with reasonable clearness.

It should be directed generally "to any constable" to execute, requiring him to bring the party before the Justice who grants it, or before any other Justice in the county. It is usually returnable "forthwith;" that is, as soon as the offender is arrested.

Where the name of an accused person is unknown, he is to be described as nearly as may be. A warrant to apprehend "a person to be pointed out," or "suspected," with no other description, is illegal and void. No officer is bound to serve such a process. 

Deputizing citizen to serve warrant 

Where a constable is not at hand to execute a warrant, and public justice requires that it be executed without delay, the Justice may appoint in writing (also sealing and signing it by his name and office) "some fit person, being a citizen of this State," to execute it, who will have all the powers of the constable. (C. 

S. 1827, § 19). In such case the Justice should indorse the appointment on the back of the warrant. 

When Justice may refuse to act 

A Justice may sometimes refuse to issue a warrant notwithstanding a complaint is filed before him. For example: The alleged crime may not be a crime in law. Under no circumstances should a warrant issue, unless the Justice is satisfied the crime charged is actually a crime in New Jersey, under either the common or statute law. Again, the complaint may be so uncertain that he would not be justified in acting upon it without some more definite or corroborating complaint. Or the person offering the complaint may be of such bad reputation that the Justice is convinced that the charge is false. The Justice must at all times use his reasonable discretion, remembering that he is bound to execute the law, but not to do injustice to the innocent. 

When a crime is positively sworn to, however, and there is no reason to believe it has not been committed, the character of the complaint cannot be considered, but the crime alone, and a warrant should issue. To wilfully refuse then or to neglect to issue a warrant, like the refusal to perform any other duty_required by law, is an indictable offense. (C. S. 1750, § 23). This same remark applies to a constable or other officer whose duty is to make arrests. 

And a Justice may not refuse to issue a warrant because no fees are tendered by complainant. He has no right to accept fees J-11

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

from a complainant. "Any magistrate or constable who shall ask, demand, or receive from any complainant, witness or other person, directly or indirectly, any fee or reward for the performance of any service in any criminal case, shall be guilty of a misdemeanor." (Ibid).

Officer making arrest upon warrant It has already been stated that a Justice, or other person, may arrest a criminal, who is caught in the criminal act, without a warrant. But when a warrant is issued, the officer must take it with him, and must exhibit it to defendant, if the latter desires to see it. Otherwise the arrest is illegal. The law is thus stated, with approval, by the late Chief Justice Beasley: "Whenever a warrant has been issued to arrest a person charged with an offense in respect of which he cannot be apprehended without a warrant, the officer must have the warrant in possession at the time he executes it; if he has not, the arrest will be illegal." (Smith v. Clark, 24 Vr. 9).

The officer must find the defendant with all speed, although if he cannot find him at once the warrant will continue good until he does. And he must find the right person. Where an arrest is made by mistake, and the officer has not the party named in the process, he should release the person arrested at once on discovering the mistake, but may then be liable for damages.

If the officer arrests the right party, but is convinced he is innocent of the crime, nevertheless the writ is to be obeyed and the party under arrest is to be taken before a magistrate. 

The arrest may be made in any place and at any time, even on Sunday.

If the crime charged is more than a misdemeanor, and amounts to a felony, (such as murder, burglary, etc.), the officer, or even a private person without warrant, may, if necessary, break open the outer door of any dwelling in order to arrest the felon. 

But he should first demand admittance. So if the person arrested escapes and flees into a house, the door may be broken open to retake him. This may be in the day or night. But in case of simple misdemeanor the door cannot be broken into. 

No actual physical touching of the body is necessary to constitute an arrest. It is sufficient if one is in the power of the officer, and is told that he is arrested in the name of the State for a certain offense, designating it. 

The degree of force the officer is authorized to use depends upon the offense charged. In case of a crime amounting to felony, if the party flees away to avoid arrest, when about to be made, or breaks away, and is shot at by the officer with no intention of killing him, and is killed by the officer, it may be justifiable

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

171 homicide. But in assault, affray, etc., killing is not justifiable, unless the party endeavors to kill the officer.

Rescues of prisoners, or the permission of escapes by the officers of the law, are indictable; and where officers are guilty of voluntary escapes in a criminal case, they shall also be disqualified from holding any office in the State. (C. S. 1746, §§ 7-13 b; but § 13 was amended by Laws 1920, p. 493; N. J. Cum. Supp. 835).

The officer, in conveying the prisoner, should be kind and humane, while using every reasonable precaution. He may search the person of the party arrested for fire arms, or concealed weapons, if he deems it prudent to do so. If the party escapes from the officer, or from jail, he escapes from the law, and may be retaken without warrant at any time, in any county in the State, and brought back to jail.

If the party is sick, or it is an unseasonable hour to convey him to a Justice, the officer may watch with him until the proper time arrives. 

Right to search prisoner

The right to search a prisoner lawfully arrested for the supposed commission of a crime, and to take from him stolen property, weapons used in the perpetration of the offense, and any other articles which may give a clue to the commission of crime or the identification of the criminal, is well established. 

No statute giving the arresting officer authority to search a prisoner for such articles is necessary. The power exists from the nature and objects of the public duty of the officer is required to perform; for, unless the arresting officer has authority immediately on making the arrest to search the prisoner, even before taking him before a committing magistrate, all evidences of crime and of identification of the criminal might be destroyed while the prisoner is awaiting a hearing.

Thus, there is no doubt of the authority and duty of an officer charged with the execution of a warrant for grand larceny, not only to arrest the accused, but to take into his custody the property described in his warrant if he finds it on the person or in the possession of the accused. To do this he may require the accused to remove his clothing, so far as necessary, to make a complete search.

He has no power under an ordinary criminal warrant to search the house or premises of the accused for concealed property. For this purpose a regular search warrant is necessary. (See general title "Search Warrant," in this volume). 

What done with prisoner

The prisoner may be brought before the Justice issuing the

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

warrant, or any other Justice, or any other magistrate, in the county wherein the warrant is issued. The statute says that "all magistrates in and for every county of this State are hereby authorized to let to bail until the next Court of Quarter Sessions or Court of Oyer and Terminer to be held in said county, all persons who are or may be arrested in their respective counties for any offense or crime therein done or attempted," except the unbailable offenses. (C. S. 1828, § 23). Consequently, the person under arrest, except in the felonious cases, may be taken to the nearest magistrate, in order that he may waive hearing and give bail, if so disposed. On authority of the Judge the county clerk or sheriff may admit to bail. (8 N. J. Misc. Reports, 154).

In case of the unbailable offenses (treason, murder, manslaughter, sodomy, rape, arson, burglary, robbery or forgery), the prisoner should be taken to the magistrate issuing the warrant and committed to jail.

The design of the law (when the offense is bailable) is that the party may be permitted to give bail as soon as possible after his arrest, before the nearest magistrate. Where the Justice who issued the warrant is almost as convenient to reach as any other the officer should bring the prisoner before him.

The question is sometimes raised whether the defendant may not exercise his option as well as the constable. The latter is to be, primarily, the judge; yet he has no right to take the prisoner to a remote place, away from bail, or counsel. 

Arrest in another county

In case a person against whom a warrant is issued charged with crime shall go to or be in any other county out of the jurisdiction of the magistrate granting the warrant, he may be arrested in such county by the officer serving the warrant, but not until the Judge of the Court of Quarter Sessions, or some magistrate of that other county, shall first indorse the warrant. The usual proceeding is for the constable, or person authorized to execute the warrant, to go to a magistrate of that other county, and make proof upon oath or affirmation of the handwriting of the Justice who granted the warrant, upon which the magistrate of that other county will indorse the warrant in the customary manner. This indorsement will be sufficient authority for the execution of the warrant in that county. (C. S. 1826, § 18).

When the accused is arrested in such other county, he may be brought either before the magistrate who indorsed the warrant, or some other magistrate or a Judge of such county. Thereupon, if the offense is bailable, such magistrate or Judge may take his cognizance to appear at the next Court of Oyer and Terminer, or of Quarter Sessions, of the county where the of-

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

173 fense was committed, and such recognizance and all proceedings relating to the accused and the alleged offense had before him shall be delivered to the clerk of the Court where the accused is required to appear. If the offense is not bailable, or the accused shall not give bail to the satisfaction of the magistrate before whom he is brought, then the constable or other person shall take the accused before the Judge of the Court of Quarter Sessions, or a magistrate of the county where the offense was committed, to be dealt with according to law. (Ibid). 

Preliminary examination of offender

A Justice of the Peace in an ordinary criminal proceedings does not try the complaint, and convict or acquit. Unless a statute does give him this special power he does not possess it. Formerly, in case of petit larceny, he could call to his aid another Justice and the two might try the complaint, but this is no longer law. There are, however, various statutes which provide for a summary hearing and conviction before a Justice in what may be termed very light crimes, or merely penal actions (many of which appear elsewhere, in this volume, under their appropriate heads). His duty in all cases (unless specially directed otherwise by statute) ends in the preliminary examination, the purpose of which is to ascertain whether there is just cause to hold the defendant to bail, (or, in default, to commit him to jail) in order that the matter may be passed upon by the grand jury of the county at its next session. 

These remarks apply to the bailable offenses. Where offenses are unbailable, the preliminary examination is not with a view to ascertain the amount of bail, but solely to ascertain what the witnesses know or what the accused may state. Therefore:

If the accused is charged with treason, murder, manslaughter, sodomy, rape, arson, burglary, robbery or forgery, (which are not bailable), the magistrate shall, when in his judgment the ends of justice so require, before he commit or send the accused to prison, take, in writing, the examination of the accused, and information of those who brought him before the magistrate of the facts and circumstances. This examination is to be signed by the magistrate and by the informant (and also by the accused, if he is willing to sign the same, but he cannot be compelled to sign the statement). The magistrate must forthwith deliver or transmit such examination and information to the clerk of the Court in which such accused is to be tried for the offense. Thereupon the magistrate is required to bind by recognizance with sufficient surety all such persons as declare against the accused to appear at the next term or session of the Court of Oyer and Terminer where the offense is cognizable, then and there to give evidence,

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

and he will also certify to such Court the recognizance. (C. S. 

1826, § 17). The magistrate is not required to assign counsel for the accused on the preliminary examination. (87 N. J. L. 515).

In bailable offenses accused to be confronted with State's witnesses

If the accused is charged with a bailable offense the magistrate must give a hearing to the person arrested, unless the defendant waives the hearing, in which case proper bail is to be received, and the defendant discharged from arrest, or, failing to give bail, committed to jail. In all cases it is the right of the accused to be given a hearing, and to have the witnesses for the State examined in his presence. He may be present by counsel if he so desires. In no case, however, (unless a trial and conviction is permitted by statute) is the accused to be permitted to bring witnesses and give the hearing the appearance of a trial. 

The issue triable is solely whether the accused is probably guilty, and the cause is necessarily heard ex parte on the part of the State. 

The recognizance of bail

The recognizance of bail should be proportioned to the magnitude of the offense. The Constitution of the State provides that "excessive bail shall not be required." (Const. of New Jersey,

Art. I, § 15). The magistrate, therefore, must be governed somewhat by his knowledge of the accused, and of his ability to give bail, as well as by the nature of the crime. In common assaults and batteries from fifty to one hundred dollars is the customary amount; in more aggravated cases, more. 

The sureties may be examined on oath as to their property when the magistrate deems it necessary; and each one of them should be worth the full amount of bail. The same rules as to examination and bail hold where the magistrate, before whom the accused is brought, is in another county from that in which the warrant is issued. But the recognizance must be to appear at the proper Court in the county where the offense was committed. 

In case the person arrested chooses to pay cash money in lieu of getting a surety on his bail, he may do so and it will be held to make good his recognizance if forfeited. (C. S. 1828, § 

25; amended by P. L. 1924, p. 657).

Fidelity or surety companies having authority to do business in New Jersey, may furnish recognizance of bail. In such cases of course, there can be no examination of sureties. (P. L. 1915, p. 332; C. S. Sup. 893). 

Bail may be taken on Saturday afternoons, or Sunday, or on any legal holiday. (C. S. 1830, § 30a).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

175 All recognizances to be in writing All recognizances in criminal cases before a Justice or other magistrate must be in writing, signed by the recognizor, or recognizors, before the magistrate taking the same or it will be void. 

(C. S. 1857, § 121). 

Requiring new recognizance Sometimes the magistrate is deceived in the bail. Whenever he discovers this, he may rearrest the prisoner (by written order to the constable) and compel him to find other sureties. But the mere death of a surety will make no difference, as his executors or administrators are liable.

Forfeiting recognizance for appearance If the offender does not appear for the hearing at the time appointed, the magistrate will note the default on the recognizance and certify it to the Court of Oyer and Terminer or of Quarter Sessions. (C. S. 1829, § 28). The recognizance is to be filed with the county clerk and will constitute a lien on lands for six years thereafter. (P. L. 1912, p. 55; N. J. Cum. Supp. 

892, § 122). 

Confessions of the accused "In practice when the party is brought before the magistrate, he is generally cautioned that he is not bound to accuse himself, and that any admission may be produced against him at his trial. 

At all events, no improper influence, either by threat, promise, or misrepresentation, ought to be employed; for however slight the inducement may have been, a confession so obtained cannot be received in evidence, on account of the uncertainty and doubt whether it was not made rather from a motive of fear or interest, than from a sense of guilt. (Chitty's Crim. Law). 

Bail after being committed to jail

When a person charged with a criminal offense has been committed to jail, it is not lawful for any magistrate, other than he who made the commitment, to admit such person to bail. But the committing magistrate may do so, in which case he must give an order to the sheriff or keeper of the jail before the prisoner shall be released. And any Judge of the Court of Oyer and 

Terminer, or Quarter Session, may admit such prisoner to bail, or the sheriff or clerk of the county may do so upon the written order of any such Judge. (C. S. 1827, § 20). 

Binding over witnesses

Witnesses may be subpoenaed by the Justice to attend before

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

him at the hearing. If there is danger of a witness absconding before the hearing, he may be brought before the Justice by a warrant.

As has been stated, in cases of non-bailable offenses the magistrate is required to bind over all witnesses to appear at the next Court where the offense is cognizable. Where, however, the offense is bailable, it is usually sufficient to take the recognizance of the witness himself without surety to appear at the next Court of Oyer and Terminer, or Quarter Sessions, (cases of treason or murder are triable in the Oyer and Terminer, but not in the 

Quarter Sessions). The statute says that every Judge or magistrate "shall, when in his judgment the ends of justice so require, bind, by recognizance of his surety, if need be, all such persons as can give testimony against the accused, to appear at the next Court of Quarter Sessions, or Oyer and Terminer." It is, therefore, a matter of judgment on his part, considering the nature of the crime and the character of the witnesses. Whenever such recognizance is taken it is to be sent forthwith to the clerk of the 

Court. (Ibid, § 25; amended by P. L. 1924, p. 657).

No witness shall be committed to jail, to secure his appearance as a witness in a criminal case, except in cases punishable by imprisonment in the State prison. (§ 30).

Whenever witnesses are bound over by recognizances to appear at Court, the magistrate shall, whenever in his judgment the ends of justice so require, take the examinations of such witnesses in writing. Both the recognizances and examinations are to be sent to the clerk of the Court, where the offense is cognizable. (§ 26). 

Adjournment of hearing

While the magistrate, in his discretion in a bailable offense, may adjourn a hearing, it must not be to exceed 10 days. (§ 27). 

Surrendering bail 

Prisoners who are let to bail are still presumed to be prisoners, in the custody of their sureties, who are considered their keepers. Such sureties may surrender a prisoner at any time for their own discharge. They may seize him anywhere as well as at any time, even if in another State or country. So the executor or administrator of the bail may surrender him.

To aid in the arrest, the bail may command the co-operation of sheriff, or constable. Or the bail may depute another person to seize him, who will possess all the powers of the sureties. The surrender will be to the magistrate who bailed the prisoner, and who must commit him in default of other bail.

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

177 

The commitment

The commitment to jail, when proper to be made, must be in writing in the name of the State, duly tested by the magistrate and under seal, and must be directed to the sheriff, or jailer. The constable will deliver it to the jailer with the prisoners. It should contain the name or surname of the party committed when it is known; if not, there must be a sufficient description of his age, stature, complexion, color of his hair, etc., to identify him, and it should be added that he refused to give his name. It must also contain a statement of the crime, and where and upon whom committed.

Commitment of person under seventeen One section of the Crimes Act provides that no magistrate "shall detain or cause to be detained, in any station-house, lockup or other place of confinement, for a longer period than twentyfour hours after such person shall be first brought before him, any person under the age of seventeen years, unless there shall have been provided in such station-house, lock-up or other place of confinement, means by which such persons under seventeen years of age may be detained separate and apart from persons above such age." (C. S. 1875, § 166). 

In case jail is insecure 

Where a common jail is insecure or inadequate, a magistrate in his discretion may direct that the person charged with the criminal offense be confined in the jail of an adjoining county. (C. 

S. 1876, § 170). 

Justice to send up papers

Within fifteen days after the taking of bail, or the issuance of a commitment, or after the discharge of a person against whom complaint is made, the magistrate must deliver the complaint, warrant, recognizance and all other papers in the case to the prosecutor of the pleas of the county. Not to do so is indictable, and he will forfeit his fees. (C.. S. 1854, § 109). But this does not apply in those cities where under other statutes the papers are to be sent to the nearest Recorder, Police Justice, or other Criminal Court of such cities. In cases where required by law an actual written record of proceedings is to be sent up with the papers. 

Fugitives from justice

It is lawful for a magistrate "on satisfactory evidence, under oath being presented to him that application has been made, or is

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

about to be made, by the authorities of any State to the Governor of this State for the extradition of any person or persons within the jurisdiction of such magistrate, to issue a warrant or warrants for the arrest of such person or persons and to commit such person or persons to the county jail, or to take bail for his or their appearance from day to day, for a period not to exceed thirty days from the date of the arrest of said person or persons provided, that any person or persons who may be so arrested and committed to the county jail shall not be detained or imprisoned for a longer period than thirty days." (§ 104; see In re Codington, 12 N. J. L. J. 151; In re Thompson, 85 N. J. E. 221). 

Commitment of boy or girl under sixteen "When a boy or girl under the age of sixteen years shall be arrested upon complaint of any crime (excepting murder or manslaughter), or of being a disorderly person, or being habitually vagrant, or being incorrigible, it shall be lawful for the magistrate before whom he or she shall be taken to forthwith commit said boy or girl to the county jail [but see above under head of "Commitment of person under seventeen"], to await trial as such trial is herein after provided [i. e., in the Juvenile Court], or to parole him to await trial, upon such conditions as the said magistrate shall determine, and forthwith send the complaint to the clerk of the Court for the Trial of Juvenile Offenders established; provided, however, this Act shall not apply to any case where two or more are jointly charged with commission of some crime, and one of them is over the age of sixteen years." (C. S. 1887, § 206).

The Court for the Trial of Juvenile Offenders is presided over by, usually, the Judge of the Court of Common Pleas in each county, but some counties have separate Judges.

The foregoing, however, does not apply to first-class cities, where, when a child under 16 is taken before a Justice of the Peace, Recorder, or Judge of the Police Court, the case must immediately be transferred to the Juvenile Court. (P. L. 1912, p. 

608. But see Laws 1929, pp. 270 et seq.). Nor to children truants from school not charged with crimes. 

Duties of Justice as to probation officers

An Act of 1906 (C. S. 1882), concerning the power of magistrates to commit persons convicted by them to the care of probation officers is so important and so much in use, that we give it below in full. It must be noticed, however (see last paragraph of the Act) that Justices of the Peace cannot proceed under this statute in any municipality wherein there is a Recorder, Police 

Justice, or Judge of a Criminal Court. Also that in criminal

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

179 cases the powers conferred are only exercised where the law gives the magistrate the right to convict. 

The 1906 statute says: "When any person is convicted before any magistrate in any municipality in this State of any crime, or of being a disorderly person, or for desertion or nonsupport of wife or minor child or children, or for neglect or abuse of minor child or children [deserters and neglecters of families not now within jurisdiction of Justice of the Peace. See Laws 1928, p. 362], and the record of the person shall so justify, the said magistrate may, instead of imposing the penalty provided by law for the offense, suspend the imposition thereof and order the person so convicted to be released on probation under the care of the probation officer of the county, if any such there be, for such time and upon such conditions as the said magistrate in his order shall determine. section, however, shall not permit such magistrate to suspend the operation of any order requiring a person adjudged a disorderly person for desertion or wilful refusal or neglect to provide for and maintain his wife or other family to pay a sum, weekly or otherwise, for the support and maintenance of his family. This "The magistrate shall forthwith send a copy of the complaint upon which said conviction has been had and of the order placing the offender on probation to the county probation officer, together with such statement of the antecedents and history of said probationer as may be required under the rules and regulations established by the Court of Quarter Sessions of said county for the government of the probation officer, and of convicted persons who shall be released on probation. "The probation officer shall have in his supervision of the person so released on probation under his care, all the powers and be subject to the same duties as are conferred and imposed upon him, with reference to offenders released on probation under his care by the Court of Quarter Sessions, and the person so released on probation under the care of the probation officer shall be subjected to the before-mentioned rules and regulations, and if he shall violate said rules and regulations, or the conditions of his probation, or shall re-engage in criminal practices, or become abandoned to improper associations or a vicious life, the probation officer shall report such conduct to the magistrate before whom the offender was convicted, and thereupon said magistrate may order him to be taken into custody by any process of law proper to be issued for the taking into custody or otherwise of any person after conviction of crime, and upon his being brought before said magistrate he may impose the penalty provided by law for the offense for which such person was convicted, and direct that he shall enter upon the sentence so imposed, and in com-

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

puting the period of his confinement, if imprisonment shall be imposed, the time between his release on probation and his re-arrest shall not be reckoned as part of the term. "If a part of the condition upon which such offender is released on probation under the care of the probation officer be the payment of money by way of fine or otherwise, said money shall inure to the benefit of the county, and the magistrate before whom said offender is convicted, if he shall collect said money or any portion thereof, shall remit the same to the county probation officer, with the copy of the complaint and order in said case, and the probation officer shall account for and turn over the same, or any money collected by him on account thereof, to the proper county officer, with the moneys collected by him from offenders released on probation under his care by the Court of Quarter Sessions; provided, all fines, penalties or moneys ordered to be paid by persons convicted of desertion or non-support of wife or minor child or children, or of neglect or abuse of minor child or children, shall be paid to the overseer of the poor of the municipality in which such conviction was had, or other proper officer, as is now provided by law, to be used and examined for the benefit of such wife or minor child or children. "The word 'magistrate' as used in this Act shall be held and construed to mean and include any Judge of a city criminal Court, any Recorder, Police Justice, Justice of the Peace or other like officer; provided, the powers hereinbefore granted shall not be exercised by any Justice of the Peace in any municipality where in there is a Recorder, Police Justice, or Judge of a Criminal Court."

The Justice as magistrate protected from suits for false imprisonment

The same remarks concerning the Justice as acting in The Small Cause Court applies to him as a magistrate in criminal proceedings. If he has jurisdiction, or has colorable jurisdiction in case of a complaint charging crime, he cannot be sued for damages by one arrested on his warrant. (Booth v. Karrus, 26 Vr. 

370; Grove v. Van Duyn, 15 Vr. 654).

Disorderly Persons, Etc. 

Who are disorderly persons

The following persons may be adjudged disorderly under the Disorderly Persons Act of 1898, (C. S. 1926 as amended), and by other Acts as named. (The numbered classification is not in the statutes, but is given in such manner here for convenience of reference. The language of the statute is condensed). But we do not mean that this list is complete, as almost every year new matters are considered disorderly. 

1. All paupers, who shall unlawfully return to the city or

township from which they were legally removed, without a certificate from the city or township to which they belong, or who shall leave their places of legal settlement. (P. L. 1928, p. 202). 

2. All persons who shall go about from door to door, or place themselves on streets, highway or passages, to beg, crave charity or collect alms, or who shall wander abroad and lodge in taverns, inns, beerhouses, outhouses, houses of entertainment, market houses, barns or other places, or in the open air, and not give a good account of themselves. (Ibid). Or- 

3. Who shall leave or threaten to leave their families to be maintained by the city, township or county, or to become chargeable thereto, or who, not having sufficient property or means for their subsistence or support, shall live idly, or not engage in some honest employment, or not provide for themselves or families. (See also No. 18). Or- 

4. Who shall use, or pretend to use, or have any skill in physiognomy, palmistry, or like crafty science, or who shall pretend to tell destinies or fortunes. (See State v. Kenilworth, 26 N. J. 

L. J. 142). 

5. All runaway servants or apprentices, and all vagrants or vagabonds, common drunkards, common thieves, burglars or pickpockets, common night-walkers, and common prostitutes. 

6. Any person who shall be apprehended, having upon him or her any pick-lock, key, crow, jack, bit or other implements with an intent to break and enter into any building or shall have upon him or her any pistol, hanger, cutlass, bludgeon, or other offensive or dangerous weapon, with intent to assault any person; or shall be found in or near any dwelling-house, warehouse, stable, barn, coach-house, smoke-house, automobile or in any place of public resort or assemblage for business, worship, amusement, or other lawful purposes with an intent to steal any goods or chattels. (See P. L. 1933, Chap. 107). 

7. Those who shall loiter or assemble on the streets, at the corners of the streets, or in the public places of any municipality, being under the influence of intoxicating liquor, or who in public places or conveyances indulge in and utter loud and offensive or indecent language, or shall address or make audible any offensive remarks or comments upon any person passing along such streets or public places, or in a public conveyance, or shall obstruct or interfere with any person or persons lawfully being in and upon such streets or public places or conveyances. (See P. L. 1912, § 

161; N. J. Cum. Supp. 944). (A saloon is not a "public place. 

Bassette v. State, 22 Vr. 502). 

8. Those who enter the building or go upon the lands belonging to any public school district of this State, or used and occupied for school purposes by any public school in this State, and

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

shall break, injure or deface such building or any part thereof, or the fences or outhouses belonging to or connected with such building or lands, or shall disturb the exercises of such public school, or molest or give annoyance to the children attending such school, or any teacher therein. Or- 

9. Who shall, by noisy or disorderly conduct in any public library or reading-room in this State, disturb or interrupt the quiet and good order of those who resort to and use said library or reading-room for reading or study. Or- 

10. Who shall be arrested at any steamboat landing, railroad depot, church, banking institution, broker's office, place of public amusement, auction-room, store or crowded thoroughfare, or other place of public resort or assemblage for business, worship, amusement or other lawful purpose, in any city, town or county in this State, and shall be proven to the satisfaction of the magistrate before whom such person shall be brought, to be a common thief, burglar or pickpocket, and to have been frequenting or attending such place or places for an unlawful purpose. 

Or disturbing schools or public libraries. (Ibid.; C. S. 1928, §§ 

4, 5). Or- 

11.
