Usual proceedings against disorderly persons, under the 

1898 Act

The proceedings generally under the 1898 Act are as stated below. But there are exceptions, and these will be noted directly following this statement of the usual proceedings.

To begin with, it is to be noted that the Disorderly Act of 1898 gives the Justice cognizance as a magistrate and not in The 

Small Cause Court. 

The Act makes it the duty of every constable, or other police officer, and it is lawful for any other person, to apprehend, without warrant or process, any disorderly person, and to take him before any magistrate of the county. By the term "magistrate" is included all Justices of the Peace, Judges of city Criminal Courts, Police Justices, Recorders, and all other persons having the power of a commiting magistrate. (C. S. 1937, §§ 36, 45).

A magistrate, on information, or on his own view, shall issue his warrant, or process, to apprehend any disorderly person. (§ 37).

But in cities in this State having Police, Criminal or Recorder's Courts, while a Justice may issue a warrant he has not jurisdiction to hear the complaint, but the offender must be taken before one of such Courts. (§ 44).

When the person apprehended is brought before the proper Court, proofs under oath are to be taken, and he may be convicted by the testimony of one or more creditable ("credible;" see State v. Kenilworth, 26 N. J. L. J. 142) witnesses. (§ 36).

The conviction must be written out and must be explicit of the offense and not simply that defendant is "a disorderly person." (State v. Regan, 38 Vr. 106). It must embrace a record of the proceedings; that is, contain the complaint or its substance; the issuing and return of process; the appearance of the person charged and his defense or confession; if he has not confessed the evidence adduced (names of the witnesses); and then state what was the judgment of the magistrate, or Court, i. e., what he is adjudged as doing under the statute which makes him disorderly, and what is to be the fine, or term of imprisonment. 

Thus a statement "Upon the law and testimony I convicted of being a disorderly person as charged" is no lawful conviction. (State v. Regan, 25 N. J. L. J. 77).

No jury trial is permitted under the Disorderly Act, except in case of deserters of families. (§ 20; see Preusser v. Cass, 25 

Vr. 532).

Within ten days after a conviction a magistrate shall file the complaint, warrant and record of the proceeding and conviction in the office of the county clerk, and not to do so makes the magistrate a disorderly person; but this does not apply to Criminal 

Courts or Police Courts. (§ 38; amend. P. L. 1932, p. 511).

It is lawful for the magistrate to sentence a disorderly person (not tramps) to the workhouse, penitentiary, or common jail of the county, for not exceeding one year, or to impose a fine, not exceeding $175. If the defendant in default of paying fine is committed, the magistrate may discharge him on receiving the fine, or such portion thereof as the magistrate may see fit to receive. If the fine is not paid, the person fined shall be discharged from custody, after serving twice the number of days that there are dollars of fine imposed. (§§ 40-42).

But the magistrate after conviction, or a plea of guilty or non-vult, may suspend sentence and put the defendant on probation with the chief probation officer of the county for from six months to one year.

This course is often followed in case of minor or first offenders. (P. L. 1931, p. 821). 

Complaint against child under sixteen 

When a boy or girl under the age of sixteen is complained against as disorderly (or of any crime, in fact, except murder or manslaughter), the magistrate is to take the complaint, when made, but, following the arrest, the offender is to be transferred for arraignment before the Judge of the Juvenile and Domestic 

Relations Court. (P. L. 1929, p. 278). 

Proceedings against tramps 

Tramps may be arrested by any constable or police officer

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

of the district where found, on notice given him by any of the inhabitants thereof. It is to be specially noted that the officer cannot arrest a tramp on his own view, but that some inhabitant must give him notice (which notice need not be in writing). (C. 

S. 1929, § 10).

On making the arrest, the officer shall convey the defendant to the local magistrate, who shall examine him, and may commit him, when "legally convicted before him by the oath or affirmation of one or more credible witnesses other than the officer making the arrest, to labor upon any county farm, or upon the streets, roads and highways of any city, township or borough, or in any house of correction, poorhouse, workhouse or common jail or penitentiary, for a term not less than thirty days, nor exceeding six months; and shall forthwith commit him or her to the custody of the steward, keeper or superintendent of such county farm, house of correction, poorhouse, workhouse, or common jail or penitentiary, or to the supervisor or overseer of highways, street commissioners, or any other officer or officers having in charge the repairs of any street, road or highway, or overseers of the poor of the respective county, city, borough or township wherein such person shall be found, as in his judgment shall be deemed most expedient."

It is also lawful for the magistrate to order that such person, (tramp) while engaged in performing the labor above specified, shall have a ball and chain fastened to his leg. (§ 16a).

Whenever, in the judgment of the custodian of persons committed under these proceedings, suitable labor cannot be provided in the place to which such persons are committed, a brief written order may be made by such custodian to bind out and keep any such persons to labor in the service of any person or persons, or corporation selected by the custodian, for a term not exceeding his original commitment, as a substitute therefor, and may compel the performance of such labor for the term fixed. (§ 11). 

It will be observed that it is not obligatory upon a magistrate to thus commit a tramp to labor upon the streets, or in a workhouse, etc.; he "may" do so.

Custodians may discharge tramps at any time during their term of commitment upon not less than ten days' good behavior, or upon satisfactory security, etc. (§ 13).

Constables or police officers, refusing to arrest a tramp on notice of any inhabitant, shall be subject to a penalty of ten dollars, to be paid into the poor fund of the district. To recover such penalty a suit must be brought in usual form. (§ 15, as amended by P. L. 1914, p. 36; N. J. Cum. Supp. 947). 

Special buildings and inclosures for the detention of tramps may be erected by counties upon the recommendation of the

Court of Common Pleas. (§ 14). But, otherwise, the "workhouses" named in the Act are declared to be "all poor houses, county farms, houses of correction, penitentiaries, and other places provided for the keeping of the poor;" and in them tramps must be provided with work when they are able, not less than six hours per day. (§ 16). 

Proceedings against deserters and neglecters of families

Formerly Justices of the Peace had jurisdiction of deserters and neglecters of families under both the Disorderly Act and Poor Act, but in 1928 it was enacted that no Justice of the Peace should have such jurisdiction, but Recorders; Police and Judicial 

District Courts could entertain complaints. (P. L. 1928, p. 362). 

Fees and costs (The fees in disorderly cases, to magistrates and officers who arrest and commit, are the same as in criminal complaint cases. (P. L. 1918, p. 243; N. J. Cum. Supp. 950, § 43). 

Filing of the record

In every case of proceedings concerning disorderly persons the magistrate, if a Justice of the Peace, and if he has convicted the defendant of being disorderly, must file the complaint, warrant and a record of the proceedings in the office of the county clerk, or the Justice himself becomes a disorderly person. (Ibid, § 38, as amend. by P. L. 1918, p. 243). On failure to do so the 

Justice will not be paid his fees. Criminal, Police and Recorders' Courts, which are by law Courts of record, are excepted from this provision.

A record necessary

I. CIVIL DOCKET 

Justices of the Peace must keep a record of both their civil and criminal proceedings. And such record must be—as all legal proceedings in every Court in New Jersey must be in the English language, and be written out in words at length and not abbreviated. (C. S. 47, § 17).

It should be stated here that there are, in fact, four kinds of records a Justice must keep. For civil causes triable in The Small 

Cause Court he must keep a Civil Docket. For criminal cases, i. e., for the entry of complaints of a crime, in which he is merely a committing magistrate, or may bail, but may not try and convict, he must keep a Criminal Docket. Where he may try summarily and convict, while he may make usual entries in his Criminal Docket, he must keep a written record on separate sheets of paper, which can be sent up to a reviewing Court when required. 

Another docket required by a law of 1922 (P. L., p. 121; N. J. 

Cum Supp. 2724) is a Summary Proceeding Docket, in which every magistrate "before whom any suit shall be brought in an action for a penalty instituted by statute under summary proceedings" shall enter facts (as stated below).

The Civil Docket 

As to the Civil Docket, the statute says: "Every Justice of the Peace, before whom any suit shall be instituted, shall enter in a book to be kept for that purpose, the names of the plaintiff and defendant, the style and nature of the action, the sum demanded or penalty sued for, the time of issuing process, and when returnable, the return made thereto by the constable, when the copy of the account, or state of the demand, or set-off was delivered by the parties or either of them, the time of taking the recognizance, of making or filing any order, the adjournment, the rule of reference, and report of referees, the jury,

when and by whom demanded, the venire, when issued and how returned, the time of trial, the names of the jurors and witnesses, the admission of evidence objected to, the rejection of evidence offered, a description of each paper offered in evidence, the verdict and judgment and when given, the execution or executions, when issued, the indorsement thereon, and how returned by the constable, the appeal, when and by whom demanded, the date of receiving notice thereof, and all the proceedings before him had, touching the said suit." (S. C. A., § 112).

The Justice cannot use any printed "Form" record for the purpose, as causes are too different in the particulars referred to in the section above quoted. He should secure a well-bound book (not cloth bound, but in buckram or good sheep) known to stationers as a "Record Book," having ruled lines as on usual foolscap paper, but with nothing printed on its pages. 

Usual form of beginning a civil docket The usual form for beginning the first docket entry will be: 

The Small Cause Court, before J. D., Justice of the Peace, of the 

Township of, County of, State of New Jersey. 

Richard Roe,

William Fox.

On Contract [or In Tort; or In Debt] 

On succeeding pages, the entitling of the Court need not be made, but in making all transcripts they should begin with such entitling. 

Miscellaneous points The full names of the parties should always be entered. 

Initials of first name will not be sufficient, unless subsequently amended.

In entering up a judgment, the full bill of costs must appear upon the docket, specifying each item and its proper fee, and the amount paid him by each party. (S. C. A., § 113). 

Correctness is what the statute requires and expects, and correctness every Justice should take pains to obtain. If dates are omitted, or are erroneous, they may prove fatal. (Marentille v. 

Oliver, 1 Penn. 379).

Thus to issue a process and not enter its date on the docket at all, either of its issue or return, would not be to make such a record as is required, and, unless it could be amended, would nullify subsequent proceedings. A transcript of such a record would be of no use in another Court, and could not be pleaded against a new action upon the same matter. 

In a ca. sa., (an execution against the body) upon affidavit, J-13

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

the Justice must not only be satisfied of the danger of delay in issuing an execution upon affidavit, but he should so record it; as otherwise it cannot be told whether the Justice acted on his own belief (to his own "satisfaction") which the law requires, in issuing the execution, or the sworn belief of another. (S. C. A., § 51; Krumeick v. Krumeick, 2 Green 39).

The judgment should be entered in words at length. If entered in figures it will be reversed. (Robinson v. Applegate, 6 

Hal. 178. See further, as to entries of judgment, under general title "Judgment”).

Nor is it proper to record the amount of the judgment entered by the words "the same," referring to the amount claimed in the demand; for example: "The plaintiff filed his demand for thirty dollars; the defendant not appearing, the plaintiff proved his demand, and I gave judgment for the same. (Polhemus v. 

Perkins, 3 Gr. 435).

In an attachment the docket must state that the plaintiff proved to the satisfaction of the Justice that the plaintiff had advertised the attachment in the manner prescribed by law. (Ditmar Powder Co. v. Leon, 13 Vr. 542).

A rule of reference should be entered at large, and so the report of referees. (Steelman v. Stewart, 1 Penn. 316. See further under general title "Reference").

In the matter of imperfections in the docket it is to be noted that a higher Court may by rule require the Justice to amend the same to conform to the facts. (S. C. A., § 112). But after giving and certifying to a transcript he must not, except by rule of Court, amend his original docket. (See general title "Amendments").

Transcripts from docket Every Justice is obliged to give a transcript of the proceedings before him to either the plaintiff or defendant when it is demanded, for which he receives a compensation, fixed by law. (§ 

112). This should be an exact, verbatim copy from the docket, which is what a transcript is. At the bottom of the copy the Justice affixes his certificate that it is genuine, and puts opposite his name his official seal, in this manner: 

I do hereby certify that the foregoing is a true and correct copy taken from my docket, and that the annexed papers consisting of [state what] are all the papers filed in the cause before 

Witness my hand and the seal of this Court this day of one thousand nine hundred and me. 

[Official Small Cause Court Seal]. J. H., Justice of the 

Peace.

As the state of demand itself is not a part of the record, and

is not written out in the docket, it is not to be in the transcript, but, in case of appeal, that and all the papers are to be sent up with the transcript. The transcript of a Justice does not need proof of his signature to make it evidence.

A justice is required to make out transcripts from his docket after his term has expired, provided it is in his possession, and certify them as "late Justice of the Peace," and such transcripts shall have the same force and effect, and be liable to the like legal objections, as though the Justice were still in commission. 114). 

(§ 

In all cases transcripts of judgments from The Small Cause Court must bear the seal of the Court. (P. L. 1911, p. 544; N. 

J. Cum. Supp. 1667). 

Docket after death or removal of Justice

While the Justice is alive and resides in the same county, he is to retain possession of his docket, even after expiration of office. But the docket shall, within one year after the death of a 

Justice, be deposited in the office of the clerk of the county wherein the Justice held commission to be there kept as a public record. And if a Justice shall be removed from office by impeachment, or if before or after the expiration of his term he shall be about to remove from the county, his docket or dockets shall be forthwith deposited in the clerk's office. After such deposit the Justice and his legal representative shall at all times have free access thereto without payment of fees to the clerk, to enable such Justice or his representative to recover any costs. (S. C. A., § 115).

For a Justice, or his executor or administrator, to neglect or refuse to deposit his docket in the clerk's office when so required by law, will occasion a forfeiture of fifty dollars, to be sued for by the collector of the county for the use of the county. (§ 116). 

The transcript from any docket deposited in the clerk's office, certified by the clerk, shall be received as evidence in any Court in this State. (§ 117).

Where a Justice removed without depositing his docket, a plaintiff was allowed to take a copy of his docket, and annex affidavits thereto, as a return to a certiorari. (Ball v. Van Houten, 1 South. 32).

Negligence in keeping docket actionable In the keeping of their docket Justices are ministerial officers, and as such are liable in damages to any one who sustains a special injury by their omission to perform, or by their negligent performance of a duty imposed upon them. (As to other points concerning the civil docket, see under

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

general titles "Warrant, Civil," "Execution," "Attachment," "Judgment," etc.).

II. CRIMINAL COMPLAINT DOCKET 

Each Justice must keep a Complaint Docket

Every Justice of the Peace and other committing magistrate is obliged to keep a Complaint Docket, as the Act directs, or shall be guilty of a misdemeanor and forfeit all costs. The Act does not apply "to any Police Justice or Criminal Court in any city of the first class in this State, except as to cases in which such Police 

Justices act as committing magistrates." (C. S. 1854, § 109).

In this Complaint Docket shall be entered "the name of every person against whom he may issue any warrant, the name and address of the complainant in each case, the names of witnesses in each case, with their respective addresses, the nature of the charge against the accused, and, whenever bail is taken in any case, the name of the bondsman and his address."

There is no provision in the law that this docket shall be filed in the county clerk's office when the magistrate's term expires, or he removes from the county, but it would be good practice so to do.

The Complaint Docket does not take the place of a written separate record of the conviction of a criminal in all those classes of cases where the record must be sent up to the prosecutor, or clerk of the county, or otherwise prepared and filed as any Act may direct. In other words it is a memorandum only to be kept by the Justice, so that he or anyone may examine it at any time. (See under Chapter on "Criminal Procedure," and also below). 

When required

III. THE WRITTEN RECORD 

In the case of proceedings under complaints made to the Justice as a magistrate and not in The Small Cause Court, beside keeping the Complaint Docket required, the steps in each cause or proceedings should be written down on separate sheets of paper, and with the same particularity as in causes entered in a Civil Docket. In other words there should be a complete record kept of any and all criminal causes coming before a Justice, and it is to be kept as a separate record in order that it may be sent up to any higher or reviewing Court in all such cases where a separate written record is required to go to the Prosecutor of the Pleas, or to be filed with the clerk of the county Court.

IV. THE SUMMARY PROCEEDING DOCKET The Act of 1922 

The Act of 1922 (P. L., p. 121; N. J. Cum. Supp. 2724) reads as follows: "1. Every magistrate or other officer, before whom any suit shall be brought, in an action for a penalty, instituted by statute, under summary proceedings, shall enter in a book to be kept for that purpose, and known as the 'Summary Proceeding Docket,' the name of the plaintiff or prosecutor, the name of the defendant, the style and nature of the action, the penalty sued for, the time of filing the complaint and the issuing of process, when returnable, the act or acts and sections thereof under which the action is instituted, the time of taking recognizance and the amount thereof and names of parties thereto, the time of hearing or trial, the names of witnesses sworn, the principal facts of evidence given, the conviction and judgment, the commitment, when issued, the execution, when issued, the endorsement thereon and how returned by the constable, the appeal, when and by whom made, the date of receiving notice of the same, and all proceedings before him had touching the said case. Also a full bill of costs, specifying each item and the fee for the same. 

"2. The 'Summary Proceeding Docket' shall be subject to the same regulations, and its records to the same provisions, as the docket now required in ' 99 The title "Summary Proceeding Docket" is somewhat misleading, because there are some summary proceedings not "for a penalty." However, it seems clear that when such proceedings are for a penalty and before a Justice as a magistrate, the docket above mentioned is to be used. But when the action and hearing is in The Small Cause Court it appears to us that the docket of that Court is the proper one to use. Under our understanding and that of the State Commissioner of Motor-vehicles, usual automobiles cases are to be entered in the Complaint Docket rather than in the Summary Proceeding Docket, since proceedings in such cases are not (usually) actions "for a penalty," which are civil in their nature. But we think the Summary Docket is to be used in complaints under all summary actions for a penalty not semi-criminal. (See topic, "Penalties and Fines").

Killing domestic animals or poultry 

Sheep-killing dogs, or any who kill, worry or wound either sheep, lamb, domestic animal or poultry may be killed by any person finding the dog engaged in it; or, if the owner, or person harboring the dog, is informed of it and neglects to kill such dog within 24 hours thereafter, he is liable to a fine of $10 with costs in an action of Debt, and also triple damages for the injury, before any Justice of the Peace of the municipality. This does not apply to cities. (C. S. 72, § 87).

There are other provisions as to claim of damages from the municipalities. (Ibid).

Various other statutes prescribe penalties for dogs which trespass, as in cemeteries (Č. S. 387); running at large in the woods except in the open season, or being used to hunt when the law forbids. (P. L. 1923, p. 252, where the penalty is $20).

Dogs not registered and straying off their owners premises without a collar giving thereon the name of the owner and registered number, may be killed by any person, and there can be no action for damages therefor. (P. L. 1916, p. 150; N. J. Cum.

Supp. 63. There may be also local penalties by municipal ordinances). 

Owners of vicious dogs who bite other persons are liable in an action of Tort if they knew them to be vicious; i. e., if they had notice or knowledge of their vicious propensities. (Gladstone v. Brunkhurst, 41 Vr. 130). But not otherwise. (DeGray v. Murray, 40 Vr. 458. See Eberling v. Mutclod, 101 Atl. Rep. 519).

To crop off ears of dogs, there are penalties named. (P. L. 

1931, p. 44). (See also under general title, "Animals, Cruelty To").

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

As disorderly persons Drunkards

Drunkards are disorderly persons, under C. S. 1927, §§ 1 and 2; also N. J. Cum. Supp. 944, 945. 

Actions against

The law makes no distinction in favor of or against drunkards, as to their bringing actions or being sued. They are to be sued in their own name. Even when a statutory guardian has been appointed by order of Court, as to all claims against a drunkard previous to the appointment of the guardian he is to be sued in his own name. (Coombs ads. Janvier, 2 Vr. 240).

But after a drunkard has been declared to be an habitual drunkard by an inquisition from the Court of Chancery, he is divested of all power and control over his property, which is vested in his guardian, "and no contract made by him shall bind either his person or estate." (C. S. 2798, § 28). 

Statute of 1916 

Elevators, (Safety of) 

By a statute of 1916 (P. L., p. 548; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1729) penalties are recoverable by the State Commissioner of Labor in municipalities having no building inspector, or by such inspector when there is one, before any Justice of the Peace having jurisdiction (outside of District Court jurisdictions) in an action of Debt, in cases where the Act is isolated. The Act provides on whom process is to be served, for a body execution, etc. 

This statute is also enforceable before Recorders of cities as well as District Courts. Evidence

General propositions concerning evidence Evidence must relate to the matter at issue, and either tend to prove or disprove it. If it relates solely to any other matter or thing it should not be admitted. Evidence relating to collateral facts (i. e., facts not at issue) should not be admitted. 

The burden of proving any fact lies upon the party who asserts the truth of it. Sometimes this is with the defendant in a cause.

EVIDENCE 

215 The best evidence of which a cause is susceptible must be produced. Where there is both written and parol evidence the written is the "best." Originals are always better evidence than copies.

It is sufficient if the substance of the issue be proved: i. e., the principal fact in the controversy. If trespass be complained of on a certain day, the trespass is the substance of the issue and must be proved; while the day on which it was committed may have been the day stated in the demand or some other day, so long as the real day is not too remote from the time alleged. 

All evidence is either primary or secondary. Primary evidence is evidence which shows for itself that there is no better evidence behind it. It is the best evidence which the party can produce; the first and chief of which the nature of the case admits. All other evidence is secondary, and cannot be introduced until it is shown that the primary evidence is out of the power of the party. Thus, a written instrument is itself primary evidence of its contents, and oral evidence cannot be introduced to show the contents until it is proved the written instrument cannot be produced. In an action upon a book account, the book in which the charge or memorandum was first made must be produced, if required; a copy of it would be secondary evidence. When a book, or instrument, or some other writing is lost, or cannot be produced, secondary evidence of its contents is allowable, because it is a necessity to admit it in order to have any evidence at all. 

When a writing is in the possession of the opposite party, if he is called upon to produce it, on due notice, evidence of its contents is admissible. 

Direct evidence is 

Evidence is also direct or circumstantial. such where the fact to be proved is directly attested by those who speak from their own actual and personal knowledge; the proof applying immediately to the fact to be proved, without any intervening process. Circumstantial evidence is such where the fact to be proved is inferred from other facts satisfactorily proved, the proof applying immediately to collateral facts connected with the fact in controversy.

There are presumptions of law which, if uncontradicted, form presumptive evidence. Thus a sane man is conclusively presumed to contemplate the nature and probable consequence of his own acts. The records of a Court of Justice are presumed to have been correctly made. A party to the record is presumed to have been interested in the suit. A bond, or note, is presumed to have been made upon good consideration. A physician is presumed to be regularly licensed. Where a magistrate takes an affidavit without stating that the person is twenty-one, it is presumed he was of full age. A non-claim for twenty years, when

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

the parties are resident and there is an opportunity for asserting demands, affords a presumption against the existence of a debt. 

Hearsay evidence, or what a person not present has said, is, as a rule, no evidence, because it does not derive its value solely from the witness himself, but rests on the veracity of another person, who cannot be subjected to the ordinary tests of a witness. The exceptions to this rule are five: 

1. Evidence of common reputation is received in regard to public facts as a claim of highway-on somewhat similar ground to that on which some public documents are admitted, the interest all have in their truth, and the consequent probability that they are true. The value of general reputation depends upon its being the concurrent belief of unbiased minds, in a situation favorable to know the truth. 

2. Evidence concerning ancient possessions. This needs no attention here, as it relates to title to property, which is not within the Justice's jurisdiction. 

3. Declarations and entries made by persons since deceased, when they are against the interest of the person making them at the time they were made, because of the extreme improbability of their falsehood. 

4. Dying declarations. They are made in extremis, (in view of death) when every hope of this world has fled, and "the terrors of a judgment to come are brought before the vision." Then "every motive to falsehood is silenced, and the mind is induced, by the most powerful considerations, to speak the truth." Gifts orally made in view of death and known as donatio causa mortis, are held good, and in actions for their value, evidence of the dying declarations of the donor is admissible. 

What a deceased witness testified to in Court may be proved by any person who will swear from his own memory, or by notes taken by anyone who will swear to their accuracy. 

Admissions and confessions

The general doctrine as to admissions and confessions is that the declarations of a party to the record, or of one identified in interest with him, are, as against such party, admissible. In the absence of fraud, if the parties have a joint interest in the matter in suit, whether plaintiffs or defendants, an admission made by one is, in general, evidence against all. But the joint interest must be real, not apparent. The admissions of the wife will bind the husband only where she has authority to make them. 

Confidential communications and admissions between attorney and client, or husband and wife, are excluded from evidence. The confessions or declarations of a party are in general good evidence against him.

EVIDENCE 

217 Parol, to contradict or explain written evidence Parol, or verbal evidence, is as a rule, inadmissible to contradict or vary the terms of a written instrument. True, written instruments may be read by the light of the surrounding circumstances, in order more perfectly to understand the intent of the parties; yet the plain meaning of words will always supersede any parol interpretation. And the rule admitting parol testimony against written instruments under any circumstances is applied only in suits between the parties to the instrument. Parol evidence may make that intelligible, and then is to be permitted. 

Thus where a note is wrongly dated, the mistake can be shown by parol and the true date proved. Conversation prior to or at the time of making an agreement, which was reduced to writing, cannot be admitted, to vary or explain the written instrument. 

Nor in case of a note given by two or more parties, although in fact signed by all but the first named party for accommodation merely, can parol evidence be admitted to alter the contract by showing they were sureties and not principals. 

Fraud may be proven

Fraud, practiced by the party seeking a remedy upon him. against whom the remedy is sought, and in that which is the subject matter of the claim, is fatal. Fraud can always be shown in defense of actions. It vitiates all contracts and renders them absolutely void; and no Court refuses to hear proof of it. In a suit brought against a maker or indorser of negotiable paper, the defendant may prove that the note was obtained from him by fraud, or that it was fraudulently put in circulation; and in such case, to entitle the plaintiff to recover, he must prove that he bought it before maturity, bona fide and for value. 

Written evidence

In the case of public records the mere production of the records, or a copy certified under the seal of the officer in whose keeping they are, is sufficient. When the cause is in the same 

Court whose record it is, the record itself should be produced; but, otherwise, a true copy is all that can be demanded. If the original record is lost, and cannot be proved by copy, its contents may be shown by the next best secondary evidence. Writs, after being returned, are to be proved by the production of the originals, if the cause is in the Court from which they issued, or else by certified copies; if lost, they may be proved by secondary evidence.

Private writings produced in evidence must be shown to be genuine. Obligations and instruments must be produced, and J-14

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

their execution proved, or their absence duly accounted for, and their loss supplied by secondary evidence. There must have been a bona fide and diligent search for an instrument before evidence of its loss will be admitted. 

The production of private writings in the hands of others may be had by subpoena duces tecum (which means bring with you), directed to the person having them in possession. Where an instrument is in the hands or power of the adverse party, there are, in general, no means compelling him to produce it; but the practice is to give him, or his attorney, notice in writing to produce the original at the hearing, describing it accurately, and, if he fails to do so, secondary evidence of its contents may be admitted.

If, when the instrument is produced, it appears altered, it is incumbent on the party offering the evidence to explain this appearance. Every alteration on the face of an instrument diminishes its credit, and makes it suspicious, and the party claiming under it must, ordinarily, remove the suspicion. Written instruments altered are thereby made void, as a general rule. spoiliated by a stranger their legal operation is unchanged, and the mutilated portions may be admitted as secondary evidence of the original instruments. 

Disputed genuineness of writings If

In all cases where the genuineness of any signature or writing is in dispute, comparison of the disputed signature or writing with any writing proved to the satisfaction of the Court to be genuine, is permitted to be made by witnesses; and such writings and the testimony of witnesses respecting them may be submitted to the Court or jury as evidence of the genuineness (or otherwise) of the signature or writing in dispute. But in such case such writings, before they can be compared with the signature or writing in dispute, must be proved to have been written before any dispute arose as to the genuineness of the writing in contro versy. (C. S. 2226, § 20; Mutual Benefit v. Brown, 3 Stew. 201). 

If, however, the action is upon a negotiable instrument, the signatures and indorsements are to be taken as admitted unless denied by affidavit. (P. L. 1914, p. 319; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1198, § 20a). 

How writings are proved

A written paper being produced, must be proved before it can be admitted as evidence. This may be either by the subscribing witnesses, or one of them, if there are any. Where there are no witnesses, proof of the signature of the person who executed the instrument is admissible. The former method of proof

EVIDENCE 

219 is to be adopted in all cases where there are subscribing witnesses. 

There are exceptions, however, even to this rule: 

1. Where the instrument is thirty years old; then it is said to prove itself. Of course, however, contrary proof may be made. 

2. Where the instrument is produced by the adverse party pursuant to notice, the party producing it claiming an interest under it. By his so claiming it he admits its execution. 

3. Where, from the circumstances of the witnesses being dead, insane, not found, or otherwise, the execution may be proved by other evidence. 

4. Office bonds, required by law to be taken and filed. 

5. Official records of Courts properly certified. 

6. Letters received in reply to others proved to have been sent to the party.

When the handwriting of the witnesses to an instrument must be proved, by secondary proof, that of the handwriting of one witness only is necessary. In such case the secondary witness must have seen the first witness write, or seen letters or documents from him which afterward were admitted by the writer to be genuine. To have seen signatures which he presumed were his will not suffice. 

Books of account "Whenever the nature of the plaintiff's demand is such that his book or books of account are requisite to the proof of his cause, a copy of the entries therein, so far as they relate to the plaintiff's demand, together with a statement of the credits or allowances if any, to which the defendant is entitled, shall be received in evidence, with the same effect as the books themselves, in case of the defendant's not appearing at the trial, or if appearing he does not require the production of the books of original entry; such copy shall be accompanied by an affidavit setting forth that it is a true copy of the original entries and that all the credits and allowances to which the defendant is entitled appear on such statement, or setting forth that the defendant is not entitled to any credits or allowances, and that the sum of money or balance claimed by the plaintiff is justly due and owing to him; a co-partnership may be proved in like case and manner.' (S. C. 

A., § 37). 

It will be seen that, by the above statute, the defendant may require the actual production of plaintiff's books of account, even though this may necessitate an adjournment of the trial. 

In general it is to be said of books of account that they are to be proved, and are not to be assumed to be correct. The personal knowledge of the Justice will not do; there must be actual proof.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Books of account should be regular, kept in the ordinary way, whose correctness with other individuals has not been disputed. A witness who has repeatedly settled by them is qualified to prove that they are regular books of account. 

Where a day-book and ledger are both kept, the former may be admitted in evidence (being the book of original entries), even if the latter is not produced, but not vice versa. Even though a book may be mutilated, or has erasures, it can be admitted; its credibility is another matter. It is also admissible where the items on the face of the book are not charged on the same day when the services were rendered, if the charge was made in the usual course of such business, but not where no prices are charged, but simply the goods sold stated. 

Corporation, its minutes, etc.

The existence of a corporation, which is a party to any suit, shall be taken to be admitted, unless the party denying the existence shall file an affidavit to the effect that, to the best of his knowledge and belief, such corporation does not exist. (C. S. 

1666, § 119a).

The books of a corporation, or of the managers of a corporation, are competent evidence of the proceedings of the corporation; and although not usually evidence against third persons, yet are evidence of such proceedings in case where it is competent or necessary to prove them. 

Evidence as to protest of notes (See under general title "Negotiable Instruments"). 

Receipts as evidence

Receipts, so far as they go to acknowledge a payment or delivery, are merely presumptive evidence of a fact, but not conclusive. Any mistake or fraud in their execution or delivery can be shown by parol and corrected, and even if it be a receipt in full. Nor does the taking of a receipt preclude the party from making other proof of payment. 

Subpoenas for witnesses

A subpoena is a writ which every party to a suit may have from the Justice, at any time, to compel the attendance of his witnesses. The writ must be in the name of the State, (Const. 

of N. J., Art. VIII., § 3), and command the persons therein named, and each of them, to lay aside all business and excuses, and appear before the Justice at the hour appointed for the trial of the cause.

It must state upon its face for whom it is issued and who are the parties defendant.

EVIDENCE 

221 The subpoena for a witness may be served in any county of the State. (S. C. A., § 9). 

The names of several witnesses may be in one subpœna. 

If the party is to be subpoenaed to produce books, or other writings, the command to produce them must be in the subpoena, as well as the command to testify, if his testimony is desired. It is then known as the subpoena duces tecum, and the book or writing must be produced by the witness, unless excused by the party calling him or the Court.

The place and hour must be described with certainty. 

The writ must be signed by the Justice and sealed with his seal; i. e., [L. S.], if he is acting as magistrate, or the official seal if in  It must be dated the day on which it is issued. (S. C. A., §§ 11, 12). The law does not prevent, however, a subpoena, being issued with a blank for the name of a witness.

Any Justice may issue a subpoena for a witness, although it be to appear before another Justice. It is not required to have it signed by him who is to try the cause, but it must be signed and dated by the issuer, although, unless the cause is to be heard by the Justice issuing the subpoena, it cannot be served in another county. (Ibid, § 9). 

Service of subpoenas

Any person may serve a subpoena. It should be read to the witness, or its contents made known to him. The proper method is to leave the copy of it with the witness, after making known the contents of the original. The original should be returned to the 

Justice before whom the witness is to appear. 

The legal fee is to be tendered the witness when subpoenaed, or he need not appear. This is fifty cents when the witness is in the same county as the Justice, or one dollar if he resides in another county. (C. S. 2224, § 12; S. C. A., § 100).

The subpoena and money may be left, when the witness cannot be found at home, at the place of abode of the witness with a person of the family above the age of fourteen years, but he must be informed of its contents. (S. C. A., § 16).

But unless the witness certainly learns of the subpoena, he cannot be subjected to a penalty for non-appearance. 

Penalty upon non-attending witness

Disobedience to the command of the subpoena, provided it is in lawful form and the proper fee is paid the witness, is punishable by a penalty not exceeding twenty dollars and not less than one dollar, to be adjudged by the Justice trying the cause. (S. C. 

A., § 35).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

In higher Courts the power to punish also summarily for contempt of Court when a witness, properly subpoenaed, does not appear, is lodged by the common law, but it does not extend to Justice's Courts (In re Kerrigan, 4 Vr. 344), unless specially given by statute in some instance; The Small Cause Court Act does not give it. 

Incompetent witnesses

There are certain objections which may be made to a witness, produced to give oral testimony, attacking his competency. 

These relate to his want of discretion, want of intellectual powers, want of religious principles, or to his manifest partiality. For example: 

1. That he is an idiot, or lunatic. No such persons can testify, as they have no intelligence. 

2. That he is a child who has not attained to years of discretion. Fourteen years is considered a proper limit, but the 

Justice may use his discretion with those younger, if he is satisfied of their capacity. If they understand the nature of an oath, about which the Justice himself should question them, and can give other intelligent answers to the Justice, witnesses may be sworn although not fourteen. (Van Pelt v. Van Pelt, 2 Penn. 657).

Evidence from those of tender years should always be received with extreme care. It is a delicate matter to put a child under oath; and he should be protected from embarrassing and improper questions, or such as will confuse or mislead him. If over fourteen, the witness is not to be interrogated respecting his capacity unless some reason creating suspicion is first shown. (Den. v. Van Cleve, 2 South. 589). 

3. That he is the Justice trying the cause, as a Justice cannot give evidence in his own Court. If he must be a witness he should dismiss the case. (McCormick v. Brookfield, 1 South. 69; 

Corliss v. Vannote, 1 Harr. 324). 

4. That he is an atheist, not believing in God, or a Supreme 

Being, and not a believer in the doctrine of punishments for false swearing. A witness, before being sworn, may be examined as to his religious beliefs, and, if a contemner of an oath, may be rejected. But this rule does not apply where the witness is himself a party to the action. The fact that a party to a suit does not believe that God will punish perjury, does not disqualify him as a witness in his own behalf. (Percy v. Powers, 22 Vroom, 432). 

Competent witnesses

As a general rule all persons of sound mind, who have attained to years of discretion, are competent to give evidence in

EVIDENCE 

223 any of the Courts of this State. Among those permitted to testify by laws of recent enactment are: 

1. Persons guilty of crime. It is now expressly declared that "no person offered as a witness in any action or proceeding of a civil or criminal nature shall be excluded by reason of his having been convicted of crime, but such conviction may be shown in the cross-examination of the witness, or by the production of the record thereof, for the purpose of affecting his credit." 

The conviction, therefore, if shown, goes to his credibility, not to his competency. (C. S. 2217, § 1). 

2. Executors and administrators. "In all civil actions any party thereto may be sworn and examined as a witness, notwithstanding any party thereto may sue or be sued in a representative capacity or as guardian of a lunatic; provided, this section shall not extend to permit testimony to be given by any party to the action as to any transaction with or statement by any testator, intestate or lunatic while of sound mind, represented in said action, unless the representative offers himself as a witness on his own behalf, and testifies to any transaction with or statement by his testator, intestate or ward, in which event the other party may be a witness on his own behalf as to all transactions with or statements by such testator or intestate, which are pertinent to the issue." (Ibid, § 4, as amend. by P. L. 1931, p. 305). 

3. Those interested in the suit. The language of the statute is: "No person shall be disqualified as a witness in any suit or proceedings at law or in equity by reason of his interest in the event of the same as a party or otherwise, but such interest may be shown for the purpose of affecting his credit; provided, no party shall be sworn in any case when the opposite party is prohibited by any legal disability from being sworn as a witness." (Ibid, § 3). 

4. Husband and wife. The husband or wife of any person interested as a party or otherwise "shall be competent and compellable to give evidence the same as other witnesses, on behalf of any party to such suit, action or proceeding;" but this does not extend to an action for criminal conversation, nor to the compulsory disclosure of any confidential communication made by one to the other during marriage, nor to any criminal proceeding. (lbid, § 5). 

5. A juror may also be called on by either party as a witness. (Popino v. M'Allister, 2 Hal. 40). 

6. Adverse party. It is allowable for one party to call the adverse party as a witness, who shall be "subject to the same rules as to the examination and cross-examination as other witnesses,' except in case of an action brought to recover a penalty or to enforce a forfeiture. (C. S., 2218, § 2).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

7. In cases of fraud, breach of trust, willful default or undue influence, the defendant may be sworn in his own behalf. (P. L. 1931, p. 474). 

Jews, Mohammedans, etc., as witnesses 

Jews may be witnesses; also Mohammedans; the former being sworn on the Old Testament, and the latter upon the Koran, if they desire it. The rule is that those not of the Christian religion are to be sworn according to the rites of their own religion. But the witnesses must believe there is One who will punish him if he swears falsely (whether in this world or the next, is immaterial); therefore an infidel may be sworn, if he believes in God and the obligations of an oath. (Penn.'s Treatise 149). 

Evidence by depositions

The law on the subject of depositions is given in S. C. A., 

§§ 109, 110. 

Evidence of signatures to negotiable paper 

See for this under the general title "Negotiable Instruments." 

Expert testimony

An ordinary witness is only allowed to state facts, not conclusions; an expert may state conclusions from given or hypothetical facts; and in this the distinction between them lies. 

While a subpoena served upon an expert will serve to bring him into Court, the same as any other witness, yet it is held generally in this country that he is not bound to answer professional questions and give professional opinions without being first compensated beyond the mere witness fee. The party calling him must first pay, or agree to pay him for his special services. But having given his opinion, the opposite party is entitled to crossexamine upon it without any employment on his part. 

This rule does not extend merely to physicians or engineers, but to a man skilled in any particular trade, whose skill entitles him to be termed an expert.

As to when such witnesses may be admitted to testify, the rule is as follows: That the opinions of witnesses possessing peculiar skill are admissible whenever the subject matter of inquiry is such that inexperienced persons are unlikely to prove capable of forming a correct judgment upon it without such assistance. 

Examination in case of injuries

In actions for injuries to the person, the Justice may, on the

EVIDENCE 

225 application of any party therein order an examination of the person injured by a competent physician or surgeon. But in such case an equal opportunity should be given to both parties to the cause to have qualified physician or surgeon witnesses present at the examination. (McGovern v. Hope, 34 Vr. 76). X-ray photographs may be proper evidence when made by and properly testified to by an expert professional. (See C. S. 2226, § 19, as amend. by P. L. 1931, p. 124). Interpreters

When a witness is produced who cannot speak the English language, an interpreter may be sworn to interpret his testimony. 

Privileged communications

A witness may refuse to answer certain questions upon the ground of privilege. Confidential relations are, in some cases, to be respected. Such relations are those of husband and wife, attorney and client, and the pastoral relation. It has long been a settled rule that facts communicated by one party to another in the relations named are to be preserved secret, unless voluntarily disclosed.

Lord Brougham long ago laid down the rule as to attorney and client, that attorneys "are not only justified in withholding such matters, but bound to withhold them, and will not be compelled to disclose the information or produce papers in any Court of law or equity, either as party or as witness.' 

Confidential communications between husband and wife remain privileged after the marriage is dissolved.

As to the pastoral relation, the rule is that communications from a penitent to his pastor, under the rules of his church, are privileged, but not otherwise. 

Justice to decide on competency of testimony

All questions relative to the competency of evidence must be decided by the Justice. The jury (where there is one) is the judge of the credit of the testimony, not of its legality. 

Witnesses out of the State

A witness residing out of the State cannot be compelled by service of subpoena to come within the State in order to give testimony. Nor can the Justice obtain it by a "Commission" to take testimony out of the State. The statute permitting such commissions limits them to the higher Courts. (C. S. 2235, § 

47; P. L. 1915, p. 141; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1200).

By consent of both parties, however, affidavits or depositions of witnesses residing out of the State may be allowed as evidence.
