I. EXECUTION AGAINST GOODS AND CHATTELS 

The writ of execution

The writ of execution is the final process in an action. It is for the purpose of carrying into effect the judgment of a Court. 

It cannot be issued until after the judgment. cause

Two kinds of execution most usual in modern practice are fieri facias and the capias satisfaciendum; the first meaning literally that "you cause to be made;" the second "that you take the body to satisfy." (The latter is sometimes called a capias-execution, and we have frequently used this term in this volume besome Justices will understand that term better). Commonly speaking, the difference in the two writs is this: that the fi. fa. only authorizes the officers to seize the goods and chattels of the defendant, while the ca. sa. authorizes the officer, for want of sufficient goods and chattels on which to levy and make the judgment and costs, to take the body of the defendant into custody and convey him to jail. The ca. sa. is the fi. fa., with the addition of a warrant of arrest. 

Ordinary execution against goods and chattels The fieri facias is used in all ordinary actions, when it is sought to collect the judgment and costs out of the goods and chattels of the defendant, without imprisoning him if they are sufficient. It follows after the judgment as a matter of course,

EXECUTION 

229 except as hereafter stated, and can be employed in all cases where the capias may be used, if the plaintiff prefers it. 

Where executors or administrators are defendants the execution is against the goods and chattels of the estate or intestate, and not of the defendants personally.

Execution against bodies politic or corporate can only be against their goods and chattels. 

An execution may be issued directly after the entry of judgment, or at any period afterward within twenty years, should the same Justice be in commission, but if more than six years have elapsed since the recovery of the judgment, a special order of the Justice is necessary, to be made upon five days' notice to the defendant and proof to the satisfaction of the Justice of the nonpayment of the judgment, or of the amount remaining due. (S. 

C. A., § 65).

When he is out of commission, or has not his docket, the judgment may be sued upon before another Justice in an action upon contract, and execution will issue upon that judgment.

A judgment may be docketed in the Common Pleas and execution then issued (as per S. C. A., §§ 72, 73), but in such case (of docketing), the Justice cannot thereafter issue an execution 

(§ 75). 

An execution must be signed and sealed by the Justice with the official seal of The Small Cause Court (if the execution issues from that Court), and be in all respects as regular and exact as any other legal process.

The writ is to be made returnable in thirty days, and the constable must then, or before, return it.

Execution in actions where defendants are responsible in a certain order

In case of an execution, where the action was upon a bill or note and the defendants are relatively liable in order, i. e., primarily and secondarily liable, etc., an indorsement to such effect must be made by the Justice upon the execution. (See for such proceeding S. C. A., § 46). Necessarily in such case the judgment will have been given and entered in the docket in such a manner as to show the order of liability. 

Execution for defendant against plaintiff "When in any action the defendant shall have judgment against the plaintiff for debt or damages, he shall be entitled to have against the plaintiff the same execution as he would have been entitled to if he had been plaintiff in the suit." (S. C. A., § 59).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

1 

Indorsement on all executions

In all cases the civil execution should be indorsed with the true amount to be made, of judgment and of costs, to which the constable may add his legal fees. 

Stay of execution

If a judgment is appealed from, or a certiorari taken to review the proceedings, the Court above, on granting the appeal or certiorari, upon application will order a stay of execution. But the Justice, himself, cannot stay an execution. He is bound, however, not to issue one, under one circumstance, viz: "If any defendant shall at any time before the issuing of execution, procure a good and sufficient freeholder, resident in the county, to join with such defendant in a confession of judgment to the adverse party for the amount of his demand, with costs, then, if the judgment shall not be more than fifty dollars, no execution shall issue until after one month from the time of rendering such judgment, and when the judgment shall exceed fifty dollars, no execution shall issue until after three months from the time of rendering such judgment; but this provision shall not apply to a suit brought upon a judgment recovered before a Small Cause Court." (S. C. A., § 60). This last clause means that it does not apply where after a judgment in The Small Cause Court a suit is brought upon that judgment before another Justice. 

Amendment of errors

All merely clerical errors in an execution may be amended by the Justice under the statute permitting amendments. But an execution, void because not based upon a lawful judgment, cannot be made good by any correction in form. 

Alias and pluries writs

A second execution is termed an alias writ, and succeeding ones pluries writs. The only differences between these writs and the first execution, is a slight change in language, and indorsement. "We command you, as before you were commanded," is the language of an alias writ; and of a pluries, “as often before you were commanded."

An alias cannot be issued before the return of the first execution. If the first is returned, with some part of the judgment collected, the second (called an alias execution), which is in reality an execution for residue, should be drawn, as the first, in amount, with an indorsement on the writ of what was paid, showing the true balance due.

As the utmost limit of time allowed for executing a fi. fa. is

EXECUTION 

231 the day whereon it is returnable, if property is levied upon under it, but is unsold, an alias should be issued; until it does, it cannot be sold. (Matthews v. Stires, 6 Hal. 295). 

Alias execution into other counties

When the constable has exhausted the powers of his execution, without collecting the judgment in full, but there are goods and chattels in another county, a special provision is made for an alias execution good in such other county. (See S. C. A., § 68). 

How long an execution is in force

Every execution will remain in full force as a lien against the goods and chattels levied on for the term of one year from the time it was issued, unless sooner satisfied. All executions which remain unsatisfied for the space of one year after their issue become void; but the plaintiff may thereupon have subsequent executions, within six years, to continue in force and become void in the same manner. After six years there must be notice to the defendant. (S. C. A., §§ 65-68). 

Priority of executions

As a rule executions have priority as liens upon goods and chattels levied upon according to the time of the levy. (S. C. A., § 69). 

One execution may be postponed to another by fraud 

Fraud will postpone one execution to another. And not only actual, positive fraud on the part of the plaintiff, but constructive fraud, arising from his granting privileges, or entering into arrangements with the defendant, whereby the rights of subsequent execution creditors would be impinged upon.

Therefore, if a plaintiff simply grants an indefinite stay upon an execution, either at the time of its delivery or afterwards, a subsequent execution creditor will acquire preference in his lien. 

Whether he grants the stay from motives of humanity toward defendant's family, or in the hope that defendant will increase his means for satisfying the execution by the permission to carry on his trade, or business, the effect is the same; the Courts will treat it constructively fraudulent as against other creditors having subsequent executions. (Cook v. Wood, 1 Harr. 254).

But the mere fact of stay, for a short period, in which the debtor does not have absolute and free control over the property under levy, will not postpone a first lien to a second.

The priority of executions as fixed by the law cannot be altered by a Justice, nor by the constable. 

---

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Surplus moneys

All surplus moneys arising upon a sale by virtue of an execution are to be paid to the defendant, or, if there are levies upon the same property under later executions, to the officer holding the next oldest execution which has been levied under, until all executions levied upon the goods and chattels of any defendant, at the time of sale under the first execution, are satisfied, or so far satisfied as there are proceeds for that purpose, according to their respective seniority. When all executions are thus satisfied, surplus moneys belong to the defendant. (S. C. A., § 69). 

The levy under an execution

A levy is the act of taking possession of defendant's goods. 

It is a seizure, and perfects the lien of the execution. The statute directs how it shall be made. (§ 70).

When the constable receives his writ, he should see that it is regular on its face, and, if so, he must act under it. 

He cannot seize property outside of the county, as his jurisdiction to serve executions is limited to his own county.

Where it is necessary to appraise the goods to give the defendant the benefit of a debtor's exemption, it may be done at the time of the levy, or at any time before the sale. 

If the writ is received too late to make a sale before the return day, still the constable must levy, so that the lien is not lost. 

And it will not matter although his term of office expires next day, or in a few days; he has this one duty to perform, to levy, and then (if his term is about expiring), to return the execution at once to the Justice. Not to do so will be to make him liable to the plaintiff in case of loss. (State v. Roberts, 7 Hal. 114).

Where there are several defendants equally liable, the constable may select of whom to make the money. But the rule is to consider them in their order; although the one important thing is to levy upon sufficient to satisfy the writ. 

A constable should not, as a rule, levy upon property not before him. It should be subject to his view, that he may inventory it by actual sight. But where the defendant gives him an inventory for the purposes of a levy, the property is transferred to the possession of the officer and placed under his control as effectually as if the inventory were made in view of the goods. (Caldwell v. Fifield, 4 Zab. 160). 

What may be levied upon

Money belonging to a defendant in execution may be levied on and returned by virtue of such execution, as so much money collected, without exposing the same to sale. It must first be taken into actual possession, however. Bank notes, bills, or other

EXECUTION 

233 evidences of debt, circulated as money, or any share of interest in any bank, insurance company or other joint stock company, incorporated under the authority of this State, or of the United States, belonging to the defendant in execution, may be taken and sold by virtue of such execution, in the same manner as goods and chattels. (C. S. 2244, §§ 3, 4). 

Bonds and mortgages are goods and chattels and subject to levy. Growing grain and other annual fruits of labor are also chattels and subject to execution. And the purchaser of them under an execution sale acquires the right of leaving the crop upon the soil until its maturity, and also the privilege of gathering and taking it away. (Terhune v. Ex'rs. of Bray, 1 Harr. 54; 

Westbrook v. Edgar, 1 Harr. 81; Bloom v. Welsh, 3 Dutch. 177).

Manuscripts secured by copyright; a building standing by consent upon another's land, where the party owning the house has no interest in the land; fuel, office furniture and stationery; a ferry boat, though it carry the U. S. mail; these and all similar movable property, in which the judgment debtor may have an ownership, and the possession or a right to possession, are subject to execution.

Shares of bank stock or other incorporated companies are not bound by mere delivery of execution to an officer, but may be transferred before actual levy. And it is not sufficient to make an inventory of such stock, but the officer must go to some proper officer and give notice of the levy; nor will making a levy by inventory bind bank notes, of which property the officer must take actual or constructive possession. (Princeton Bank v. Crozer, 2 

Zab. 383).

Rights and credits generally of a defendant (as it would seem) may not be levied upon except in the higher Courts. 

What may not be levied upon

Under an execution from The Small Cause Court no real estate can be levied upon. Real estate is fixed and immovable property, such as houses, lands, timber uncut, etc. Nor can choses in action be the subject of levy and sale. A chose in action is something which a person has not in possession or enjoyment; a right one has which can be enforced against a reluctant party only by suit. Such are promissory notes, coupons, notes for the payment of interest on bonds, judgments, accounts, account books, etc.

The uniforms, arms, equipments and other military property of the National Guard and its members are exempt from execution and every process of law. (P. L. 1918, p. 794; N. J. Cum. 

Supp. 1939).

If a warehouseman has possession of goods and has issued J-15

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

a negotiable receipt for them, they cannot be levied upon under an execution unless the receipt be first surrendered to the warehouseman or its negotiator enjoined (by an injunction). (C. S. 

5781, § 25). (See, further, under the following head of "Property exempt from execution"). 

Subsequent levies on new property

The officer holding an execution may make a levy and inventory of part of defendant's goods, and afterwards, before the writ is returnable, may levy on and inventory other goods. 

But after the execution is returned, no new levy can be made unless upon a new (alias) execution issued. (Lloyd v. Wyckoff, 6 Hal. 218). 

Where a new execution against the same defendant comes into the constable's hands subsequent to a levy on the first execution, it is not necessary for him to view the property again. He may make a copy of his former levy and attach it to the writ. Nor need he notify the defendant. (Millville Bank v. Bethel, 13 Vr. 550). 

Notice of lien to purchasers

The purchaser of goods of a defendant in execution after the writ has been regularly issued and placed in the hands of an officer, and levy made, purchases with notice of the lien, notwithstanding they have remained in defendant's possession; and if after such purchase he intermixes his own goods with those subject to the lien, the burden of proof will be upon him, and not the officer to show what specific articles were the exclusive property of the purchaser. (James v. Burnet, Spen. 635).

The plaintiff in execution, if he purchases under his own execution, is supposed to have notice of every step of the proceedings, and is not entitled to special notice in order to void his purchase should the title turn out to be defective or the sale unlawful. Bona fide purchasers, who are third parties, must have notice, however, or their title will be superior to that of other claimants of the judgment debtor's property, who allowed the execution sale to pass without proclaiming their interests. 

Execution against corporation "Every agent or person having charge or control of any property of a corporation, on request of any public officer, having for service a writ of execution against it, shall furnish to him the names of the directors and officers thereof, and a schedule of all its property, including debts due or to become due to it, so far as he may have knowledge of the same. If any officer holding an

EXECUTION 

235 execution, shall be unable to find other property belonging to the corporation liable to execution, he or the judgment creditor may elect to satisfy such execution, in whole or in part, by any debts due to the corporation; and it shall be the duty of any agent or person having custody of any evidence of such debt to deliver the same to the officer, for the use of the creditor, and such delivery, with a transfer to the officer in writing, for the use of the creditor, and notice to the debtor shall be a valid assignment thereof; and such creditor may sue for and collect the same in the name of the corporation, subject to such equitable set-offs on the part of the debtor as in other assignments; and every agent or person who shall neglect or refuse to comply shall be himself liable to pay to the execution creditor the amount due on said execution, with costs." (C. S. 1637, §§ 61, 62).

Execution against partnership property If the execution is against one of several partners the officer may seize and levy upon the interest of the defendant in the whole of the partnership property; selling off his interest only, however, be it more or less. It is the undivided share of the debtor which the purchaser receives. And the levy is made subject to the prior rights and liens of the other partners, and of other joint creditors. In other words, the partners who are not concerned have their rights in the firm property which cannot be disturbed; and the creditors of all the partners have also rights superior to that of a creditor against one partner. 

Partnership property is first liable to pay the partnership debts, and then that of the individual partners. This latter principle has long been conceded as a general rule of law. (Linford v. Linford, 4 Dutch. 115).

The seizure must be of all the goods of the firm, even if the execution be against one partner only; and all must be taken into the constable's custody, and not a moiety only.

Possession of goods taken under execution 

Must the constable take actual possession of defendant's goods, and guard them until the sale, or place them under lock and key? The solution is with him. That officer is responsible for their safe keeping, and their final sale, and he must use what means seem to him best to insure the end designed. The only obligation imposed upon him by the writ in his hands is that he shall cause to be levied and paid to the plaintiff, or, in his absence, the Justice, so much money, etc. That he must inventory them has been stated; otherwise he cannot be considered as having possession, so as to maintain an action for them, if taken out of his possession.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

There is no law, however, to compel him to remove the goods levied upon and inventoried, or to take them from the actual possession of the defendant till the day of sale. Circumstances ought to govern him in the execution of his duty rather than arbitrary rules. (Wintermute v. Hankinson, 1 Hal. 140; Caldwell v. Fifield, 4 Zab. 155).

Property exempt from execution 

Goods and chattels, shares of stock or interest in any corporation, and personal property of every kind, not exceeding in value (exclusive of wearing apparel) the sum of two hundred dollars, and all wearing apparel the property of any debtor having a family residing in this State, is reserved, as well after as before the death of the debtor, for the use of his family; and is not liable to be seized or taken by virtue of any execution or civil process, whatever, issued out of any Court of this State. (C. S. 2245, § 10).

It will be noticed that under the above rule it is requisite that the debtor have, first, a family, and second, that such family be resident in this State. It does not matter whether the debtor resides at the time of the service of execution in the State or not; if his family does, the exemption can be claimed.

As to what constitutes a "family," the decisions are pretty much in harmony. A married man, living with his wife, has a family; so if she is a resident within the State, although he may not be. The same in case he has children. Persons related to him, for whom he is bound to law to provide, constitute his family. (As to whether and when a married woman can claim the exemption as the head of a family, see Muir v. Howell, 6 N. J. 

L. J. 184; Briggs v. Bell, Passaic Circuit, 8 N. J. L. J. 251. If actual head she can).

When the goods or the property levied on are the foundation of the demand in the suit, they are not entitled to exemption. The statute giving the exemption of two hundred dollars and wearing apparel, expressly notes that "nothing therein shall be deemed or held to protect from sale, under execution or other process, any goods, chattels or property, for the purchase whereof the debt or demand for which the judgment on which such execution or process was issued shall have been contracted." (C. 

S. 2245, § 10).

Thus if defendant purchased a cow of plaintiff, and the suit was for the collection of the price or value of such cow, upon execution the cow could be seized and sold, irrespective of the exemption clause. So with clothing.

But the debt must have been contracted for the purchase of

EXECUTION 

237 such property, and not simply be connected with it in an indirect, or remote manner.

In many States tradesmen's tools are excepted, but not in 

New Jersey. Rings, jewelry and watches are not wearing apparel; nor trunks, satchels, or bags. But a lace shawl has been held to be such, it being clothing. Apparel is what is worn upon the person, not for ornament merely, but from necessity. 

Bonds and mortgages given by cemetery associations to secure the purchase money of the lands owned by them are exempt from execution. (C. S. 375, § 8). (See further, a preceding subhead of "What may not be levied upon"). 

Proceedings to set aside the $200 exemption

In order to ascertain what property equals the value of two hundred dollars and what shall be set aside to a debtor having a family, it is necessary under the statute for the constable to take certain proceedings before selling under the execution, if his levy covers everything, viz.: 

1. Inventory all the goods, and appoint, in writing, three discreet and judicious persons of the county to appraise them. 

These appraisers must be sworn. The constable himself may administer the oath, or it may be administered by anyone legally authorized to administer oaths. (C. S. 2246, § 11. For the oath, see Form 187 infra). 

2. The appraisers must give five days' notice to the plaintiff, or his attorney, of the time and place of making the appraisement, and must then appraise the articles separately, in writing. 

3. If the appraisement does not exceed two hundred dollars, the constable must suffer them to remain in the possession of the defendant's family. If they exceed it, the defendant may select out two hundred dollars' worth, in writing, and sign his name to it, and thereupon the constable will proceed to sell only the residue. 

4. The selection may be made by the wife or family of the defendant, if he is absent or cannot be found, or refuses to select, or by the appraisers. 

5. The statement of the appraisers, and also of the defendant, is to be annexed to and returned with the execution. 

6. If the defendant in execution dies before a levy and sale is made and leaves a wife or children, the executors or administrators may apply to the surrogate, and have appraisers appointed, and allow the widow to make the selection of two hundred dollars' worth of goods and chattels, moneys and effects. (C. S. 

3831, § 60).

The question was once raised in this State whether the fam-

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

ily of a debtor could have their property, which in the total did not exceed $200 in value, levied upon and seized by the officer until an appraisement was regularly made. Their goods were in transitu, and the officer stopped them, although they were worth but $50. It was held that the officer only fulfilled his duty. It was not his judgment which determined the value of the goods but that of appraisers chosen according to law. For, until the two hundred dollars worth of goods allowed to a debtor's family are ascertained and selected in conformity to the statute there is no privilege of exemption from a levy. But when once appraised and set aside the officer's power is gone, and he would be a trespasser if he should hold them or sell them. (Bonnell v. Dunn, 5 Dutch. 439).

Claim of title to property levied upon If a constable levies upon property not the property of the defendant, or alleged not to be his, the claimant may deliver to the constable a notice in writing claiming such of the goods and chattels as he may allege to belong to him, specifying them. 

Thereupon the constable must delay his sale of the same for the space of ten days, that the claimant may, within such time, apply to some Justice of the Peace within or near the place where such goods or chattels were seized for a venire to summon a jury of six lawful men as jurors, to try the right of the claimant to the property. Such Justice of the Peace will issue the venire and direct a return thereof to be made to him, and proceed therein as in other cases of trial by jury. (S. C. A., § 62). The statute does not say this application must be to another Justice than the one issuing the execution; hence it may be made to the Justice issuing the execution if he is "within or near the municipality" where the chattels are located. The object of the law is to have the claim tried before a nearby Justice.

The claimant must in all cases give notice in writing to the plaintiff of the time and place of the trial. If, however, the claimant shall not, within the ten days, apply to a Justice and have his right tried, the claim is to be considered abandoned, and the constable must proceed as if it had not been made. (Ibid; Lucas v. Van Marter, 35 Vr. 182).

The verdict of the jury in case of trial will protect the constable from any action for taking and seizing the property or the delivery thereof to the claimant. (S. C. A., § 63). 

If the property shall be found to belong to the claimant, the constable is to proceed no further with the seizure or sale of it; but if it shall be found to belong to the defendant, he must dispose of the same, as is directed in the execution. 

The costs attending such trial must be taxed by the Justice

EXECUTION 

239 before whom the claim is tried as in other cases, and it is to be paid by the plaintiff at whose suit the property was taken and seized, if the claimant obtain a verdict in his favor; and by the claimant if the verdict is found against him. 

If the plaintiff, upon notice given by the claimant to the constable, shall indemnify him against claimant's demand, the constable shall proceed to sell as if no claim had been made. 

In case of a jury trial to settle ownership the Justice trying the claim must be careful that his record shows the proceedings to be according to the scope of his authority, i. e., that he has jurisdiction. The claim must be filed with him, to give him jurisdiction; and it must so appear on his record; also, that the execution was out of a Small Cause Court, who were the parties, by what constable the levy was made, who is the claimant, etc. 

The claim is not to be vague or uncertain, and the proof must be confined on the trial to the articles claimed. The claim cannot then be amended to include different or other articles from those incorporated in the original notice. (Baird v. Johnson, 2 Gr. 120).

The judgment awarded will be as to the ownership of the property, and not for an amount of money. Consequently, while it should state who is to pay costs, there is no judgment for costs so that execution can issue. If the parties to the trial of the claim to property do not voluntarily pay the costs as adjudged, the remedy is by an action for them. (Ibid).

A claim to property levied upon may be made by a landlord who has a lien upon the chattels for rent; and in order to allow of such claim being made, it is enacted that, in case any goods or chattels shall lie or be in or upon any messuages, lands or tenements which are leased, they shall not be sold, even if removed from the premises, until ten days after such removal; and then, before the sale, all rent due up to the time of the sale shall be paid to the landlord, not exceeding one year's rent; provided, however, that the landlord shall claim the same within ten days from the time of removal by written notice to the constable. (C. 

S. 3067, § 5). If the constable does sell before ten days, he must pay the landlord the rent first, out of the proceeds, and an action will lie against him for any deficiency. The mere sale within ten days will be considered as a removal of the goods under the statute so as to make the constable responsible for a violation of his duty. (Ryerson v. Quackenbush, 2 Dutch. 249). 

Sale under execution

The property levied upon, if not claimed by others, or exempted from sale by an appraisement, etc., as heretofore stated, is to be sold as follows: The constable shall give notice by ad-

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

vertisements, signed by himself and put up in three of the most public places in the municipality where the goods and chattels were taken, of the time and place where they will be exposed to sale, at least five days before the time appointed for selling them, and therein describe the goods and chattels so taken. At the time and place so appointed, he shall expose them to sale by public vendue, and strike them off to the highest bidder, and pay the money thence arising to the plaintiff, or in case of his absence to the Justice. Within thirty days from the time he shall receive the execution he is to make return to the Justice who issued the same of the proceedings had thereon (see below), and the Justice must make a record thereof in his docket. (S. C. A., § 62). 

The sale must be public, and above every suspicion of fraud. 

Only that which is levied upon and advertised can be sold. 

The constable should cry the sale himself, in person, if possible, and the same constable who made the levy. He may sell for cash only, or make other conditions, if thereby he can realize more for the property and if the plaintiff consents. The law contemplates a sale for cash, and, at all events, will hold the constable responsible for the payment of actual money in satisfaction of the judgment. Where, however, the plaintiff in execution purchases at the sale, the custom is to consider the amount of his purchase so much paid upon the execution, for which the plaintiff will give the constable his receipt.

A private sale is not lawful, nor a sale upon the Sabbath. 

And it must be before sunset.

The constable may make the usual rules of a public auction. whereby it is conditioned that in case the highest bidder refuses to pay his bid, the property may be sold again, and the latter must make up any deficiency, and also making the constable the judge of the disputes of bidders. He must have some conditions and adhere to them.

The property must be sold in separate articles, unless a sale in lots would realize a greater price. When the constable has sold sufficient to satisfy the execution he must stop; he has no right to sell on because he has advertised more property. Any of the parties concerned may purchase, except the constable, who cannot, either directly or indirectly.

The constable must adjourn the sale if there are no purchasers, and may, at the request of either party, at his discretion. He should give every indulgence to the defendant consistent with his duty in obeying the process, and without compensation. If he has illegally advertised, he must advertise again. 

Constable may demand a bond

When no written claim is put in to the constable for prop-

EXECUTION 

241 erty, he will nevertheless be liable in damages if he sells goods and chattels not belonging to the defendant. Accordingly, where he has doubt about the ownership, and a third party claims, or whether any claim at all be made or not, but doubt exists, he may demand a bond of indemnity from the plaintiff before selling. 

But unless demanded, the plaintiff is not obliged to tender it, nor will the want of such voluntary tender excuse the constable from executing the writ. (Harris v. Kirkpatrick, 6 Vr. 393).

Liability of the constable 

If the constable to whom any execution is delivered shall not perform the duties prescribed by the statute respecting such execution, he shall be liable to pay to the person in whose favor the execution issued, the debt or damages and costs to be recovered by action on contract, with double costs by the person so injured. 

(S. C. A., § 71). 

If it shall appear that the constable has received the money or any part thereof on any execution for which a suit is brought and not performed his duty in paying it over, he shall pay the plaintiff treble costs. (Ibid). 

Merely putting an execution into the hands of a constable does not make him liable for the debt. There must be a nonperformance of some positive duty. (Bennet v. Bozorth, 2 Penn. 543). 

Return of execution

Every execution must be returned by the constable to the Justice who issued it within thirty days from the time he receives it. (S. C. A., § 61). The Justice is not permitted to make it returnable at a later date, nor the constable to withhold it by consent of parties. It must be returned with the constable's written indorsement as to how he has executed the writ. An alias execution may be issued immediately after its return; and goods levied upon by the first execution will continue to be bound by the levy.

The constable must return any money made upon the execution at the same time that he returns it into court. He cannot apply it in payment of another execution in his hands against the person who is plaintiff in the first execution, and defendant in the second; for it is not the goods and chattels of the former until paid over to him. (Crane v. Freese, 1 Harr. 305). 

Should the return day be on Sunday he should return it the preceding Saturday. 

A void writ the constable is not bound to return at all. But he will not be excused from returning the execution by an agreement between the parties to suspend proceedings.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Should the plaintiff direct the constable to return the writ to the Justice unsatisfied, the lien of his levy will not continue, but it will leave the property free of control. 

Execution against wages, salary, etc.

By an Act of 1915, which was amended last by P. L. 1933, Chap. 102, when a judgment has been recovered and an execution thereon has been returned wholly or partly unsatisfied, and "any wages, debts, earnings, salary, income from trust funds, or profits are due and owing to the judgment debtor, or shall thereafter become due and owing to him to the amount of $18 or more per week, the judgment creditor [the plaintiff] may apply to the Court in which said judgment was recovered or the Court having jurisdiction of the same, without notice to the judgment debtor" for an order for an execution against the same.

This statute is thought by some lawyers not to be applicable to The Small Cause Court, and, on the whole this is our view. 

We know of no decision on this subject in any of the high Courts. 

II. EXECUTION AGAINST BOTH CHATTELS AND BODY 

Execution against the body (capias)

This writ, known as the capias ad satisfaciendum (“that you take the body to satisfy") directs the constable to take the body of the defendant into custody, yet only if he has not sufficient goods to satisfy the judgment; and he is not necessarily brought before the Justice, but is conveyed to jail without any other or further order.

The language of the writ must follow the statute, which directs that the constable, "for want of sufficient goods and chattels whereon to levy" shall "take the body" of the defendant, "and convey and deliver him to the sheriff of the county." (S. C. A., § 64). 

Foundation of the capias-execution

The foundation of the execution against the body is, first, a judgment; second, where a warrant had issued and remains in force; and third, that the action, being founded on Contract or 

Tort, due proof of concealment of property, of the value of $50 or more is made by affidavit. It is to be used only in the cases stated in the statute. (See S. C. A., § 51). 

It cannot be used against a woman. (§ 50). 

Order for a capias-execution

If a capias be proper, and is desired by plaintiff, a written

EXECUTION 

243 order that the execution be against the body, in default of goods and chattels, must first be made by the Justice. (S. C. A., § 52). 

This order should specify the ground upon which it is based, so as to show on its face that it comes within the provisions of the statute. It is not the mere adjudication of the Justice that "proof was made to his satisfaction that the defendant had fraudulently contracted the debt," or "that he has property or rights in action which he fraudulently conceals," etc., that must appear in the order, but the facts, or such of the facts in the affidavit or affidavits filed, which actually satisfied the Justice. (Browne ads. 

Titus, 1 Vr. 340).

At the time of the delivery of the defendant to the sheriff, the constable should deliver to the sheriff or jailer a copy of the execution, take his receipt upon the original execution and return the latter to the Justice who issued it, the Justice making a record thereof in his docket. (S. C. A., § 64).

The constable cannot refuse to execute the writ and arrest defendant on the ground of any irregularity in the process or proceedings, provided the Court has jurisdiction of the matter. 

He is bound to serve it and is expressly protected by statute from legal liability for damages. (Ibid, § 55; Woodruff v. Barrett, 3 

Gr. 40).

The Justice must furnish the defendant, or his agent, on request, a certified copy of the order or affidavit upon which the warrant of execution is founded. (§ 57). 

Application for discharge from jail of person under capias-execution

The defendant, after the order of arrest is made, has four opportunities to become free, viz.: 

1. He may apply to a Justice of the Supreme Court, or a 

Circuit or Common Pleas Judge, or a Supreme Court Commissioner, to set aside the order for a capias, so far as it authorizes the taking of the body, the defendant having first given reasonable notice to the plaintiff of such application; and if such Judge or Commissioner shall deem the proofs made insufficient to warrant the issuing of the process against the body, he may make order that the Justice's order, so far as it authorizes the taking of the defendant's body, be set aside. (S. C. A., § 53). 

There is an exception as to the application to a Justice of the Supreme Court, however. If he was applied to under S. C. A., § 15, for a capias and refused it, defendant cannot reapply. But if a Circuit or Common Pleas Judge, or Commissioner, refused it before, a Supreme Court Judge may rehear the matter. (Ibid, §§ 53, 58). 

For the purpose of such review of proceedings the Justice

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

of the Peace shall furnish to the defendant, or his agent, on request, a certified copy of the order and affidavits upon which the capias issued and such copy may be used before the Judge or Commissioner, who may make order thereupon in the same manner as if the original order and affidavits were produced before him. (§ 57).

The effect of an order of a Judge or Commissioner setting the order for the capias aside is to discharge the defendant from arrest, or liability to arrest. The order is to be filed with the Justice, and a copy of it (certified by the Justice) served on the sheriff, or jailer, whereupon the defendant is to be discharged. 

(§ 56). 

2. He may apply for his release, under the "Insolvent Debtors Act," to the Court of Common Pleas. (C. S. 2824, § 2). 

3. If the action arose upon contract, he may apply to a 

Supreme Court Justice for relief from imprisonment by writ of habeas corpus. (C. S. 2639, § 2).

Upon habeas corpus the question of the legality of the imprisonment is decided, and defendant is not subject to re-arrest for the same cause; but that determination has no bearing upon the plaintiff's right to collect his judgment. 

4. By payment, or satisfaction of the judgment, whereupon the prisoner is to be discharged by order of the Justice issuing the capias. 

Effect of an escape under a capias-execution 

If a prisoner upon capias makes his escape from jail, he may be re-arrested upon a new warrant of execution or have other writs of execution against him the same as if the first warrant had not been issued. (C. S. 2248, § 21).

If an officer permits him to go at large and he escapes, the officer is liable to an action for the amount of the judgment and costs. (Woodruff v. Barrett, 3 Gr. 40). It is also a misdemeanor and the officer is to be disqualified from holding any office under the State. (C. S. 1746, § 8). 

Return of a capias-execution

The usual return to an execution against the body is that the officer has taken the defendant whose body he has ready to deliver and does deliver to the sheriff of the county. Thereupon the sheriff or jailer is to give a receipt for defendant's body upon the execution, which is then to be returned to the Justice, who must make a record of it in his docket. Or the return may be that the defendant is not to be found in the county. If the return is made that he is not to be found, the plaintiff may proceed against his bail, if he has any.

Executors and Administrators

Actions by and against executors and administrators Executors, administrators, guardians, etc., are to sue in their representative characters. Formerly all the executors had to join, by name, in an action brought by them, whether they had all qualified under the will or not. (Cole v. Smalley, 1 Dutch. 374). 

But now those who have qualified and not renounced may bring suit. (C. S. 4058, § 25).

In actions against executors, etc., only those who have administered need be joined; and the executors of a deceased obligor cannot be joined in an action with a surviving obligor, but the suit is to be brought, or will survive (if begun in the lifetime of the deceased), against the survivor only. Thus where,

in a suit on a promissory note against three defendants as joint and several makers, one of the defendants dies pending the suit, the action survives against the other defendants, but cannot be continued against the survivors and the representatives of the deceased. (Fisher v. Allen, 7 Vr. 203).

An executor or administrator obtaining letters in another State may prosecute an action in this State if he first file with the Register of the Prerogative Court or with the Surrogate of any county wherein there are lands affected by the suit, an exemplified copy of the will and his letters. (C. S. 2266, § 22).

Administrators, having a joint power, must sue and be sued jointly. If they are separated in the action, no written plea is necessary to be filed with the Justice, but a non-suit may be asked for and should be given upon motion, if there is sufficient proof of the non-joinder. (Ryerson v. Ryerson, 1 South. 363).

But the administrators of a deceased partner are not to be sued with the survivors. (Hedden v. Van Ñess, 1 Penn. 84).

Miscellaneous 

As to limitation of actions on bond of executor, etc., see general title "Limitation of Actions."

As to executors, etc., being witnesses, see general title “Evidence."

An executor or administrator may be held to answer in civil actions, if he wastes the estate or converts it to his own use. (C. 

S. 2261, § 6). [For a Form of affidavit to an account filed with an executor or administrator, see Form 10]. 

Fees and Costs

I. IN CIVIL OR SEMI-CIVIL ACTIONS 

Rule as to who shall pay costs

The first general rule is that the party making the costs is primarily responsible to the Justice for their payment. That is to say, the plaintiff, who asks for a summons, becomes indebted to the Justice for the cost of issuing it. When he files his demand, or asks for a venire, he makes such costs, and is the party directly responsible for them. Should he withdraw his suit at any time previous to judgment he is liable to pay these costs, and perhaps more, but in the first instance these, which are his own. 

So, when the defendant files a written plea, he owes the cost of filing it to the Justice. If he demand the venire, or obtain subpoenas for witnesses, the Justice makes it a charge against him, and not the plaintiff.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

In a word, every performance by the Justice of a duty in civil cases, to which there is attached by law a fee, is, as a rule, at the request of one party or the other, and of him the fee should be collected. When both parties ask for the performance of a duty as in the case of an adjournment agreed upon by the parties-the one-half of the cost should be charged against each party. 

If neither party makes a cost, but the Justice himself-as in case he voluntarily adjourns to suit his convenience—there are no proper costs to be paid. 

Costs on final judgment

The costs of the successful party form part of his judgment. 

When the plaintiff succeeds, judgment is given him for a sum, due on contract or for damages, as the case may be, and costs, the amount of which is entered in words at length, the same as the entry of the judgment proper, but distinct from it. The costs are always to be noted separately from the judgment in the docket, and so indorsed on the execution. 

When the defendant succeeds, the judgment is in his favor, with costs against the plaintiff for what the defendant has expended, or is liable for, and no more. 

The Justice sometimes makes the mistake of including in the judgment the costs of both parties, because such costs are due him. Thus, if the verdict is for defendant, it is an error for him to include with the defendant's costs the costs of the summons, etc., which make the plaintiff's costs, and which the plaintiff is bound to pay to the Justice (not to the defendant), irrespective of the judgment. The costs included in the judgment must be of the prevailing party.

Exception to general rule-executors and administrators There is an exception to the general rule concerning costs in the case of plaintiff executors and administrators, who sue only in a representative capacity, and are nonsuited, or discontinue or withdraw an action without defendant's consent, but where they may lawfully do so. Then defendant's costs are not to be taxed against the plaintiff and a judgment given for them. (S. C. A., § 47). 

Costs of jury

Ordinarily the costs of a jury will fall wholly upon the unsuccessful party, but the statute also says: "When the plaintiff in any action on contract shall demand a jury of twelve men, and the jury shall find a sum in favor of the plaintiff, not exceeding fifty dollars, then the plaintiff shall pay one-half of the costs of the jury." (S. C. A., § 102).

This applies to actions on contract only. If the action is in 

Tort, the costs will follow the judgment irrespective of the amount involved. 

Justice's remedy for unpaid fees

The Justice may demand his fee of a plaintiff or defendant as soon as a service is rendered and sometimes in advance. (See infra). But he is not to look entirely to the party against whom judgment is given for fees due the opposite side; otherwise he might often be unable to collect his fees. He should, unless he chooses to wait, collect them of the party making the costs; then, on the payment of the judgment, if the other party has advanced the fees to him they are to be returned. 

If either party fails to pay his own costs, the remedy is by an action on Contract. The Justice may bring the action before another Justice of the Peace, to recover his fees the same as any other legal demand. 

Prepayment of costs

The Justice may require prepayment of fees to a limited extent, if he deems it proper to do so. In other words before he issues a summons, he may require payment of his fees and also the constable's fees for its service; so before he files a demand, or draws a venire. It is not usual to do so unless there is doubt of their payment, but it is his right under the common law, not under any statute. He cannot, however, require prepayment of fees for the jury when the demand for it is made (see 

39 Vr. 232), unless a statute so declares, for these are not fees due to him. Under the Bastardy Act, however, it is expressly stated that he is to require the costs of issuing the venire and of the jury. (C. S. 185, § 6).

The statute takes care of the advance fees of a constable by declaring that "no constable, or other officer, authorized to serve a subpoena, summons, or other mesne process issued out of The Small Cause Court, shall be required to serve such process until his legal fees and mileage for so doing shall have been paid to him." (S. C. A., § 103). An execution is not a "mesne" process. 

In case of appeal, it is enacted that: "No appeal from the judgment of a Justice shall be allowed until the party applying for the same shall, in addition to the matters now required by law, pay to said Justice all costs incurred by him, except such as shall be adjudged to the prevailing party." (Ibid, § 104).

So, too, certain costs must be prepaid to the clerk of the Common Pleas before that Court can be required to hear the appeal. (Ibid, § 105).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE Effect of tender 

It frequently happens that a defendant tenders to the plaintiff, in presence of witnesses, the sum which he believes to be lawfully due to the plaintiff. If it is refused, and the plaintiff afterward sues but recovers no more than the sum tendered, he is not entitled to costs. But the tender must be proved, and it must not be made on a Sunday.

If his tender is made after suit brought, it must be by payment into Court, from which period, if the judgment entered be not for a greater sum, there can be no more costs recovered of defendant than was incurred up to the time of the tender. 

There is no provision made in The Small Cause Court Act respecting tender after suit brought, but the common law rule prevails as stated above. 

Action stayed if prior costs unpaid

When judgment for costs are adjudged to either party, and there is a failure to pay, whether with or without execution, further prosecution of the action by the defaulting party may be stayed upon application by the opposite party. So in case of nonsuit, or dismissal, and a subsequent action for the same cause between the same parties, the suit may be stayed until the costs of the former action are paid. The matter is in the discretion of the Justice. (Sooy v. M'Kean, 4 Hal. 86). 

Witnesses' fees allowed

The law allows the fees of but three witnesses and for the service of subpoenas upon but three witnesses, to be taxed against the defeated party. (S. C. A., § 100). But only if subpoenaed. 

Doubling costs

Costs are sometimes to be doubled or trebled as a punishment for those liable in penal or quasi-criminal actions, but only when the statute so requires. This is done by taxing the single costs, and multiplying them by two, or by three. (Shields v. 

Lozear, 5 Vr. 530). 

Settlement out of Court

When the parties settle out of Court and make no provision for the costs, the rule is that each party pays his own costs to the Justice. 

On report of referees

The referees should report what costs are incurred before them, including the number of days in which they took testimony,

the number of witnesses examined, etc., and award them to the victorious party; and the Justice on entering up judgment shall include the lawful costs. (S. C. A., § 108; see also under general title "Referees"). 

Of expert witnesses

There is no law in this State as to the fees to be paid expert witnesses for expert opinions. Of course the ordinary subpoena fee will bring the witness into Court, and no other is taxable, but perhaps he may decline to testify to professional opinions until paid by the person whose witness he is. (See 1 N. J. L. J. 97; 6 

N. J. L. J. 240). 

Entry of costs in docket

To carry out the rule to charge each party for his own costs requires a careful entry of every item of costs, which should be put in the margin of the docket. These should be grouped under the two heads of "plaintiff's costs" and "defendant's costs." The statute requires the entry of costs in detail in the docket, and the amount paid him by each party. (S. C. A., § 113).

Comments on some foregoing items

Below are brief comments upon most items of the fee bill, so far as they relate to the Justice: 

1. This is for preparing the summons, and will not be increased or diminished by the number of defendants, as all the names are to be in one summons. It includes the drawing, signing, sealing and indorsement, but no copies. In 

2. The copies necessary are one for each defendant. case of partners, one copy is allowed for each. In case of corporation, one only is necessary, if the service is upon one officer, as the law designs in all ordinary instances. 

3. Governed by the same rule as the summons. above. 

See (1) 4. A single order only is necessary, for which this one fee is given. 

5. Applies to every civil suit, and also in case of confessed judgment. 

6. This is for recording the return in the Justice's docket. 

7. This is for taking and accepting the recognizance in cases where defendant is held to bail. If the constable takes the recognizance, this fee of 50 cents goes to the constable, (see S. C. A., § 20) and the Justice will receive only 15 cents for filing the same. 

8. Although this motion is made by the defendant, the costs will fall upon the plaintiff (in the judgment), and is for the entry in the docket. 

9. For the entry in the docket, usually upon the plaintiff's motion, and, therefore, his costs. 

10. This is for the writ calling a jury, and includes drawing the writ, signing, sealing and recording the fact in the docket, including the constable's return; and it is a charge in the first instance against the party calling the jury. 

11. This fee is for each separate oath administered, whether to the constable who takes charge of a jury or to witnesses, but not the oath to the jury; see (13) below. Each oath to the witness is to be charged to the party whose witness he is; that to the constable in taking charge of a jury to the party demanding the jury. The charge does not apply to affidavits outside of a civil cause before the Justice. 

12. This charge is permitted to the Justice for each witness, no matter how many, but no additional charges are allowed for "copies," (and it is to be remembered that subpoenas can only be taxed in the bill of costs on three witnesses). 

If the cause is adjourned, no new subpoenas being necessary for the same witnesses there can be no fees for new subpoenas to the same witnesses. The witnesses must attend on the adjourned day under

the original subpoena, although they may first demand their fees for the adjourned day. 

13. It is immaterial whether the jury is composed of six or twelve men; the fee for swearing them is the same and is to be charged against the party calling the jury. 

14. This is for the record in the docket. 

15. This is also for the record in the docket. 

16. For each copy of the rule of reference, to be charged to the party demanding it. One should be given to each of the referees, and the cost may be taxed against the unsuccessful party. 

17. For the record in the docket, to be charged against the party who obtains the judgment. 

18. For issuing the execution, and making record thereof in the docket. In an alias execution, and the pluries writs, the same fee attaches to each. 

19. For recording in the docket the return of the constable. 

20. To be charged against the party applying for the certiorari. 

21. One hundred words make a sheet or folio. Any excess less than an additional hundred are usually charged as another folio. Thus four hundred and twenty words are considered to be five folios. The party asking the copy must pay the fee. It is not taxable in the bill of costs against the opposite party. This charge is not to be made when a complete transcript is given. (See next item). 

22. This is when no transcript is necessary, but simply the statement now required in docketing a judgment. 

23. Applies to all suits in which no summons or warrant is employed. 

24. Applies to summons, state of demands, affidavits, recognizances and every paper required to be filed before the Justice. 

25. To be taxed to the party asking the commission, and cannot afterward be recovered from the opposite party. 

26. Same as last stated; it is for the docket record. 

27. For entering the costs in the margin of the docket. 

28. For taking an affidavit which a Justice is authorized to take, in any action under "The Small Cause Court Act." It does not apply to taking ordinary affidavits not in a cause brought under that Act; then the legal fee is 12 cents. (C. S. 2289, § 3). 

29. To be paid by the party seeking the adjournment; can not be taxed in final costs as part of judgment. 

30. This is the trial fee, whether the Justice or a jury determines the cause, and goes against the party losing the cause. 

31. When the defendant is not present, or, if present, offers no testimony to rebut plaintiff's case, and does not cross-examine, the case is not contested, and the Justice only receives fifty cents

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

for the hearing. But cross-examination may amount practically to a contest. 

32. This is a charge in addition to making the transcript of the judgment, and is charged against the appellant. 

33. This is the fee of the Justice for taking a deposition by commission. "Per folio" means 100 words. 

34. The fee is for drawing, sealing and issuing the same. 

35. The Justice is liable to a penalty of $50 for taking an excess of fifty cents for drawing a paper necessary in any proceeding in his Court. (S. C. A., § 10). The fee is to be paid for by party asking Justice to draw the paper and is not chargeable in bill of costs. 

36. Usually applies to forcible entry and detainer cases. 

Fees to witnesses in Common Pleas

The following are the fees allowed to witnesses in the Common Pleas. (C. S. 2288):

For every witness attending a Court, or commissioners, or referees, or arbitrators in his own county, for each day

Every witness from a foreign county, attending a Court, or commissioners, or referees, or arbitrators, after the rate of one dollar a day, in which shall be included his or her going to and returning from the same, allowing one day for every thirty miles from his or her place of residence ... 50 1 00 The fee and mileage must be tendered the witness to make the subpoena effective and compulsory. And where a witness is subpoenaed for one day, and is asked to return upon the next, or an adjourned day, another day's fees and mileage must be tendered him, although no second written subpoena is necessary. 

A witness out of the State, who consents to come into the State, is entitled to mileage for his travel from the New Jersey 

State line, and no farther. (Den v. Johnson, 1 Green 156).

Costs on docketed judgment

On docketing a judgment in the Common Pleas the Justice receives 75 cents for issuing the statement required, and the clerk of the Court for docketing the judgment, $2.00. (S. C. A., § 

100, as amended; but see P. L. 1926, p. 396 as to clerk's fee). 

Costs on trial of property

In a trial of property seized by final process, the Justice must tax the costs as in other cases, and they must be paid by the plaintiff at whose suit the property was taken and seized, if the claimant obtains a verdict in his favor, and by the claimant, if the verdict is found against him. But the Justice cannot render a judgment for the costs, or award execution for their payment. When he has taxed and awarded the costs his jurisdiction ends; and if they are not paid voluntarily by the party liable, the only remedy for their recovery is by an action on the award of costs; and such award furnishes conclusive evidence of liability and right to recover. Nor need any copy of the taxed costs be served on the party liable to pay them before suit brought. (Cole v. Lunger, 13 Vr. 381; Baird v. Johnson, 2 Gr. 120).

Costs under Landlord and Tenant Act 

The usual fees are allowed for services under this Act; the language of the statute being that "the same fees shall be allowed to the Justice, constable, witnesses and jurors as are provided for like services by "The Small Cause Act;' and the constable, for executing the process of possession, shall receive the sum of one dollar." (C. S. 3074, § 19; S. C. A., § 100, as amended).

Mode of obtaining costs in criminal cases 

As the Criminal Procedure Act (C. S. 1852, § 106, as amended by Laws 1924, p. 443; N. J. Cum. Supp. 891) states, a magistrate or constable cannot demand or receive of a party, who applies to them to set the criminal machinery in motion, any fee or reward. The State is the real complainant in all criminal matters, and it is a part of its functions, through the several counties, to pay all bills incurred in prosecutions.

The following is the statutory mode for obtaining payment of fees in ordinary criminal proceedings: "Every magistrate shall make a bill of particulars of the costs in each criminal case before him and send up the same with

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

the papers in the case to the clerk of the grand jury in his county, if there be such a clerk, and if there be none, then to the prosecutor of the pleas in such county, and if an indictment be found in the case, said bill shall be handed by such clerk or prosecutor, as the case may be, to the county clerk, who shall review and correct the same, if necessary, and shall certify the correct amount to the county collector, who thereupon shall pay the amount so certified to the magistrate; and if no indictment be found in any case, or if the proceedings in any case be dismissed by the magistrate, and in the judgment of the prosecutor of the pleas the proceedings in such case were taken by the magistrate honestly, in good faith, and were calculated to promote the administration of justice, and the costs therein ought to be paid out of the county treasury, and he shall so certify on the bill of particulars of costs in the case, said bill shall be paid by the county collector; provided, that no fees or costs shall be paid by the county collector for the services of any Judge, Justice or officer of any Police or Criminal Court where such Judge, Justice or officer receives a salary." (See, however, next subhead as to exceptions in certain municipalities). "In case a person is convicted before a Justice of the Peace for any offense and sentenced to imprisonment, or to pay a fine and costs and committed until fine and costs are paid, it shall be the duty of the Justice before whom any such conviction is had, to make a bill of the particulars of costs in such case, attached to the commitment, and also certify and send up a copy of said bill of particulars of costs, with the conviction in said case, to the county clerk, who shall review and correct the same, if necessary, and shall certify the correct amount to the county collector, who thereupon shall pay the amount so certified to the said Justice; for his services in taxing said bill of particulars of costs the county clerk shall be paid a fee of twenty-eight cents for each bill of particulars of costs so taxed." (C. S. 1854, § 108; but see as to clerk's taxing fee, P. L. 1926, p. 398).

The costs are usually indorsed upon the back of the warrant -both those of the Justice and of the constable. In making out bills of particulars, however, to send up for payment, it is customary for the Justice to make out his own bill of costs separately and send it to the clerk of the grand jury, if any, otherwise to the prosecutor of the pleas. The constable makes out his bill also separately. He is to receive his costs whether there is indictment or not, under the following enactment: "The several constables of this State shall be entitled to receive from the collector of the county wherein any warrant issues, their lawful fees for serving any criminal warrant that may be issued by any Justice of the Peace or Police Justice duly quali-

fied and commissioned as such in any county in this State, whether any such offender be indicted or not for the offense of which he, she or they may have been charged." (C. S. 2293, § 25).

In usual practice, therefore, this separate bill of the constable, when certified to by the Justice, goes direct to the county collector and is paid by him. In cases of doubt the Prosecutor of the Pleas should be consulted.

Prevention of forest fires Fires

A new Act as to forest fires was passed in 1931. (P. L., p. 

857). It is elaborate and must be consulted by any magistrate acting in the matter. Jurisdiction is given to District and Judicial 

Courts, all Justices of the Peace, and every Police Justice and 

Recorder. The prosecutor is the Board of Conservation and De velopment. 

Municipalities may make ordinances

Municipalities may make ordinances as to the use of inflammable and explosive materials, so as not to cause fire. (P. L. 

1917, p. 354).

Inquiry into origin of fire of building, maliciously caused Whenever the affidavit of a creditable [credible] witness is made before any coroner, sheriff, or Justice of the Peace, that there is ground to believe that any building has been maliciously set on fire or attempted to be, and the request is made to him by the president, secretary or agent of any insurance company to investigate the truth of such belief, such officer or magistrate must investigate. The officer will proceed much as coroners in

FIRES 

277 case of inquests, and he will possess the powers coroners have in such inquests. (See general title "Coroners"). 

Necessarily the officer or magistrate must call a jury. Such jury, after being sworn, will inspect the place of the fire, and, after receiving testimony, will deliver their inquisition to the magistrate. This inquisition must certify how the fire happened, or was attempted, and who is guilty thereof as principal or accessory if the jury are so able to certify. The magistrate may then issue a warrant to arrest the guilty party, if he is not already in custody; may bind over witnesses; must take down the testimony before the jury in writing, and tax the costs as in other inquests. 

The testimony and all the papers in the case must be sent to the next Court of Oyer and Terminer (i. e., to the clerk). The expenses must be borne by the insurance company directing the investigation. (C. S. 2324).

In this matter the Justice acts as magistrate, and not in The 

Small Cause Court.
