Fish and Game 

Statutes for their protection

The general statute "for the protection of certain kinds of birds, game and fish, to regulate their method of capture and provide open and close seasons for such capture and possession," is the Act of April 14, 1903, (C. S. 2506), but with many amendments and supplements every year. As to birds, this Act applies to game birds only. There are other statutes relating to birds other than game. (Ibid, p. 90, etc.). If a Justice desires to know the present condition of these laws, and exactly what is or what is not lawful, application should be made to Mr. Walter H. 

Fell, Secretary, Board of Fish and Game Commissioners, of

Trenton, for a pamphlet copy of the laws. 

We do not undertake to give even a résumé of all the game laws, but a few of statements of what is illegal follows: 

What is illegal at all times 

To hunt without a proper license. 

To sell any squirrel, deer, migratory or non-migratory game bird or song bird, but rabbits, killed in this State, are excepted during the open season and 10 days thereafter; provided that rabbits coming from another State may be sold at all times; provided that game birds and game animals raised under a wholly enclosed preserve license may be sold at any time if legally tagged, but no pheasant raised under a license to propagate pheasants in a semi-wild state shall be sold. Migratory water fowl shall bear a well defined mark in the form of a "V" which must have been removed from the web of the foot before the birds attain the age of four weeks. Certain imported game, also deer and pheasants, mallard and black ducks, coming from another State may be sold if legally tagged by State authorities.

It is illegal to sell any black or Oswego bass, except for propagating purposes, and their importation into or exportation from the State for commercial purposes is illegal.

To have in possession in the woods or fields during the open

season for killing deer any missile except buckshot or to have any missile larger than number two, [now number four] shot in possession in the woods or fields at any time other than the open season for killing deer.

To use in hunting fowl or animals of any kind any firearm holding more than two cartridges at one time, or that may be fired more than twice without reloading, or to use a rifle for hunting in the woods or fields. 

To take or attempt to take any game except by the use of guns held at arm's length. 

To use a silencer on any gun or firearm for hunting game.

To have ferrets in possession in woods or fields. 

To hunt migratory or other game birds between sunset and one-half hour before sunrise. They cannot be taken with airplane, powerboat or boat under sail, or from any boat, seaweed or structure anchored, placed or staked at a greater distance than 100 feet from shore or ice, or naturally heaped seaweed, or with a gun larger than 10 gauge. 

To capture, kill, injure or to have in possession insectivorous and certain other birds, and to rob birds' nests. 

To remove the skin or feathers or to mutilate any wild bird or animal in the fields or woods for the purpose of concealing sex or identity.

To sow, deposit or place any rye, wheat, oats or corn or other cereal, except wild celery and wild rice, in any of the salt or fresh waters of this State within four hundred feet of any gunning point for the purpose of decoying or baiting wild fowl.

For a person to go into the woods or fields with a hound or firearm, or for dogs to run at large in the woods or fields, except during the rabbit season, but the occupant of a farm may allow his dogs to run at large on land which he occupies, except during the deer season; and persons may train dogs without firearms in daylight at any time except during the deer season, or hunt foxes with hounds and firearms in daylight from November 10th to

April 30th, both dates inclusive, except during the deer season; no permits required. The law does not prohibit the legal hunting for deer, woodcock, snipe, rail, mudhen, raccoon or water fowl during the legal season therefor. Penalty $100 for persons hunting foxes who kill any protected bird or animal. All foxes killed shall be reported to the warden of the county or to the Fish and 

Game Commission at Trenton within 48 hours. No Sunday hunting permitted. Persons may hunt raccoons with dogs and firearms (and without permit) from November 1st to December 31st, excepting during the deer season, between sunset and sunrise. 

To have any live fox in possession without permission of the

Board of Fish and Game Commissioners, or to liberate any fox in the State regardless of where said fox was obtained.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

To have trapped game in possession. To shoot into any squirrel's nest.

To set any trap, snood or snare above level of the ground. 

To pursue, shoot at or kill any bird or animal while in an automobile or to hunt for and shoot at same by aid of lights carried on such automobile.

To hunt on Sunday or carry firearms in the fields or woods or on the waters on Sunday. 

To hunt for any squirrel, quail, partridge, pheasant, woodcock or rabbit while there is snow upon the ground in such condition that such game may be tracked in any area where hunting is being done. 

To hunt ducks and snipe on Shark River or on the shores thereof. 

To take trout, bass, pike, pickerel and pike-perch between 9 

P. M. and daylight.

To take or attempt to take any fish in any manner excepting with hook and line, but minnows for bait may be taken with a seine not over 50 feet long in ponds and lakes of over 100 acres and in other waters with a seine not over 30 feet in length. Eels may be taken at all times with wicker baskets anchored on the bottom of streams and ponds. For Delaware River and other tide waters see special laws. 

To pollute streams. To use medicated bait or explosives of any kind for taking fish. To draw off water or place screens in water without permission of the Board of Fish and Game Commissioners. To permit the erection or maintenance of unlawful contrivances for taking game or fish; applies to owners and tenants of lands. To use carp for bait or in any other way to put carp in fresh water.

To haul seines beneath the ice in salt waters. To take fish through the ice in fresh waters, except carp and suckers, which may be taken with a net under the ice between December 1st and March 1st; penalty $20 for any fish taken other than carp and suckers, and from January 1st to January 20th, pike, pickerel, pike-perch and.perch may be taken through the ice in fresh waters with not more than ten lines, each line to have attached thereto not more than one hook; said pike, pickerel, pike-perch and perch caught through the ice not to be sold.

To use set lines in waters inhabited by pickerel, pike, pikeperch, bass or trout, or to use any contrivance in fishing having more than three hooks, or more than one burr of three hooks, or to have such contrivances in possession. 

To spear fish in fresh waters.

To take female crabs with eggs or spawn attached thereto. 

To take crabs in any tidal waters, except Delaware Bay, with a line with more than ten baits attached.

[NOTE.-The taking of white and yellow perch, catfish, sunfish, suckers, carp and eels with hook and line is permitted at all times in all waters of the State, excepting there is a season for white and yellow perch in the Delaware River and its tidal tributaries between New Jersey and Pennsylvania, which is from June 

15th to December 1st].

Additional Acts of 1933 

By Act of June 26, 1933, the Fish and Game Commission shall issue hunting and fishing licenses direct to all clerks and wardens mentioned in the law instead of through the county clerk. 

Also, Act of same date, continues the close season on quail in the counties of Warren, Passaic, Bergen, Sussex, Morris, Essex, Hudson, Union, Somerset and Hunterdon until June 26, 1938. 

By Act of June 26, 1933 (Chapter 319) it is made unlawful for any non-resident male person above the age of fourteen years to angle for fish in the Delaware River throughout its entire length within the jurisdiction of New Jersey or in any inland tidal water of the State unless he first shall have procured a nonresident's and alien's fishing license. This act does not apply to fishing in the Delaware Bay or bays or waters of the Atlantic 

Ocean within the jurisdiction of the State. 

An Act of June 21, 1933, amends Section 3 of the deer law to provide that it shall be unlawful to have any missile larger than number four shot in possession in the woods or fields at any time other than the open season for killing deer. 

An Act of May 10, 1933 (Chapter 153) amends the breeders' license act providing that quail may be raised under the semi-wild provision and changing the time for shooting pheasants under the semi-wild from the regular open season for hunting to the season as follows: November 10 to the following February 28.

There are also a very large number of special laws as to fish or game in various parts of the State. Hunters or fishermen should obtain a full copy of the "Fish and Game Acts," in pamphlet form, from the Secretary of the New Jersey Board of Fish and Game Commissioners in Trenton.

Enforcement of Fish and Game Act 

Actions for penalties under the various Game Acts are not to be brought as in cases of usual penalties when before a Justice, in The Small Cause Court, because there is a specific and exclusive method pointed out, which must be followed, and the jurisdiction is by a Justice as magistrate and not in his civil Court. (Minard v. Dover, 47 Vr. 132).

By the Act of 1897 (C. S. 2556, § 2, as amended Mar. 24, J-18

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

1921; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1341), Justices of the Peace, District

Courts, Recorders and Police magistrates have jurisdiction over persons or corporations accused of violating the fish, game and bird laws; and this whether such officials are in the county where the offense is committed, or where the offender is first apprehended, or where the offender may reside; but Justices have no jurisdiction within the judicial district of a District Court (as per a Supreme Court decision).

The first usual proceeding is a complaint in writing, duly sworn to, of the violation of law. This complaint, if for a penalty, can only be made by a duly commissioned fish and game warden, or a deputy fish and game warden, or a police officer, or constable, or a member of an incorporated fish and game protective association, or the fish and game protector of the State. (§ 16). Proceedings may be begun and process issued and served on Sunday. (§ 15).

The complaint must specify the particular section of the Act violated, the time, place, etc. In all cases a copy of the complaint is to be sent to the Board of Fish and Game Commissioners, addressed to Trenton, N. J. This is done after judgment is rendered on the case, and there should be indorsed on the complaint whether defendant was convicted, or acquitted, or the case appealed. Upon receipt of such complaint the magistrate shall issue a warrant directed "to any constable, police officer, fish and game warden, fish and game protector, or deputy fish and game warden of this State," for the arrest of such person, and shall thereupon determine the guilt or innocence of defendant in a summary way, no jury trial being permitted. (See 87 N. J. L. 512). Upon conviction he shall impose the penalty prescribed in the particular Act violated, together with costs, and if the defendant shall fail to pay the penalty imposed, with costs, he shall be committed to the common jail for a period not exceeding ninety days, or until said penalty and cost are paid. (§ 3 as amended Mar. 24, 1921, and April 12, 1921).

In case a corporation is complained of, the magistrate shall issue a summons, directed as before, to be served on the president, vice-president, secretary, superintendent or manager of such corporation at least five days before the return day, and thereafter the proceedings shall be as in cases against individuals. 

The prevailing party shall recover costs against the other, and the same fees and costs shall be allowed as in trials in The 

Small Cause Court. 

Adjournments may be had for good cause shown, for a period not exceeding thirty days from the return day or from the date of any arrest, but in such case the magistrate shall detain the defendant in custody, unless he shall enter into bond to the State for his appearance upon the day for the hearing, and

thence to any adjourned day, etc., until the final hearing, in double the amount of the penalty to be recovered. 

Moneys recovered as penalties under the fish and game laws of the State shall be paid over to the Board of Fish and Game Commissioners as a rule, but the magistrate should consult the 

Secretary of the Board of Fish and Game Commissioners when in doubt.

In prosecutions instituted under the Act "no further pleadings than the filing of the complaint and the issuing of a warrant shall be necessary on the part of the prosecutor, nor shall any such proceedings be invalidated on account of lack of endorsement of the complaint or the warrant or for insufficiency in the recital of the offense charged; provided, however, that said complaint shall specify the section and the title of the Act charged to have been violated, the time of the commission of the alleged offense and the location where it is charged the offense was committed." (C. S. 2560, § 268).

Proceedings to recover penalties under the Act are to be entitled in the name of the State of New Jersey, with one of the fish and game wardens, or deputy fish and game warden, or a police officer or constable, or member of an incorporated fish and game protective association as prosecutor, and no other person may institute such proceedings. (Ibid, § 264). Appeal

Any party to the proceedings named may appeal from the judgment or sentence of the magistrate to the Court of Common Pleas of the county, by serving a written notice of appeal upon the opposite party within ten days after the date of the judgment and paying the cost of the proceedings, and also by delivering to the magistrate a bond to the opposite party, in double the amount of the judgment appealed from, with at least one sufficient surety, conditioned to prosecute the appeal and to stand to and abide by such further order or judgment as may hereafter be made against said party. [See amendment by P. L. 1933, Chap. 201].

The magistrate shall then send up all papers together with a transcript of the proceedings to the next Court of Common Pleas. 

(§§ 10, 11, C. S. 2558). 

Arrest without warrant

Where the law is violated in view of any constable, police officer, fish and game warden, fish and game protector, deputy fish and game warden, or an officer or member of an incorporated game protective society, such person is authorized without warrant to arrest the offender and carry him before the magistrate of the county (or District Court, if that has the jurisdiction), wherein the arrest is made. Such person shall then make writ-

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

ten complaint under oath, after which the magistrate or Court shall hear the proceedings as otherwise in a summary way. (C. 

S. 2557, § 253 as amend. Mar. 24, 1921; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1342). 

Search Warrant 

Justices of the Peace, District Courts and Police magistrates, "upon receiving proof of probable cause for believing in the concealment of any bird, animal or fish caught, taken, killed, had in possession, under control or shipped, or about to be shipped contrary to law, shall issue a search warrant and cause a search to be made in any place, and to that end may, after demand, and refusal, cause any building, enclosure or car to be entered, and any apartment, chest, box, locker, crate, basket or package to be broken open and the contents thereof examined by the Fish and 

Game Commissioners, fish and game protector or fish and game wardens; all birds, animals or fish, or nets, or fishing appliance or apparatus, seized by the Fish and Game Commissioners, fish and game protector or any of the fish and game wardens, shall be disposed of in such manner as may be directed by the Justice of the Peace, District Court, or Police magistrate before whom the offense is tried." (C. S. 2559, § 267).

Miscellaneous provisions 

Fish and game protectors, fish and game wardens, and deputy fish and game wardens, may serve processes in cases under the Act and be entitled to the same fees as constables. 

No person shall be excused from giving evidence on the ground that it may tend to convict him, or render him liable to prosecution, but such evidence shall not be received against him in any such prosecution.

If persons or corporations are found making use of boats, seines, nets, traps, etc., being apparatus for the unlawful taking of fish, he shall in addition to the penalties prescribed, forfeit such apparatus, and all constables, sheriffs, fish and game wardens, and fish and game protectors, shall seize such apparatus and give notice to the magistrate of such seizure. Such magistrate shall hear and determine in a summary way whether the same was unlawfully used, and if so to make an order directing the confiscation and forfeiture of the same to the use of the Game and Fish Commissioners. (C. S. 2558, § 13, as amended, Mar. 

24, 1921).

Judgments obtained for penalties against a corporation may be docketed in the office of the clerk of the Circuit Court. 

The Act prescribes that where a person is convicted a second time the magistrate, besides imposing the penalty, shall, upon pres-

entation of the record of the former conviction revoke any fishing or hunting license issued to the defendant. 

Trespassing after notice against hunting or fishing When on occupied lands a notice is posted forbidding gunning or fishing, there is a penalty for hunting thereon of $20 and costs, recoverable before any Justice (having jurisdiction), Police Court or Recorder, and the offender may be arrested by the occupier or an officer without warrant and taken to the magistrate. (P. L. 1912, p. 198; § 3, as amend. Mar. 20, 1923; N. J. 

Cum. Supp. 1355).

Flour and Meal Food Products, Etc. 

The manufacture of flour and meal food products The statute makes certain requirements concerning the daily and weekly employment hours of employés in biscuit, bread and cake bakeries and confectionery establishments. Also as to the buildings or rooms employed for the manufacture of biscuit, bread and cake. (C. S. 2586). Various other Acts appear from time to time and need to be consulted. 

Special provisions for recovery of penalties

A supplement of 1903 to the above Act provides that any penalty incurred may be recovered in an action of Debt in any Court having jurisdiction of civil causes, to be brought in the name of any person of full age, or corporation, which action may be commenced, as in ordinary cases, by summons, which need not

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

be indorsed as in qui tam actions, and shall be proceeded with as in ordinary cases. The finding shall be that the defendant has or has not (as the case may be) incurred the penalty claimed in the demand ($100 for the first and $200 for the second offense), and judgment given accordingly. In case of recovery one-half of the amount recovered shall belong to the person or corporation by whom the action is brought and the other half thereof shall be paid by the person or corporation recovering the same to the treasurer of the State; in case execution shall be issued and returned unsatisfied, the Court, on application and two days' notice to the defendant may award execution to take the body of the defendant. (C. S. 2588, § 107).

Food, Drugs and Dairy Products 

Proceedings under Act to secure purity of foods, etc., of 1907 This Act "to secure the purity of foods, beverages, confectionery, condiments, drugs and medicines, and to prevent deception in the distribution and sale thereof," of 1907, is an important one, enforceable by the State Board of Health and also by local Boards. The provisions and penalties are too numerous to state here. (See the Act, C. S. 2564, with various amendments since, e. g., P. L. 1920, p. 432; 1921, p. 155; 1922, pp. 17, 198; 1923, p. 595, and various later ones).

It is sufficient to say that adulterated or misbranded meats, drugs, confectionery, milk (as to skimmed milk, see P. L. 1912, p. 199), cream, vinegar, etc., cannot be sold without penalties, which vary in different cases. Bob veal cannot be sold. There are provisions for cleanliness of establishments where foods, etc., are put up or distributed.

The Act is one in which, when a Justice of the Peace is called upon to act, he acts in The Small Cause Court. (Department of 

Health v. Monheit (1917), 101 Atl. Rep. 413. See also P. L. 

1933, Chap. 243).

Every local board of health has a copy of the Act and its amendments, and, in bringing an action, the Justice should see the Act and learn its exact scope and effect. The plaintiff is to be the State Department of Health or local board of health, and all penalties are to be paid for the use of the State, or local municipality, as one or the other sues (as per P. L. 1911, p. 739; N. J. 

Cum. Supp. 1404).

FOOD, DRUGS AND DAIRY PRODUCTS 

291 In case of judgment for the plaintiff the execution is to be issued against the goods, chattels and body of the defendant, without any express order to the latter effect.

The Act does not provide for a trial by jury, nor for an appeal, but because cognizance is in The Small Cause Court an appeal lies, as in all actions in that Court, except where appeal is expressly excluded by the statute, to the Common Pleas. (Department of Health v. Monheit, supra). 

Condemnation of food 

There is also a provision in section 45 (C. S. 2575, as amended by P. L. 1913, p. 216; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1405), that when a member of the State Department of Health or local board of health or an employé of such board, finds any meat, milk, fish, bird, fowl, vegetable or other food of a perishable nature offered for sale in violation of the Act, or in a state of rottenness, he is to condemn it and may apply to any Justice of the Peace in the county, or District, or Common Pleas, or Circuit Court to have it seized for condemnation and confiscation. Proceedings are begun by a verified complaint, whereupon a warrant issues, directed to the sheriff of the county or any constable to seize and take the articles into possession and bring them to the Justice (or Court); and also a summons (which may be incorporated in the warrant) to be served as a summons. The hearing is to be summary, without jury, and the articles, if the law is violated, are to be confiscated and destroyed or sold. The Act contains other important provisions. The proceeding would be before a Justice as a magistrate. 

Cold storage Act

An important Act of 1916 provides for penalties relating to foods kept in cold storage. (P. L., p. 223; see Supp., P. L. 1921, p. 113; Ñ. J. Cum. Supp. 1437). 

Goods sold in packages

Penalties are provided in an Act of 1916 as to selling food in packages without the net quantity being conspicuously marked on the outside in terms of weight, measure or numerical count, and the Small Cause Court or police magistrate is given jurisdiction. (P. L. 1916, p. 383, as am. by P. L. 1921, p. 157; N. J. Cum. 

Supp. 3856). 

Proceedings under Oleomargarine Act 

There is a special oleomargarine and butterine Act of 1886. (C. S. 2579), but, probably, it is rarely violated in this State, as there seem to be few penalty suits brought under it. The Act

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

is enforceable in every District Court and before any Recorder in any city, or the Justice of the Peace in any county. (C. S. 

2581, § 72, etc., as amended by P. L. 1912, pp. 173, 599; N. J. 

Cum. Supp. 1409).

No person is allowed to offer or expose to sale, or sell, or have in possession for the purposes of sale, any oleomargarine, butterine, suine, or any substance in imitation of actual butter or cheese, etc., unless in tubs and other packages plainly labelled according to the Act. The penalty for violating the Act is $50 for the first offense, and $100 for each subsequent offense. 

On oath or affirmation being made in writing, designating the person who has violated the Act and specifying the particular section violated, the magistrate or Court will thereupon issue a summons or warrant in the name of "The Department of Health of the State of New Jersey," or of a local board of health, which is to prosecute for the penalty or penalties. If a warrant, it is to be returnable forthwith; if a summons, in not less than one nor more than ten entire days; and the process must state what provision of the Act is alleged to be violated. 

On return of the process, or at any time to which the trial may be adjourned, the magistrate or Court shall proceed to hear testimony and give judgment for plaintiff or defendant without the filing of any pleadings. In case judgment be for the plaintiff (which is to be a judgment of conviction in the form stated in the Act; see Form No. 226), execution is to be issued forthwith in the nature of a capias-execution, being against the goods, chattels and person of the defendant; and if he does not pay the amount of the judgment or appeal to the Quarter Sessions within. ten days, he is to be committed to the county jail, the period not to exceed ninety days.

The conviction must be signed by the magistrate or Judge trying the case, and if the penalty be for $200 it must state the reason therefor, namely, that it appeared that the defendant had been previously convicted of a violation of the said Act. 

The hearing may be adjourned from time to time not exceeding thirty days from the return day, in which case the person charged may be bailed in such sum as the magistrate or Court shall deem proper for his appearance at such adjourned date. 

This should be a written recognizance with surety or sureties. In default of bail the defendant may be committed to the common jail until the hearing.

No trial by jury is allowed by the Act. (Newton v. Reed, 10 N. J. L. J. 175; Carter v. Court, 20 Vr. 600).

Within ten days after the trial either the complainant or defendant, upon paying all costs incurred, may appeal from the decision of the Justice to the next Court of Quarter Sessions of the

Proceedings under New Bottle Act of 1925 

By the "New Jersey Bottle Act" of 1925 (P. But this Act does not apply to sales of milk products, for which see P. L. 1933, Chapters 243 and 271.

There are other requirements and the Act must be consulted.

What condensed or evaporated milk must be, in content, and penalty for violation, are stated in an Act of 1922 (P. L., p. 198; 

N. J. Cum. Supp. 1399).

Any person having knowledge of the offense may make complaint before a Justice of the Peace of the county, Police Justice, or Recorder, who shall issue either a summons or warrant.

Forcible Entry and Detainer

The offenses defined The statute makes three classes of entries and detainers. The first is known as forcible entry and detainer; the second as forcible detainer; the third as unlawful detainer, and are thus defined:

I. "If any person shall enter upon or into any lands, tenements or other possessions, and detain or hold the same with force or strong hand, or with weapons, or by breaking open the doors, windows or other part of a house, whether any person be in it or not, or by any kind of violence whatsoever, or by threatening to kill, maim, or beat the party in possession, or by such words, circumstances or actions, as have a natural tendency to excite fear or apprehension of danger, or by putting out of doors, or carrying away the goods of the party in possession, or by entering peaceably and then turning by force, or frightening by threats, or other circumstances of terror, the party out of possession; in such case every person so offending shall be guilty of a forcible entry and detainer within the meaning of this Act.' 

S., 2598, § 2). (C. 

II. "No person, who shall lawfully or peaceably enter upon or into any lands, tenements, or other possessions, shall hold or keep the same unlawfully, and with force, or strong hand, or weapons, or violence, or menaces, or terrifying words, circumstances or actions aforesaid; and it is hereby declared, that whatever words or circumstances, conduct or actions, will make an entry forcible under this Act, shall also make a detainer forcible. 

III. "If any tenant or tenants, for term of life or lives, year or years, or other person or persons, who are or who shall be in possession of any lands, tenements or hereditaments, by, from, or under, or by collusion with such tenant or tenants, shall wilfully and without force, hold over any lands, tenements, or hereditaments, after demand and notice in writing given for the delivery of the possession thereof, by his, her or their landlord or landlords, lessor or lessors, or the person or persons, to whom the remainder or reversion of such lands, tenements or hereditaments shall belong, his, her, or their agent or attorney, thereunto lawfully authorized, then such person or persons so holding over shall be guilty of an unlawful detainer." (§ 5).

The first two classes embrace terms for years, and all estates, whether freehold or less than freehold. But the Act does not extend to any person who has had the uninterrupted occupation for the space of three whole years together, immediately preceding "the complaint so exhibited to the said Justice," and whose estate therein is not ended. (§ 23).

J-19

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

The two offenses of "forcible entry" and "forcible detainer," are by our statute, and always have been, distinct offenses, their difference consisting in the lawfulness of the entry. When the entry is unlawful, whether forcible or not, and the subsequent conduct is forcible and tortious, the offense committed is a forcible entry and detainer. But when the original entry is lawful, and the subsequent holding forcible, then the offense is an unlawful detainer. (Pullen v. Boney, 1 South. 125).

By comparing the first and second with the third class above, it will be observed that in the cases of forcible entry and detainer, and detainer forcible, the tenant in possession, and not the landlord, is the party who may prosecute; while in the case of an unlawful detainer, the landlord prosecutes. This is the only difference in the entire proceedings, except that in the latter case the landlord must give the required notice in writing. (Bennet v. 

Montgomery, 3 Hal. 48).

Until the amendment of 1923 to § 1 of The Small Cause Act that Court was not given jurisdiction of forcible entry and detainer cases, but the Justice acted as magistrate. But now The 

Small Cause Court has jurisdiction. 

The complaint

The complaint must be made in the county where the offense was committed, and cannot be brought elsewhere. It will be without notice to the party, except in case of a landlord for an unlawful detainer, when a reasonable notice must be given. (Crane v. 

Dod, 1 Penn. 341; Mead v. Kirkpatrick, 3 Hal. 368).

The complaint must state that the complainant was in possession, either in fact or in law. (Corlies v. Corlies, 2 Harr. 167). 

The summons

Summons for a jury will thereupon be issued, to be served upon the defendant by the sheriff at least six entire days before the return day. It does not matter where the defendant lives, if in the State; the Justice has cognizance of the offense if it happens in his county, and the summons may be served as well without as within the county. (C. S. 2599, §§ 6, 9).

The forms of summons and venire for the jury are both statutory, and must be exactly followed.

The proceedings are stated by The Small Cause Act to be in that Court (S. C. A., § 100 as am.), and writs, etc., by the Justice should have his official seal. Subpoenas 

The Justice may issue subpoenas for witnesses at the request of either party, in the usual manner, which may be served in any part of the State. (§ 24).

FORCIBLE ENTRY AND DETAINER 

299 Adjournment

Upon the return day of the summons it is not customary to adjourn the trial, as the jury will be present, and it will usually inconvenience every one; but if either party requests it, and "good reasons" are assigned, the Justice may adjourn, not exceeding fifteen days, requiring the applicant to pay costs of such adjournment. (§ 16). 

The hearing 

If the defendant appears and pleads "not guilty," the trial will proceed; so if he does not appear, or, appearing, does not plead to the complaint. The practice, and also the suggestion in the Act, is for the defendant to plead "not guilty," or "that he hath been three years in quiet possession, and his estate therein not ended or determined." This is to be done at the time of appearance and before the jury is sworn. Thereupon the proceedings are at issue. (§ 10).

The Justice, in all cases, should ask the defendant to plead, if he is present, before swearing the jury.

The jury being sworn, either party may have the benefit of counsel, and the trial will usually proceed as in other cases; except that the Act requires the Justice to read, or cause the complaint to be read to the jury, and he must distinctly call upon the complainant to support the same. (§ 12).

The merits of the title to the property cannot be the subject of inquiry by the jury; but simply whether the defendant is guilty of a forcible entry and detainer, or forcible detainer, or unlawful detainer. The defendant cannot set up that complainant's title is not as set forth in the complaint.

Upon such trial actual possession must be proved; constructive possession is not sufficient. The difference should be stated by the Justice in the charge to the jury. (Boylston v. Valentine, 1 Harr. 347; Mairs v. Sparks, 2 South. 513). 

If the action be for unlawful detainer, then the notice in writing required to be served in advance for delivery of possession must be proved.

No amendment can be allowed to the complaint which substantially changes the original charge made to defendant's detriment. (Waters v. Haynes, 20 Vr. 598; Wilson v. Bayley, 13 Vr. 132). 

The verdict and judgment

If the verdict of the jury be for the defendant, judgment will be entered by the Justice against the complainant, to include costs, and execution for costs will issue against the goods, chattels and body of the complainant. But if for the complainant, judgment 1

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

of restitution will be entered against the defendant and for treble costs, and execution will issue against his goods and chattels and, if insufficient to pay the judgment, the body. (C. S. 2601, §§ 

13, 15).

If there are two defendants charged as joint tenants in an action for unlawful detainer, both must be found guilty; there cannot be a verdict against one only, and of not guilty against the other. (Snediker v. Quick, 7 Hal. 129; Hildebrandt v. Linninger, 3 Gr. 38).

To treble the costs, the ordinary costs, when taxed, are multiplied by three. (Crane v. Dod, 1 Penn. 340).

The jury do not find a verdict for damages, but simply that the defendant is "guilty," or that "his plea of possession is not good;" hence the only pecuniary punishment of the defendant is the treble costs, with an impending execution directing the sheriff to convey him to jail if the costs are not made of his goods and chattels.

The judgment entered by the Justice will be for restitution, and there may issue afterward a writ of restitution to the sheriff directing him to put the complainant in possession of the premises violently entered upon or detained. (C. S. 2601, § 13).

But the writ must be withheld until eight days after the judgment is rendered, exclusive of Sundays. The writ is to be returnable in three months. (§ 14). 

The Justice's record The

The record in the minutes must be precise and full. statute says it must contain true copies of the complaint exhibited, and of the summons and return; also the time of issuing the venire and how returned, the names of the jurors, the verdict, and judgment; and also the names of the witnesses, and the admission of evidence objected to, and the rejection of evidence offered, etc. 

But not at large the oath administered to the jurors. (§ 17; 

Drake v. Newton, 3 Zab. 111).

There is no requirement that the copy of the complaint be entered in the minutes before the Justice actually issues the summons. (O'Hogan v. Crossman, 21 Vr. 516).

Penalties on sheriff and jurors If the sheriff does not carry out the duties required by this Act, he is subject to a penalty of two hundred dollars, to be recovered in an action of Debt by the party aggrieved. Or if a juror summoned does not appear, or refuses to serve, he may be fined by the Justice from one to five dollars; and a witness from five to twenty dollars; for which fine judgment and execution may be issued. When collected, the fine is to be paid to the county collector for the use of the county. (C. S. 2602, §§ 18, 26).

FORCIBLE ENtry and DeTAINER 

301 

No appeal

There is no appeal from the Justice to the Common Pleas, or Quarter Sessions. The only remedy for error is by certiorari to the Supreme Court. But none of the proceedings under the 

Act will prevent the complainant from bringing suit against the defendant for a Tort, if he is so injured in property or possession as to sustain damages. (§ 22).

A Supreme Court Justice may try the cause At any time after summons issued and before its return, either the plaintiff or defendant may apply to a Justice of the Supreme Court, who, if he shall deem the case of sufficient importance, may issue an order to the Justice of the peace to file forthwith the complaint and other papers in the office of the clerk of the Circuit Court, which Court shall then have cognizance of the case. As to the proceedings there, see the statute prescribing this method of trial. (§§ 27-34).

Premium on foxes killed in this State

In order to insure the killing of foxes in this State "for the benefit of agriculture and the protection of game," a premium

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

of three dollars for each fox killed is to be paid by the county wherein the animal is slain. (C. S. 94). Formerly counties could avoid this payment by a two-thirds vote of a board of chosen freeholders against carrying out the Act, but not now. 

L. 1917, p. 531; N. J. Cum. Supp. 82). (See P. 

To secure such premium the special provisions of the Act must be followed, viz: "It shall be the duty of any person, having killed any fox within this State, who is desirous of availing himself of the premiums therein provided, to produce such slain animal before any Justice of the Peace of said county in which the same was killed, and make affidavit of the time and place of killing the same; provided, that the pelt, if entire from tip of the nose of any such animal, may be produced in lieu of such animal, when so preferred; and upon the production of any such animal, or pelt, it shall be the duty of said officer, in the presence of said person killing such animal, and one qualified voter of said county, to cut off the ears of such animal, and, in the presence of said persons, burn the same." (C. S. 94, § 2). 

The affidavit is to be filed by the Justice "forthwith" with the county collector, upon which he shall receive fifty cents in full for his (the Justice's) services.

The Act then provides how the premium of three dollars is to be secured from the county. (§ 3, as amended by P. L. 1917, p. 531; N. J. Cum. Supp. 82).

To wilfully and fraudulently collect a premium under the Act is a misdemeanor, punishable by fine of not over $500, and imprisonment in the county jail not over one year, or both.

The Fish and Game Act of 1903, § 24 (as amend. by P. L. 

1932, p. 266) provides that persons may hunt foxes with hounds and firearms in daylight from Nov. 10 to Apr. 30, except during the open season for deer. If one kills a fox he must report it within 48 hours to a fish or game warden of the county or to the 

Board of Fish and Game Commissioners at Trenton under a penalty of $5. It is unlawful to liberate a fox; or to have one in possession except by permission of the above Board. (P. L. 1920, p. 386; N. J. Cum. Supp. 83). 

Frauds and Perjuries 

What the "Statute of Frauds" is

What is popularly known as "The Statute of Frauds" is the statute, dating originally from 1689, which requires certain contracts to be in writing, in order to be enforced. The statute, so

FRAUDS AND PERJURIES 

307 far as it applies to actions cognizable before The Small Cause Court or other Courts, may be thus stated (C. S. 2612, §§ 5-10): 

No action shall be brought unless the agreement upon which it is founded, or some memorandum or note of it, be in writing, and signed by the party to be charged with it, or his authorized agent, in the following cases:

First. To charge any executor or administrator upon a special promise to answer damages out of his own estate. 

Second. To charge the defendant, upon any special promise to answer for the debt, default or miscarriage of another person. 

But a promise to pay one's own debt to a third person is not within the statute, nor a promise to pay over money collected. 

And the promise to pay the debt of another based on a beneficial and substantial consideration is good, although not in writing. It is a new consideration moving to the promisor. (There are other exceptions under this head. See Parsons on Contracts, 498; articles in 4 N. J. L. J., pp. 197, 229, and various decisions in this State).

Third. To charge any person upon any agreement made in consideration of marriage. (See Manning v. Riley, 7 Dick. 39). 

Fourth. Or upon any contract for sale of lands, tenements or hereditaments, or any interest in or concerning them. 

Fifth. Or upon any agreement that is not to be performed within one year from the making thereof. There are three classes of cases to which this rule does not apply, viz: 1. Where the thing promised is to be done when a certain event occurs which may occur within a year; as, for instance, to pay money on the day of the promisor's marriage; to pay it on the death of a third party, etc. 2. Where the promise is to continue to do something until the contingency occurs, as, for instance, to pay during the life of another; to educate a child, etc. 3. Agreements to refrain altogether from certain acts; as not to engage in the practice of medicine in a certain town, not to sell musical instruments within certain limits, etc. 

Sixth. Or upon any contract for the sale of goods, wares or merchandise for the price of thirty dollars or upwards, unless, (1) the buyer shall accept part of the goods so sold, and actually receive the same; or (2) shall give something in earnest to bind the bargain; or (3) pay some part of the purchase money. The term "goods" is equivalent to "personal property," and embraces everything not included in the phrase "lands, tenements and hereditaments.' Therefore a parol contract for the sale of a promissory note, a bond and mortgage, shares in a stock company, etc., come within the rule and is void. (Greenwood v. 

Law, 26 Vr. 168). 

---

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Seventh. Or upon any promise made after full age to pay any debt contracted during infancy, to which infancy would be a defense. This does not apply to contracts made in infancy under seal, which, while voidable by the infant, are not ipso facto void, but may be confirmed and made binding when he attains his majority. (Eaton v. Eaton, 8 Vr. 117).

Eighth. Or against any person who is a discharged bankrupt upon any verbal promise made after the discharge to pay a debt from which the discharge has released him. But a promissory note, or other engagement in writing will bind him.

Ninth. Or by a broker, or real estate agent to obtain commissions for the sale or exchange of land, unless the authority for selling, or exchanging is in writing and signed by the owner, or his authorized agent, or the authority of broker or agent to make the sale or exchange is recognized in a writing or memorandum signed by such owner or agent before or after the sale or exchange is effected, and the rate of commission is stated therein. (See C. 

S. 2617, § 10, as amended by P. L. 1918, p. 1021; a lengthy section as amended which must be consulted. See Heyman v. Stoppen, 85 N. J. L. 128, and various later decisions).

All leases, uncertain interests in land, etc., not put in writing, have the effect of leases or estates at will only, except all leases not exceeding the term of three years. Assignments of leases, etc., are to be made in writing, signed by the assignor, or his agent lawfully authorized by writing, unless made by act and operation of law. (§§ 1, 2). 

The writing required

It is sufficient if one only of the parties to a contract signs the contract, provided it is the party sought to be charged. He, at least, is estopped from denying that the contract was validly executed. It is sufficient, likewise, if the memorandum be made by an agent, who is authorized in writing to act. 

The signature may be in lead pencil. And the mark of one unable to write, if duly witnessed, is sufficient. 

The contract must be stated with reasonable certainty, so that recourse need not be had to parol proof to understand it. 

It must be noted in making a contract to do or not to do a particular thing, that the time stated is of the essence of the contract. 

Effect of part performance

If an agreement not made in writing, which would otherwise be void under the statute, is partly performed, it may be rendered valid, even as to the part not performed. But in the latter case

GAMING (INCLUDING LOTTERIES) 

309 there must be such a part performance on the part of the plaintiff as would render it a fraud upon him if the defendant refused to comply with the contract on his part. In such case jurisdiction is founded upon the fraud rather than the contract. 

Proceedings for debts fraudulently contracted

Whenever a debt or obligation shall be fraudulently incurred, it is lawful for the party defrauded to institute suit, at any time after the obligation is incurred, to recover the money owing on such obligation, notwithstanding that by the terms of such obligation the debt contracted or the money secured to be paid thereby is not then due or payable, and in such cases, upon discovery of the fraud, the party defrauded may either rescind the contract wholly, and recover any property so obtained by fraud, or proceed by action on Contract for the recovery of the moneys owing thereon. (§ 17).

Sale of merchandise in bulk The sale in bulk of a large part of a stock of merchandise and fixtures, or of either, is void as against creditors unless the purchaser in good faith obtains from the seller a list in writing of all his creditors and gives them personal notice of the proposed sale at least 10 days before consummating the same; but such sale cannot be questioned after 90 days. (See P. L. 1932, p. 502). 

Gaming (including Lotteries)

Gaming an indictable offense 

Gaming for money, or other valuable thing, whether with cards, at pool tables, tennis, bowls, shuffleboards, faro-bank, on horse races, or by lottery, etc., are made misdemeanors, or high misdemeanors, in this State. (C. S. 1764, §§ 57-65). 

Any selling of tickets or chances for lotteries is a misdemeanor. This applies to secular, society or church fairs as much as to regular advertised "lotteries." 

Penalties for gaming

Besides the ordinary criminal procedure against gaming and gamblers, there may be a civil action brought to recover lost wages. 

Persons who pay, deliver or deposit any money, etc., upon the event of any wager, may sue for and recover the same, within six months. (§ 57). And it does not matter that the thing wagered about (as a horse race) comes off in another State. (Hessler v. Jennings, 33 Vr. 209).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

In the action it shall be sufficient to declare for so much money had and received for the plaintiff's use, without setting forth the special matter. (C. S. 2624, § 5).

All promises, agreements, notes, contracts or other securities or conveyances given, where the whole or any part of the consideration shall be for a wager, are made utterly void. (§ 3). 

Where a person loses money on a wager and does not sue to recover the same within the six months stated, any other person may sue for and recover the same, provided such suit be instituted within six months after the expiration of the first named six months. (§ 6). In such suit the plaintiff must aver in his state of demand all the essential facts under the statute. (See Fitzgerald v. Schloss, 33 Vr. 472).

There is also a penalty of two thousand dollars to be recovered in a civil case for opening or drawing a lottery in this State, and every transfer of goods of real estate made in pursuance of any such lottery is invalid and void. (C. S. 2625, §§ 8, 9; see 

Wolcott ads. Skahill, 27 Vr. 221). (As to proceedings for penalties, see general title "Penalties and Fines"). Glanders

Complaint to Justice of case of glanders If complaint upon oath is made to a Justice that any person or corporation has any horse, mare, gelding, ass, or mule in possession having the glanders, he shall order an inquiry made under the supervision of a competent veterinary surgeon; and if by his report the Justice is satisfied the charge is true, he shall issue his warrant directed to the owner forthwith to destroy such animal. (C. S. 82, § 131). As in all cases before him, the Justice must keep a record of the facts.

The warrant should set forth the affidavit, order of inquiry, report of surgeon, determination of the Justice, etc., so as to contain all the essential facts upon which such warrant is based. 

The above proceedings would be before a Justice as a magistrate.

It is also a misdemeanor to sell or offer for sale a horse having glanders or one which cannot be worked in this State; the sale is punishable by a fine of from $10 to $100, or imprisonment not more than six months, or both. (P. L. 1923, p. 104; N. J. Cum. 

Supp. 59, §§ 26a, 26b).

HEALTH BOARDS 

311 

Health Boards 

Penalties of local boards recoverable in The Small Cause Court

In case any local board of health prescribes penalties (not to exceed $100) for the violation of its ordinances or code, proceedings to collect the penalties may be taken before the District Court or Police Justice or Recorder in any city, or a Justice of the Peace in any county; the latter, of course, not to have jurisdiction as against the exclusive cognizance of a District Court. 

Mayors in boroughs are also given the same authority. (C. S. 

2666, § 18; P. L. 1913, p. 641; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1490).

Where in a city there is neither District Court, Police Justice or Recorder, a Justice of the Peace may act. (See Bourgeois v. Ocean City Health Board, 48 Vr. 162). 

The proceedings are to be begun by the usual written complaint by the local board of health, whereupon process shall issue at the suit of such board and may be a summons or warrant; if the former, returnable in from one to ten days, or, if a warrant, forthwith. The process must state what section or what code or ordinance is violated.

There may be adjournments, if necessary, but the hearing will be summary and without any written pleadings. 

The usual proceedings for recovering penalties for such violations of health board ordinances or code are to be, when before a Justice of the Peace, in The Small Cause Court (so held in 

Board v. Cattell, 44 Vr. 516), and, accordingly, if under_The

Small Cause Court Act, there is an appeal to the Common Pleas but not a trial by jury. Yet there may be instances under health board ordinances based on particular statutes where proceedings are so summary that the Justice hears the matter as a magistrate; then proceedings are regulated by such statutes. (See under general title "Penalties and Fines").

The defendant, in default of payment of judgment and costs, may be committed to the county jail for a period not exceeding ninety days. For a second offense within six months, the imprisonment may be one day for each dollar of penalty.

The form of conviction is given in the statute, and must be strictly followed. The conviction must be signed by the Court, Justice or magistrate, and in case it is for a second or additional violation (within six months after the first), the conviction must set that fact out. (C. S. 2671, § 40).

Such judgment of conviction may be docketed in the Common Pleas, the same as other judgments in The Small Cause 

Court. (8 41).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Review of proceedings when actions are in cities

By a law of 1895, when the proceedings are before "any city Judge, Police Court or other inferior Court" they "shall be reviewable by writ of certiorari in according with the rules and practice of the Supreme Court, or on application for that purpose, made by the defendant within 3 days after such judgment has been rendered, the Court of Common Pleas of the county may order such judgment and all the proceedings had in the case to be certified to said Court by the Court in which such judgment was had," etc. (C. S. 408, as amended by P. L. 1915, p. 413; 

N. J. Cum. Supp. 255). The review is not by appeal. (4 N. J. 

Misc. Rep. 246). 

Penalties recoverable by county boards County boards of health are also given power to make ordinances for the protection of health, etc., and the proceedings before a District Court, Police Justice, Recorder, or Justice of the Peace of a county are similar to those in case of ordinances of local boards. (C. S. 2689, § 115).

Directions as to how summons in an action for penalty begun by county boards shall be served, are given in the Act. (Ibid, § 127).

Warrant to search buildings for nuisances 

All magistrates are authorized on complaint founded on information and belief, supported by oath or affirmation of any officer or agent of the Department of Health, or a local board of health, that there is in any building of any kind any nuisance affecting health, or any person sick of any contagious or infectious diseases, or any condition of contagion or infection, to issue a warrant directed to the sheriff, constable, marshal, police officer, or to any officer or agent of such Department or local board, directing him to search in such building for such nuisance, or person sick of such disease, or for any condition of contagion or infection, and if found to abate the same. The officer shall make return of his proceedings to the magistrate. (C. S. 2673, §§ 47-49).

Proceedings for penalties under the Act concerning contagious diseases

By an Act of 1895 and amendments physicians are required to report to the assessor or designated officer of a local board of health persons suffering from certain contagious, etc., diseases. 

Householders are also required to report the same, when no physician has been in attendance. All such reports to be within twelve hours after discovery of the disease. (See P. L. 1911, p. 

787; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1499, § 247). Common carriers are not to accept for transportation, or to transport, persons affected with such diseases, or infected articles, etc. Penalties for these and other offenses named are from fifty to one hundred dollars. 

By an amendment to this Act, it is provided how penalties incurred can be recovered in summary proceedings, viz: either in the name of the Board of Health (now Department of Health) of the State of New Jersey, or in the name of the local board of health of the local municipal government, within whose jurisdiction the penalty may have been incurred. The health inspector, registrar of vital statistics, or member of any local board of health, who shall know or be informed of any violation of the Act, is to make, and any other person having such knowledge, may make, under oath or affirmation, a complaint against the person incurring such penalty, setting forth the facts of such violation, "which complaint shall be filed with the clerk of the District Court or any Justice of the Peace of the county within which the offense may have been committed, or with any Police Justice or Recorder of the township, city or municipality within which any local board bringing suit shall have jurisdiction." (P. L. 1898, (P. L. 1898, p. 162; C. S. 2725).

The Justice, Police Justice or Recorder with whom any complaint shall be filed is required to issue process, either a summons or warrant, which process, when a warrant, shall be returnable forthwith, and when a summons, shall be returnable in not less than five nor more than fifteen days. On the return of such process, or at any time to which the trial shall have been adjourned, the Justice, etc., shall proceed to hear the testimony and give judgment without the filing of any pleadings. If judgment shall be given for the plaintiff, execution shall be forthwith issued against the goods and chattels of the defendant for the amount of the penalty, with costs. (Ibid).

There is no jury trial allowed by the Act. J-20

Proceedings for penalties for transporting dead human bodies contrary to Act of 1900

By a statute of 1900 (C. S. 213) it is forbidden for an undertaker, or any person, or any common carrier, to have transported across or within the State any human body dead of small-pox, Asiatic cholera, yellow fever, typhus fever or bubonic plague except the same be enclosed in a hermetically sealed casket, and having a license in writing from the Department of Health of the State, or an officer or inspector thereof, under a penalty of $100. 

Certain other forms are to be observed, as to which see the Act. 

A complaint of violation of any provision of this statute is to be made by a member, inspector or other officer of the State Department of Health, or of a local board of health, if the violation is within its jurisdiction, under oath, and it may be upon information and belief. Jurisdiction is given to "every District 

Court and every Justice of the Peace in any city or county, and every Police Justice or Recorder in any city." The suit for the penalty is to be in the name of the Department of Health of the State of New Jersey as plaintiff, for the use of the State of New Jersey if that Department institutes the suit, or in the name of any local board of health for the use of the township, city, borough or other municipality it represents. A summons or warrant may then issue; if a summons to be returnable in from one to ten days and if a warrant forthwith; and such process must specify what section of the law is alleged to be violated. 

On the return day, or an adjourned day (not to exceed 30 days) there is to be a hearing, with testimony, without the filing of any pleadings, and the judgment, if for the defendant, is to be according to the form provided by the statute (in § 8 of the Act. 

See C. S. 216 and "Forms," infra).

The judgment is to be signed by the Justice (or by any Judge or magistrate hearing the cause and rendering the judgment), and the execution to follow will be against the goods and chattels and body of the defendant.

If a warrant has been issued and the matter is adjourned, the defendant may be required to enter into the usual bond for his appearance at the hearing in the penal sum of $200. 

When Justice may issue burial permit

While this topic is one not embraced in any Health Act, yet it is somewhat related thereto and is given place here. 

In case where, on account of the absence of the local registrar of vital statistics, or municipal clerk, "or for any other sufficient reason," it is impossible to obtain a permit for burial of a dead person in time, any Common Pleas Judge or Justice of the Peace of the county, on presentation of the certificate of death

HEALTH BOARDS 

315 (from a physician, as the Act directs), and being satisfied that it is genuine, and that no permit can be obtained from the registrar, etc., may issue a special permit of burial. (The statutory form of same is given in Forms, infra). (C. S. 210, § 5). But such certificates physicians are not to give where the death was caused by the misconduct of another. (See § 2).

Idiots and Lunatics 

Definition of "idiot" and "lunatic"

An idiot is usually a person having no understanding from nativity, although idiocy may occur later in life. A lunatic is one who has had understanding but has lost it. 

Contracts and actions 

A lunatic may have sane intervals, and if, during those intervals, he does an act, it will bind him as it will any habitually sane person. An idiot does not have sane intervals.

The executed contract with a lunatic, if for full consideration and made with knowledge of his incompetency, will be sustained. (For a review of the cases, and an interesting discussion of the law concerning contracts by lunatics, see Matthiessen v. 

McMahon, 9 Vr. 536).

As may be inferred from the foregoing general principles an idiot, having no reason, cannot enter into contracts. A lunatic may, in sane moments. But in all cases necessaries supplied to them may be sued for.

If an action should be brought against an idiot or lunatic, it is to be against him in his own name; but, if he be an infant, before proceeding farther the Justice must appoint for defendant a proper guardian to defend him in the action. It may be done orally, but the guardian must be present and consent to act, and it should be entered in the docket; the better way would be for the guardian to sign his consent. (See under general title, "Infancy").

A lunatic who is of age, when sued, must appear in Court by some one; an attorney (approved by the Court) or guardian, or

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

some one actually and legally representing him, before the action can proceed. The process, however, is to be served upon him, personally, as the law prescribes no other way. (Van Horn v. 

Hann, 10 Vr. 207).

Lunacy may be pleaded as a bar to an action, but it will be for the Justice or jury, whichever tries the cause, to determine the weight of the proof of lunacy.

The period of lunacy is not calculated under the Statute of Limitations. 

Cannot be held to bail

No capias can issue against an idiot or lunatic. He cannot be detained in prison in any civil action, or proceeding for a penalty. (C. S. 2794, § 20). 

Dangerous lunatics to be apprehended

Whenever a lunatic is considered to be dangerous to the public, any constable or police officer is authorized to arrest him without warrant and take him to the nearest Justice of the Peace or Police Justice, who shall in a summary way inquire and determine whether he is of unsound mind and dangerous to the public. 

If so, the lunatic is to be committed to the place provided by the board of freeholders of the county as one of temporary confinement for the insane, unless discharged or removed in lawful manner. (Ibid, § 21d).

The costs of the apprehension and hearing, and maintaining a lunatic as last set forth is to be borne by the municipality wherein such lunatic is found.

The proceedings, of course, are before the Justice as a magistrate and not in

Some general principles Infancy

It is a well settled common law rule that, until a person is twenty-one years of age, he cannot bind himself by any contract, except for necessaries. He is supposed to be of immature mind and subject to the artifices of others.

Accordingly, as a rule whenever an infant (or an adult) is sued in an action upon a claim or demand which was incurred during minority, (except for necessaries), he may plead infancy as a defense. The plea need not be in writing. The fact may be stated and proved, and when proved will bar the plaintiff's recovery.

An infant, when he becomes twenty-one, may by promise in writing signed by him, obligate himself in law to pay a debt contracted in infancy. (C. S. 2616, § 7).

An infant's contract is voidable, not void. Hence there is no obligation for him to set up infancy as a defense. He may waive it, and defend on other grounds. But, unless for actual necessaries furnished, he may void any contract he enters into, and the plaintiff has no remedy at law. 

However, an infant may deposit money with any bank or

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

41 trust company, and make withdrawals by checks, and deposit there checks for collection. (C. S. 2823).

The defense of infancy cannot be employed in actions in Tort. An infant is as liable in trespass as an adult. A tort partakes of the nature of a crime, and in crime the guilty party has no shield of this kind after he attains the age of ordinary intelligence, and of perception between right and wrong. A contract may be founded in fraud and thus an action in Tort be sustainable and in that case he cannot plead infancy in bar. But as an infant cannot legally create an agent, so he will not be liable in Tort for any acts committed by persons presuming to act under his authority.

The plea of infancy extends only to the person making it. 

An adult co-defendant cannot plead it to abate the action against him.

As previously stated, an infant may make contracts for the necessaries of life, and will be bound for them. Thus he may bind himself to pay for his necessary meat, drink, apparel, medicine and the like, and also good teaching and instruction. 

No debt contracted by an infant (with exceptions) can be collected from him or his parent or guardian, etc., when he is a scholar or student of any college, academy, or school, without special permission of his parent or guardian, or the principal, etc., of the school (but with exceptions as to "reasonable entertainment" on the way to or from such place) or to board and lodging at the institution. (C. S. 2813, § 32). 

Should the infant, or his natural guardian, sue?

The general principle of law is that infants, who are residing at home with their parents, are not entitled to sue for and recover their earnings, because such earnings belong to their parents. A father may bring an action for the wages of his child, or the mother, if the father is dead. He is the natural guardian of his child during the child's infancy, and at his decease the child's mother is the natural guardian. But if the infant is emancipated, and leaves home "to do for himself," he is entitled to his own wages and may sue for them. Or, if the infant is at home, but the parents refuse to provide for him, and thus compel him to seek his own maintenance, he may contract for his own labor, and receive the earnings of his own industry. (Campbell v. Campbell, 3 Stock. 268).

The question, in all actions by infants, which is first to be determined, is, whether it is the infant who has the right to sue, or his natural guardian. If the infant is allowed to receive earnings and invests them for himself, he may bring an action for such investment; his father cannot claim the benefit of it and sue in his

INFANCY 

321 own name, or call the infant to account for it after he arrives at full age. (Ibid).

It would seem to be a safe general rule that the infant may sue in his own name for whatever contract he personally makes, with the consent of his parents, such consent being either express or implied; but not for contracts his parents enter into concerning him, and which they, as his natural guardians, have a legal right to make, unless in their agreement the wages are to be paid not to themselves but to the infant, in which case the infant alone has the right of action to recover such wages. (Snediker v. Everingham, 3 Dutch. 143).

In an action in Tort for a personal injury done to an infant, the rule is much the same as in actions on Contract; if the infant is under the care and protection of the parent, he ought to sue, but if not the infant may sue for himself. For torts or wrongs committed by the infant, he must be sued and not his parent, unless his wrongful act is done expressly by parental command. (M'Calla v. Wood, 1 Penn. 86).

An infant may sue for a legacy due him, but it must be by his guardian or next friend. 

An infant cannot be held to bail

An infant cannot be held to bail in a civil action when the plea of infancy would be a bar to the action. 

Civil actions by or against infants

An infant under twenty-one years of age may sue or be sued the same as any other person, but as a rule he must prosecute or defend by his guardian.

Therefore, if he is the plaintiff, while the first process in the action may be taken out in his own name, yet, if so, before there are further proceedings, some one must appear for him, either his regular guardian at law, or his "next friend" to be selected by him, and admitted by the court, as a proper person to appear in his behalf. (Groff v. Groff, 1 Penn. 656; Lang v. Belloff, 8 Dick. 298).

If objection is made by defendant that plaintiff is an infant and there is no proper person to represent him, the Justice must allow proof to be made of the fact and, if the fact appears, and there is no proper person of full age present to represent the plaintiff, the action should be dismissed. (Smith v. Van Houten, 4 Hal. 382).

Where an infant is defendant, he is to be sued in his own name, but before the Justice can try the cause, he must appoint a guardian ad litem to defend him. Where practicable, the Jus-

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

tice should appoint the parent or relative, because naturally the father, or one closely related, has the first right to act as guardian, or "next friend;" but the appointee should be in fact a friend of the infant, and not adverse to his interest. (Rue v. Meirs, 16 

Stew. 377; Anonymous, 10 N. J. L. 142).

Should one guardian ad litem be appointed by the Justice, but fail to act, the Justice should appoint another who will act. 

As a guardian, or "next friend," stands in place of the infant, he can act as his own attorney in prosecuting or defending the action. (C. S. 4055, § 18).

Miscellaneous statutes concerning infants or minors A minor under the age of eighteen years may not play billiards or pool in a room where liquors are sold; the keeper of such place is liable to a penalty of twenty dollars at the suit of a parent or guardian, or of an incorporated humane society, one of whose objects is the protection of children from cruelty. (C. S. 

2814, §§ 43, 44). Also made a crime unless attended by a parent or guardian or with their written permission. (C. S. 1768, § 70). 

No person may sell cigarettes or tobacco to any minor under eighteen years under a penalty of ten dollars for the first, and not exceeding twenty-five dollars for each subsequent offense. (P. L. 1917, p. 113; N. J. Cum. Supp. 856). 

By an Act of 1911 (P. L., p. 752; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1725, § B1), no person under the age of twenty-one in cities of the firstclass, nor under eighteen in other municipalities can be employed as a messenger by a corporation, firm or person before 5 a. m. or after 10 p. m., unless the Commissioner of Labor grants a permit under extraordinary circumstances. Penalty for violation of 

Act, $100, to be sued for in debt. District and Recorders Courts of cities, and Justices of the Peace having jurisdiction, have power to issue summons, hear the cause and award execution-to be against the body if the usual execution is unsatisfied. (For particulars see the Act).

Pawnbrokers may not take in pawn any articles from a person under eighteen; penalty, fifty dollars. (C. S. 3931, § 16, as amended by P. L. 1911, p. 586; N. J. Cum. Supp. 2676).

It is a crime to hire out minors for mendicant or immoral purposes. (C. S. 1763, § 56).

Also to seduce an infant under promise of marriage. (C. S. 

1761, § 50), or to carnally abuse a female under sixteen (Ibid, § 113, as amended by P. L. 1906, p. 430). In both cases the crime is a high misdemeanor. (See also general title "Children, Cruelty to," "Labor," etc.).
