Judgment (Civil) 

How and what to be entered

When a verdict is rendered by a jury, (or when a Justice, who tries a cause, determines upon and announces his judgment) an entry of the judgment is made in the Justice's docket. Without such entry no execution can be issued. 

Perhaps an entry in the Justice's minutes is a sufficient entry of judgment upon which an execution may issue, provided he subsequently enters up the judgment in his docket. It is so held in New York. (Hall v. Tuttle, 6 Hill 68). But this entry should be made before any execution is issued, and be full and certain. 

And the amount of the judgment must be written out in

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

words, and not put down in figures, which any one who may have access to the docket can alter at will; nor be left in blank to be filled out subsequently. (Cole v. Petty, 1 Penn. 60; Hann v. Gosling, 4 Hal. 248; Meirs v. Bussom, 28 Vr. 383).

A judgment must also be only against the plaintiff or defendant in the action and cannot include others. Thus, judgment cannot be entered against two obligees in a bond, when one only is sued.

A judgment of a Justice must be at the time of the hearing, or at a day and hour and place then fixed and known to both parties.

It must not exceed the amount demanded. 

The Justice after a hearing must pronounce a judgment, unless the parties settle, or agree to withdraw the suit. He cannot dismiss after he has heard the merits. (Miller v. Miller, 1 Gr. 165).

Entries against special parties, as infants, executors, etc. 

Judgment against an infant is against him, and not the guardian appointed to defend the suit. (Steelman v. Cox, 2 Penn. 644).

In the case of administrators and executors, while the judgment is against them, it must not be a general one, but the words are to be added, "to be levied and made of the goods and chattels, which were of the said — -, deceased," etc. (Quicksall v. 

Quicksall, 2 Penn. 457). There may be exceptions, however.

Where facts are shown by which an executor should be personally liable for debt or damages to an extent beyond the costs, the judgment may be that so much (naming it) as he is personally liable for, and the costs, shall be levied of his own goods. But the rule is that executors shall be answerable so far only as the goods and debts coming to their hands will satisfy. (Ibid). 

Entry of judgment on special verdicts 

If there is a "special" verdict by a jury the Justice should set out the special finding of the jury, and add that, "having considered the matters of law involved in the cause, and submitted to my discretion by the jury, I gave judgment," etc. 

Entry of judgments for penalties (See under general title "Penalties and Fines"). 

Entry of judgment on verdict on Sunday

When the jury renders a verdict on Sunday, the Justice should simply make a note of it, and enter the judgment on Monday. The Justice himself has no right to give judgment on Sun-

JUDGMENT (CIVIL) 

325 day, unless in a case where the statute permits it. But if dated on Sunday by mistake, it is amendable. (Yorks v. Ackerman, 2 

Penn. 900; Van Riper v. Van Riper, 1 South. 159). 

Entry of judgment on report of referees

Upon the report of referees, the Justice should copy the report in his docket, and enter judgment thereon in words at length, notwithstanding that it may be a repetition to do so. 

Entry of judgment against indorsers

In case of indorsers on promissory notes there may have to be special entries against parties primarily and secondarily liable; in such case particulars must be noted. (See under general title "Negotiable Paper"). 

Judgments to be only on sworn proof

There is no such thing as "judgment by default" in The Small Cause Court; that is, judgment entered up simply because defendant fails to contest or to appear. There must be sworn proof offered to substantiate plaintiff's claim (or defendant's if he puts in a set-off. Snyder v. Hummel, 1 Penn. 87; Clarke v. 

Clarke, 2 Penn. 724).

But it is not compliance with the rule requiring proof for a Justice to call a witness or two, who know nothing about the case, and to swear them, so as to enter their names as witnesses upon the docket. Such a practice was severely censured by Chief Justice Hornblower in Crane v. Brundage, 2 Gr. 603, and it was intimated that it might be a cause for the impeachment of the Justice. 

Judgment for interest

As every action is for some actual debt, or for damages, up to the date of the suit, judgment must be for the amount then due, and no more; but lawful interest will be calculated up to the date of the judgment. Where the jury erroneously calculate interest, by consent of parties the Justice may change the verdict. The lawful rate of interest (six per cent. since July 4, 1878) is understood where none is expressed in the contract.

The New Jersey method of calculating interest when there are partial payments is as follows: To cast the interest upon the principal to the time of the first payment; if the payment equals or is greater than the interest deduct the payment; if the payment does not equal the interest, it is not to be credited, until, with the future payments, the interest is equalled or exceeded by them. (Baker v. Baker, 4 Dutch. 15).

If a less amount of interest has been demanded (by the state

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

of demand) than the lawful rate, in order to reduce the amount claimed to a sum below two hundred dollars (beyond which the Justice cannot enter up a judgment) judgment may be rendered upon that basis. Or the plaintiff may waive interest altogether upon his demand. (Griffith v. Clute, 4 Hal. 264). 

Judgment for costs

When costs go with the judgment, as is the rule, the entry in the docket should be, where the action is on Contract, for so much due on contract; or if in Tort for so much damages; or if for a penalty for so much debt-unless a statute specifically points out a different entry; and then adding "and for dollars and cents, costs of suit," the judgment for costs being always separately set forth.

It is thought by some Justices that no harm ensues if they add the costs to the sum due, or the verdict, and enter judgment for the sum total. But this is erroneous. The costs must be entered separately, not only in the docket, but also in the execution; and it must be separately noted in all subsequent proceedings where the amount of judgment is mentioned. 

Where judgment is rendered for treble costs, it is not necessary to state first the amount of the single costs and then the treble sum. Thus, if the single costs are five dollars, it is sufficient to state thus: "fifteen dollars, being treble the costs and charges of the plaintiff." For

As a rule, a judgment for either party carries costs. example, if the judgment be for a defendant (and the plaintiff is not an executor or administrator), the rule is that the defendant shall have judgment for costs. This will be the case where the plaintiff is nonsuited, or shall discontinue his action. The statute says: "If a plaintiff, other than executors or administrators, in any action shall be nonsuited or shall discontinue or withdraw his action, without the consent of the defendant, where he may lawfully do so, then judgment shall be given against such plaintiff for the costs which have accrued." (S. C. A., § 47).

A judgment stands until reversed A judgment once rendered in The Small Cause Court will stand good as a judgment for twenty years, unless reversed or set aside by a higher Court, on appeal or certiorari, or paid, but the time during which the person entitled to the judgment may be under age, or insane, is not computed. (C. S. 3166, § 7). After twenty years a judgment is presumed to be paid. (Bird v. Inslee, 8 C. E. Gr. 363).

The Justice cannot open a judgment once entered, nor set it aside, to afford the parties, or either of them, a rehearing. The

JUDGMENT (CIVIL) 

327 right to grant a new trial is reserved to higher Courts only. (Terhune v. Barcalow, 6 Hal. 38). But on review by certiorari, the higher Court may order a rehearing, in which case the judgment is opened as of course. (S. C. A., § 99).

The cause of action is destroyed by a judgment, so that no new suit can be brought upon the same cause of action. (Cheesman v. Leonard, 2 Penn. 549). Even though a judgment be based on one form of action and the new action be stated in another form, if substantially for the same matter the judgment bars. (Smith v. Finley, 2 Penn. 1005).

A judgment of nonsuit, however, is no bar to a new action. (Snowhill v. Hillyer, 4 Hal. 38).

How judgment before suit brought may be obtained by confession

Confessed judgments are frequently given by parties before a suit is brought. In such case both the parties to a demand must attend, and not only one. Without the presence of the defendant and also the plaintiff (or his attorney), and also the filing of an affidavit as stated below, the Justice is not authorized to enter up judgment by confession so as as to bind any outside parties. (Young's Adm'r v. Stout, 5 Hal. 302; Parker v. Griggs, 1 South. 

161; Ballinger v. Sherron, 2 Gr. 145).

On their appearing before a Justice, and before the latter can proceed to enter the judgment, the plaintiff, or his attorney, must produce an affidavit (which may be made by either the plaintiff, or his attorney, or agent), of the true consideration of the bill, note, or other matter, for which the judgment is confessed, and further set forth that the debt or demand is justly and honestly due and owing to the person to whom the judgment is confessed, and that the judgment is not confessed to answer any fraudulent intent or purpose, or to protect the property of the defendant from his other creditors. (C. S. 221, § 11). Such an affidavit must be filed with the Justice as a prerequisite to the entry of the judgment, and as essential to its validity, and must be preserved by him; without it the judgment is inoperative against other persons, though binding as between the parties. (S. C. A., § 48; Clapp v. 

Ely, 3 Dutch. 555; Wright v. Wood, Spencer 308).

The parties confessing judgment must confess for a definite amount. No demand is needed, all technical proceedings being waived by the confession. It cannot be for a fictitious debt; or a debt to grow due in the future; or to secure future advances; or for a larger sum than is due. It must be for a lawful debt, founded on a legal consideration, and for a debt owing at the time of the entry of the judgment.

When the judgment is entered by confession the effect is

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

precisely as in case of verdict and judgment in a contested cause, except that, if before execution the defendant procures a good freeholder of the county to join with him in the confession (by a bond) for the amount of the judgment and costs, the judgment being below $50, there is to be a stay of execution of one month, or, if over $50, of three months. (S. C. A., § 60). 

Confessed judgment after suit brought

The affidavit required as stated above, is not necessary where the judgment is confessed after suit is brought. The statute does not apply when the defendant has been first sued and brought into Court by process, and then may choose to confess to the judgment. (Budd v. Marvin, 1 South. 248; Elliot v. Woodhull, 7 Hal. 126). In such latter case a confessed judgment will operate as a judgment with the usual effect, but with this special advantage to the defendant, that he may stay execution by entering into bond in the manner noted in the previous paragraph. 

If the suit is against two or more persons, one cannot confess judgment for all. He can only confess for himself. And the suit will then proceed against the other defendants. (Wiggins v. 

Kleinhans, 4 Hal. 249).

The effect of a confession of judgment after suit instituted is to stop all further proceedings in the nature of a judicial investigation of the merits of the cause. But the costs of the plaintiff up to the period of confession should be embraced in the costs of the judgment, unless otherwise agreed upon. 

How confessed judgment is reviewable

A judgment obtained by confession is reviewable by certiorari only and not by appeal, as the Act permitting appeals to the Common Pleas expressly excepts judgment by confession. (S. C. A., § 80; Ritter v. Kunkle, 10 Vr. 259). 

Proceedings on foreign judgment

A foreign judgment can have no binding effect in this State until it is made a judgment in our Courts. If below two hundred dollars it may be sued upon in an action on Contract before a Justice of the Peace. To this proceeding there can be no defense upon the merits existing anterior to the rendition of the judgment in the foreign State. Upon a judgment obtained on such foreign judgment (which will include the original judgment and costs), execution may issue, and in all respects the second judgment will be one of this State, and subject to its laws relating to judgments. 

Satisfaction of judgment

Satisfaction of judgment by the plaintiff in writing is not entered verbatim in a Justice's Court. If the constable returns

JUDGMENT (CIVIL) 

329 the execution satisfied, or the defendant pays the judgment, an entry of the same is made by the Justice, and this is evidence of satisfaction.

Where the parties settle the matter themselves, the plaintiff ought to give the defendant a satisfaction receipt, which, if he shall file it with the Justice, should be noted by the latter in the docket, and this will be sufficient evidence of payment. 

The acknowledgment of satisfaction, or a discharge of a judgment by an attorney, binds his client. (Wyckoff v. Bergen, Coxe, 214).

Less than the true amount may be received in satisfaction by the plaintiff, and, if he gives his release, under seal, any further proceedings to collect the balance are nugatory. (Braden v. 

Ward, 13 Vr. 518). 

Assignment of judgment

A judgment in a Justice's Court may be assigned by the plaintiff, whether with or without a consideration. The execution, if any, thereafter, must be issued in the name of the plaintiff, or, if the judgment be sued upon elsewhere the action must be in the name of the original plaintiff. (Sharp v. Moore, 2 Penn. 844). 

Scire facias to revive judgment (As to revival of judgments in certain cases by scire facias, see general title “Scire Facias”). 

Execution on judgment after six years

After a judgment has been rendered for six years, an execution can be awarded by the Justice who gave the judgment only upon an order on five days' notice to the defendant, and proof to the Justice of the amount remaining due. (S. C. A., § 65). 

Docketing judgment

The reason for docketing, in the Common Pleas, a judgment obtained before the Justice is, usually, to acquire a lien upon real estate, or to reach property of one kind or another which an execution from The Small Cause Court will not reach. 

The execution issued by the Justice is not a lien upon realty, but against goods and chattels only. Accordingly, a judgment subsequently obtained by another party in another county Court, or before a Justice and first docketed, would supersede any Small Cause Court judgment not docketed as to its lien upon realty. 

In order to be docketed in the Common Pleas, the judgment or balance due thereon must be for not less than ten dollars, excluding costs (S. C. A., § 72); and if an execution has been issued against goods and chattels, it must have been first returned J-21

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

unsatisfied; but it is not necessary that such execution shall have been issued. (See Barr v. Fleming, 32 Vr. 431).

To effect this docketing, a statement must be made out and signed by the Justice (such as the Act requires), and an affidavit made by the plaintiff, or his attorney; and both must be filed with the clerk of the Common Pleas. (See S. C. A., § 73).

If the docket of the Justice has been filed with the county clerk, such clerk may make the "statement" required by the Act, and it will have the same force for the purpose of docketing a judgment as if made by the Justice. (S. C. A., § 73).

Effect of docketed judgment The effect of docketing a judgment is to make it a lien upon real estate, as well as upon personalty levied upon, the same as if judgment had been originally obtained in the Common Pleas. 

After docketing the judgment the proceedings before the Justice are at an end, unless he grants an appeal (which can be granted only within twenty days after judgment; see S. C. A., § 

80); or responds to a writ of certiorari, in which case the judgment docketed "shall be stayed and suspended until the final determination of such appeal or certiorari." (S. C. A., §§ 75, 78).

The Common Pleas can vacate a docketed judgment (see 

Curtis v. Stout, 40 Vr. 124), or defendant may have it certified to the Supreme Court to determine its validity. (Roller v. Roller, 17 Vr. 511). (For other references to subject of "Judgment," see general titles "Trial," "Penalties," "Scire Facias," etc., and see also Index).

Actions for penalties 

Various statutes concerning labor, especially in factories, shops, etc., prescribe penalties, usually recoverable in The Small 

Cause Court when a Justice has jurisdiction. We notice some

By an Act of 1911 no child under fourteen shall be employed or allowed to work in any mercantile establishment; the employer of such is to be adjudged a disorderly person and the place a disorderly house if such employment is habitual. If a child is under sixteen there must be an age and schooling certificate. There are other provisions as to such child working in places detrimental to health. (P. L. 1911, p. 194, as amended by P. L. 1918, p. 745). Justices of the Peace have jurisdiction as to penalties if not within District Court jurisdiction. (Ibid, § 13).

By an Act of 1912 (P. L., p. 337, as variously amended.

(But see Act referred to below). Canneries engaged in packing perishable products are excepted. Fines up to $50 for a first, and to $200 for a second offense, are recoverable as penalties, by an action of Debt, and are to be paid to the State. 

As the Commissioner of Labor is to bring the necessary actions, which are cognizable before any District or Recorder's Court of a city, or a Justice of the Peace having jurisdiction, we do not give further details of the Act, to which, if proceedings are brought, we refer the Justice or Recorder.

In these proceedings to recover penalties the requirements in the Practice Act (C. When a Justice of the Peace may issue subpoenas in labor disputes

By an Act of 1886, disputes that arise between any employer engaged in manufacturing and his or its employés may be submitted by mutual consent in writing to a board of arbitrators for a hearing and settlement. In such case it is lawful for a Justice of the Peace to issue subpoenas for the production of books and papers, and for the attendance of witnesses before said board. (C. S. 108). 

Landlord and Tenant 

Justice's Jurisdiction

Until the amendatory Act of 1923 extending the jurisdiction of The Small Cause Court to landlord and tenant and to forcible entry and detainer cases, the Justice's jurisdiction was as a magistrate and not in  Now that Court has jurisdiction, excepting where District Court jurisdiction may deny any civil jurisdiction to the Justice. Just how far this jurisdiction may extend under present statutes relative to all tenures the Courts have not decided. We cannot assume it applies in cases of dispossession by two Justices, nor in strict actions of ejectment.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

but it must usually apply to the usual dispossession cases for default of rent, expiration of lease, objectionable tenant, etc., as well as ordinary actions to recover rent. 

Landlord's right to dispossess without recourse to law A landlord, where the term of tenancy ceases, and his right to take immediate possession is clear, may take possession of his own property without recourse to law, but without injury to another's person.

In our Court of highest resort it has been laid down as an established principle that "the landlord may take possession by any means short of personal violence; that he may break into a dwelling house for the purpose, because no one ought to complain of him for such an injury done to his own property; that he may remove goods which he finds there, because they are an unlawful encroachment upon his rights; that once in possession he may protect that possession, as well against the individual who, in violation of his contract, has attempted to wrong him, as against a stranger who intrudes upon his possession." (Todd v. 

Jackson, 2 Dutch. 532, and cases there cited).

But the landlord does this at his peril as to his method and rights; hence such a proceeding is not to be advised when a safer statutory one is sufficiently prompt in its remedies, (see Kaufman v. Longworth, 2 N. J. L. J. 231), and especially since recent statutes do not make the rights of landlords as clear as they formerly were. 

Landlord's statutory remedies

Where the landlord has a claim against his tenant for rent due and unpaid, or for any other legal reason has the right to regain possession of his property, there may be one of several legal remedies open to him, according to the circumstances: 1. 

Distress to recover rent due. 

2. An action on Contract to recover the rent due. 

3. In case the premises are deserted, and one year's rent be due, he may make application to two Justices of the Peace to be put into possession. 

4. Take proceedings to dispossess, because of expiration of term, or default in rent, or because tenant is objectionable under a statute so permitting. 

5. Bring an action of ejectment, if one year's rent be due (but not in The Small Cause Court). (C. S. 2054; 3068). 

6. If the tenant is within the provisions of the "Act concerning forcible entries and detainers," he may bring an action of unlawful detainer. (See general title "Forcible Entry and Detainer"). 

Of course none of these remedies apply to a Justice of the

Peace where the District Court has exclusive jurisdiction.

I. REMEDY BY DISTRESS 

Justice not applied to for distress

The remedy by distress is in the landlord's own hand; with it a Justice of the Peace or other magistrate has nothing to do, unless a house is to be broken into. The landlord himself distrains, or authorizes some person to do it. 

The main features of the law of distress (C. S. 1939) are: 

The rent must be fixed and certain and must be due and in arrear; the distress must be reasonable and not too great; the last articles to be distrained are beasts of the plough, sheep and implements of trade; beasts distrained must be put in the public pound; there must be an appraisal after 10 days; the distress cannot be for more than one year's rent and must be within six months after being due; the tenant may have the $200 exemption. 

Goods locked up in a dwelling

If the property to be distrained has been locked up in a dwelling, such house may not be broken into without oath first being made before a Justice of the Peace of the fact, upon which said Justice should issue his warrant to the landlord or his bailiff, directing that the house may be broken into. (C. S. 1944, § 

16). Without such warrant, an outer door of the house, if not locked, may be opened in the ordinary way by turning the knob, raising the latch, etc., or a window, if open, may be entered, but the dwelling house may not be broken into, or the person so breaking may be arrested for a forcible entry. When a person is once in lawful possession of a dwelling house where the goods and the chattels have been concealed, he is justified in breaking open the outer door in order to regain possession. (Wood's Land. & Ten., § 545).

Landlord's lien preferred to liens under distress, execution, etc.

By virtue of the fourth section of the "Landlord and Tenant 

Act" (C. S. 3066), it is enacted that "no goods or chattels whatsoever, lying or being, or which shall lie or be in or upon any messuage, lands or tenements, which are or shall be leased for term of life or lives, year or years, at will or otherwise, shall be liable to be taken by virtue of any execution, attachment or other process, unless the party at whose suit the said execution or other process is sued out, shall, before the removal of such goods from off the said premises, by virtue of such process, pay to the landlord of the said premises, or his bailiff, all rent due for said premises, at the time of the taking such goods or chattels by virtue of such process, or which shall have accrued up to the day of the

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

removal of the goods from off the said premises, whether by the terms of lease the day of payment shall have come or not, making a rebate of interest on the sum, the time of payment of which by the terms of the lease shall not have come; provided the said arrears of rent do not amount to more than one year's rent.' 

It is not required, therefore, that a landlord shall take out a distress warrant to seize such goods for rent, because he knows some execution or other process has been or is about to be served and the goods levied upon, for the officer is bound not to remove them, if rent be due, without making payment of the arrears of rent, not exceeding one year's arrearages. 

This does not make the constable or sheriff liable to pay rent before the removal of a stranger's goods, because the landlord has no right to distrain such goods for rent. 

If there is no certain rent fixed, however, such as would give a landlord the right to distrain, the landlord has no right to have his rent paid before the tenant's goods are removed. (Kirkpatrick v. Cason, 1 Vr. 331).

II. REMEDY BY CIVIL ACTION AGAINST TENANT 

An action will lie for rent

Whenever rent is due and unpaid, an action (in Debt) will lie, as a matter of course, against the tenant; and it will lie where the rent is due upon a lease for life, as well as upon a lease for years. (C. S. 3065, § 1).

Where a tenant for life shall happen to die before, or on the day on which any rent is payable, where the lease terminated on the death of the tenant, the executors or administrators of such tenant for life may recover from the under-tenants. (Ibid, § 2). 

Where the agreement to lease is not in writing, the landlord may recover a reasonable satisfaction for the use and occupation of the same. (§ 3).

Actions to recover rent may be in The Small Cause Court if within its jurisdiction.

III. REMEDY WHEN PREMISES ARE DESERTED 

Two Justices to put landlord in possession

Two Justices of the Peace may act in the case of the desertion of premises where the tenant shall be in arrear for one year's rent, and put the landlord in possession in the following manner: 

The landlord, his bailiff, or agent, must request the Justices to view the premises. They will go, and affix on a notorious part of the premises a written notice, stating what day they will return -to be not less than fourteen days thereafter. Then they must take a second view, when, if the tenant does not appear or pay the

rent, and there is not sufficient distress, the Justices may put the landlord in possession. The lease thenceforth becomes void. (C. 

S. 3069, § 10). 

Note that the Justices may put the landlord in possession, not shall. There rests with them a discretion.

IV. REMEDY BY DISPOSSESSION 

When a Justice may dispossess in case of definite term or definite rent

There is another and the usual proceeding open to a landlord where a tenant does not pay his rent when due, or when he does not surrender possession of the property leased at the expiration of his term. It is known in law as "Dispossession," or "Removal" proceedings, and may be instituted under amended section 

1 of the Small Cause Act and the general Landlord and Tenant 

Act as Revised in 1877, with numerous amendments thereto. As before stated, the Justice has jurisdiction only where the District Court does not have jurisdiction, but, under the amended section, when proceedings are before a Justice they will be in The Small 

Cause Court.

This form of action is so common when a landlord desires to take possession of premises leased by him for a term which he considers has expired, or when rent is unpaid, that the law respecting it should be clear and not constantly changed. 

By Act of 1903 amended several times (N. J. Cum. Supp. 

1773, § 18a, et seq.), it is provided: "I. Where any such person [tenant, etc.] shall hold over and continue in possession of the demised premises, or any part thereof, after the expiration of his or her term, and after demand made and notice in writing given for delivering the possession thereof, by the landlord or his agent for that purpose, which notice shall be served either personally upon the tenant or such person in possession by giving him a copy thereof, or by leaving a copy thereof at his usual place of abode, with some member of his family above the age of fourteen years; or where for any reason such service cannot he had, then the same may be served by affixing a copy of such notice to the door of any dwelling, or such demised premises, occupied by such tenant. "II. Where such person shall hold over after any default in the payment of the rent, pursuant to the agreement under which such premises are held."

Ünder another Act, however, if in any letting no term is agreed upon, and the rent is payable monthly, so long as the tenant pays the rent as agreed, and is not disorderly, it is unlawful to dispossess him before the first day of April, succeeding the commencement of such letting, without giving the tenant three J

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

months' notice in writing to quit. If disorderly, or he injures landlord's premises, etc., he may be served with notice to quit in three days. (C. S. 3079, § 32; Finkelstein v. Herson, 26 Vr. 

217; 2 N. J. Misc. Rep. 727).

As to the matters in foregoing paragraph, and others relating to "holding over," etc., see under the head, "V. Various Important Statutory Provisions, Rules and Decisions."

The statutory proceedings before the Justice The following are the statutory proceedings as applicable to a Justice of the Peace, when he has jurisdiction. The Act is exactly quoted, except the omission of references to the District Court, which has primary jurisdiction: "Any landlord or lessor, his legal representatives, agents or assigns, may make oath in writing to the facts which, according to the preceding section [see I and II above] authorize such proceedings against a tenant and describing therein the premises claimed; and if proceedings are begun under subdivision II of section one of this Act, then said oath shall state the amount of rent claimed to be in default, and may file the same with any Justice of the Peace of the county in which the premises are situated; and on filing such affidavit the Justice of the

Peace with whom the same is filed shall issue a summons describing the premises, in respect of which such proceeding is had, and requiring such tenant or any person in possession of said premises or claiming possession thereof, forthwith to remove from or surrender the same, or to show cause before the 

Justice of the Peace at a certain place and time to be therein specified, not less than five nor more than fifteen days from the date of such summons, why possession of such premises should not be delivered to such claimant, which summons shall be served in the manner prescribed in the Act constituting 

Courts for the Trial of Small Causes," [see § 16 of that Act] 

"and either party may demand and have a trial by a jury of twelve men; provided, that if proceedings shall be instituted under the provision of subdivision II of the preceding section, then if the tenant or person in possession of the demised premises shall at any time before the time of appearance specified in said summons pay to the 

Justice of the Peace by whom such summons was issued, the rent claimed to be in default by the oath filed with the said

Justice of the Peace, together with the accrued costs of the proceedings, all proceedings shall be stopped and the receipt of said 

Justice of the Peace shall be evidence of such payment, and the said Justice of the Peace shall forthwith pay all moneys so received to the landlord or to the person making oath for him." (C. S. 3071, § 18b, as amended by P. L. 1913, p. 744; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1774).

"If at the time appointed in the said summons, or at the time to which said suit may be adjourned, no sufficient cause be shown to the contrary, and it shall appear to the said . . . Justice of the 

Peace that the summons has been duly served and (in cases arising under subdivision II of section one of this Act) that the rent claimed and costs accrued have not been paid, the said ... Justice of the Peace shall forthwith enter a judgment for possession, and shall issue a warrant to any constable of the county, in which the premises are situate, . commanding him to remove all persons from the said premises, and to put the said claimant into full possession thereof, and to levy and make the costs out of the goods and chattels of such person or persons in possession; provided, it shall be necessary for said claimant, if required by the defendant, to prove to the satisfaction of the .. Justice of the Peace, or of the jury if there be a trial by jury, the facts which, according to the first section of this Act [see I and II above] authorize such proceedings against the tenant; and whenever in any suit for dispossession of a tenant on the return day of summons, or any adjourned day, there is no appearance by or on behalf of any tenant named therein, or if any defendant shall appear, but make no defense, the . . . Justice of the Peace may, if it appear that the summons has been duly issued and served, hear and determine the cause upon the affidavit filed, without the production of any witnesses or other proofs; provided, that no such warrant of removal shall issue until after the expiration of three days after the entry of judgment for possession." (Ibid, § 18e). It is further provided that in case admission to the dwelling or premises occupied by the tenant "is denied to the officer attempting to serve any summons issued under the provisions of this Act, or where the tenant resides out of or absent from the county in which the demised premises are located, and there is no person in actual occupation thereof, it shall be lawful service of such summons if the said officer shall post or affix a copy of the same upon the door or other conspicuous part of such dwelling or premises, and the said officer shall make a return of such service of such summons accordingly; provided, that in case the tenant shall not be a resident of the county in which said demised premises are situated, and the same shall be in the occupation of any other person or persons, then such summons shall be served either personally upon such person or persons, or by leaving the same with a member of his or their family above the age of fourteen years." (§ 18d). 

What gives the Justice jurisdiction 

To give a Justice jurisdiction (the holding over the_term) and waiving the matter of any exclusive jurisdiction by District 

Court, it must appear:

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

1. That the relation of landlord and tenant exists between the parties. 

2. That the tenant's term has expired, and that, notwithstanding this, he holds over. 

3. That the landlord, or his agent for that purpose, has made demand, and given the legal notice in writing to the tenant to deliver up possession: at present three months in all cases of monthly tenure. 

To give the Justice jurisdiction in the second class of cases (where rent is in default) it must appear: 

1. That the relation of landlord and tenant exists. 

2. That default has been made by the tenant in payment of the rent, according to the agreement under which he holds. (Fowler v. Roe, 1 Dutch. 549).

The statutes must be strictly followed. As the matter is of great importance, because cases will frequently come before a Justice of the Peace for his action, attention is called to the following leading points as to procedure (C. S. 3071, §§ 18a and 18b, as amended by P. L. 1913, p. 744, 1915, p. 97): 

1. The affidavit filed with the Justice must in all cases show on its face all the facts necessary to give him the jurisdiction. 

That affidavit is the whole basis for the proceedings before the Justice. It must be in legal form, presenting the facts about the rental, the term, etc., and not the conclusions of the affiant; because, if the affidavit does not make clear that the tenure is ended, or that the rent is actually due and unpaid, the Justice cannot take jurisdiction. (See Layton v. Dennis, 14 Vr. 380; Wooley v. 

Lane, 22 Vr. 504; Scheifele v. Irving, 24 Vr. 180; Gray v. Reynolds, 38 Vr. 169). 

2. If the proceedings are because the tenant holds over, such affidavit must show that there was notice in writing, by the landlord or his agent for that purpose, and that such notice was served according to the Act. 

3. If the proceedings are based upon a default in the payment of rent, notice by the landlord to the tenant, if necessary, must be according to the statute, and the affidavit must state the particulars as to when the rent fell due, the amount of rent, etc., according to the lease, or agreement. 

4. The affidavit being in order, the summons to be issued should recite the facts, and then require the tenant, or any person in possession of the premises, or claiming possession, forthwith to remove from or to surrender the same, or to show cause before the Justice why possession of such premises should not be delivered by the tenant. 

5. This summons is to be made returnable not less than five nor more than fifteen days from its date, and is to be served precisely like other summons in The Small Cause Court; that is to

say, it is to be served at least five days before the time of appearance, by reading the same to the defendant, and delivering to him a copy, if he shall be found, and if not found, by leaving a copy thereof at his usual place of abode with some person of his family above the age of fourteen years, who shall be informed of the contents. (S. C. A., § 16). Or, if service cannot be so made, it is to be made by affixing a copy upon the door or other conspicuous part of the premises; while if the tenant is not a resident of the county and the premises is in the occupation of another person, then it may be served upon such person or a member of his family above the age of fourteen. (C. S. 3073, § 18d). 

6. On the return day either party may demand a trial by a jury of twelve men, in which case the Justice will issue a venire to a constable, and proceed with the trial before the jury in the usual manner. If no jury be demanded, the Justice will try the proceeding himself. The Justice cannot demand fees in advance for the costs of a jury. (Story v. Walker, 42 Vr. 256). 

7. The proceeding, if for default for non-payment of rent, can be stopped at any time before the time of appearance mentioned in the summons by payment of rent and costs to the Justice, who must "forthwith" pay it to the landlord. 

8. If the defendant does not appear at the time appointed in the summons, or on the adjourned day, should there be an adjournment, and if no sufficient cause is shown to the contrary, and if the action be for dispossession because the tenant holds over, the Justice must take the proof of the plaintiff or his witnesses, as to the facts alleged in the affidavit, as the affidavit alone will not be sufficient. Then, if it appears that the summons was duly served, and the proof is that the tenant holds over his term after due notice, the Justice should enter judgment for possession, and after three days may issue his warrant for possession and costs. (§ 18e). 

9. If, however, the action be for dispossession, because the tenant defaults in rent, and the defendant makes no defense, the Justice, it appearing that the summons has been duly issued and served, may hear and determine the cause upon the affidavit filed, without the production of other proofs. It is to be noted that the language of the statute in such a case, is that the Justice "may hear and determine the cause upon the affidavit filed without the production of any witnesses or other proofs;" not that he shall. Hence, if he is not satisfied that the affidavit is complete enough to warrant his determination that the defendant defaulted in rent without further proofs, it is not only his right, but his duty, in order to protect the defendant against wrong, to demand further proofs. 

10. If the defendant enters into any defense, however (and he may call a jury), the proofs are to be heard, whether the action

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

be for removal because of holding over, or because of default in rent. 

11. If the judgment is for plaintiff, such judgment is to be a judgment for possession, and must be so entered on the Justice's record. (Halsey v. Sauer, 50 Vr. 159). 

12. The proceedings are to be recorded in the civil docket of The Small Cause Court, which has now jurisdiction of ordinary landlord and tenant cases instead of the Justice as magistrate. 

Warrant not to issue under three days 

Note that in no case shall a warrant of removal issue "until after the expiration of three days after the entry of judgment."'

The reason for this is to prevent the hardship of instantaneous dispossession after the decision is adverse to the defendant, and before he has time to secure a place to which to remove. After that time the officer holding the warrant of removal must remove all persons from the premises so as to put the landlord in possession. 

If title to land comes in question 

Where, upon the trial, the plaintiff shall not be able to prove by lease or other evidence his right to possession without proving title to the lands, the Justice must dismiss the action. (C. S. 3074, § 18f). 

Neither appeal nor certiorari allowed; exception 

Proceedings under section one of the Act (§ 18a) shall not be appealed from (i. e., to the Common Pleas, or in any usual form of appeal) nor removed by certiorari, but the landlord shall remain liable to an action of trespass (in Tort) for any unlawful proceedings. (Ibid, § 18g).

But if after summons has been issued and before its return, application is made by the landlord or the defendant to a Justice of the Supreme Court and he shall "deem the case of sufficient importance," he may order the Justice to file the papers in the Circuit Court for cognizance there. (C. S. 3074, § 24a).

V. VARIOUS IMPORTANT STATUTORY PROVISIONS; 

ALSO RULES AND DECISIONS 

"In case of any Right of landlord where tenant has made assignment general assignment, where the assignor shall be a tenant, all the goods and chattels of such tenant on the premises in the possession of such tenant shall be subject to a lien for the payment of the rent to his landlord; and the said

claim for rent in favor of the landlord, not exceeding one year's rent, shall be first paid and satisfied by the assignee out of the goods and chattels of the said tenant which were on the demised premises at the time of the assignment." (C. S. 119, § 12, as amend. by P. L. 1928, p. 410). 

Lien of landlord paramount over execution or other process

Rent due and unpaid must be first paid to the landlord, or his bailiff, before goods and chattels on the premises can be taken by virtue of any execution, attachment or other process. But this rule is qualified. (The full section on this point is in C. S. 3066, § 4).

Where there is rent due which the landlord has a right to have paid, and the goods on the premises, which are liable for the rent, are seized by virtue of an execution, or other process, the constable, sheriff, etc., who levies on or seizes the goods, should have notice that rent is due. This should be notice in writing, although if the officer has knowledge of the fact of the rent due and the lien of the landlord, he cannot proceed and dispose of the goods, except at his peril, because these goods are subject first to the lien of the landlord. (Hand v. Howell, 32 Vr. 142).

When holding over may be foundation of action for double rent

In case a tenant gives notice of intention to quit the premises leased at a time mentioned in such notice, and then shall not deliver up possession at that time, the landlord, or his heirs or assigns, may sue for and recover double the rent to afterward accrue. (C. S. 3077, § 28).

Termination of lease from other causes than end of term or default in rent

If the lessee of any dwelling-house or other premises uses the same for purposes of prostitution the lease thereupon becomes immediately void and the landlord may have the same remedies to recover possession as in the case of a tenant holding over. (Ibid, § 30).

If the tenant becomes so disorderly as to disturb the peace and quiet of other tenants in the house or neighborhood, or wilfully injures the premises or violates the landlord's rules, a copy of which is conspicuously posted on the premises, and holds over after a written notice to quit within three days, he may be dispossessed by a Justice of the Peace, if he has jurisdiction. In such case an affidavit setting forth the facts and service of notice is to be filed with the Justice, summons issued, proof made at the

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

hearing, and then there may be a judgment for the landlord and a warrant of removal as in other cases of summary removal of tenants. (C. S. 3079, § 32).

If a building is injured by fire without the fault of the lessee, the landlord must repair as speedily as possible, or, in default, the rent will cease until it is in complete repair; or, if it be totally destroyed, the rent is to be paid up to the time of destruction and then the lease comes to an end, unless the agreement of lease otherwise stipulates. (C. S. 3078, § 31). Where tenant refuses to allow the landlord to make repairs after a fire, the rent will not be suspended. (7 N. J. Misc. Rep. 612). 

The rule as to "holding over"

The rule as to "holding over" when there is a lease is not always well understood. It may here be stated as follows:

Where premises have been rented for a period of one month, or, as is usually the case, month by month, expiring, however, at the end of a certain period, and, after the expiration of the lease, the tenant holds over, with the consent of the landlord, a monthly tenancy is established; that is to say, in order thereafter to terminate the monthly tenancy three months' notice to quit [under the 1923 Act] is necessary, and the landlord must give such a notice if he wishes the tenancy to end and the tenant to vacate; or the tenant must give such a notice to the landlord if he wishes to leave the premises. Without such notice by either one to the other the tenant will be responsible for the three months' rent. This notice must be to quit or, if by the tenant, that the tenant will quit on one of the recurring periods of the holding. (See Hanks v. Workmaster, 46 Vr. 73).

Precisely the same principle holds good as to rentals for the period of one year. If, at the expiration of the year as per terms of a lease, the tenant holds over with the consent of the landlord, he becomes a tenant for another year and cannot be dispossessed during that year so long as he pays the rent fixed by the terms of the original lease. Supposing the year of the hold-over tenant to end on the first of April, the landlord must notify the tenant on or before the first day of January that the tenant must quit on the first day of April, or the tenant may remain and will have again another year's tenure. On the other hand, if the hold-over tenant wants to leave on the first of April, he must notify the landlord to that effect on or before the first day of January, or he will be held to be a tenant for another year. 

If a landlord does not consent to a "hold over," of course he will immediately make it known in some way. Silence or inaction may be construed as consent.

It must not be understood from the foregoing that where

there is a lease for a definite time and that time expires that the landlord must give a previous notice to the tenant to quit, but as many lawyers feel uncertain as to the effect of various statutes we advise that three months' notice be given in all cases.

Some important decisions relative to dispossession cases If the landlord, after the expiration of a term of years, consents to a continued occupation, a tenancy from year to year arises, and such consent may be inferred from the words or conduct of the parties. (Yetter v. Kings, 37 Vr. 491).

Where no term is agreed on, or annual rent reserved, then the tenure is determined by the intervals of the payments agreed on, and if to be made monthly, the hold over tenancy is limited to a month, or if weekly to a week. (Yetter v. Kings, supra).

Where a tenant in possession of land under lease for a term of years which provided for a rental during the term to be paid in equal monthly sums in advance, holds over according to the agreement, which the landlord unconditionally accepts, a tenancy from year to year is created, in the absence of any proof from which want of consent by the landlord may be inferred. Maier v. 

Champion. (Recent Sup. Ct. decision, per Justice Bergen).

Unless a lease contains a provision restraining the lessee from underletting the demised premises or assigning the lease, the lessee is entitled to do either at his own pleasure, notwithstanding the landlord's objection. (Braunstein v. McCrory, 116 Atl. 707).

Where a person is occupying farm buildings, while under contract to the owner of the farm for a share of the crops, he is not removable as a tenant holding over his term, or for non-payment of rent. (State, Gray v. Reynolds, 25 N. J. L. J. 144). So if one occupies premises under an agreement to purchase and fails to purchase, he is not such a tenant that the usual summary proceedings for his removal can be had, but he may be sued for use and occupation, or removed by action of ejectment in a higher 

Court. (Young v. Investment Co., 48 Vr. 410).

Any one of a number of joint tenants in common who are landlords may join in the proceedings to dispossess. (Mallone v. 

Klein, 26 Vr. 479).

An assignee of a landlord's reversionary interest can file the affidavit to dispossess. (Lloyd v. Richman, 28 Vr. 385).

If the defendant does not appear on the return day of the summons, he cannot afterward say that title to land came in question and there was not jurisdiction. (Watson v. Idler, 25 Vr. 467).

A tenancy which by express agreement was in its origin a tenancy from month to month remains such notwithstanding an increase of the monthly rent by agreement. (Stein v. Porter, 115 

Atl. 656).

J-22

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Where one employed as a workman by the month occupied a tenement of the employer, having its use as part remuneration for his services, his holding possession of such tenement, after the term of service is ended, does not give jurisdiction to a Justice of the Peace to remove him under the law. The relation between the parties is that of master and servant, not of landlord and tenant. 

The right of occupancy in such case ends with the service, and the employer may remove the incumbent without suit. (Mc- 

Quade v. Emmons, 9 Vr. 397).

A contract between the owner of lands and a third person, that the latter shall work the farm on shares, is not a lease, and does not create the relation of landlord and tenant. (Edgar v. 

Jewell, 5 Vr. 259).

Where a condition is annexed to a lease, on breach of which the rights of the tenant under the lease are to be forfeited—as, for instance, that the lessee will not assign the lease or sublet the premises or any part thereof without the landlord's written consent the actual breach of such conditions does not terminate the lease so as to make the "expiration of term" of the statute. The statute means expiration by lapse of time. (Wakeman v. Johnson, 3 N. J. L. J. 84).

The relation of landlord and tenant, so as to require the three months' notice to quit, does not exist where a party is let into possession under a contract to purchase, and the purchase is not afterwards completed. (Ross v. Van Aulen, 13 Vr. 49).

A notice to quit sooner or later than the conclusion of the tenancy will not be lawful; it must be to quit on the precise date of the conclusion (or desired conclusion) of the tenancy, and the day must be named in the notice. (Finkelstein v. Herson, 26 Vr. 217).

This day, however, for the tenant's removal may be the last day of the term, or the day corresponding with the day of rental. 

For example, if a tenancy began April 1 for one month, April 30 may be said to be the last day of the tenure, yet May 1 is the running calendar day, and, whether the notice specified April 30 or 

May 1, it would be lawful. (See Steffens v. Earl, 11 Vr. 128).

Where the form of farm lease uniformly used in a certain locality forbade the tenant to remove manure or compost, and it was the custom for the tenant to leave the manure when no agreement was specifically made, a tenant under a parol lease containing no specific stipulation was not entitled to take the manure, though it exceeded in amount what he received when he went into possession. (Whitesell v. Collison, 118 Atl. 277).

If there are formal defects in the summons issued by the Justice, yet, if defendant appears, secures an adjournment and begins trial before objection made, such defects are waived. (Palmer ads. Sanders, 22 Vr. 408).

A tenant at sufferance is not entitled to notice further than a demand of possession. (Moore v. Smith, 27 Vr. 447).

A tenant who disclaims his landlord's title is not entitled to notice. (Hankinson v. Blair, 3 Gr. 181). Nevertheless it seems safer always to give a notice in dispossession proceedings. 

In removal proceedings the description of the premises is to be such as to advise the tenant of them, and the officer concerned, with certainty. (Newing v. Stilwell, 38 Vr. 96).

In case of a mistrial because of the disagreement of the jury, the Justice should adjourn the cause to a date fixed and call a new jury. (Frost v. Chandler, 25 Vr. 128).

Legal Holidays 

Legal holidays in New Jersey

The statute now makes the following public legal holidays: the days and half days of January 1, February 12, February 22, Good Friday, May 30, July 4, first Monday of September, October 12, November 11, December 25, any general election day, every Saturday from twelve noon until midnight, and every 

Thanksgiving day or fast day, etc., or bank holiday, appointed by the Governor of this State, or the President of the United States. (P. L. 1921, p. 508; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1787; amended by P. L. 

1933, Chap. 37).

These holidays shall be considered such for all purposes whatsoever as regards the transaction of business in the public offices of this State, or counties of this State, the protest of notes, etc. 

If any of the days named above (excepting Good Friday) falls on Sunday, then the Monday next following shall be a public holiday. (Ibid).

Such Act (respecting holidays) "shall not be construed as

356HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

interfering with any person, or corporation, transacting business in this State, either private or public, but every such person or corporation shall be permitted to conduct business on any holiday or half-holiday." (C. S. 3092, § 7).

Another Act (of 1892) declares that sales of real and personal property made by any public officer or citizen on Saturday shall be valid and legal. (Ibid, § 12).

Still another Act (of 1892) provides in effect that it is valid for any process issued out of any Court in this State to be served on Saturday, between twelve M. and midnight, provided it is in other respects lawfully served. (Ibid, § 8). 

Construction of above Acts 

It is reasonably clear, therefore, that the law does not prevent the issuing of process, whether summons, attachment, civil warrant, execution, venire, subpoena or other process, upon any of the legal holidays or Saturday half-holidays if the Justice chooses to issue them, nor their service; but neither the Justice, nor the constable, is obliged to issue or serve these processes on those days, unless criminal processes. If issued, or served, however, they will be legal. (Kinney v. Emery, 10 Stew. 339).

It was questioned whether a civil Court can be held to try causes on legal holidays, because that would mean compulsory attendance upon Court of officers, suitors and witnesses. (Glenn v. Eddy, 22 Vr. 255). In that case Mr. Justice Magie drew the distinction between "legal holidays" and Sundays, and held that while certain acts done (as processes served, etc.), on Sundays are invalid, they may be valid if done on legal holidays, if they do not involve the attendance of other persons, but did not decide on holding Court. Afterwards, however, the Supreme Court held 

Court could be held on holidays. (Atlantic City v. Feretti, 41 Vr. 489).

The better plan is for the Justice not to issue civil writs in ordinary suits on legal holidays or half-holidays if it can be avoided, and especially not to make them returnable on those days.

As to summary penal actions, special provisions sometimes allow summons or warrants to issue on Sundays; for example, in bastardy, fish and game, motor vehicle and various other proceedings. 

Do not apply to criminal writs, however

The Acts referred to do not extend to criminal proceedings. 

The Justice, as magistrate, may receive complaints and issue warrants and prisoners may be held to bail on legal holidays and on Sundays.

Its meaning

Limitation of Actions 

Limitation of actions means that, by reason of statutes to that end, the time for bringing an action or prosecuting a crime is to end at a certain period after the cause for action or for prosecution began. After that period elapses no proceedings taken will be lawful. The limitations as to prosecutions for crime are as stated under general head, "Criminal Procedure." In civil actions they are as follows (not all of which directly concern the Justice): 

Limitation of two months 

Where a sheriff or other officer (as a constable) attaches, or levies, on personal property under any writ of attachment, or execution, and there is a written claim to such property made by some other than the defendant, such claimant must bring his action to enforce his claim within two months after such notice, or be forever barred. If the claimant does not give such notice, the officer may give him the notice, if such officer has reason to suppose it is so claimed. (C. S. 3171, §§ 23-25). 

Limitation of six months

Actions to recover a sum of money by the loser in a wager, prohibited by the "Act to prevent gaming," must be brought within six months after payment, and not after. (C. S. 2624, § 5).

So, also actions for penalties under the Act of 1877 (Revision), against peddlers who have no license must be brought within six months, and may be begun by warrant. (C. S. 3935, § 9). 

Limitation of nine months

Assignees in the case of assignments under the general Assignment Act, charged with appropriating, selling, etc., any part of the trust estate belonging to him under the assignment, are to be sued within nine months from the time when the cause of action shall arise, and not after. (C. S. 125, § 28). 

Limitation of eighteen months 

Actions for cutting timber under the Timber Act must be brought within eighteen months. (C. S. 5397, § 6). 

Limitation of one or two years

In cases of actions for penalties, known as "penal actions," in which the time is not otherwise designated, the law restricts their prosecutions as follows: If the forfeiture be limited to the

State of New Jersey only, to two years; if the forfeiture goes in whole or in part to any person prosecuting, to one year; but in the

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

latter case the action may be brought solely for the benefit of the State within the next year thereafter. If the forfeiture be to a county, township, town corporate, or an officer thereof, or for its or their use, or the use of the poor, the limitation is one year. 

If it be limited to the benefit of the party aggrieved, an action may be brought within two years. (C. S. 3170, § 21).

Actions accruing for injury to persons caused by the wrongful act, neglect or default of another are to be commenced within two years after the cause of action accrues, and not after. (C. S. 

3164, § 3). This would include actions for trespass, for assault, battery, etc., being all actions for injuries to the person by the wrongful act or neglect of another. (Tomlin v. Hildreth, 36 Vг. 438).

Actions for damages for the death of a person caused by the wrongful act, neglect or default of another, must be brought within two years after the death of such deceased person. (P. L. 1913, p. 586; N. J. Cum. Supp. 927). 

Limitation of four years

In case of an action upon a constable's bond the limitation is four years, after the date of the bond. (C. S. 3165, § 5). 

Limitation of six years "All actions of trespass quare clausum fregit, all actions of trespass, detinue, trover, and replevin for taking away of goods and chattels, all actions of debt [now "on Contract"] founded upon any lending or contract without specialty, or for arrearages of rent due on a parole demise, and all actions of account, and upon the case [now in Tort], except actions for slander, and except also, such actions as concern the trade or merchandise between merchant and merchant, their factors, agents, and servants [i. e., running accounts on both sides], shall be commenced and sued within six years next after the cause of such actions shall have accrued, and not after." (C. S. 3162, § 1).

Under this limitation it has been held that on a note, payable on demand, the statute begins to run from the time of making the note, but when due on a certain day, it runs from the time it is due; it bars an action brought by an executor to recover money overpaid to a legatee; it applies to a set-off by the defendant; it applies to a suit against a sheriff, or a constable, for money collected on execution, running from the time of such collection; it applies to a suit brought on a foreign judgment; and where one receives money, as an agent of another, the time runs, not from the date of the receipt of the money, but from the day it is demanded by his principal.

In short most civil actions to recover debts or for torts are limited to six years.

Limitation of nine years

Suits on bonds of sheriffs, or collectors of taxes are limited to nine years. (C. S. 3165, § 5). 

Limitation of ten years

Official bonds of Justices of the Peace must be prosecuted within ten years. (C. S. 3168, § 15). 

Limitation of sixteen years

Every action for rent, founded upon any lease under seal, or on a sealed bond or obligation, whether in a penal sum or not for the payment of money only, or upon award of arbitrators, under their hands and seals, or bond given to the sheriff by an insolvent person arrested upon a ca. sa., shall be commenced within sixteen years after the cause of the action accrued, or the date of the bond, and not after. But if plaintiff during that period has been an infant or insane, such time is not computed. (C. S. 

3165, §§ 6, 14). 

A promissory note having a mere wafer or scroll seal after the name of the maker is not "sealed," and an action thereon is barred after six years as in other notes. But if the fact of its being a sealed instrument is set out in the body of the note, and the signing and sealing is witnessed, it becomes a "sealed obligation," and to it the sixteen years' rule applies. 

Limitation of twenty years

An action must be brought upon a bond given by any executor, administrator, guardian, trustee, receiver, or assignee, within twenty years from the date of the bond (with exceptions; see 

C. S. 3168, § 13).

Forbearance to collect a judgment, if unexplained, and unaccounted for, will extinguish it in twenty years, but a period of infancy or insanity is not computed. (C. S. 3166, § 7).

In actions in which persons or corporations are impleaded by the State of New Jersey for "rents, revenues, issues or profits" of lands; and in all actions for lands, tenements or hereditaments, the limitation is also twenty years. (C. S. 3170, §§ 17, 20). (As to limitations for longer periods in matters concerning possession of lands, see C. S. 3172, §§ 28, 29, etc.). 

Exceptions to the operation of the statute

There are exceptions made by the statute or Courts to the operation of the statute of limitations; exceptions arising from the acts of the defendant, or from circumstances beyond the plaintiff's control. These are: 

1. Infancy: The time during which the plaintiff may be an in-

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

fant is, usually, not to be computed in reckoning the period when the statute of limitations begins to run, but he is at liberty to bring his action within the number of years named in the statute after his arriving at full age. (C. S. 3164, § 4). 

2. Insanity, etc.: If a person entitled to bring an action shall be, at the time the cause of action accrued, non compos mentis, the statute does not run against him until he becomes sane. (Ibid). Deaf and dumb persons, being prima facie incompetent to contract or to sue, the statute does not run against them unless they are shown to have sufficient intelligence to comprehend their legal rights and liabilities. But if a lunatic becomes sane, the statute begins to run from the day of his sanity, and it will not cease to run notwithstanding the lunacy returns. The rule that when the statute begins to run it does not cease has also been applied to the case of a note, where, some time after the note became due, the payee became a lunatic. (Steelman v. Steelman, 1 Harr. 68). 

3. Non-residence: In all actions where the limitation is to six years, or upon a sheriff's or constable's bond, or upon sealed instruments, or to revive a judgment, or against sureties upon the bonds of executors, administrators, guardians, trustees, receivers or assignees, where the person against whom there is a right of action becomes a non-resident after the right accrues and before the time of limitation, the time or times during which such defendant shall not reside in this State is not to be computed as part of the limited period. The mere fact of non-residence at the time of trial will not debar a defendant from taking advantage of the statute, if when the action was brought he had resided in the 

State for over six years after the right of action. (C. S. 3166, § 8; Halsey v. Beach, 1 Penn. 123).

Non-residence must be bona fide, in order to suspend the operation of the statute; merely being out of the State for a few weeks or months, on business or pleasure, will not suspend it. (Paterson Bank v. Ludlow, 6 Hal. 354). 

4. Death: In cases where the limitation is, as set forth above, six years, or sixteen years; or where actions are brought upon judgments, or on a sheriff's bond, if the debtor shall have died before the expiration of the time of limitation, six months next succeeding the death of such person shall not be computed as part of the limited period. (C. S. 3167, § 9). 

5. Reversed Judgment: In case a plaintiff, after suit brought and judgment obtained, has that judgment reversed, he is allowed one year in which to commence a new action. But this does not apply to a judgment of nonsuit, nor to an action commenced and not prosecuted to judgment. (C. S. 3170, § 19; Ivins v. Schooley, 3 Harr. 269). 

6. Mutual Accounts: In actions on Contract, in which the

limitation is to six years, the statute expressly excepts "such actions as concern the trade or merchandise between merchant and merchant, their factors, agents and servants." (C. S. 3162, § 1.)

No length of time is a bar in such a case, if the accounts are mutual and continuing. And not simply "merchants" are allowed to have advantage of this saving clause, but all persons between whom there have been mutual dealings, a current account, unsettled and unadjusted. (Belles v. Belles, 7 Hal. 339).

A single transaction between two merchants is not within the exception; nor accounts between one partner and another; nor a single payment on an account; nor the mere holding of a due bill against the vendor of goods. Where there are many items previous, but only one item charged within six years, it is not sufficient to bring the account within the statute; nor will the part of an account of more than six years standing be excepted from the operation of the statute where the defendant has a set-off extending back six years only. Items on both sides must be within six years, and to bring in items beyond that period, in connection with those since, the transactions beyond that time must not be too remote or unconnected with the later items. 

Where parties have adjusted an account it ceases to be an account; and the statute will run, as to a suit for the balance due, from the date of the last item on either side. This balance may be carried forward into a new mutual account, when the statute will bar the items of the first account, but the balance will be saved unless the balance is incorrect. Nor will the payment of a sum of money on an open book account, which has never been presented or recognized in its entirety, be a fact from which alone a promise to pay can be inferred. 

7. Acknowledgment, or Part Payment: "In actions grounded on any simple contract, no acknowledgment or promise by words only shall be deemed sufficient evidence of a new or continuing contract, whereby to take any case out of the operation of this Act, or to deprive any person of the benefit thereof, unless such acknowledgment or promise shall be made or continued by or in some writing to be signed by the party chargeable thereby; and where there shall be two or more joint contractors or executors, or administrators of any contractor, no such joint contractor, executor, or administrator shall lose the benefit of this Act so as to be chargeable in respect, or by reason only of any written acknowledgment or promise, and signed by any other or others of them; provided always that nothing herein contained shall alter or take away or lessen the effect of any payment of any principal or interest made by any person whatsoever; provided also that in actions to be commenced against two or more such joint contractors or executors or administrators, if it shall appear at the trial or J-23

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

otherwise that the plaintiff, though barred by this Act as to one or more of such joint contractors or executors or administrators, shall, nevertheless, be entitled to recover against any other or others of the defendants by virtue of a new acknowledgment or promise, or otherwise, judgment may be given, and with costs allowed for the plaintiff as to such defendant or defendants against whom he shall recover, and for the other defendant or defendants against the plaintiff." (C. S. 3167, § 10). "No indorsement or memorandum of any payment written or made, after this Act shall go into effect, upon any promissory note, bill of exchange, or other writing, by or on behalf of the party to whom such payment shall be made, shall be deemed sufficient proof of such payment so as to take the case out of the operation of this Act." (Ibid, § 11). "This Act shall be deemed and taken to apply to the case of any debt on simple contract alleged by way of set-off on the part of the defendant." (Ibid, § 12).

The language used above is unmistakable. A mere promise to pay a debt, to revive it as against the statute of limitations, must be in writing. Such writing may be separate, or on the back of the written obligation itself. It may be intended to revive the action, or it may be a letter simply acknowledging the existence of the debt, and agreeing to pay it; in either case it does revive responsibility in law.

A part payment is to be proved, and it must be proved by other evidence than the mere indorsement of the plaintiff on the back of his note, check or other writing. The holder of a written obligation can so readily make a false indorsement or give a fictitious credit, that independent proof of the part payment, or payment of interest, is now demanded. Further, there must, beside indorsement of payments, be some act or declaration to show that the debtor recognized the whole claim and intended to appropriate the payments upon the whole account. (Vaughn v. 

Hankinson, 6 Vr. 79; Romaine v. Corlies, 18 Vr. 108).

A new promise in writing will revive the debt from the day on which such writing is made, or from the day when the new obligation created by such writing is due, and continues the obligation for another full period. For example, A gives a note to 

B and, when the six years is about to expire A makes a payment upon it. From that day the note will have six years to run; i. e., it can be sued upon during any time of that additional period. 

8. The State as a Party: The statute of limitations is held not to apply to the State itself, unless so expressly designated, under the common-law maxim that "no laches can be imputed to the King." 

9. Actions by Public Officers for their Salaries: The sal-

ary of a public official is not a debt in the nature of a contract, express or implied. "When a citizen is elected to a public office there is no agreement on the subject between his electors and himself; they require him to take the office, and no option to accept or refuse it is left to him, for he is constrained to perform its duties under pain of a criminal prosecution. Nor can he stipulate for his compensation; he must perform the official functions even though he is obliged to do so gratuitously." Therefore the statute of limitations does not run as against him. (Outwater v. 

Passaic, 22 Vr. 352; Cowenhoven v. Middlesex, 15 Vr. 232). 

Effect of statute upon torts

The limitation of actions in cases in Tort runs from the date of the commission of the injury. If the illegal act committed creates an immediate injury, it runs from the date of the act; but if the injury is consequential, whenever such injury results and is actionable, however much later that day may be than the date of the commission of the wrongful act, on such actionable day the statute begins to run. (Del. & Rar. C. Co. v. Wright, 1 Zab. 469). 

Waiver of statute

The statute of limitations may be waived in legal form, and such waiver will estop the party from pleading it. A written agreement will always waive it; a parol agreement will not, unless there was valuable consideration for such parol agreement. (Quick v. Corlies, 10 Vr. 12). 

Computation of time

As a rule the time limited by the statute of limitations is to be computed from the day on which a right of action accrues upon the obligation, or upon an injury done. If there is a condition attached to the contract, that condition must first be performed; or if money is to be paid at a future period, such period must first elapse before the right of action accrues, and hence before the statute begins to run. In computing the time the rule is to exclude the first day; so that where a debt was due October 6, 1862, a suit, brought October 6, 1868, was held not to be barred by the statute. (McCulloch v. Hopper, 18 Vr. 189). 

The law of place

As all remedies on contracts are to be regulated according to the law of the place where the action is instituted, and not of the place where the contracts are made, it is the statute of limitations of the State where the suit is begun that is to be pleaded by a defendant, and not of the State where he made his bargain. The

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

exception to this is where the debt itself is extinguished by the statute of the State where it was incurred. 

Statute of limitations need not be pleaded in writing No written plea is necessary in The Small Cause Court in order to give a defendant the advantage of the statute of limitations. When such defense is set up, and proved, the Justice must dismiss the action. 

Act to protect Lobsters

By an Act of 1911 (P. L., p. 189, amend. by P. L. 1913, p. 

266; N. J. Cum. Sup. 1391), it is made unlawful to take from salt waters, by means of boats, pots or otherwise, or have in possession, buy or sell, or offer to buy or sell, any lobster less than 42 inches long, or any spawning lobster under $20 penalty; and the procedure to enforce the Act is the same as under the Fish and 

Game Act of 1897. 

Nature of writ Mandamus

The writ of mandamus is a command issuing from a superior Court, having competent authority, directed to any person, corporation, or inferior Court, requiring the performance of some duty as to a particular thing therein specified. The term is derived from the opening Latin word of the writ, "mandamus,” "we command you." 

When it will lie

It will lie (i. e., may be issued) by a Judge or Court to a Justice of the Peace to compel him to render judgment on a verdict which he had no power to set aside; or to compel him to issue an execution on a judgment, even where the Justice had granted an appeal, but where, in fact, he had no lawful right to grant such appeal; or to proceed with the trial of a claim to property levied on under an execution from his Court, etc., etc.

It is to be granted on motion, upon presentation of affidavits or the record of the Court below. 

The alternative and peremptory writ It is customary to issue first an alternative writ of mandamus. The object of this is to give the opposing party the bene- 4334

MARRIAGES 

365 fit of a return, and a full hearing on the merits. The Justice must make a return to the writ. It is only when the parties are both heard in the first instance, and the facts and law have been fully discussed, or when the mandamus is based upon a previous order of the Court in which all the facts appear, that a peremptory writ will issue in the first instance. 

How to be served

The alternative mandamus is usually served by delivering it to the Justice who is required to obey it, or to return a sufficient cause for not doing so; the person serving it preserving a copy by which, if needful, to prove the service. 

A peremptory mandamus is served by showing the original to the person required to execute it, and reading or explaining it as may be necessary and giving him not the original but a copy. 

It is not necessary that an officer should serve it, although it is better so done.
