Justices of the Peace may not perform marriages 

Until a statute of 1912 Justices of the Peace could solemnize marriages in New Jersey, but it is no longer the law. Marriages can now be solemnized only by the Chief Justice and Associate Justices of the Supreme Court, the Chancellor and Vice-Chancellors, Circuit Court Judges, Common Pleas Judges, Judges of

Criminal Judicial Courts where such exist in counties, Recorders, Police Justices, Mayors, and ordained ministers; "and every religious society, institution or organization in this State may join together in marriages such persons as are members" of the same,

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

"or when one of such persons is a member" of the same, "according to the rules and customs" of such society, etc. (P. L. 1912, p. 306, as amended by P. L. 1927, p. 578). 

License to marry

A license to marry must first be obtained at least 24 hours before the ceremony, before any ceremony of marriage, from the registrar of vital statistics in municipalities, if there be such officer, otherwise from the municipal (i. e., city, borough or town) clerk; and in townships, in case there is no registrar of vital statistics, from the assessor. The license fee is $2.00. (P. L., 1926, p. 334). But no license is to be issued when either party is infected with gonorrhea, syphilis or chancroid, or intoxicated (for such to marry is a misdemeanor), or using narcotics, or is an imbecile, epileptic or of unsound mind, or inmate of insane or indigent institution unless satisfactorily discharged therefrom. (P. L. 1921, p. 128; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1828). (P.

The male must not be under 21, nor the female under 18, but, if so, consents are necessary by parents or guardians. 

L. 1912, p. 310; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1830).

The registrar, clerk or assessor, before issuing a license may require the parties to attest, by oath or affirmation, the legality of the proposed marriage, to be verified by a witness of lawful age. (P. L. 1917, p. 483; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1829).

As to the place of obtaining license, it must be the municipality where the female party resides, or, if she is non-resident, where the male party resides. If the license officer is absent, his deputy may issue it.

Penalties are recoverable in an action of Debt in the usual way (in The Small Cause Court when it has jurisdiction) in actions by and in the name of the local board of health, or by the

Married Women 

Some points of New Jersey law

Some of the principles laid down by our New Jersey statutes or Courts respecting married women, about which Justices of the Peace or other magistrates may be concerned, are the following: 

A married woman may now sue or be sued without joining her husband in any case where he would be an unnecessary party if he were not her husband. (P. L. 1912, p. 416; N. J. Cum. 

Supp. 1838). But neither can sue the other at law.

Thus she may bind herself by contracts, as if unmarried, and

MORTGAGE 

367 enforce them, or be subject to have them enforced against her and in her own name, apart from her husband. (P. L. 1927, p. 83).

Deeds, mortgages and other instruments made by her husband and herself (if she be of 21 years or more) she need not acknowledge, as formerly, by a separate examination "privately apart from her husband." But as to a married woman under 21, the private examination must still be had. (P. L. 1916, p. 321; 

N. J. Cum. Supp. 628).

If a wife conveys real estate or interest therein separately, her husband needs to convey his interest in it by separate deed, to give complete title. (P. L. 1926, p. 310).

A wife may testify for her husband, and she is a compellable witness in any ordinary action. (See under general title "Evidence").

A married woman may make a will (if she is above 21 years of age) the same as if she were unmarried, but not to dispose of any interest her husband may have in the real estate. (C. S. 3235, § 9).

The husband is not responsible for his wife's debts contracted before marriage; nor is he liable for her debts contracted in her own name after marriage. (Ibid, § 10).

While ordinarily a wife is not responsible for her husband's debts, yet there are exceptions. For example, she may purchase her husband's debts, and give a binding note therefor. (First National Bank v. Dohn, 23 Vr. 363). 

A wife's wages and earnings belong to her, and she may carry on business in her own name. (C. S. 3225, § 4; amend. by P. L. 1928, p. 422). 

Arrest of married woman

No woman, married or unmarried, can be arrested on any first intermediate or final civil process. (C. S. 4072, § 64; S. C. 

A., § 11). If she and her husband are sued for her tort, and a capias issues, the order to hold to bail must be against both, but he only can be arrested. (Damiano v. Corello, 16 Ñ. J. L. J. 376). 

What a mortgage is Mortgage

A mortgage, as usually understood, is a conveyance of real property as security for a debt, and to become void on payment of it. It must be a written instrument and in the English language. Where the mortgage is on personal property it is called a

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

chattel mortgage. No special form of mortgage is required by law, but it should conform to the usual requisites of the mortgage and be under seal. 

Execution, recordation and cancellation

A mortgage is to be acknowledged and executed precisely like a deed, and is also to be recorded in the same manner in the office of the county clerk, or registrar of deeds. The fee for recording is, usually, 15 cents per folio. (P. L. 1920, p. 46; N. J. 

Cum. Supp. 1238). Or an abstract of it may be registered (which we do not advise), the fee for which is 40 cents. (P. L. 1923, p. 

155; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1967).

A short form of mortgage is allowed (P. L. 1918, p. 816; 

N. J. Cum. Supp. 1967), but it should contain, what is not in the form stated in that Act, the words, "his heirs and assigns." 

Mortgages are cancelled by the county clerk or register only when produced with proper receipt, acknowledged. (P. L. 1929, p. 104). If a corporation mortgage (not building and loan) certain officers may authorize cancellation. (P. L. 1931, p. 52). (As to chattel mortgage, see general title "Chattel Mortgage").

Motor Vehicles 

Regulations concerning motor vehicles

The Act of March 23, 1903, was the first attempt made in 

New Jersey to control by uniform law the use of "automobiles, locomobiles, and all other vehicles propelled otherwise than by muscular power, excepting the cars of electric and steam railways and other motor vehicles running only upon rails or tracks." (P. 

L. 1903, p. 80, § 1). This Act was repealed by the substitution of the "Frelinghuysen Act" of 1906, which applies to automobiles, motor cycles, etc., under whatever name, when propelled otherwise than by muscular power and not running on rails or tracks, but excepting fire engines, steam road rollers, and vehicles not for hire, pleasure or business. (C. S. 3427).

Many Acts have been passed since, and the magistrate should secure the latest copy of all the Motor Vehicle Statutes from the 

Commissioner of Motor Vehicles, State House, Trenton, unless obtainable from the local licensing agent. The General Act of 1921 

is in force, but with scores of amendments and supplements. 

There is also a Road Traffic Act regulating vehicles, etc., on all public roads passed in 1928, which is of equal importance to users of automobiles and other motor-vehicles as the Motor Ve-

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

hicle Act. (See under general title "Roads"). Some of the matters under this Act appear in various parts of what follows. 

The Acts fully provide as to speed, lights, passing other vehicles, etc., and requires a State license, and must be examined as to provisions and penalties by any Justice or magistrate who takes charge of a complaint. 

Drivers' licenses 

Seventeen years is the minimum age limit.

Applicants must establish their age to the satisfaction of the Department, preferably by means of a birth certificate, if obtainable, and if not obtainable, then a baptismal certificate or a school certificate. Affidavits are not acceptable. cense.

Examination is necessary for first New Jersey driver's li- 

Driver's license certificate shall expire on the thirty-first of

December of each year; annual fee three dollars; learner's permit necessary before examination can be taken; holder of learner's permit must be accompanied by licensed driver; holder of permit, as well as the licensed driver, shall be held accountable for all violations of the Motor Vehicle Act committed by the holder of the permit while in the presence of such licensed driver; fee for permit fifty cents.

Every license shall have endorsed thereon the name of the licensee, in the handwriting of the licensee.

License must be in possession of the driver at all times when the driver is in charge of a motor vehicle or motorcycle. Licensee, when requested by any motor vehicle inspector, police officer or magistrate, shall exhibit said license to said officer, and write his name in the presence of said officer, to the end that he may thereby determine the identity of said licensee. 

Non-resident drivers licensed in their resident State may operate under reciprocity privilege vehicles bearing New Jersey plates, as well as non-resident registered vehicles. 

Drivers seventy-five years of age or over must be re-examined each year before the Department will renew their licenses. 

Drivers' licenses obtained for the following year on and after November 1st of the current year may be used on and after 

December 15th of the current year.

Drivers' licenses are renewable for three years without examination. 

Motor vehicle registrations

Every automobile or motorcycle must be registered before operation on the highways. 

Registration certificate expires on December thirty-first of each year.

MOTOR VEHICLES 

371 Registrations and licenses for the ensuing year will now be issued from November 1st of the current year, and registrations and licenses for the ensuing year may be legally used on and after December 15th of the current year.

Initial or original registration for motor vehicle will be issued only upon production of satisfactory original bill of sale. 

Renewals for following years are obtainable upon presentation at agency of registration card issued for preceding year. 

Commissioner may refuse registration to any vehicle that in his estimation is not a proper vehicle to be used on the highways. 

Non-residents who obtain New Jersey registrations are required to file a power of attorney with their application for registration naming the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles as their attorney to accept service in the event of a civil suit. 

New Jersey allows full reciprocity privilege to passenger vehicles and to commercial vehicles owned by non-residents who have complied with the laws of their resident State with regard to the registration and operation of motor vehicles. This reciprocity privilege is granted on condition that similar privileges are extended by the laws of the State in which the non-resident resides to motorists from the State of New Jersey who are touring in such non-resident State.

A registration cannot be transferred from one owner to another.

A registration can be transferred from one car to another by the same owner, upon production of the bill of sale for the new car and the original registration certificate. 

Duplicate registration or driver's license certificates may be obtained on written request to the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles at Trenton, New Jersey, setting forth that the original card has been lost. The fee for each duplicate is one dollar. 

Duplicate plates may be issued to replace lost or defaced plates. In the event of the loss of a plate, it is the duty of the owner to apply to the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles or the local agent within twenty-four hours of the discovery of the loss of the plate or plates, but the motor vehicle may not be operated with one plate in the meantime. The agent will issue new plates upon payment of the fee of one dollar for each lost plate. 

No person shall counterfeit any number plate or marker, nor make any substitute or temporary marker. Any person who shall violate this provision shall be fined not less than fifty nor more than one hundred dollars.

The license plates shall be affixed to the front and rear of the motor vehicle in a horizontal and stationary manner and shall be not less than fifteen inches nor more than forty-eight inches from the ground; they shall be kept clear and distinct and free

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

from grease, dust, or other blurring matter, so as to be capable of being easily read at all times. The rear plate should be illuminated at night by the white rays from the tail lamp.

No person shall drive a motor vehicle, the owner of which vehicle shall not have complied with the provisions of the law concerning the proper registration and identification of the same nor shall any person drive a motor vehicle which shall display on the front or back thereof a fictitious number or a number other than that designated for such motor vehicle in the registration certificate.

It shall be the duty of every registered owner and of every licensed driver to notify the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles of any change in his or her place of residence within one week after such change is made. (Sections 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13 of Law).

If the operator of a motor vehicle fails to produce the registration certificate, a complaint may be made for not having the registration certificate in possession. This applies to residents as well as non-residents. The registration certificate should be in the possession of the person in charge of the car at all times while the car is operated on the highways. 

The law provides for braking systems on automobiles, signaling device and lights after sunset, mufflers and tire chains.

Making complaints and procedure

Any citizen who observes a violation of the law is entitled to make a complaint against the motorist committing such violation. The complaint may be made to any magistrate having jurisdiction where the violation occurs, and must be brought within thirty days from the date of the violation.

In cities no Justice of the Peace can act. Otherwise all Jus tices of the Peace, Judges of City Criminal Courts, Police Judges,

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Recorders, Mayors and other committing magistrates may act. (Laws 1926, p. 202). The magistrate may issue a summons or a warrant for the appearance of the person charged with the violation, may hold a hearing to determine the innocence or guilt of the defendant, and upon conviction may impose the penalty provided by the Motor Vehicle law or Road Traffic Act. 

The proceedings are summary and, if before a Justice, not in the Small Cause Court but before him as magistrate. 

All proceedings are to run in the name of The State of New Jersey with the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles, or a motor vehicle inspector, or a police officer, or constable, or any private person who institutes proceedings, as prosecutor. But any magistrate may, at discretion, refuse to issue a complaint of a private person until he gives a bond for the costs. 

The summons or warrant is to be directed to any constable, police officer, inspector of motor vehicles or the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles of the State and is to name what provision of the Act has been violated, and the time, place and nature of the violation. (See Revision of 1929, approved April 22, 1929; amended by P. L. 1933, Chap. 63).

The case may be adjourned in the discretion of the magistrate, for a period not exceeding thirty days from the return day named in any summons or warrant, or from the date of any arrest without warrant, as the case may be; but in such case the magistrate may require a bond to insure the future appearance of the defendant; forfeited bail is returnable to the Commissioner of 

Motor Vehicles in the same manner as fines for violations are returnable.

Any person arrested for a violation of any of the provisions of the Motor Vehicle Law shall, upon demand of the magistrate hearing the complaint against said person, produce his license for inspection. 

Proceedings for violation of the Motor Vehicle Law are valid if taken on Sunday, and any process served on Sunday shall be as valid as if served on any other day of the week. Process may also be served in any county of the State. Appeal

The defendant, if not satisfied with the decision of the magistrate, may within ten days appeal his case to the Court of Special Sessions; the defendant is required to file an appeal bond with the magistrate; an appeal acts as a stay of any judgment or sentence, with the exception that it does not operate to restore during the pendency of such appeal, a license revoked for driving while intoxicated. (R. L. 1933, Ch. 97).

Arrest without warrant "Any constable or police officer, or motor vehicle inspector, or the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles is hereby authorized to arrest, without warrant, any person violating, in the presence of such constable, or police officer, or motor vehicle inspector, or the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles any of the provisions of this Act, and to bring the defendant before any magistrate of the county where such offense is committed. In the event of any violation of subdivision three of section fourteen of the Act of which this Act is amendatory, such magistrate, clerk or deputy clerk is not readily accessible, the constable, or police officer, or motor vehicle inspector, or Commissioner of Motor Vehicles, apprehending the offender is authorized to detain in any police station, lockup, or other place maintained by any municipality for the detention of offenders, or in the common jail of the county, for such reasonable time as will permit the said officer to obtain a warrant for the further detention of the offender; provided, however, that the temporary detention in this section authorized shall not exceed twenty-four hours from the time of the said arrest. In the event of any violation other than a violation of subdivision three of section fourteen, the person so offending shall be detained until the officer making such arrest shall make oath or affirmation, which he shall do declaring that the person under arrest has violated one or more of the provisions of this Act, and specifying the provision or provisions violated, whereupon said magistrate shall issue a warrant, and the said magistrate shall proceed to hear or postpone the case as provided in sections twenty-six and twentyseven of the Act, of which this Act is amendatory. And any such constable or police officer, or motor vehicle inspector, or the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles, upon satisfying himself that such offender is a resident of this State, may, instead of arresting such offender as hereinabove provided, serve upon him a summons in the name of any police court, recorder's court or other court of competent jurisdiction in the county, city, town, township, village, borough or other municipality wherein such officer shall be authorized to discharge his duties, directing such offender to appear and answer such charges as may then and there be preferred against him, and for this purpose, the county, city, town, township, village and borough clerks respectively, shall provide the said officer or officers with a form of summons, which, when filled out, executed and issued by the said officer or officers, in such case as herein provided, shall be good and effectual according to the purpose and intent thereof. 

Any person arrested for a violation of any of the provisions of this Act shall, upon demand of the magistrate hearing the complaint against said person, produce his license for inspection, and if said person shall fail to pro- J-24

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

duce his license or give satisfactory excuse for its non-production, he shall, in addition to any other penalties imposed by said magistrate, be subject to a fine of not more than twenty-five dollars." (P. L. 1926, p. 249). 

Fees and costs (See under general title "Fees and Costs," pp. 267, 270). 

Payment of fines; report

Fines are to be forwarded to the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles, at Trenton within 30 days, under heavy penalty. In case the complaint is under a municipal law, the penalty goes to the municipality.

Every magistrate hearing a motor vehicle case must make a report to the Commissioner within three days after the disposition of the case (on blanks the Commissioner will furnish), stating the nature of the violation, the disposition, and any recommendation he may deem of value as to whether action be taken against the licensee or owner of the motor vehicle. (1921 Act, § 39). 

Intoxicated driver as disorderly person

The Road-Tariff Act forbids driving when intoxicated on the public highway under penalty of the driver being convicted as a disorderly person and applies to all vehicles. 

But the Motor-Vehicle Act, in § 14, also forbids driving when under influence of intoxicants or narcotics, under penalty of from 30 days to six months imprisonment and forfeiture of license. (N. J. Cum. Supp. 1993). 

Garage keeper's lien

Garage keepers and automobile repairmen have a lien upon a motor vehicle, or any part of it, for the sum due for storing or repairing it, or furnishing supplies for it, and, after demand for payment, may detain the motor vehicle without process of law until the sum due is paid. Or, if the vehicle be removed, the lien will not be lost, but the vehicle or parts of it may be seized wherever found within the State. After being held thirty days from the date of detention, it is to be sold at public auction upon notice published for two weeks in a newspaper circulating in the municipality, and after five days' notice of the sale set up in five most public places. When sold and the lien and expenses are paid, the balance goes to the owner; or, if unclaimed for sixty days, to the support of the poor.

There are other important provisions of this Act, as amended, to be examined by any garage keeper or repairman interested.

Acts in force 

Negotiable Instruments

Two Acts are still in force in this State in so far as they do not conflict with each other, the one being "An Act concerning 

Promissory Notes," etc., (Revision of 1877; C. S. 3757), and the other "A general Act relating to Negotiable instruments," etc. (C. S. 3734), being an Act of 1902.

The law of 1902 concerning negotiable paper is a lengthy and important one, in the matter both of actions and defenses, and

PARTNERSHIP 

383 should be examined with care when appealed to during the progress of a suit. It has been amended. (See N. J. Cum. Supp. 2558).

Actions on bills and notes in The Small Cause Court The Small Cause Act gives important directions concerning procedure on actions on bills and notes in §§ 38-45, which must be carefully consulted, especially where there are more than one defendant.

The two very important sections, as to proving plaintiff's case by affidavit, are §§ 38 and 39. 

For special provisions as to set-offs, see § 44.

There is also a provision as to how the constable, after a levy under execution, shall make the money out of the property of the person primarily liable. (8 46). 

Indorsers on a promissory note are held liable only after notice of dishonor and protest (unless protest has been waived), and a certificate of protest by a notary public under his hand and official seal accompanying such note is conclusive evidence of the facts therein certified, if a copy of the same has been annexed to the state of demand, unless (if the action is in The Small Cause Court) notice is given by a defendant that he intends to dispute the notice of dishonor, etc. (C. S. 2227, § 21).

Sometimes the authenticity of a signature or indorsement to a negotiable instrument is disputed. In such case the statute says (in its applicability to The Small Cause Court) that in every suit brought on such instrument the authenticity of any such signature or indorsement "shall be taken to be admitted" unless the party to the suit denying the authenticity of such signature or indorsement shall file with the Court an affidavit stating that to the best of his or its knowledge and belief such signature or indorsement is not the true signature or indorsement of the person purporting to have made the same." (P. L. 1914, p. 319; N. J. Cum. 

Supp. 1127, § 20a).

Partnership Various statutory and common law rules Some general principles follow, based on the statutes and on the common law.

There is an Act of 1919 on limited partnerships repealing inconsistent Acts that may need to be consulted in limited partnership actions (P. L., p. 471; N. J. Cum. Supp. 2652). This Act may occasionally conflict with some matters named below, which are more or less general principles.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

The firm name of an ordinary partnership will not be sufficient to be used in an action, (as "Burke & Clarke"), but the particular name of the individuals composing the firm must be used. 

No persons may transact business in this State using the designation "and Company" or "& Co." as part of the partnership name, unless duly incorporated, or unless they file a statement, duly executed and sworn to, in the office of the clerk of the county where the business is conducted, stating the nature of the business and the full names and residences of all the partners. Noncompliance with this statute is a misdemeanor. (C. S. 3686; amended in 1922, p. 313).

A new firm is not liable as such for debts of an old firm which it succeeds, unless under some express or clearly implied agreement.

Where a member of one firm is also a member of another firm, the one firm cannot sue the other, as no man can sue himself.

The property of a partnership is bound to pay the partnership debts, and the liability of the property of individual partners follows afterward.

When a partnership has been dissolved and a settlement made and balance struck, one partner may sue the other for the balance.

Culpable neglect will make one partner liable to the other for the amount lost by such neglect.

Persons who are not partners will be held liable as such if they give themselves out as partners.

Where one of two or more partners, who are defendants, is a secret partner, unknown to the plaintiff, and his contract has been with the known partners, such of them as are known may be sued without joining the unknown. 

No secret agreement between partners will prevent their being liable as partners if they hold themselves out to the world as such.

Dissolution of partnership will not alter the liability of the partners for their debts, but they may sue and are to be sued as "late partners in trade.”

A discharge of one partner in bankruptcy or insolvency proceedings will not affect the liability of the remaining partners. 

A separate creditor of one partner may attach that partner's interest in partnership property. (Hill v. Beach, 1 Beas. 31).

Separate claims of a partner cannot be set off in an action against partners for a partnership debt. (McAdams v. Randolph, 13 Vr. 332; Williams v. Hamilton, 1 South. 220).

One of several partners has the right to use the name of the firm in order to bring an action. The principle that each partner

PEACE WARRANT 

385 is an agent of his co-partner within the scope of the partnership business applies to the institution of suits at law for the recovery of debts due the partnership or of damages for the infringement of the partnership rights.

If partners reside in different counties, so that one only can be served with process, then the action against them will not abate, but proceedings may be continued against the partner served with process, and the judgment recovered will bind the partnership as to any property within the county belonging to them. 

Peace Warrant 

All magistrates may issue 

Under the Revised Criminal Procedure Act of 1898 the Judge of the Court of Quarter Sessions, the Judge of the Juvenile Court, and all magistrates duly appointed, or elected and commissioned "shall have power to cause to be kept all laws made or to be made for the conservation of the peace and for the good government of the citizens and inhabitants of this State, within the said counties respectively and to apprehend and to cause to come before them and imprison and punish all persons offending against said laws or any of them in the said respective counties, in such manner as, according to said laws, shall be right and proper, and to perform and execute all such matters, acts and things as by law appertain to their office," etc. (C. S. 1825, § 16, as amended by P. L. 1915, p. 399; N. J. Cum. Supp. 880). This Act does not include what was in the former Act (G. S. 1119, § 19), that they shall "cause to come before them all persons who have used or shall use threats to any of the citizens or inhabitants of this State concerning his or her body, or the firing, injuring or destroying" of his or her property, etc., "to enter into recognizance with sufficient surety" to keep the peace, etc. 

Nevertheless the common law also gives a magistrate such a right. 

Under the common law, therefore, a Justice of the Peace as magistrate has the right and it is his duty to bind over persons to keep the peace, in the following cases: 

1. When they break the peace. 

2. When they have used, or shall use threats to any of the citizens or inhabitants of this State, concerning his or her body. 

This is the most frequent instance in which a Justice is called upon to issue a "peace warrant," as it is usually called. 

3. When they use threats concerning the firing, injuring or destroying of one's house, barn, building or other property.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

4. When they are not of good fame where they are found. "The lowest person may demand sureties of the peace against the highest, if he has reason to believe his person or property in danger."

A wife may demand sureties of her husband, or vice versa. 

Infants are in the same category, with the difference that their own recognizance cannot be taken; if complained against they must find sureties or be committed. If a stranger or foreigner uses threats, although transiently in this State, he is subject to our laws and may be required to give sureties. 

According to the early English authorities the authority of the Justice, ex officio, to "keep the peace," extends "to those who in his presence make any affray; or threaten to kill or beat another; or contend together with hot and angry words; or go about with unusual weapons or attendance, to the terror of the people; and all such as he knows to be common barrators; and such as are brought before him by the constable for a breach of the peace in his presence; and all such persons as, having been before bound to the peace, have broken it and forfeited their recognizances. Also those "who are not of good fame," specified as "night-walkers, eavesdroppers, cheats, idle vagabonds," etc. 

The common law upon this subject is as old as the Saxon days of England. It is a fundamental principle at the basis of every government that each citizen must keep the peace with his neighbor, and not harm him in person or estate. Blackstone speaks of the demand of sureties of the peace as "preventative justice," and declares that it "is, upon every principle of reason, of humanity and of sound policy, preferable in all respects to punitive justice." 

How issued

The Magistrate may, at his discretion, issue a warrant, with or without complaint, to compel suspected or bad persons to give security to keep the peace.

Where the parties are threatened, or they have cause to suspect harm, the usual course is for the aggrieved to file an affidavit with the Magistrate, setting out the facts and averring that he has no malice, and also to file the affidavits of other parties who may have heard the threats, where such can be obtained. Thereupon a warrant should be issued, to be served as a warrant in any other case by a constable, or, where it is necessary, a special constable deputized for the purpose. Such officer may break into a house to arrest the defendant if he first asks admission and is refused. 

The surety

The return of the peace warrant is to be made to any magistrate in the county. In the custody of the officer the party ar-

PEACE WARRANT 

387 rested should be first permitted to see his friends, that they may go his security, and then must be taken to a Justice. To the latter proper sureties must be given. These must be offered, in fact, by the prisoner, as the Justice is not obliged to ask him for them, but may commit him to jail; which he will do, at all events, in default of sureties.

The sum required for surety to keep the peace is in the discretion of the Magistrate. It should be sufficient, but not excessive. The recognizance should be not only to keep the peace and be of good behavior until the next Court of Quarter Sessions, but to appear thereat, when and where, if the party complaining desires and can make out a sufficient case, the Court will command that new sureties be given and for a greater length of time. 

The jurisdiction of a Justice, or the constable, in such case is strictly confined to his county, and the matter comes before the Justice as a magistrate and not in

Penalties and Fines 

Enforcement of laws by penalties and fines The statute book is full of penalties and fines, and there are municipal and health board, etc., ordinances equally numerous that provide for penalties against offenders against such ordinances. The instances in which they may be sued for penalties in 

The Small Cause Court, or before Justices as magistrates (and Recorders, etc.), are too numerous to detail. Statutes are used to punish the neglect of duty in officers, and to enforce laws whenever a forfeiture is deemed a proper satisfaction for breaking them. Sometimes, in order that everyone may have an interest watching the violators of the law or of ordinances penalties are given in whole, or in part, to whoever will complain. When a suit is brought to recover a penalty the Justice should consult the Act or ordinance itself, where the penalty is prescribed, to see its wording as to just what constitutes the offense and as to whether any particular mode of procedure for recovery of the penalty is set forth.

Some general principles about penalties and fines Where a statute gives a penalty or prescribes a fine for an injury for which an action lies at common law, the common law remedy is not taken away. To illustrate this: A obstructs and hinders B in driving upon the public road. By the statute a pen-

alty of dollars may be sued for and recovered. The suit for this penalty, however, will not bar an action for any special damages B sustained.

If the penal statute authorizes a penalty to be sued for by the party injured, any one of several parties jointly injured by the offense may sue for and recover the penalty. 

And where a penalty is prescribed for an omission to perform a particular duty, which is enjoined upon a class of public officers, the offense is in its nature several or single, and each offender must be prosecuted separately. 

The person who first commences an action for a penalty, and whether the penalty is to be received by him in whole or in part, cannot be divested of his right to the penalty by a prior recovery by a second prosecutor, who commences an action later than the first prosecutor.

The complainant is not always sole plaintiff. Sometimes the proper name of the State, or city, etc., as well as the actual prosecutor's name must appear in entitling the cause and in the body of the summons or warrant.

Justices of the Peace may or may not have jurisdiction to recover some penalty or to enforce some fine, according to what some statute may direct as to jurisdiction. In all cases he should be sure of his jurisdiction before entertaining a complaint. 

An important distinction to be observed

It is of the utmost importance, in proceedings for penalties, to know when the action is a civil one in The Small Cause Court, and when such a summary or semi-criminal one as to give jurisdiction to the Justice as a magistrate. The next few paragraphs are intended to clear up the distinction (often quite misty) so far as possible.

When jurisdiction by The Small Cause Court, and when by magistrate, in actions for penalties

As suggested above, it is not always easy to determine whether an action for a penalty is to be brought in The Small Cause Court as a civil action, or before the Justice of the Peace as a magistrate in a very summary or semi-criminal proceeding. It is important, however, to determine the matter, when the proceeding is begun, because in The Small Cause Court there may be a trial by jury, an appeal to the Common Pleas, a docketing of the judgment, etc., unless the statute declaring the penalty withdraws one or more of those provisions; whereas in a summary or semicriminal action there may not be these incidents, unless they also are expressly inserted in the statute conferring the power upon the Justice to adjudicate a penalty. In one case docket-entries are

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

to be kept; in the other minutes of the proceedings as well as entries in the Criminal or Summary Complaint Docket. It is also important because, if wrongly acted upon as to the proper tribunal, a reviewing Court could nullify the proceedings. 

So far as the decisions in this State indicate, the following may be laid down as rules by which to determine whether an action for a statutory penalty is to be brought in The Small Cause Court, or before the Justice as a magistrate. When a Small 

Cause Court has jurisdiction, however, the Justice must be sure that he is not ousted of jurisdiction because of his being within the territorial limits of a District Court that, when it exists, may have exclusive jurisdiction. As to his jurisdiction as a magistrate, that will depend on the statute creating the offense complained of, which always needs to be consulted. 

1. All ordinary actions for the recovery of penalties, when no steps of procedure are specified, are civil actions, and to be in The Small Cause Court (provided, of course, that the amount of the penalty exclusive of costs does not exceed two hundred dollars. (S. C. A., §§ 1, 4; Koch v. Vanderhoof, 20 Vr. 619). And jury trials are to be had if called for. 

Illustrative case: Where, under the Pharmacy Act (C. S. 3946, §§ 7, 8) a penalty of $100 was prescribed for violating the Act, at the suit of "The Board of Pharmacy of the State of New Jersey," and "any Justice of the Peace in the county or any District Court in the city," where the offense was committed was given "jurisdiction to hear and determine said action, and to render judgment therein, with costs according to the laws and practice governing said courts in similar actions;" held to be a civil proceeding in  (Harmon v. State Board 

Pharmacy, 38 Vr. 117). 

2. All other actions for penalties will be deemed to be civil where the procedure described is: a beginning of the action by summons, or warrant (or even by complaint) and then a regular conduct of the case to a judgment of forfeiture (and imprisonment only in case the forfeiture is not paid), and notwithstanding various of the steps of procedure named in the statute are made somewhat divergent from The Small Cause Court Act. In other words, if the terms of the statute show that it is essentially a civil proceeding.

Illustrative case: Where, under the charter of Perth Amboy, an action was brought for a penalty for violating an ordinance of that city in relation to inns and taverns, and the ordinance gave the magistrate (in that case the Recorder) jurisdiction, and the proceedings were, the filing of an oath, process by summons or warrant, judgment without filing of pleadings, an execution against defendant's goods for the penalty and against his body if

the penalty was not paid (half the penalty to go to the informer), and an appeal was given to the Common Pleas : held to be a civil proceeding. (Brophy v. Perth Amboy, 15 Vr. 421).

Another: Where in an action brought for a penalty for a violation of a malt liquor ordinance of Passaic city, where the city charter prescribed that penalties might be enforced by imprisonment or fine, proceedings to be by action in Debt before "any Justice of the Peace of said county," and if judgment was unpaid for five days execution to issue against the body; held that the charter meant a civil action in  (Greely v. Passaic, 13 Vr. 429; see also Murphy v. Montclair, 10 Vr. 673).

Another: Where, under an ordinance of a borough passed under an Act respecting licenses in boroughs, the Justice was empowered to issue process after complaint filed, hear testimony, give judgment and issue execution, it was gathered from the whole that the proceeding was essentially a civil one. (White v. 

Neptune City, 27 Vr. 222).

Another: The charter of a city provided that in actions for penalties under its ordinances should be regulated, as near as may be, by The Small Cause Act. That took the action out of the category of summary proceedings before a magistrate. (Winard v. Dover, 47 Vr. 132). 

3. Where the statute expresses that the action for a penalty must be begun by a complaint under oath, process by warrant, or permissibly a summons, and pleadings are unnecessary, and there are both a conviction and a judgment, the judgment being, at the discretion of the Justice, either for fine or imprisonment, it is in the nature of a criminal proceeding, and the jurisdiction is in the Justice as magistrate. And this may be so even when the proceeding, under an ordinance of the municipality, states the first procedure is to be an action in Debt. (Board of Health v. Meyer, 14 N. J. L. J. 302). 

Illustrative case: Where under the Oleomargarine Act a complaint is to be filed, and pleadings afterward are unnecessary, and the Justice tries the case without a jury, and the defendant's goods, chattels and person may be taken for the penalty: held to be a summary and semi-criminal proceeding. (Hoeberg v. Newton, 20 Vr. 617).

Another The Fish and Game Act has some points in procedure under it similar to those in The Small Cause Court including an appeal to the Common Pleas. But it is so summary otherwise that it is to be classed as a summary proceeding. (Minard v. Gas Co., 47 Vr. 132). 

Another Where an ordinance of the city of Bridgeton made a penalty for merchants and others to place boxes in the public

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

street, and where the charter permitted such ordinances to be enforced by a fine or imprisonment without trial by jury, and the proceeding was to be begun by an action in Debt: held to be of a criminal nature. (McGear v. Woodruff, 4 Vr. 216). 

Another: Where an Act gave the town committee power to pass ordinances to prevent immoderate driving, or riding on any street or highway, the penalty to be by imprisonment in the township lockup, or county jail, or a fine, and authorizing an arrest without a warrant, on view of an officer, held to be in the nature of a criminal procedure. (Unger v. Fanwood, 55 Atl. Rep. 42).

It will thus be noticed that there are penal statutes constantly being enacted where the proceedings are somewhat of a summary nature, but where doubt will arise as to their proper classification. They are close to the border line between the civil and summary in their uncertain intent. As to such statutes, we can only say that, until they are construed by a higher Court, the Justice must use his best judgment in their classification. If they can be consistently classified as a civil proceeding, the tendency of the Supreme Court is to so classify them. (See White v. Neptune 

City, 29 Vr. 222, which is a leading case). The fact that the beginning is an action in Debt makes a presumption that the proceeding is civil, but this alone is not determinative. What is stated under paragraph 3, above, shows what is more determinative.

It is well in issuing process for the Justice to be guided by legal advice, and not improperly that of the counsel for the prosecutor, who is clearly interested in the proper construction of the law, as, if he advises a mistake in the procedure, it will be at the peril of losing in the end. 

How actions for penalties are classified

There have been different classifications of actions upon common information for penalties, but that which is most approved by long usage divides them into two kinds: 

1. A "qui tam" action, which is one in which the penalty is divided between the common informer, or person who sues, on the one hand, and the State, township, or poor, etc., on the other. 

2. A "popular" action, which is one in which the whole penalty is given only to the informer, or only to the public (poor, State, municipality, etc.). If a statute or ordinance does not state where the penalty or fine is to go, it goes to the county, and that makes of it a "popular" action. 

Proceedings on information for penalties of a summary nature before the Justice as magistrate 

Where the information, (complaint, under oath) to secure a penalty, is filed with the Justice as magistrate or any other com-

petent magistrate, and the proceeding is of a summary nature, the statute may make it throughout a strictly summary proceeding, or largely so. In any event, the mode of procedure laid down in the statute, so far as it goes, must be followed with great strictness. Everything done must be done that the Act requires and in the manner required. 

Amendments going to the substance of the information as originally made, or departing from the exact line of requirement, cannot be permitted, except with defendant's consent. 

Such proceedings not being civil actions, no indorsement of the statute and day, month and year of institution of action, etc., need be made upon the summons. (Murphy v. Montclair, 10 Vr. 

673; Johnson v. Barclay, 1 Harr. 1). (Such indorsement must be made in certain cases in  See under next subhead).

The complaint must aver all the facts required, which would constitute defendant's guilt, and not complainant's suspicion or belief. (Mowrey v. Camden, 20 Vr. 106).

Unless the Act states there can be a jury trial, there can be none, but the magistrate will hear and determine the complaint. (McGear v. Woodruff, 4 Vr. 213).

His judgment is not to be a judgment alone, but, first, a conviction, and then a judgment. (Murphy v. Montclair, supra). 

Such a conviction must show: 1. Such facts as are necessary to constitute a statutory offense; time, place and particular matter. 2. That defendant was convicted thereof. 3. Upon what evidence. 4. Judgment of forfeiture (penalty or fine). (Buck v. Danzenbacker, 8 Vr. 359; see also Asbury Park v. Layton, 55 Atl. Rep. 86).

Unless an appeal is given by the Act, there can be none. (Carter v. Camden Dist. Ct., 20 Vr. 600). 

The magistrate shall keep full minutes of the proceedings on separate sheets of paper, as in criminal procedure, as well as enter the same, in short form, in his docket, the Criminal, or Summary Docket, according to circumstances. (See "The Docket,' below). Such minutes must show all the facts, and all that was done before or by him. (Schlachter v. Stokes, 34 Vr. 138). 

In the case of certiorari, these minutes, and all papers in the cause, are to be sent up; not a transcript of them, unless the Act so requires.

These minutes, however, do not take the place of certain special matters which must also be written out separately. If there is a judgment of conviction for a fine, or fine and imprisonment, such conviction must be written out as a separate matter; or if it is necessary under a statement to make an order for an execution, following a conviction, that, too, would be a separate matter.

Civil procedure to recover penalties in The Small Cause Court

In civil actions to recover penalties in The Small Cause Court the following rules are to be observed, unless the Act concerned specifies a different procedure: 

1. Generally speaking, the proceedings designated in The

Small Cause Act are to be followed, except where otherwise stated in the particular Act that is the foundation for the proceedings. But, as a rule- 

2. The action is to be styled in Debt, as The Small Cause 

Act (§ 24) does not apply to the form of the action for a statutory penalty, which is not in the nature of a contract. A statute may state, however, that the action may be brought in another form, in which case such statute is to be followed. For example, actions under the Timber Act. (See general title "Timber”). 

3. Of great importance is a determination as to whether the action is a qui tam one (that is, whether the penalty goes, part to the informer and part to the public), or whether it is a "popular" action and the penalty all goes to one party (person or corporation), and is not divided. Because if it is a qui tam action, in the first place the Justice must at once note in his docket the very day, month and year of the institution of the action. If he waits until the summons is returned, the judgment will be bad. (Ackerson v. Zabriskie, 2 Hal. 167; Griffith v. West, 5 Hal. 301). In the second place (at the same time) he must indorse on the information (the complaint) the day, month and year of the institution of the action. In the third place, upon the process, whether it be a summons or warrant, he must indorse the name of the party who prosecutes and the title of the statute or statutes upon which the action is founded. (C. S. 4120, § 219). Not to do so may deprive the Justice of jurisdiction.

Should such indorsements not be made in a qui tam action and the defendant does not object, the Justice will retain jurisdiction, but if he objects the cause must be dismissed. (Hageman v. Van Doren, 6 N. J. L. J. 310; Williamson v. Common 

Pleas, 13 Vr. 389; Hayes v. Storms, 35 Vr. 514).

If it is a "popular" action such indorsements are not necessary. (Ibid, § 223). 

4. The writ must not be ante-dated. This is necessary to distinguish between the right one informer has to prosecute his suit as before another who may sue for the same offense before the same, or another Justice. 

5. The first process must be a summons, not warrant, unless the latter is specially authorized by the Act concerned. 

6. The defendant may plead orally that he is not guilty, or that he owes nothing. If he does not plead at all, or if he does not

appear in answer to a lawfully served process, of course the cause will proceed in the usual manner. 

7. Unless otherwise directed by the Act there will be the right to a jury, and also to an appeal to the Common Pleas. In case want of jurisdiction is to be urged the right of the Common Pleas to consider it and of the Supreme Court to consider it on certiorari is concurrent. 

8. No "conviction" is necessary in a civil action, but simply a judgment (Murphy v. Montclair, 10 Vr. 673), unless the statute otherwise requires. 

9. Where the special statute, or ordinance sued upon, does not state to whom the penalty shall go, the Justice will, as a matter of course, give judgment that it shall go "as the law directs;" and such phraseology has been approved. (Vandergrift v. 

Meihle, 37 Vr. 92. See below, subhead "Disposition of Fines"). 

10. If the Justice has an option as to the penalty (which is very rarely the case), the judgment must specify to whom, or to what such penalty shall go, and this should also be embraced in the execution. (Ibid). 

11. Where there is jury trial permitted, the jury is to determine whether a penalty has been incurred, and the amount of it. 

If an action be for several penalties, it is to determine particular offenses on which the verdict is founded, and the amount of the penalties incurred; it cannot be left to the Justice to designate the number of penalties in making up his judgment. (Bowden v. 

Overseer, 12 Vr. 462; Bloodgood v. Vanderveer, 2 Penn. 928). 

12. If the prosecutor of a qui tam action compounds, or discontinues the action, unless with consent of the Justice, the prosecutor will be liable to pay to the State, or to any other person who benefits with him by the action, the full penalty due. The statute says: "No recovery by verdict or otherwise obtained by covin or collusion in any such action shall be a bar to any other action prosecuted in good faith, and if the prosecutor of an action for the recovery of any penalty not wholly appropriated to the use of such prosecutor shall compound with the defendant to direct such action to be discontinued, unless it be by leave of the Court, then such prosecutor shall be liable for so much of the penalty to the State or any other person than the prosecutor, as the State or such other person would have been entitled to if the defendant had been convicted." (C. S. 4121, § 221). 

13. If the prosecutor fails to press and sustain his suit, the prosecutor will have judgment against him for costs, and an execution may issue against his goods and body. The Act says: "Every informer on a penal statute shall pay costs to the defendant if he discontinues, be nonsuited, or judgment pass against

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

him, for which costs the defendant shall have execution against the goods and body of such informer." (Ibid, § 222). 

14. The prosecutor in a qui tam action will not recover any costs unless expressly given to him by the statute creating the penalty. In a popular action costs will go with the penalty. 

15. The prosecutor in an action to recover a penalty or enforce a fine cannot compel the adverse party to testify. (See C. 

S. 2218, § 2). 

16. The foregoing points apply generally whether the proceedings are under a statute, or under an ordinance of a municipality, or health board, etc.

In cities, towns and boroughs, on suits for violation of ordinances, it is only necessary to state in the complaint the number of the section violated, briefly setting forth enough of the language of the section to apprise the defendant of the charge. (C. S. 3985, § 56).

It is to be noted, however, that enforcement of ordinances, municipal or of health boards, are not always under civil proceedings, as has already been stated. 

The docket

As stated under the general head of "The Summary Proceeding Docket," proceedings in actions for penalties which are distinctly summary are to be entered in a Summary Proceeding Docket. Sometimes, however, the Criminal Docket should be used, as (so the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles holds) in automobile cases; sometimes the Civil Docket, but only when actions for penalties are in  

Review of penalty proceedings

When the action for a penalty is in The Small Cause Court, appeal is given to the Common Pleas in the usual manner, or, when jurisdiction is to be traversed, certiorari to the Supreme Court may be taken, although on appeal the jurisdictional question can be ruled upon by the Common Pleas. When the proceeding is before the Justice as magistrate, the statute acted upon may direct how review is to be had; if not, certiorari is the usual remedy for the correction of error. Where proceedings are on account of violations of a city ordinance, or a city board of health, there may be either certiorari or, within thirty days after judgment rendered, application being made to the Court of Common Pleas, that Court may "order such judgment and all the proceedings had in the case to be certified to said Court," and on the return to such order that Court may review the judgment, etc. (C. S. 408, as amended by P. L. 1915, p. 413; N. J. Cum. 

Supp. 455).

Always consult the statute or ordinance concerned We here repeat that it is not safe for a Justice of the Peace or any magistrate to take cognizance of and try an action for a penalty without reading over the actual statute or ordinance on which the proceeding is based. While elsewhere in this volume under various heads we have made abstracts of certain important statutes embracing penalties (and also fines), and pointed out the modes of procedure under them, yet in all cases the full text should be consulted. Usually the attorney for a prosecutor can and should produce the statute or ordinance if the Justice does not have it on hand. 

Disposition of fines and penalties

Statutes and ordinances awarding penalties or providing for fines usually state their disposition. But when not they go to the county. The provision of law as to this is the following: "All fines which may be authorized under any proceedings before any Justice of the Peace, and which have not been appropriated by law to any distinct use, shall be and they are hereby appropriated and made payable to the county collector of the county in which the Justice may reside, for the use of the county." (C. S. 3017, § 7). 

Strictly speaking there is a difference between a "fine" and a "penalty." A fine is usually imposed for a criminal or semicriminal offense, and a penalty for a civil offense. But our statutes have often made the two indistinguishable, and, while the provision above cited uses the term "fine," it must also apply to penalties, as there is no distinct provision for the payment over of what may be termed in the statute a "penalty," when the law does not state to what or whom it is to go.

These fines and penalties belonging to the county must be reported and paid over to the county collector on the first of each month after their collection. The law is: "Every Justice of the Peace shall report monthly, during his term of office, on the first of each month, to the collector of his county the amount of fines imposed and received by him during the preceding month, and shall at the same time pay over all fines so by him imposed and received, the said fines to be received and held by the county collector for the use of the county; provided, this Act shall apply only to such fines as are declared to be for the use of the county.' (C. S. 3017, § 5). Failing to do this, and if the collector gives the Justice a thirty-day written notice and he still fails to do it, such Justice will be guilty of a misdemeanor and, therefore, subject to indictment. (Ibid, § 6). 

In automobile cases and many others, not usually in The Small Cause Court, the fines go to the Commissioner of Motor

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Vehicles and is paid over by him to the State Treasurer for the use of roads. (P. L. 1928, Chap. 59).

Some decisions concerning actions for penalties The state of demand filed must distinctly set out the offense with certainty of time and place, and if more than one offense be charged, each must be set out with particularity. (Chew v. 

Thompson, 4 Hal. 249).

The penalty cannot be varied; the precise sum given by the statute is to be recovered, or none at all. (Broadwell v. Conger, 1 Penn. 210; Adams v. Scull, 1 Penn. 311; Sayre v. Sayre, 2 

Penn. 597).

Where a statute states the Justice has jurisdiction "upon receiving proof by affidavit or affidavits of one or more persons of the violation of any of the provisions of this Act," it means that such affidavit shall embrace positive testimony, according to the rules of evidence; an affidavit made "upon information and belief" will not be "proof." (Inglis v. Schreiner, 29 Vr. 120. This was a case under the Gaming Act of 1893).

Where the statute provides for an alternative judgment (as a fine or imprisonment) the Justice cannot sentence doubly; he cannot adjudge that defendant pay a fine and be imprisoned. (In re Emmitt, 20 N. J. L. J. 130).

One penalty only is recoverable for one offense, or entire transaction, and not a separate penalty for each particular act into which the offense may be divisible. So for the offense of performing one's worldly employment on Sunday, there can be a conviction for only one offense on the same day. (Mayor v. 

Ordrenan, 12 Johns. [N. Y.] 122; Crepps v. Durden, Cowp. [Eng.] 640).

In a suit to recover penalties under the Gaming Act for setting up a lottery in this State, the affidavit must not only set up the title of the Gaming Act, but also the title of the Crimes Act, and that section of the latter which declares which lotteries are prohibited. (Wolcott ads. Skahill, 27 Vr. 221).

In penalties for violations of city ordinances, a summary conviction must show a case clearly and distinctly within the provisions of the ordinance. (Atlantic City v. Turner, 38 Vr. 

520; Hosburg v. Newton, 20 Vr. 617); must set out the offense and the names of the witnesses. (Leek v. Kreps, 41 Vr. 120). 

For example a conviction of violating a borough ordinance which finds the defendant "guilty of violating section 76 of the ordinance" is not a lawful conviction. (Board of Health v. State, 25 

N. J. L. J. 146).

In the recovery of a penalty under the summary Fish and Game Act when the fines go to one party (the Board of Fish and

Game Commissioners), the action is not qui tam and, therefore, the special indorsements on the complaint and summons as required in qui tam proceedings are not necessary. (Minard v. 

Dover, 47 Vr. 132).

The statute making special indorsements required in qui tam proceedings has no application to the recovery of penalties before a magistrate, but only in " (Ibid). 

Execution by warrant of distress 

In all cases where a Justice is empowered to issue a "warrant of distress" for the levying of a penalty and no mode for the disposal of the distress is pointed out, the Justice may in such warrant order a sale within a certain time not less than four nor more than ten days. (C. S. 1946, § 23, which see).

Exemption from civil process in penalty actions Members belonging to the National Guard of New Jersey, while going to, remaining at or returning from any place at which they are required to attend, for military duty cannot be served with a civil process of arrest for penalties (or in other civil actions). (P. L. 1917, p. 177; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1953). (For penalties, procedure, etc., under some of the special statutes, see under their appropriate titles in this volume).

Police, Recorders', Mayors' and Other Magisterial Courts

General remarks 

In almost every city and in certain municipalities in this State there is at least one Police Court, or a Recorder's Court, or a Mayor's Court, or all three kinds of local Courts, as well as Justice's Courts. Their jurisdiction and powers are defined in both general and special Acts, and in some special charters of cities. 

Usually they may try suits for penalties for violations of city ordinances, health board ordinances, etc.

They are also empowered to act in a variety of criminal, summary and sometimes civil proceedings. Some of these Courts have, by statute, regular clerks, and have authority to punish for contempt, a power hitherto denied to Justices of the Peace. 

Unfortunately no attempt has been made by the Legislature to enact a uniform law respecting these magistrates or Courts, even in cities. By statutes affecting only this or that class of cities, and this or that class of towns and townships, the result is so great un-uniformity that it is puzzling to know what is the full or restricted scope of these several Courts. In fact, the law on this general subject is in a state closely resembling confusion, and both new Acts and repealers of Acts need to be carefully studied to be certain as to the extent of the duties of Police Justices, Recorders and Mayors on the topics named under the heads below.

We have endeavored below to cite all important laws relating to all the magistrates and Courts which properly belong to the foregoing general title, but may have omitted some or noted some which possibly have been repealed.

I. JURISDICTION ON SPECIFIC SUBJECTS 

Jurisdiction by statutes on specific subjects applicable to certain of these Courts

Regardless of the statutes creating and naming the jurisdiction of the Courts above mentioned, a large number of Acts on specific subjects, criminal and semi-criminal, and also relating to summary proceedings for the collection of penalties or enforce-

ment of fines, give jurisdiction to one or another, or perhaps all of the minor Courts. This appears under appropriate heads in this volume (where the subjects are treated, as most of them are if they affect Justice of the Peace), but we name these several matters here for convenience of reference. It may be those so stated below are not all the matters in which jurisdiction is conferred by particular penal, summary, etc., statutes upon the Courts named, but it is believed to be a substantially complete list. In no case can a Justice of the Peace act where jurisdiction is given only to other officials, or, where the action is civil and would be in The Small Cause Court, and not then if a District or other 

Court has exclusive jurisdiction.
