II. SOME SPECIAL JURISDICTIONAL POWERS OF MAYORS 

Mayors having criminal powers of Justices of the Peace, Police Justices, etc. 

Under a former head (viz., "I. Jurisdiction on Specific Subjects") we have named a variety of matters in several of which the Mayor of any municipality is named as having jurisdictional powers. There are also other statutes giving sometimes jurisdictional powers to hold a "Court," to quell insurrections, to be commissioner of deeds, etc., and we name such so far as we have found them.

In cities adopting an Act of April 24, 1894, "relating to and regulating the government of cities" upon a referendum (but inoperative as to first-class cities), the Mayor is vested with all the J-26

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

powers of any Police Justice of the city in quelling any insurrection, riot or disorderly assemblage, and may call out citizens and the militia to preserve public peace. (C. S. 1107, § 1849). 

In cities adopting an Act of April 3, 1902, of similar import, the Mayor is vested with all the powers of the Recorder of such city to quell insurrections, riots, etc., and may call out citizens and the militia to preserve public peace. (C. S. 1137, § 1941). 

In cities adopting an Act of April 8, 1903, of similar import, the Mayor is vested with all the power of a constable or police officer to quell insurrections, riots, etc., and may also call out citizens and the militia to preserve public peace. (C. S. 1177, § 2072).

In cities adopting an Act of April 11, 1908, of similar import, the Mayor is vested with "all the powers and duties" of the Recorder and of a commissioner of deeds, and also of a Justice of the Peace and may quell insurrections, riots, etc., and call upon citizens or the county sheriff for aid. (C. S. 1223, §§ 2206, 2228).

Ín cities adopting an Act of April 14, 1908, of similar import, the Mayor is vested with "all the powers which the Recorder or any Justice of the Peace have by law;" and may also quell insurrections, riots, etc., and may call out citizens and the militia. (C. S. 1243, § 2284).

In cities of the second class adopting an Act of April 16, 1912, of similar import, the Mayor is given power to call on citizens, the sheriff, the Governor, etc., to quell insurrections, riots, etc. (P. L. 1912, p. 879, § 52; N. J. Cum. Supp. 446).

In cities of the second class of less than 20,000 inhabitants adopting an Act of April 23, 1907, of similar import, the Mayor is vested with "all the powers of the Recorder in other cities of the like class" and of a commissioner of deeds, and all the powers of a Justice of the Peace, and may quell insurrections, riots, etc., and may call upon the sheriff and citizens for aid. (C. S. 1416, §§ 

2786, 2844).

In cities of over 12,000 inhabitants, incorporating under an Act of March 24, 1899, of similar import, the Mayor is vested with all the powers of a Police Justice in quelling insurrections, riots, etc., and may call out citizens and the militia. (C. S. 1375, § 2680).

In cities of less than 12,000 population adopting an Act for their government of March 21, 1899, of similar import, the Mayor is vested with all the powers of a Police Justice to quell insurrections, riots, etc., and with power to call on citizens or militia for aid. (C. S. 1346, § 2590).

In cities of less than 12,000 population adopting an Act of April 23, 1907, for their government, which provides for the crea-

tion by ordinance of a Recorder's Court, in case no such Court is established, the Mayor is to have the jurisdiction and powers vested in such Court until it is established (C. S. 1433, § 2844), and also afterward. (Ibid, § 2786). He is also vested with power of a commissioner of deeds and of a Justice of the Peace, and may quell insurrections, etc., and call out citizens. (Ibid).

In cities of less than 10,000 and over 6,000 inhabitants, adopting an Act concerning cities of March 12, 1879, the Mayor is given all the powers of a City Judge in the event of the latter's absence or inability to act (C. S. 1279, § 2362), and also that of a 

Justice of the Peace in criminal cases. (Ibid, § 2346).

In all boroughs Mayors not only possess power to suppress all riots and tumultuous assemblies, but have jurisdiction in all criminal matters and those relating to cases of bastardy, poor, breaches of the peace, vagrancy and disorderly conduct, as is conferred by law upon any one or two Justices of the Peace, and may try and determine all actions for the recovery of any penalty prescribed for the violation of an ordinance, and try and determine offenses committed in violation of such ordinances for which the punishment is by fine or imprisonment. His Court is one of record, and he may punish for contempt of Court, as in higher 

Courts. (C. S. 232, §§ 10, 11). 

Besides what are named above, some cities have special charters which give jurisdictional powers to mayors to act as magistrates, hold proceedings over violations of ordinances, etc.

III. SOME SPECIAL JURISDICTIONAL OR OTHER POWERS OF RECORDERS AS DISTINCT FROM THOSE OF POLICE JUSTICES 

Distinction between Police Justice and Recorder

The real distinction between the duties of a Police Judge or Justice and Recorder is often in the designation only. Charters or statutes sometimes give the one name or the other to magistrates whose functions are generally similar. The jurisdiction and authority of each, or both, are always specifically defined, however, as they are officials created by statute, or municipal charter, and are not constitutionally-created officers. Neither can hold a Small Cause Court (but see an exception below) although in various matters they may, by some particular statute, be given jurisdiction over matters otherwise cognizable by that Court, with a statement that certain of the proceedings shall be as in that Court. The main duties of both classes of officials, however, is to hear criminal complaints and those under ordinances for penalties, or to enforce fines. 

Whenever the statute gives jurisdiction to "all magistrates,"

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

this includes Recorders and Police Justices, and also those mayors who have the powers of Justices of the Peace. 

Under subdivision I, above, "Jurisdiction on Specific Subjects," we have named various jurisdictional powers of the Recorder. Others are noted below. 

A Recorder's Small Cause Court 

An unusual Recorder's Court Act is a statute of April 14, 1913, where it is enacted that in "any township or borough in any county of this State (other than counties of the first class), having a population of more than 3,000 inhabitants and forming a part of and located in any county of this State in which one or more District Courts are established," there may be what is to be known as "The Recorder's Court for the Trial of Small Causes." To secure such a Court the Mayor and Council of the borough, or township committee of the township, are to apply to the Governor, who shall appoint "an attorney-at-law residing in such township or borough" as Recorder. Term of office three years; compensation not to exceed $500. (P. L. 1913, p. 760; amend. by P. L. 1931, p. 829).

The jurisdiction of this Court is to be, in civil matters, where the amount in dispute does not exceed $200, but there are excepted from jurisdiction actions of replevin, slander, trespass for assault, battery and imprisonment, and where title to lands comes in question. Except in attachment suits the defendant must reside in the township or borough. As to criminal matters the Act says the 

Recorder "shall have the same jurisdiction, power and authority in criminal matters, cases of bastardy, relief, removal and settlement of the poor" (but this proceeding is now outside of his cognizance, unless given by some Act later than 1923), "breaches of the peace, vagrancy and disorderly conduct, as is by law conferred upon Justices of the Peace." (Ibid, §§ 2, 3, as am. by P. 

L. 1920, p. 396; N. J. Cum. Supp. 2711). He is also empowered to try actions for penalties for violation of by-laws or ordinances of the township or borough, and offenses concerning the same for which the punishment is fine or imprisonment. (§ 4).

Proceedings are to be as nearly as may be according to The Small Cause Act, including appeal therefrom, but in case a jury is not demanded the determination of fact by the Recorder is to be final (as is that of a jury verdict), so that an appeal is to be only on questions of law and the legality of admission or rejection of evidence. (§ 5). 

Provisions as to Recorders in certain other municipalities In all boroughs the council may appoint a borough Recorder, who will possess "the same jurisdiction and power in criminal

matters, cases of bastardy, relief, removal and settlement of the poor" (not now practicable under the Poor Act of 1911), "breaches of the peace, vagrancy and disorderly conduct and violations of borough ordinances as is vested in the Mayor; the same power to issue process, try and determine such cases, and fine or imprisonment upon conviction." (C. S. 234, § 13). This Act did not give Recorders jurisdiction over health board ordinances (Streeter v. Bd. of Health, 55 Vr. 67), but a 1913 Act does.

In towns exceeding 4,000 inhabitants adopting the incorporating Act of March 7, 1895, provision is made for a Recorder to be appointed for a term of two years, whose jurisdiction is over the violation of town ordinances, with power to fine and imprison, and with "the same powers in criminal matters within the territorial limits of the town as are possessed and exercised by Justices of the Peace of this State." Details of procedure are stated. 

In case of absence or inability he may appoint either an attorneyat-law or a Justice of the Peace to act in his place. (C. S. 5526, § 351 et seq.).

In all towns the governing body may appoint a Recorder to have criminal jurisdiction, including cases of bastardy, relief, etc., of the poor, breaches of the peace, vagrancy, disorderly conduct and violations of ordinances as Justices of the Peace and Police 

Justices have in towns. (P. L. 1921, p. 503; N. J. Cum. Supp. 2724).

In any township the township committee may appoint "a fit person" in the township as Recorder for a term of three years, to have the same jurisdiction in criminal matters, bastardy, poor, breach of the peace, vagrancy, disorderly conduct and violation of township and board of health ordinances as Justices of the Peace. (P. L. 1914, p. 112; N. J. Cum. Supp. 3677). This makes of the 

Recorder a "magistrate," so that when a statute gives jurisdiction to "all magistrates" the Recorder is necessarily included. (See also 

P. L. 1932, p. 528).

In any village with a population of over 5,000 the governing body may appoint a Recorder for the term of three years, who will have the same jurisdiction in criminal matters, bastardy, poor, breach of the peace, vagrancy, disorderly conduct and violation. of municipal ordinances as conferred on Justices of the Peace. (P. L. 1914, p. 100; N. J. Cum. Supp. 3787).

In any municipality (other than cities and boroughs) having a population of more than 15,000, the governing body, by an Act of March 21, 1916, may appoint a Recorder for the term of three years, to have the same jurisdiction in criminal matters, bastardy, poor, breach of the peace, vagrancy, disorderly conduct and violation of municipal ordinances, as conferred upon Justices of the 

Peace. (P. L. 1916, p. 519; N. J. Cum. Supp. 2723).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

In cities of more than 12,000 population adopting an Act of March 24, 1899, for their incorporation and government, the Recorder has jurisdiction over violations of city ordinances, and may inflict fines of not exceeding $20 or commit in cases of persons convicted of vagrancy, disorderly conduct or breach of the peace. (C. S. 1377, § 2686 et seq.; amend. in 1918, N. J. Cum. Supp. 

548, § 2686a et seq.).

In cities having a population of from 133,000 to 200,000, an Act of April 12, 1907, gives power to the board of fire and police commissioners to appoint a Recorder or Police Justice, who must be an attorney-at-law. (C. S. 2361, § 136; amend. by N. J. Cum. 

Supp. 1269).

In cities adopting an Act of April 3, 1902, for the government of cities, a Recorder's Court is provided for, with jurisdiction and powers in civil and criminal matters as is conferred upon Justices of the Peace, except those conferred by the Small Cause, Landlord and Tenant, Attachment, and Forcible Entry and Detainer Acts, and that increasing the jurisdiction of Justice of the Peace; also of violations of city and city board and department ordinances. It is to be a Court of record and may punish for contempt. (C. S. 1160, § 2026 et seq.).

In cities adopting an Act for the government of cities of April 8, 1903, a Recorder's Court is to be established with the same jurisdiction, powers, etc., and with the same exceptions as in the preceding paragraph stated. (C. S. 1195, § 2134, et seq.).

In cities adopting the Act of April 14, 1908, providing for a city government, etc., a Recorder's Court is to be established, having jurisdiction over violations of city ordinances, and with the powers of Justices of the Peace in criminal matters, and it may punish for contempt. The Recorder may appoint a Court clerk. 

Details of procedure given in the Act. (Supplement, P. L. 1914, p. 234; N. J. Cum. Supp. 510). 

In cities adopting the Act of April 14, 1908, for the government of cities, a Recorder is to be elected, who is to have jurisdiction over violations of city ordinances and in criminal matters the same powers as a Justice of the Peace. (C. S. 1247, § 2293). 

In cities of the second class having a population of less than 20,000 adopting an Act of April 23, 1907, for their government, there may be created by ordinance a "Recorder's Court of (name of city), which will possess all the jurisdiction and powers in civil and criminal matters conferred upon Justices of the Peace except such conferred by the Small Cause, Landlord and Tenant, Attachment and Forcible Entry and Detainer Acts; and it will have exclusive jurisdiction over the recovery of penalties for violation of ordinances of the city, or any board or department thereof. The Recorder must be a three years' resident of the

city. Details of procedure are set forth in the Act. If council fails to establish the Court the Mayor may appoint a Justice of the Peace to act temporarily. (C. S. 1431, § 2840 et seq.; amend. by P. L. 1926, p. 430, and P. L. 1928, p. 718).

In cities of the second class adopting the Act of April 16, 1912, regulating their government, a Recorder's Court is to be established having jurisdiction of violations of any ordinance of the city or any board or department thereof, and of disorderly conduct, breach of the peace, "or any other offense" within its jurisdiction. In his absence the Recorder's clerk may serve in his place. It is to be a Court of record with power to punish for contempt. (P. L. 1912, p. 892, et seq.; N. J. Cum. Supp. 454).

In any third-class city having a population of over 4,500, by an Act of 1914 the governing body may appoint a Recorder for a three years' term, who will have the same jurisdiction in criminal matters, bastardy, poor, breach of the peace, vagrancy, disorderly conduct and violation of municipal ordinances as conferred on Justices of the Peace. (P. L. 1914, p. 546; N. J. Cum. Supp. 454).

In any third and fourth class city, borough, township or village with a population of over 1,000 (but not in a county having a 

Criminal District Court), the Recorder, or Police or other Municipal Court may try various cases, under the practice stated. (P. L. 1930, p. 956; am. by P. L. 1931, p. 157). 

By an Act of 1933 (P. L., Chap. 160), criminal complaints in cities of the fourth class may be taken by Justices of the Peace, and if bail is given it is to be to appear before the Recorder, Police Justice, etc. (See the Act). Otherwise the prisoner is to be committed to jail.

It is possible some of the foregoing Acts are repealed or set aside by subsequent Acts in part, but only a careful study will determine the fact. And there may be other statutes applying to other municipalities. 

Temporary Recorder

When the term of a Justice of the Peace expires in any municipality, and, by reason of change of date in holding an election his successor cannot be appointed until after his term expires, the governing body of the municipality may appoint a Recorder to hold office until the Justice's successor is elected and takes office, and he will have the jurisdiction of a Justice in criminal matters, breaches of the peace, vagrancy, disorderly conduct and violations of municipal ordinances. (C. S. 4004, §§ 132, 133). 

Substitution for Recorder

Any Recorder of this State, in case of his temporary absence

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

from his Court, or inability from any cause to act therein, may designate and appoint an attorney-at-law resident in the county to act in his place. (C. S. 4005, § 36). Any Recorder of any city under the same circumstances may appoint a Justice of the Peace to act in his place. (C. S. 3980, § 31). 

Recorders may take affidavits

Ordinary affidavits required to be taken by any statute or to be used in Court or for any lawful purpose, may be taken before any Recorder, Mayor or Alderman of any city, town or borough. (P. L. 1916, p. 90; N. J. Cum. Supp. 2563).

IV. SOME SPECIAL JURISDICTIONAL OR OTHER POWERS OF POLICE JUDGES AS DISTINCT FROM THOSE OF RECORDERS 

Police Judges in cities of the first class

Cities of the first class having a population of 360,000 or over are to have three Police Justices. (P. L. 1916, p. 603; N. J. Cum. 

Supp. 2701). 

In cities of the first class the Police Judge may request a

Judge of any Police Court of his city, or any duly qualified Justice of the Peace or clerk of his Court to sit in his place and with all his power and authority. (C. S. 3994, § 87, as amended by P. 

L. 1912, p. 292; N. J. Cum. Supp. 2703).

In first- and second-class cities any police officer of the municipality may take the recognizance with sureties of any person arrested and in the custody of the Police, for offenses against the Vice and Immorality or Disorderly Persons Acts for their appearance before the Police magistrate. (P. L. 1913, p. 776; Ñ. 

J. Cum. Supp. 2157). 

Other Acts relating to Police Judges in cities

By an Act of April 6, 1886, the common council of any incorporated city, where there is no Recorder, Police Justice or Police magistrate appointed under the city charter, may appoint one or more Police Justices not to exceed one for every 20,000 inhabitants; term, not to exceed five years, to be fixed by ordinance. 

Provisions are made for removal, oath, bond, etc. Jurisdiction is over all criminal matters, and in bastardy, poor, vagrancy and disorderly persons' proceedings, and actions for penalties under by-laws or ordinances of the city. Details of procedure are given at length. (C. S. 3980, § 32 et seq.).

In cities adopting the Act of April 24, 1894, regulating their government, a city Police Court is to be established having all the civil and criminal powers of Justices of the Peace, excepting those

under the Small Cause, Landlord and Tenant, Attachment and Forcible Entry and Detainer Acts and the Act increasing the jurisdiction of Justices of the Peace (this jurisdiction is to be exclusive of all other Courts, Judges and Magistrates, excepting the county Courts); also over violation of city and city board ordinances; also to try cases of simple assault and battery and petit larceny when committed within the city, provided the person charged with the offense waives indictment and trial by jury. It is to be a Court of record and may punish for contempt. Details of certain procedures are stated in the Act. Common Council is to appoint the Police Justice. (C. S. 1121, § 1903 et seq.). 

In cities of less than 12,000, acting (by referendum vote or otherwise as provided) under an Act of March 24, 1897, a City

Police Court may be established by ordinance, with jurisdiction and powers substantially the same as stated in the preceding paragraph. The appointment is by Common Council. (C. S. 1332, § 

2554 et seq.).

In cities of less than 12,000 acting under another Act, of 

March 21, 1899, if adopted by referendum, a City Police Court may be established by ordinance, with jurisdiction and powers substantially the same as in the second preceding paragraph. (C. 

S. 1362, § 2643 et seq.). 

In second-class cities where police magistrates are temporarily absent by inability, he may appoint a resident attorney-at-law to act. (P. L. 1929, p. 137). 

Police Justices in third-class municipalities

By an Act of 1883, in every incorporated borough, town or city of the third or fourth classes one or more Police Justices may be appointed "in the same manner as other appointed officers," not to exceed one for each 3,000 inhabitants, but each such municipality may have one, the term to be five years. The jurisdiction and powers of such Police Justice are to be in all criminal matters and all cases of bastardy, the poor, vagrancy and disorderly persons; but not any civil actions except those brought to recover a penalty prescribed by the by-laws or ordinances of the municipality. 

Particulars of procedure are stated at much length. (C. S. 3975, 

§§ 9, 29, etc.). 

Police Justices in town governed by boards of commissioners

In incorporated towns governed by a board of commissioners where there are Police Justices, an Act of April 16, 1891, provides that the Police Justice shall have jurisdiction over violations of ordinances, and there are provisions for procedure. (C.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

S. 5503 et seq.). This Act has nothing to do with the later Walsh 

Act for the government of municipalities by commissions. 

Police Justice in villages

By an Act of 1918 the board of trustees of villages may appoint a "Police Justice" for the same term as Justices of the Peace, but not to try civil actions except to recover penalties under a village ordinance, when he is given Justice of the Peace powers. (P. 

L., p. 312; N. J. Cum. Supp. 2723).

Substitution of Justice of the Peace by Police Judge 

By an Act of March 14, 1879, any Police Justice may in case of his temporary absence from the Police Court, or inability to act, designate a Justice of the Peace to act in his stead. (C. S. 

3974, § 1).

V. SOME JURISDICTIONAL OR OTHER POWERS GIVEN TO ALL OR SEVERAL MUNICIPAL COURTS 

Sureties to keep the peace

Under the general powers of "all magistrates" to compel persons who make threats, etc., to give sureties to keep the peace, all 

Recorders, Police Justices, etc., may act. (P. L. 1915, p. 399; 

N. J. Cum. Supp. 880; see general title "Peace Warrant"). 

Criminal Courts in first-class counties

An Act of March 30, 1905, as to counties of the first class (P. L., p. 137), provides that, upon the recommendation of the 

Prosecutor of Pleas, with the approval of the Supreme Court Justice holding the Circuit, or the Judge of General Sessions, the Act shall be effective in such first class county, and shall apply to all Criminal Courts, Recorder's or Police Court or Courts. Such 

Courts may punish for contempt; may make rules for its business; and shall try and determine all cases of assault, assault and battery, petit larceny, malicious mischief, embezzlement (of not over $20), obtaining money under false pretences (of not over $20), receiving stolen property (of not over $20), and other criminal offenses, the penalty for which does not exceed a fine of $100, or imprisonment not exceeding six months, where the crimes are committed within the municipality, and provided the offender, in writing, waives indictment and trial by jury. (§§ 2, 3). On such trial no jury is permitted except in suits for violation of ordinances or regulations of such municipality, and in cases under § 13 of the 

Disorderly Persons Act, and the Bastardy Act. (§ 4). All vio lations of the General Crimes Act of June 14, 1898, and supple-

ments (not excluded as above), this Court may try. Those waiving indictment and trial by jury may be held to bail to appear for trial. (§ 6). A Justice of the Peace may sit in place of the regular magistrate at the latter's request. (§ 10). The Act may be found in C. S. 3999 et seq.

By an Act of April 1, 1912, as amended, creating Juvenile 

Courts in counties of the first class, when a child under sixteen years of age who is a "delinquent," that is, who violates any penal law or municipal ordinance, or who commits any act or offense for which he could be prosecuted in a method partaking of the nature of a criminal action or proceeding (except the crimes of murder or manslaughter), or who is a disorderly person, or habitually vagrant, or incorrigible, or immoral, or who knowingly associates with thieves or other vicious or immoral persons, or is growing up in idleness and crime, or knowingly visits gambling places or patronizes other places or establishments, or idly roams streets, or who is habitually truant from school, etc., is taken before a Justice of the Peace, Recorder, Judge of a Police Court or other magistrate the case shall immediately be transferred to the Juvenile 

Court. (P. L. 1912, p. 606, §§ 5, 10; am. by P. L. 1926, p. 353, and P. L. 1929, p. 90). 

Criminal Courts in certain second-class cities

In all cities of the second class having a population of over 

50,000, by an Act of March 16, 1916, the "Recorder, Police Justice or other official presiding over any Recorder's Court, Police Court or municipal Court, having jurisdiction of criminal offenses and power of committal," is authorized to try and determine all cases of assault, simple assault and battery, malicious mischief, larceny or embezzlement where the price or value of the article or property taken is under $50; also obtaining money or property under false pretenses, or receiving stolen property, where the value is under $50, and also all other criminal offenses where the penalty does not exceed a fine of $100 or imprisonment not exceeding six months; but only where the crime is committed within the municipality and provided the person charged in writing waives indictment and trial by jury; but the Act is not to apply where defendant has been previously convicted and is on probation. Details of procedure by Justices of the Peace in taking complaints, taking bail, etc., and of the practice in the Courts are stated in the 

Act. (P. L. 1916, p. 143, as am. by P. L. 1919, p. 351; N. J. 

Cum. Supp. 2713). 

Criminal courts in certain fourth-class cities

In all cities of the fourth class having a population of over 

10,000, an Act of March 20, 1916, provides that Justices of the

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Peace shall transmit complaints to "the Recorder, Police Justice or other official presiding over any Recorder's Court, Police Court or other municipal Court having jurisdiction over criminal offenses and power of committal" in such city. Such municipal 

Court is given jurisdiction and power over assault, simple assault and battery, malicious mischief, larceny or embezzlement where the value of the property is under $50, obtaining money or property under false pretenses, or receiving stolen property or unlawfully converting property, up to same value, fornication, adultery, selling cigarettes to minors, allowing minors to congregate in pool rooms, and other criminal offenses named, provided the person charged waives in writing indictment and trial by jury and requests trial in such Court. Details of procedure given. (P. L. 

1916, p. 453; N. J. Cum. Supp. 2718). 

Criminal Courts in certain cities

In cities adopting an Act of Mar. 24, 1899, the Recorder, Police Court, or other official presiding over any Recorder's, Police or municipal Court, with jurisdiction of criminal offenses and power to commit, may try cases of assault, simple assault and battery, malicious mischief, larceny under $20, obtaining money under false pretenses under $20, receiving stolen property under $20, and other criminal offenses where the fine does not exceed $100, or imprisonment of six months, if occurring within city limits. (P. L., p. 283, as amended by P. L. 1918, p. 147; N. J. Cum. 

Supp. 548).

Jurisdictional Courts in boroughs and towns 

By an Act of April 9, 1913, the Recorder or Police Justice and the Mayor of any town or borough is given jurisdiction over all actions to enforce ordinances passed by the local board of health, and police officers of such municipalities are empowered to serve all papers, process and orders to enforce such ordinances. (P. L. 1913, p. 641; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1490).

By an Act of May 15, 1907, concerning the enforcement of ordinances in incorporated towns, "the Recorder, Police Justice, or other officers having criminal jurisdiction," and who are appointed by the governing body, are given jurisdiction over violations of town ordinances, and to hear and determine complaints respecting them without the filing of pleadings. The Act gives some details of the mode of procedure, and provides for appeal to the Common Pleas. (C. S. 5423, §§ 26, 27). 

Juvenile Courts

Beside reference made above to Juvenile Courts there are various other Acts affecting such Courts, which are beyond the province of this work to treat.

VI. MISCELLANEOUS MATTERS 

Review of certain municipal Court proceedings 

All judgments or other judicial proceedings of any city

Judge, Police Court or other inferior Court for violation of city ordinances, or ordinances of city boards of health, whether with or without trial by jury are reviewable by certiorari, or, on application by the defendant, within thirty days after judgment rendered, the Court of Common Pleas may order such judgment and all proceedings certified to that Court for review. (C. S. 408, as amended by P. L. 1915, p. 412; N. J. Cum. Supp. 255). 

Fines to go to municipality

As a rule the various statutes concerning all special municipal Courts is that all fines, and all penalties not otherwise designated by law, go into the city, borough, etc., treasury. 

Returning fines

Where a defendant in a proceeding before a Recorder or Police magistrate has paid a fine on being found guilty of any offense, and on appeal has obtained a decision in his favor terminating the case of a city or municipality against him, the body controlling the finances of the municipality wherein the trial was had may return to him the amount of the fine. (P. L. 1911, p. 30; 

N. J. Cum. Supp. 2704). 

Salaries and fees

In most cases Recorders and Police Judges and Justices are paid salaries, fixed by the governing body but limited by statute. 

Where they receive fees the rule is that they are to receive the same fees as Justices of the Peace for like services. Where civil or quasi-criminal actions are within their jurisdiction, and costs are receivable from plaintiff or defendant, and the above-named officers are paid salaries, such fees go into the municipal treasury. 

Solemnization of marriages 

Recorders, Police Justices and Mayors may solemnize marriages. (See under general title "Marriages"). 

Complaint docket 

All magistrates are to keep Complaint and Summary Proceeding dockets. (See general title "Dockets"). Some Acts relating to Recorders or Police Justices also give other directions concerning such dockets.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Terms of office

The terms of office of the foregoing officials and by whom appointed or elected are so varied by the provisions of the several statutes that no general statement concerning them can be given. 

Ordinarily the terms vary from two to five years. 

Forms by Recorders, etc. 

Where Recorders or Police Judges, etc., are given jurisdiction over certain proceedings which are also under the cognizance of Justices of the Peace, and no special manner is pointed out for procedure, the same laws and steps of procedure and the same Forms for process, etc., as used by Justices of the Peace and as given in this work are applicable to them, except that the title of the Recorder or Police Judge is to be substituted for that of Justice of the Peace, and the designation "The Small Cause Court" is not to be used. 

Use of official seals

While there is no general law requiring all Recorders or Police Judges to use an official seal (some particular Acts regulating the Courts of these officials in certain municipalities require a seal), it is well for all to have one by which to authenticate their writs. 

Remarks on Act of 1911 Poor

Until 1911 the Poor laws of the State devolved many duties upon Justices of the Peace or local magistrates, concerning the determination of place of settlement, removals, application for relief, etc. But in 1911 and later all this was changed, and the overseers of the poor are now charged with most of the duties heretofore lodged with magistrates. The only jurisdiction conferred now, as a rule, upon Justices and other magistrates relates to deserters of families, when they are treated as disorderly persons and liable to indictment as such. (See general title, "Disorderly Persons"). 

What it is 

Power of Attorney

A power of attorney is an instrument in writing designating a person to act as an attorney-in-fact of the signer of the instrument, and specifying therein the purpose. It confers a power,

REFERENCE 

423 usually to sign or execute papers, checks, etc. If to be used to execute a conveyance, under seal, it must itself be acknowledged and recorded; or, if the acknowledgment is recited in the conveyance, it will be prima facie proof of its existence, provided the deed has been recorded for ten years, and if an affidavit of it be made and recorded. (C. S. 1561, § 69).

A married woman may join her husband in a power of attorney to execute a conveyance, but it must be acknowledged in the usual manner. (C. S. 1549, § 40). She may give power of attorney to another person to perform any act which she might do alone, without her husband.

A power of attorney is not like an agreement, which is signed by both parties; it is signed only by the person who gives the power, and it is usual to acknowledge it. 

The power should be sealed and witnessed; a scroll seal is sufficient.

A power of attorney may be given for almost any purpose, such as to convey or mortgage land; to collect debts, rents or a legacy; to enter a satisfaction of judgment; to transact mercantile business, etc., etc.; or it may be given to an attorney-at-law authorizing him to appear and plead in a suit in Court. To revoke a power of attorney it must be done by the same formal instrument as that which created the power.

Reference 

When and how referees may be appointed Any civil action may be tried before a referee or referees, provided both the plaintiff and defendant request it, or assent thereto. This assent need not be in writing; it may be made orally,

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

but if made in an action before a Justice he must note a rule of reference in his docket. (Schooley v. Thorne, Coxe, 71).

The Act permitting it is S. C. A., § 108, which applies also to appeals in the Common Pleas, and the general statute to be followed is the Act of 1877 (Revision; C. S. 103).

The person or persons to act as referee or referees are to be those whom the parties shall nominate. The Justice cannot name them against the will of the parties, nor can he be one of them. (Little v. Silverthorn, 2 Penn. 680).

The practice is to nominate an uneven number, one or three, but in a matter of account one is more usual. This is because the statute contemplates that, if more than one be selected, a majority shall arrive at a certain determination. In what is stated below three are supposed to be acting.

The suit must first be actually instituted, by process served and returned, unless parties meet and agree to waive process, and the suit is entered by consent for the purpose of a reference. Consent will cure previous irregularities in the process, even to the form of the action. (Burroughs v. Gennung, 1 Penn. 103; Applegate v. Schureman, 2 Penn. 868). 

The oath to be taken

After the referees are selected, they must make oath to faithfully determine the issues in controversy. This should be in writing, that it may be filed with the award. The oath must follow the statute, and declare that they "will faithfully and fairly hear and examine the cause in question, and make a just and true report according to the best of their skill and understanding," and may be taken before any Judge of any Court, or Justice of the Peace of this State. It is usual to take it, if convenient, before the Judge or Justice in whose Court the suit is instituted. (C. S. 106, § 4; 

Reeves v. Goff, 1 Penn. 143; Parker v. Crammer, Ibid, 271). 

The proceedings

The proceedings before referees must be according to law. 

The time of their meeting must be known to both parties. Attorneys may conduct the examination if they appear for the litigants. 

The capacity of witnesses, propriety of admitting papers and other matters of proof are to be determined by the referees the same as by a Justice. They should hear legal objections and decide them. They must also swear the witnesses examined before them in legal form. Subpoenas for the attendance of witnesses before the referees may be issued by the Justice in the usual way. In short, there is no material difference between the mode of proceeding before referees and before the Justice.

REFERENCE 

425 

State of demand unnecessary

A state of demand in case of reference is not required by the statute. It would be better to have one, however, to give regularity to the proceedings. 

The report

The referees can adjourn the case from time to time but they cannot nonsuit. They must report for either plaintiff or defendant, and a sum certain (or "no cause of action") and not some unlawful verdict.

The report must be made in writing, and signed by all or a majority of the referees, and cannot be altered after delivery. It must appear by this report that the cause was regularly and legally heard. If the defendant did not appear it should state that he was duly notified of the meeting. It should also state that the referees were sworn. If all the referees do not sign the report the reason should appear. (Steelman v. Stewart, I Penn. 316; Egbert v. 

Smith, 2 Penn. 923).

If one refuses to act the others cannot report. (Hoff v. Taylor, 2 South. 829). 

Fees and costs

The fees allowed each referee for his services are "one dollar for every day necessarily spent in the business of the reference, besides a reasonable allowance for his expenses, which, in the first instance, shall be paid by the prevailing party, and shall afterwards be allowed to such party in the taxation of costs where costs are recoverable." (C. S. 106, § 5). 

Subsequent duty of the Justice

When the report is submitted to the Justice-as it should be, and not to the parties-he should file it, and must copy it in full in his docket, and notify the losing party of the time when he will enter up judgment in the cause according to the report. The costs on the judgment will go to the prevailing party, and is also to be entered in the docket. 

The Justice does not enter the judgment as of course upon receiving the referees' report; for if the defendant appears and objects to the regularity or validity of the proceedings before the referees, as that they were not sworn, or considered matters not submitted to them, etc., it is his duty to adjudge upon those objections. But the truth of such objections must appear from the report itself; he cannot swear witnesses and enter into a trial. If he finds their report illegal on its face, he may refuse to confirm it. J-27

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

An appeal will lie from judgment on report of referees From this judgment, however, there is an appeal to the Common Pleas in the regular way. The words of the Act that the "report shall be final and conclusive to the parties," (S. C. A., § 108), applies only to the report, to preclude its reopening, or being set aside, and not to the judgment, which is subject to review, the same as if the judgment were upon a hearing before the Justice or jury.

What a riot is Riots

A riot consists of a number of persons, twelve or more, armed with clubs, guns, swords, or other weapons; or thirty persons or more, "unlawfully, routously, riotously or tumultously assembled." (C. S. 4380, § 1). 

Duty of Justices and others

The Justice, sheriff, under-sheriff, or constable, must attempt to disperse the rioters in the following manner : He must first come as early as he safely can to the rioters, demand silence, and make this proclamation: 

"State of New Jersey: By virtue of an Act of this State, entitled 'An Act to prevent routs, riots and tumultuous assemblies,' I am directed to charge and command all persons being here assembled immediatèly to disperse themselves, and peaceably to depart to their habitations, or to their lawful business, upon the pains and penalties contained in the said Act. God save the State!" (Ibid).

The officers above named are required to do this when made acquainted with the fact of a riot. After the proclamation, if the rioters do not disperse within one hour, the Justice and other officers must command all persons to aid in the arrest of the rioters.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Those arrested are to be taken before a Justice of the Peace and committed to jail, unless bail is given in the usual way. If in pursuit of the rioters any of them are killed, through their resistance, no one of the pursuers shall be held guilty. (§ 2). 

By various statutes Mayors of municipalities are also given power to quell riots.

Riots are also misdemeanors, punishable by imprisonment ranging to three years, and by fines up to $1,000. (C. S. 1759, §§ 

42, 43; 1811, § 215).

Road Traffic Act Highway Regulation Act of 1928 

A most important Act of 1928, with amendments since, generally known as the Road Traffic Act, which is to regulate vehicles, animals and pedestrians on all public roads, sets forth a large number of provisions as to speed, stopping, turning, passing, crossing intersections of streets, control and treatment of horses and motor-vehicles, street cars, accidents, etc. (P. L. 1928, p. 769; P. 

L. 1929, pp. 332, 385; P. L. 1931, pp. 220, 609. It is a completely 

Revised Act, the former one being of 1915). Everyone driving horses on the public road must also conform to the provisions of this Act.

The provisions of this Act, making 53 pages in the Pamphlet Laws of 1928 and more pages in the amendments are too voluminous to give here, even by abstract. The proper thing for a magistrate to do is to secure an up-to-date separate pamphlet of both the automobile and traffic laws issued by the Department of Motor Vehicles. Sometimes one may be procured of the local licensing agent; otherwise by writing to the Department, State 

House, Trenton. Changes are likely to be made in this as in the 

Motor Vehicle Act at every session of the Legislature. Various ones are to be found in P. L. 1933, in various Chapters. 

The enforcement proceedings

The enforcement of the Traffic Act is vested "in all police officers, peace officers of, or inspectors duly appointed for the purpose by any town, township, city, borough or other municipality, or by any county, or by the State, and in the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles and the inspectors appointed under his authority." 

(Act XV, § 1). But no Justice of the Peace can act within the limits of any municipality having a Police Judge, Police Justice,

Recorder's Court or City Criminal Court. The penalty for any violation is "not more than $50, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding 15 days or both."

SCIRE FACIAS 

429 Any magistrate of the county, or any municipality, or any Judge of any Criminal Judicial District Court of any county in which the offense is committed may take a complaint, to be in writing, under oath or affirmation, and to be made within 30 days after the commission of the offense, but not a Justice of the Peace of any city. (See P. L. 1933, Chap. 340). Either a warrant or summons may be used. The Act provides for an adjournment, appeal, etc., such appeal now being to the Court of Special Sessions. And proceedings may be instituted on Sunday. The proceedings are to run in the name of the State of New Jersey, with the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles, or a motor vehicle inspector, or a police officer, peace officer or a constable, "or such other person as shall by complaint institute the proceedings, as prosecutor."

It is also provided that if the complainant is not the Commissioner or inspector of motor vehicles or a police officer, the magistrate may refuse to entertain the complaint until a sufficient bond to secure costs has been filed. The officers heretofore named may also arrest without warrant. (Ibid, §§ 8, 9). 

Provision is also made for cash deposit or recognizance, and for arrests in other counties. 

As to the fees, see under general title "Fees and Costs."

One or more Forms to be used under this Act and some portions of the Act itself may be found under the general subject, "Motor Vehicles." 

What the writ is

Scire Facias 

The scire facias is a writ founded upon some record, requiring the person designated in it to show cause why the party bringing the writ should not have advantage of that record. The words mean "that you cause to know." Among the cases in which it may be employed in civil proceedings in The Small Cause Court are the following: 

1. To revive a judgment in order to issue execution when the term of office of a Justice of the Peace has expired, or he has resigned, provided his docket is still lawfully in his possession. 

(See S. C. A., §§ 7, 8). 

2. To revive a judgment, in case the plaintiff or defendant dies. Then a scire facias may issue on behalf of, or against the executors or administrators, and thereafter execution will issue in their names as representatives. But if one of two or more plaintiffs, or defendants, dies, the death may be suggested on the record, and the action proceed in the name of the survivor. (C. S. 

3, §§ 1, 2). This Act seems to have been drawn as if only appli-

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

cable to the higher Courts, but has been applied in practice, when applicable, to  

3. In an attachment, after judgment, a scire facias may issue against the garnishee to show cause why execution should not issue against him, even if garnishee resides within a city where there is a District Court. (See under general title "Attachment;" 

N. Y., L. E. and W. R. R. v. Cookson, 6 N. J. L. J. 237). But it can only be used when it can be served as a summons, and not against a municipal corporation. (Mayor v. Horton, 9 Vr. 88). 

Service and return of writ and proceedings

There are no special provisions in The Small Cause Act for the service of this writ, but in the higher Courts it is to be served as a summons, and such is the practice in The Small Cause Court. 

The writ is to be returned at the time therein stated with the constable's indorsement of service, and thereupon it will be regular (though perhaps not essential) for the plaintiff to file a demand, to contain a recital of the writ, with a request for execution. 

The scire facias is, usually, in the nature of a continuance of an action, being based upon former proceedings taken in the same matter, and may be amended, after it issues, to be conformable to the record. (Condit v. Gregory, 1 Zab. 429).

When the writ is intended to secure an execution, the defendant may plead payment, discharge as an insolvent debtor, or release, but nothing in defense to the original action. The judgment will not be for a sum of money, but merely "that execution issue" for the amount of the original execution and costs, and the additional costs then adjudged. (Tindale v. Carson, 1 Harr. 94; 

Woolston v. Gale, 4 Hal. 32).

What it is 

Search Warrant 

A "search warrant," as generally understood, is a warrant commanding an officer to search for stolen goods, or goods which the law directs shall be found by a special warrant of search; and usually it also commands the arrest of the person in whose possession they are found. It is applicable in cases of larceny, or graver offenses including larceny, as robbery, or burglary, and in certain statutory cases, as under the game laws, etc. 

So important a matter is it, under our form of government, that the right to be protected from illegal searches should remain inviolate, that we find incorporated in the Constitution of the United States the following national law, as among one of the first amendments to it demanded by the people: "The right of people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers and effects against unreasonable searches and seizures shall not be violated; and no warrants shall issue, but upon probable cause, supported by oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized." (Const. of U. S., Amend., Art. IV). 

The basis for a search warrant in most cases is the common law, but there are statutes for certain special matters. 

Requisites for search warrant

It is requisite, in the issuing of a search warrant for stolen goods: 

1. That it be granted only after the filing of an affidavit.

This affidavit must show that a theft has been actually committed, and that the party complaining has cause to suspect where the goods are. It must also show his grounds for such suspicion. 

2. The rule is for the warrant to command the search to be made in the daytime, but, when there is positive proof, it may be made without limitation, and executed in the nighttime. 

3. The warrant should command that the goods found, as well as the party in whose keeping they are, should be brought before the Justice, that he may examine and make a lawful disposition of them.

SEARCH WARRANT 

433 

How executed

The party from whom the goods are stolen should accompany the constable in order to identify the goods. Other assistants may be called to aid if it is necessary. Accompanied by these, and armed with the warrant, the constable can enter in the daytime any suspected house, if the doors are open, and make search. 

If the door is shut, demand should be made to have it opened, and, if refused admittance, the constable may break open the door. 

If the goods are not found, the officer or his assistants will not be liable in an action, as they are fully protected by the warrant.

The search must be made only where the warrant authorizes it. A warrant to search a certain house will not justify a search in a barn, or in another dwelling.

If the officer finds other property besides that described, which he knows is stolen, or which may be necessary to convict the possessor, he may seize it. 

Proceedings after return of warrant

Upon the return of the warrant, if the goods brought before the Justice are proved to have been stolen, they are to be restored to the owner or possessor. The party arrested, if not the thief, or an accessory, must be discharged. He will be an accessory if he did not steal the goods but received them with knowledge. If he claims to be and it is reasonable to believe he is innocent, his recognizance should be taken for him to appear as a witness against those of whom he received the property. 

Special cases for search warrants

These are some of the special instances in which, by statute, a magistrate may issue a search warrant: 

1. In case of complaint to any magistrate under oath, founded on information and belief, of the existence, in any place, of obscene and indecent books, papers, pictures and articles, he must issue a search warrant directing their search and seizure. They are to be brought before him and specimens of the same are to be transmitted by the magistrate to the prosecutor of the pleas of the county, enclosed and under seal, and the remainder deposited, enclosed and under seal, in the county jail, or some other secure place. As the Act then refers to the conviction of the person in whose possession they were found, it would seem to follow that the prosecutor of the pleas must follow up the matter, secure arrest of the offender, and if a magistrate convicts him such magistrate is to "forthwith destroy, or cause to be destroyed, the remainder" of what was seized and enter the fact on his records. (C. S. 1854, § 110).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

www. 

2. In case of dispute between the inspectors or repackers and the possessors of herring, concerning the soundness or package of the same or of the casks, a search warrant may be issued by a Justice to two indifferent persons of skill, etc., to view and search the herring and casks. (Č. S. 2745, § 15). 

3. In case of the secreting or unlawful use of bottles owned by manufacturers or sellers of bottles, boxes, kegs, etc., bottles of mineral waters, beer, ale, cider, milk, etc., by some persons not the owners. (P. L. 1925, p. 681). 

4. In case of public nuisance affecting health, which the officer serving the warrant may abate. (C. S. 2673, § 47). 

5. In case of belief that animals are cruelly treated. (C. S. 

58, § 31). 

6. In case of concealment of fish or game killed or had in possession contrary to law. (C. S. 2559, § 267). 

7. In case of concealment of diamond-backed terrapin. (C. 

S. 2519, § 85).

These, or other statutes, permitting search warrants, must be carefully consulted by the justice before he proceeds, as the method of procedure, from complaint to conviction, or judgment, is wholly technical, and varies according to the language of each Act. Set-off and Recoupment The law of set-off and recoupment In case a person is sued in an action on Contract and he has any lawful set-off, or counterclaim, against the plaintiff, he should make out his claim and set it up in defense, or thereafter may lose the benefit of it. In other words, if he fails at such a time to present his set-off, or (when proper) his counter-damages by way of recoupment, it may be that he cannot subsequently bring an action for either. (See S. C. A., § 24).

Where, however, the balance, which would be found to be due to the defendant, exceeds two hundred dollars, the Act says: "If the defendant file as a set-off or recoupment a demand against the plaintiff for more than two hundred dollars, and at the trial it shall be proved that a balance exceeding two hundred dollars is due to the defendant, then the suit shall be dismissed, unless the defendant consent to accept a judgment for two hundred dollars and costs in full settlement of his claim." (§ 25). 

The reason for the exception is, that where the defendant's account (the balance due) would exceed two hundred dollars, he

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

is not required to divide the sum into parts in order to recover upon it. (Sipley v. Wass, 18 Vr. 187; see also 11 N. J. L. J. 9). 

Explanation of the law that:

Under the foregoing statute and decisions it must be noted 1. Where the balance due defendant, after allowing the setoff, will not exceed two hundred dollars, it must be filed, or an action cannot be maintained for the demand afterward. 

2. Where the balance due defendant, after allowing the setoff, will exceed two hundred dollars, it may be filed, if the defendant so wills; in which case the Justice, should he find at the trial that there is actually due to defendant more than two hundred dollars, must dismiss the action, unless the defendant waives the excess over two hundred dollars. But if defendant does not choose to file such set-off, so as to secure dismissal of the action, he will not be precluded from bringing a new action on his claim at a future time.

While the decision of Sipley v. Wass, supra, was based upon a different language of the statute concerning set-offs from that at present incorporated in The Small Cause Act, it does not appear that the principles of that decision are disturbed in relation to the point that it is not obligatory to file a set-off if a balance of more than two hundred dollars is actually due to the defendant upon a demand which defendant has against plaintiff. 

3. If the action, being on Contract, is subject to recoupment, the defendant must set up such claim of recoupment or he will afterward be precluded from bringing an action thereon. 

There is no provision in the Act as to what is to be done if the counterclaim of recoupment is found by the Justice to exceed two hundred dollars, and perhaps it is to be assumed that there is not likely to be a balance due on recoupment greater than that of the original contract itself.

If a defendant neglects to file his proper set-off, and afterwards assigns his account to a third person for full value, the account or debt will probably still be barred against such third person by the statute quoted above. (Henry v. Milham, 1 Gr. 266).

The defendant may not so far disregard the statute as, before the return day of the summons to bring a new, or crossaction against the plaintiff before the same or another Justice. 

The action first brought must be responded to; the second will go for naught. It matters not which return day is made first; the plaintiff in the first action has a right to a trial of the whole matter of indebtedness between him and defendant (until it transpires that defendant would be entitled to a judgment for beyond

SET-OFF AND RECOUPMENT 

437 two hundred dollars) and the Justice, in the second suit, upon the facts being presented to him, must dismiss the action. (Johnson v. Pennington, 3 Gr. 188).

If the set-off is filed but not allowed, or but partly allowed, no subsequent action upon it may be brought by the defendant, provided the whole set-off was properly before the Justice, or jury, and passed upon by them. In such a case the claim is res adjudicata; is forever settled, except by appeal or review on certiorari.

Where, therefore, the set-off of over two hundred dollars is filed, the Justice will proceed to the trial regardless of the amount, but, if the balance actually found due the defendant should prove to exceed two hundred dollars, he cannot render judgment for that amount, any more than he could render judgment for an excess of two hundred dollars for the plaintiff; then he should state in his docket that fact and dismiss the action, "unless the defendant consent to accept a judgment for two hundred dollars and costs in full settlement of his claim." 

What kind of set-offs are allowed 

The statute says "any demand against the plaintiff" may be set off, but the Courts have held that the subject matter of the account should be restricted to one of the following classes:

I. To such as contain an independent cause of action in itself. In other words, the defendant's claim must be such as that he could sue the plaintiff upon it and recover. 

II. To such as are actionable at the time the set-off is filed. 

A debt barred by the statute of limitations, or statute of frauds, cannot be set off; nor a note made and indorsed by the plaintiff and obtained by the defendant, after an action has been commenced. (Whitaker v. Turnbull, 3 Harr. 172). 

III. To such as are due in the same right. Where a man is sued for his own debt, he cannot set off a debt due to him as executor, administrator, trustee, or to his wife. But if he is sued as an executor or trustee, a debt due him as such executor or trustee may be the subject of set-off. So a debt due to another person cannot be set off by the defendant, unless he is bona fide the creditor of the plaintiff by reason of an assignment of the debt to him for value received, before suit is brought. Nor can the separate claims of the partners be set off in an action by or against partners for a partnership debt. (McChesney v. Rogers, 3 Hal. 

272; Bowne v. Thompson, Coxe 2; Williams v. Hamilton, 1 

South. 220).

Under these general principles it has been held that stock in a bank is not a set-off against a note given in bank, nor deposits with a firm of bankers, after the withdrawal of a partner, by the

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

4 maker of a note given to them before such withdrawal. The debtor of an insolvent corporation has the same right of set-off against a claim of the receiver that he had against the corporation at the time of its insolvency. In an action to recover money received by an officer in his official capacity, a debt due from the plaintiff to the officer, in his private capacity, is not a subject of set-off. A public officer cannot blend his public duties with his private transactions. A defendant, in a suit brought by a State, may set off a claim against it. But not against a suit for taxes. 

An assigned judgment is not a proper subject of set-off, because the defendant could not maintain an action upon it in his own name. A judgment obtained by the defendant against the plaintiff is a proper set-off if it be admitted, but the Justice cannot order one judgment set off by another judgment recovered in another Court.

The maker of a note, after maturity, cannot set off an independent claim, in no way connected with the note, which he has against the indorser, in an action brought against the maker by the indorsee. But if there is any connection between the note in the hands of the indorsee and the account, or any agreement between the parties before the indorsement, that the one should balance the other, a set-off would be good. A claim of the defendant against a bank which discounted a note, upon an action by the indorser against the maker, such note being payable at that particular bank, cannot be set off. The claim of a debtor against an insolvent corporation does not constitute a legal account under the general account of set-off, as against the receiver. 

Claims against an agent cannot be offset against the principal. It is a general rule, under this head, that the same parties and only the same parties must be interested in both the accounts to allow one to be filed against another. Thus if A sues 

B, and B and C have joint account against A, or B has an account against A and D, it cannot be offset. This rule applies to partners, husband and wife, and executors, as well as to others. 

The filing of a set-off does not waive any other lawful defenses the defendant may have to plaintiff's demand. (Price v. 

Combs, 7 Hal. 188). 

Affidavit to set-off

If a defendant does not deny the plaintiff's claim, but merely asks that his set-off be allowed against it to reduce the amount of judgment, no affidavit is required. He is at full liberty to file and on the hearing to prove his set-off and thus secure a reduction of the account. 

But if the defendant denies that he will owe the plaintiff when both their accounts are adjusted, and seeks to recover judg-

SET-OFF AND RECOUPMENT 

439 ment against the plaintiff for balance actually due to defendant, he must accompany his set-off with an affidavit, to be filed at the time of filing his set-off, setting forth that this counter-demand "is not filed for the purpose of delay, and that he verily believes he does not owe the plaintiff anything, or that he owes only a certain sum, stating such sum, and that the plaintiff is indebted to him in a certain sum, stating such sum." (S. C. A., § 36). Only so can defendant secure a judgment in the action. 

Without such affidavit the plaintiff may withdraw his suit at any time, unless he has called a jury and the merits of his side have been presented. (§ 49). An affidavit to the set-off is, therefore, advisable, even if the defendant is only anxious to have his set-off adjudicated. 

Form of the set-off

The claim must not only be in writing, but in form as clear and explicit as the state of demand. The same certainty is required, because it must apprise the plaintiff fully of the defense to be made. It should be entitled with the action, signed and indorsed.

Defendant's execution on judgment for set-off If the defendant recovers on his set-off and obtains a judgment against the plaintiff, he may have execution for the judgment and costs, the same as if he had been plaintiff in the suit. 

(S. C. A., § 59). 

Nature of recoupment

Recoupment differs from set-off in that the latter is a counterclaim of fixed or liquidated money value. Recoupment is in the nature of an equitable set-off, not fixed in amount, but growing out of the contract on which the demand of plaintiff is based. 

Recoupment seeks to abate the contract sum, or amount said to be due by the plaintiff, by reason of a defect in, or partial failure of the consideration, or for damages sustained by reason of nonperformance, or defective performance, of the contract by the plaintiff. 

Bill of particulars in recoupment

When the defendant seeks to recoup, he must file a bill of particulars of such defense or counterclaim. (For the language of the Act concerning the filing of a bill of particulars for recoupment, see S. C. A., § 40).

Recoupment in actions on Contract 

A defense setting up recoupment of damages may be made

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

only in actions on Contract; not in actions in Tort. In the latter case facts which might reduce the damages claimed may be proven, and are matters for the consideration of the Justice, or jury, in mitigation of damages; they may even wholly defeat plaintiff's action. But in Tort a defendant cannot secure a judgment for damages against the plaintiff. In other words, the principles both of set-off and recoupment are applicable in The Small Cause Court upon actions on Contract, but in no other actions.

SHIPWRECKS 

441 Shipwrecks 

Statement, etc., by coroner, or Justice as acting coroner

In case dead bodies are thrown upon shore, after a shipwreck, a Justice of the Peace may act as coroner when the latter cannot be had in due time. In such case he must make out a written statement, containing the name of the ship or vessel, the date of the wreck, and place where it occurred together with as full a description of the body as he can give, time of burial and location of grave, and record the same in a book for that purpose. He is to preserve all letters, writings, coins or other articles which may serve for identification. He must also send a copy of this statement, sworn to, to the treasurer of the State of New Jersey. (C. S. 1588, §§ 4, 16, 33).

If in a state of nudity he is to furnish necessary graveclothes (and bury the body, as of course). Clothing found on the body not necessary to the interment must be kept twenty days, when, if not claimed by relatives or friends, it may be sold, after due notice, at public auction, the proceeds, after paying interment expenses, to be paid to the State treasurer. (C. S. 1589, §§ 19-21). (As to fees and costs, see under general subject, "Fees and Costs").

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

What it is 

State of Demand

A "state of demand," is a statement in writing of the plaintiff's demand in a civil action. It is his "case;" the basis for his cause of action. Ordinarily, no civil suit can progress without it, because the defendant must be properly apprised, in writing, of what he is to demand before he can be made to answer. 

The demand need not be signed by an attorney, or even by the plaintiff, but the proper custom is to attach the plaintiff's name, which may be done by plaintiff's agent, or attorney. 

Form of demand 

The demand should: 1. Set forth a legal cause of action within the jurisdiction of the Justice. 2. Set forth the same style of action for which the summons was issued. 3. Demand a sum certain and not an indefinite amount. 4. Be intelligible, so as to show the real ground of the action. 5. Be sufficiently specific so that no subsequent action could be brought upon the same items. 6. Agree with the summons as to number, names etc., of the parties. 7. Conform to the statute where it directs what it shall contain. 

Amendments to demand

As to amendment to state of demand, see general title, "Amendments." 

When to be filed

It must be filed with the Justice on or before the return day of the summons; or, if the process against the defendant is a warrant, upon the return of the warrant. (S. C. A., § 24). 

To hurry up the hearing, it may be served with the summons. (S. C. A., § 30). In such case the return of the constable is sufficient proof of the service of the state of demand, and he receives no extra fee for serving the same. It is advisable for the constable in returning the summons to add to his return "the state of demand being attached," or words to that effect. 

The plaintiff may file his demand with the Justice personally, or by any one who acts for him. 

If it be not filed at the time required, the defendant may ask for a nonsuit, and the Justice must grant it, with costs against the plaintiff. (Ibid, § 24).

The Justice should indorse the demand with the date of filing. The paper is a public one, to be seen by the defendant or any party interested, but it must be retained by the Justice, unless in case an appeal or certiorari is taken, when all the papers in the cause will go to the higher Court of review.

STATE OF DEMAND 

443 If, without a demand being filed, the Justice goes on notwithstanding the objections of the defendant, the judgment will be set aside. Or if he adjourns the cause because no demand is filed, and the defendant objects, the proceedings subsequent will be illegal. So if the plaintiff alters the demand after filing without regular motion made, when both parties are present. (Blackwell v. Leslie, 1 South. 112; Hunt v. South, 2 South. 495).

The defendant may waive an irregularity, however, and he may do it inferentially as well as by words. If he appears and goes to trial, or if on adjourned day the demand is filed, and he does not object but himself asks for an adjournment, it will be too late to take advantage of the irregularity in the filing. (Shreeves v. Liveson, 1 Penn. 247).

And it has been held that going to trial under an agreement that a note sued upon should be considered to be a state of demand concluded the defendant from objecting afterward that no demand was filed. Also that where a plaintiff sued upon a promissory note but filed no demand, and the defendant, in his set-off, gave the plaintiff credit for the note, and no objection was made to the want of a demand, it was held a waiver. (Steward v. Sears, 7 Vr. 174).

But it must be noted that it takes the consent of the defendant, express or implied, to constitute a waiver. 

When state of demand unnecessary

A state of demand is not necessary upon a confessed judgment (Hunt v. Shivers, 1 South. 89); nor when a cause has been submitted to arbitrators or referees by agreement, although in the latter case it is proper and better to file a demand with the arbitrators or referees. (Ayres v. Burt, 2 Penn. 739).

A state of demand is also not necessary in summary actions for penalties, the "complaint" filed being equivalent thereto.

Where executors, firms, assignees, etc., are plaintiffs 

In cases where administrators or executors are plaintiffs their representing relation should be set out. It has been held that where the demand is headed by the name and title of the action, and in such the plaintiff is set out as administrator or executor, it is sufficient, but the proper way is to set it out in both the heading and body of the demand. (Reid v. Crawford, 2 Penn. 622).

In actions by or against firms, the names of the individuals composing the firm should be stated. (Tomlinson v. Burke, 5 

Hal. 295; M'Creedy v. Vanneman, 2 Penn. 870).

When an assignee sues, the suit should run throughout in his name as assignee, and, further, the demand must show the instrument sued upon to be such as could be legally assigned. (Stroud v. Howell, 3 Penn. 649).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Demand on money bond

A demand on a money bond should be for the real sum and not for the penalty. 

Demand against a married woman

A demand against a married woman for contracts of her own making is to be made against her just as against any other individual, or as if she were unmarried. (P. L. 1929, p. 110). 

Demand against indorser

Where an action is brought against both the maker and indorser of a bill of exchange or promissory note, the plaintiff should annex to his state of demand a copy of the bill or note with the indorsements, and stating that the action is brought to recover the amount due thereon. (S. C. A., § 42). 

Interest and credits

A lower rate of interest than that allowed by law may be demanded in order to reduce the amount due to a sum below two hundred dollars. Or the plaintiff may waive interest altogether. Where no rate of interest is mentioned, however, and it is demanded generally, the legal rate is to be computed. 

If credits are given at all they should be correct. The plaintiff may not put in fictitious interest, or fictitious credits, in order to secure jurisdiction in  (Griffith v. 

Clute, 4 Hal. 264; Saddle River v. Colfax, 1 Hal. 115; Howell v. Burnett, Spencer, 265). Miscellaneous

No provision is made in the Small Cause Court Act for the defendant to require plaintiff, before trial, to serve him with any further "bill of particulars" than appears in the demand. 

In an action in Tort, in the nature of trover, where defendant came into possession of plaintiff's property lawfully, a demand of property is necessary before an action will lie, but it need not be set out in the demand. It is a matter to be put in evidence and mere matters of evidence are not to be pleaded.
