Steam Boilers and Steam Engines 

Act to license engineers and firemen of stationary and portable boilers and engines

An Act of 1913 (P. L., p. 782, as amended), established a bureau in the State Department of Labor, providing for the examination and licenses of engineers and firemen having charge of stationary and portable steam boilers and steam engines. No person may operate such boiler or engine without a license, and

STEAM BOILERS AND STEAM ENGINES 

451 no owner or other person or corporation having charge of the building or work where such engine or boiler is used shall use it unless it is in charge of a licensed person (except in emergency). 

There is an exception in the case of engines or boilers in U. S. 

Government control, railroad locomotives, steam boilers used in road vehicles, or in connection with fire departments, boilers used exclusively for heating purposes not carrying a pressure of more than fifteen pounds per square inch, and engines and boilers of less than six horse-power. (See amendments by P. L. 1917, p. 

856; 1918, p. 769; 1919, p. 326).

The penalty for violating the Act is of not less than $10 nor more than $100. 

Jurisdiction and procedure

Jurisdiction to enforce the Act and recover penalties is given to District Courts and police magistrates; also to Justices of the 

Peace of the city or county, but not in any city or judicial district having a District Court. (P. L. 1918, p. 774, § 18, as amend. 

1919, p. 329; see P. L. 1917, p. 860).

Actions are to be brought in the name of the Commissioner of Labor of the State as plaintiff. There must first be a verified complaint in writing, which must be sworn to. There may be either a summons or warrant issued; if summons returnable in from five to fifteen days, if warrant forthwith.

The hearing may be adjourned, but not beyond thirty days from the return day without consent of both parties. If the process issued was a warrant and there is adjournment, the acting magistrate or Court must commit the defendant to the county jail pending the hearing, unless the latter enters into the usual bond, with surety, in $200, conditioned for his appearance at the hearing and to abide the judgment, etc.

The hearing is to be summary and if before the Justice as magistrate; not in  No pleadings need be filed. The Justice is to determine (of course on sworn evidence produced) the guilt or innocence of defendant and, if convicted, impose the penalty. 

Execution is to be against the goods and chattels of defendant, and, in case it be unsatisfied, against his body for a period not exceeding thirty days. In case of a corporation defendant it will be against its goods and chattels only. 

The judgment may be docketed in the Common Pleas "as judgments recovered in District Courts are docketed," and the costs are to be taxed as in civil actions in the District Court. (P. 

L. 1917, p. 858, § 9; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1755). As to docketing as "in District Courts," any judgment may be docketed in the Common Pleas or directly in the Supreme Court, if final judg-

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

ment is not less than ten dollars including costs, upon filing a statement conformably to the District Court Act. (See P. L. 1931, p. 295). 

Service on witness

Subpoenas 

No person is obliged to come into Court and testify without service of a subpoena. He, may do so voluntarily, however. 

Witnesses, when legally served with subpoenas, must appear and testify, if called on. (See more fully on this subject under general title "Evidence," and as to number to be included in costs). 

Justices may issue subpoenas for witnesses to testify before arbitrators, referees, and in other cases named in the statutes. 

When a witness is under the subpoena of any Court he is privileged from arrest in civil actions (not criminal) during his necessary attendance at Court, and in going to and returning from the same, allowing one day for every 30 miles from his place of residence (C. S. 2224, § 14). The same section gives power to the Court from which the subpoena issues to discharge the witness from arrest, and hold one who makes the arrest in contempt of Court; but this contempt feature has not been held to apply to 

The Small Cause Court, where there is no power lodged to hold persons for contempt. (As to other matters concerning subpoenas, see under general title "Evidence," and also consult the Index).

FORMS 

(For Forms of subpœnas, see Index under head of “Subpœna"). 

Beginning an action Summons

Every civil action at law in The Small Cause Court is begun, either: (1) By voluntary agreement in writing by the parties, defendant waiving process; or, (2) By summons to the defendant; or, (3) By warrant to hold the defendant to bail; or, (4) By writ of attachment. 

Issuing summons

The usual first process is a summons and is lawful in all cases in beginning civil actions, unless (as rarely happens) the

SUMMONS 

453 statute requires a warrant. It is also the only process which can be used in cases wherein the defendant is privileged from arrest by warrant, or where the defendant is a female. 

The Justice is required to issue a summons upon application, if he has jurisdiction and is otherwise competent to adjudge. To make it optional with him to do so or not, according to any whim or caprice of his, or disrespect to the plaintiff, or friendliness to the defendant, would be to have justice frustrated. If he has not jurisdiction, of course he cannot, lawfully, issue a summons. If he is in doubt, he should seek advice, or give the benefit of the doubt to the plaintiff, until the matter can be heard before him, and then, if he has no jurisdiction, dismiss the case. If he is disqualified to adjudge the matter from any of the reasons which debar he should not issue the summons. 

Form of summons

The object of the summons being to cite the defendant to appear at a given time and place to respond to the plaintiff's action, it needs to be legally drawn, dated, impressed with his official seal (if the Justice is acting in The Small Cause Court; otherwise by an [L. S.] or a wafer seal), signed and served, to accomplish its object. As to its form, attention should be given to the necessary parts of a summons, viz.: 

1. Its direction. The common form is "to any constable of the county." It should not be directed "to any constable of the township." Sometimes a statute prescribes how; for example that it be directed "to the sheriff or any constable of the county," etc., but ordinarily it is "to any constable of the county." 

2. Its date. The statute directs that "every proc- ess issued out of said Small Cause Court shall be tested the day on which it is issued." It is not allowed to ante-date, nor to postdate a writ. It may be altered by the Justice for correctness, but he cannot give to a constable or other person a general authority to do it, nor issue it in blank. That would void the writ. (S. C. 

A., §§ 11, 12). 

3. Its seal. It is to be "signed and sealed" by the Justice. (Ibid, § 11), to be the official seal in The Small Cause Court, when the Justice is acting in that Court. 

4. The return day. This must be "not less than five nor more than fifteen days from the date of such process.' (Ibid, § 16). That is, if the summons is dated on Monday, January 

2, it must not be returnable until on the Saturday next following, January 7, at the shortest, nor beyond the next day two weeks, January 17, at the longest.

Some statute may vary what is required as to the earliest or

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

latest return day, but under The Small Cause Act the five to fifteen day rule is the lawful one. 

If the return day is Sunday it will be illegal and cannot be amended. It ought not to be made on a holiday, but if it is, there can be an adjournment, although it will not be unlawful to try a civil cause on a holiday. As witnesses are compelled to answer subpoenas, they ought not to be summoned to attend a civil Court on a holiday if it can be avoided. (See general title "Legal Holidays"). 

5. The time and place for appearance must be particularly expressed in the summons; as the day, hour of the day, and the place for the defendant's appearance. (S. C. A., § 16). 

The time should be in words at length, although if in figures it will not prove fatal. The statute expressly directs that the summons shall be returnable only "between the hours of nine o'clock in the forenoon, and three o'clock in the afternoon both inclusive." 

To summon the defendant to appear at "two o'clock noon" is defective. So at "twelve o'clock afternoon." If the copy of the summons be to appear at ten, instead of two o'clock, the proper hour, which was in the original and the defendant does not appear at all, and cannot show injury from the mistake, the defect is immaterial. But if the hour in the original summons is omitted, or is an impossible one, there can be no amendment without the defendant's consent. (Camman v. Perrine, 4 Hal. 253; Titus v. 

Whitney, 1 Harr. 86). 

6. The style of the action. This must be stated; whether on Contract, or in Tort, or in Debt. 

7. The amount demanded. This must specifically set out, and must not exceed two hundred dollars (S. C. A., § 18), or it will be void on its face for want of jurisdiction, but it may be for less than the sum demanded in a state of demand subsequently filed, as the amount named in the summons may be amended at any time before trial. (Hopper v. Steelman, 2 Penn. 907). 

8. The true names of the parties concerned. The Christian name of the plaintiff (and the defendant) whether of an individual or a firm, must be used. (McCrady v. Vanneman, 2 Penn. 870).

If a summons should give only an initial for the defendant's first or Christian name, and is properly served, and defendant appears, whether in person or by attorney, the Justice may amend the summons and proceed. (Abrahams v. Jacoby, 40 Vr. 178).

Two Christian names are not necessary, as the law knows only one Christian name; therefore even the use of the middle letter is not necessary. But it should be used if one exists and is known. (Dilts v. (Dilts v. Kinney, 3 Gr. 130). Where a summons was 44442

SUMMONS 

455 issued without a middle name and the state of demand contained a middle name, a judgment was set aside (in Bowen v. Mulford, 5 Hals. 230).

If the defendant is a minor, the name of a guardian appointed for the purpose of bringing an action is not required in a summons; nor does his suit run in his name after his return; although a guardian must appear for him. (See under "Infants").

If plaintiff or defendant sues or is sued as executor, or administrator, or trustee, or receiver, etc., the summons should so state. 

9. The authority by which it issues; that is, it is by the authority of the State of New Jersey, while issued by a Justice of the Peace in and for the county in which it issues. The Constitution expressly declares that "all writs shall be in the name of the State;" hence such a form as this: "I, A. B., Justice of the

Peace, to any constable of the county," etc., is unconstitutional and void. (Const. of N. J., Art. VIII, § 3). 

It is not to be forgotten that every process, summons, warrant, execution, writ of attachment, scire facias, etc., is to be in the name of the State. 

10. The signature of the Justice to the summons is expressly required. The Justice may sign the initials or a contraction of his Christian name, giving, however, the surname in full. He must sign the process himself; he cannot delegate his authority. (S. C. A., § 12; Veal v. Brown, 1 Penn. 72; Wood v. Fithian, 4 

Żab. 33, 838). 

11. The indorsement. The Small Cause Act directs that not only in the body of every summons and civil warrant but also indorsed on the summons there shall be stated the debt and damages, or sum, demanded, in order that, if the defendant desires, he may pay the debt and costs and avoid further proceedings. (S. 

C. A., § 18). 

Service of Summons

The statute directs the time and mode of the service of the summons, viz.: That it "shall be served at least five days before the time of appearance mentioned therein, by reading the same to the defendant, and delivering to him a copy thereof, if he shall be found, and if not found, by leaving a copy thereof at his usual place of abode, with some person of his family above the age of fourteen years, who shall be informed of the contents thereof." (S. C. A., § 16).

It must be served by the officer to whom it is directed, viz., a constable, if directed to "any constable" as is usual. A private person cannot serve a summons.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

The statutory and only correct method of service upon the defendant himself, is as follows: 

1. The constable to read the summons through. To read a part of it is not to "read it" as the Act prescribes; and the reason for this particularity, namely, that the defendant, if too ignorant to read, may have no excuse for not knowing its contents, would be lost by any such halfway method of service. The same is the case if the defendant reads it and not the constable; it will not comply with the law. (Moore v. Miller, 1 Harr. 233; Ayers v. 

Swayze, 2 South. 812). 

2. To leave with defendant an exact copy (indorsed "A true copy"). The constable ought to know that it is a copy which he leaves, and a correct one; he should know it by actual comparison. 

The same rule holds in the computation of the "five days" which obtains in fixing the time for the return of the summons. 

Thus, if it be returnable on Saturday, it must be served not later than on Monday preceding; one day, and not both, will be excluded in the count. When Sunday intervenes between the time of service and the return, it is counted the same as any other day. (Bray v. Drake, 3 Halst. 303).

The constable is to find the defendant if he can. Should he be not found-not otherwise the constable may serve it "by leaving a copy" of the summons "at his usual place of abode." 

Said the Supreme Court in interpreting this section: "It is only when the defendant is not found that a service by leaving a copy at his house is sufficient. 

Otherwise a constable might pass a defendant in the street, or at his very dooryard, and instead of serving the summons upon him proceed to his house and leave a copy there; or the defendant may be at home, and yet the officer, without even inquiring for him, may content himself with leaving a copy with some person at his door. The law contemplates and requires a personal notice to the defendant, when the officer can find him in the exercise of ordinary and reasonable diligence; and only substitutes a secondary kind of notice in case the defendant is not found." At the same time "the officer is not bound to ransack the county." (Polhemus v. Perkins, 3 Gr. 436).

The defendant's "usual place of abode" has been clearly decided to be his bona fide residence, and is not where he may be on business, or visiting, or merely stopping in his travel. It is where defendant is actually living at the time when service is made; not where he has been living, and which may be his "legal" residence; nor any of his several residences, if he has more than one, but where he is actually abiding; and should he be temporarily absent from such abode, service may be made there. (Mygatt v. Coe, 34 Vr. 510; Camden Safe Co. v. Barbour, 37 Vr. 102).

SUMMONS 

457 It matters not that a defendant is not a resident of the county. If he is in it temporarily he is amenable to process. But if induced to come into this State by a deception practiced upon him, and a summons is served, the service will be set aside. (Williams v. Reed, 5 Dutch. 385; Steinger ads. Bonn, 3 N. J. L. J. 370).

Service by leaving a copy with the defendant's wife is not a good service unless the wife is, at the time of service, at the residence of defendant. (Vigars v. Mooney, 2 Penn. 909; Rogers v. Jarman, 2 Penn. 527).

The simple delivery of a copy is not a good service (Rape v. Titus, 6 Hal. 314); though if the defendant will not listen when the writ is being read to him, the service is good nevertheless, because no defendant can take advantage of his own wrong. (Slaight v. Robbins, 1 Gr. 340). 

To leave a copy at defendant's store and read it to his agent is not sufficient. (Penny v. Harrison, 2 Gr. 24).

If a summons against two debtors on a joint account is served upon one, the plaintiff may proceed against both. But it must appear by the return that the other debtor could not be found in the county. But if against two not on a joint account, both must be served, or the judgment can be entered only against the one served. (Reid v. Crawford, 2 Penn. 622; Mannings v. Randolph, 1 South. 144; Ford v. Munson, 1 South. 93; Stults v. Outcalt, 1 Hal. 130). 

The service may be made at any time of the day or night, as well as at any place and on a legal holiday, or half-holiday, but not on Sunday, unless a statute expressly permits it. 

The constable may not break into a dwelling to serve any civil process. His rights and liabilities in regard to the service are the same as those of a sheriff under similar circumstances. If the outer door of the defendant's house is shut, the officer will be a trespasser if he enter without leave to serve the summons. He may ring a bell, or knock, and then enter, if the door is opened, and he is invited in. If the defendant is within his dwelling and admission is refused, the constable should make service by reading the summons aloud at the door, and leaving the copy there. 

If, as is usual, the summons is directed "to any constable" of the county, such constable as the writ may be given to may serve it. If not directed at all to any constable, by name or by class, the writ cannot be served.

The constable to whom a summons is given must serve it, if he can do so lawfully. He may not refuse at his option, any more than the Justice may refuse to issue the writ. He can, however, require prepayment of fees, from the plaintiff; the Justice is not expected to advance them. (S. C. A., § 103). 

If it be not possible for him to serve a summons, as if he is

J-29

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

sick, he would be excused; but otherwise to refuse or neglect to serve the summons, after prepayment of fees, will render him liable in an action for damages; while if he refuses to serve, or mis-serves it, with intent to injure and delay the plaintiff, he will be indictable.

Should the constable, by mistake, be outside of the line of the county wherein he may act, or serve the summons on Sunday (unless the statute so permits), or otherwise unlawfully serve it, the defendant may: (1) Appear and object, and ask the Justice to dismiss the suit, which the Justice must do; or, (2) he may not appear at all, and subsequently obtain a reversal of any judgment founded on the summons upon certiorari to the higher Court. 

If the summons is not served at all by the return day, it is dead. (Van Cleef v. New Brunswick, 8 Vr. 394). So it will be ineffectual if not served full five days before its return. 

Service on a business corporation

Summons against a business corporation is to be served as follows: "If the defendant is a domestic corporation the summons may be served on the president or head officer or agent in charge of its principal office in this State, either personally or by leaving a copy at his usual place of abode, at least six days before its return; and in case the president or other head officer or agent cannot be found to be served with process, and has no usual place of abode in the county, the summons may be served on the clerk or secretary of the corporation, if any there be within the county, and if no clerk or secretary, then on one of its directors, and if no director then upon the agent in charge of any office maintained in the county, either personally or by leaving a copy at his usual place of abode within the county, six days before its return. If the defendant is a foreign corporation, process may be served upon the agent in charge of its principal office in this State, or upon any officer, either personally or by leaving a copy at his usual place of abode, or by leaving a copy at the office, depot, or usual place of business of such foreign corporation within the county, with any person in charge thereof." (S. C. A., § 17).

By the wording of this statute it is made clear that in the case of domestic (i. e., New Jersey) corporations (1) the president, or head officer, or agent, in charge of the principal office in this State, is to be served, if found. If not, (2) a copy is to be left at his usual place of abode, but this only where such president, etc., may be found within the county. If not found within the county, it may be served (3) on the clerk or secretary of the corporation; or, if neither of them is in the county, on (4) a director; or, if no director, (5) the agent in charge.

The order of the above service must be followed. Service

SUMMONS 

459 cannot be made on the clerk, etc., unless the president, or head officer or agent in charge of the principal office cannot be found. (See 82 N. J. L. 45).

In a summons against a foreign corporation doing business in this State, the constable likewise is not to go outside the county, where neither he nor the Justice has jurisdiction, but must find the agent, or officer, or person in charge of the office, depot, etc., within the county. In such case the language of the statute seems to permit the constable to serve it either upon the agent in charge of the principal office, or an officer, (personally at his abode), or with any person in charge of any office, depot, or usual place of business of the corporation.

A person whose only connection with a corporation is a contingent one is not "an agent of the company." (Haas v. Security Ins. Co., 28 Vr. 388).

The provisions of the general Corporation Act as to service of summons do not apply to  (Railroad 

Co. v. Kreitzman, 58 Vr. 60).

An Act of 1916 (P. L. 410; N. J. Cum. Supp. 695) states that in actions "in any Court in this State" against a domestic corporation "the summons may lawfully be served personally on any officer or agent in charge of its principal office or on any ticket agent or freight agent employed in any of its offices in the county in which the venue is laid," and if against a foreign corporation "upon any officer or director, or upon any ticket agent or freight agent of such corporation personally, in the county in which the venue is laid." 

Service on a municipal corporation Notwithstanding that the Small Cause Act states that "a body politic or corporate may sue and be sued," etc. (§ 6), yet a line of decisions in the Supreme Court of this State has held that, inasmuch as the Act provides no method for a service of a summons upon a municipal corporation, or even a quasipublic corporation, such as school boards, etc., this feature of the 

Act is inoperative. (See Inhabitants of Princeton v. Mount, 5 

Dutch. 299, and other cases, one being Kunz v. Dech, 50 Vr. 37).

But by a Township Act of 1899 (C. S. 5609, § 92) there may be a summons served upon the township committee chairman, or township clerk "at least ten days before the return day." 

Return of the summons

The statute only says of the return of the constable on the summons that the "constable serving such summons shall indorse thereon a return of the time and manner he executed the same, and sign his name thereto." (S. C. A., § 16).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

This return is usually made on the return day, at or before the hour named in the summons, but it may be made to the Justice at any time between the service and return day. The return is to be written upon the back of the summons, usually upon one of the sides which is folded under, instead of beneath the Justice's indorsement. The constable simply writes and signs the return; he does not make oath to it, because he is considered to be always acting under his oath in performing his duty. 

Should the constable knowingly make a false return, an action will lie against him at the suit of the party injured, and he may also be indicted, the same as in case of an intentional misservice.

The Act says "the manner" of the return must be stated; i. e., whether the service was personal, or by copy left at defendant's abode, and, in the latter case, with whom. The hour need not be stated, but the day must. If there are several defendants, it must state how each was served. Should the return show a proper service upon one only, the Justice would have jurisdiction against that one only. In case of service upon a corporation the return must be equally explicit. The person not only must be named upon whom the writ was served, but his office the relation he bears to the company-that it may appear he is one of those authorized by the statute.

If the return made by the constable on his writ is made after the return day, or after the hour named, and when the defendant has appeared and left, it is not good. 

Amending the return

The return, if not according to the facts respecting the service, may be amended, and the truth stated. Where the constable has complied with all the requirements of the statute in serving the writ, but the return, as made, does not show it, he may, on or before the trial of the cause, but not later, amend it to conform to the truth; and this whether the defendant appears or not, or objects or not. (S. C. A., § 107). 

Curing defective summons

Notwithstanding a summons may be defective in substance, or in its service or return, if the defendant appears at the return day, and, without objection, goes to trial, the illegality will be considered waived, the defect cured, and no advantage can be taken of the irregularity upon appeal. Or if the defendant appears to ask an adjournment the defect in the return of a constable is cured, but he may, on the adjourned day, object to any important defect in the process itself. (Stediford v. Ferris, 1

SUMMONS 

461 

South. 108; Doughty v. Jones, 2 Penn. 653; Murat v. Hutchinson, 1 Harr. 46).

Sunday

Statute concerning Sunday, as to Courts and legal proceedings

The Christian Sabbath, known as Sunday, is made more than a legal holiday by the common law as well as by the statutes. 

It is considered a holy, a sacred day, in England and America, and in most Christian countries, and as such is protected by law from invasion by business of any kind. There is an exception in this 

State in the case of Jews, Seventh Day Baptists, and others, who observe Saturday as the Sabbath Day. (See infra).

In New Jersey legal business cannot be transacted on that day, and Courts are not open for the purpose of serving processes in civil actions as a rule; there are exceptions, as under the Mo

SUNDAY 

463 

tor Vehicle Act, the Fish and Game Act, etc. The exceptions are noted under the treatment of each such subject in other parts of this volume.

Criminal warrants, however, and other criminal and certain semi-criminal processes are not affected by the Sunday laws. The statute says: "That no person or persons, upon the first day of the week, commonly called Sunday, shall serve or execute, or cause to be served, or executed, any writ, process, warrant, order, judgment or decree (except in criminal cases or for breach of the peace), but that the service of every such writ, process, warrant, order, judgment, or other decree, shall be void to all intents and purpose whatsoever; and the person or persons so serving or executing the same shall be as liable to the suit of the party aggrieved, and to answer damages to him, for doing thereof, as if he or they had done the same without any writ, process, warrant, order, judgment, or decree." (C. S. 5715, § 5).

This section, when construed together with section one of the same Act, which prohibits "all worldly employment or business, ordinary or servile labor, or work, either upon land or water (works of necessity and charity, excepted)," constitutes the basis for the decisions of our Courts, prohibiting all business, employments, contracts, etc., on that day, but with exceptions in 1933 

Act. (See under general title, "Vice and Immorality").

However, in civil proceedings it is proper for a Court to receive a verdict by a jury, where such jury has been over the preceding night and could not arrive at a verdict until Sunday. But the Court then may simply make a note of the verdict, which is to be entered on the following day. A jury may also be discharged on Sunday, when it has failed to agree on a verdict. 

What is known as the "Vice and Immorality Act" enumerates most of the offenses against the Sabbath (Sunday), and they are enumerated, for the most part, under that general head in this work.

The exception as to Jews, Seventh Day Baptists and others 

The following is the statute concerning the exemption of

Jews and others from prosecutions on Sunday, and from obligation to answer processes on Saturday. "Every inhabitant of this State, who religiously observes the seventh day of the week as the Sabbath, shall be exempt from answering to any process, in law or equity, either as defendant, witness, or juror, except in criminal cases; likewise from executing, on the said day, the duties of any post or office to which he may be appointed or commissioned, except when the interest

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

of the State may absolutely require it, and shall also be exempt from working on the highways, and doing any militia duty on that day, except when in actual service. "If any person, charged with having labored or worked on the first day of the week, commonly called Sunday, shall be brought before a Justice of the Peace to answer the information and charge thereof, and shall then and there prove, to the satisfaction of the said Justice, that he or she uniformly keeps the seventh day of the week as the Sabbath, and habitually abstains from following his or her usual occupation or business, and from all recreation, and devotes the day to the exercise of religious worship, then such defendant shall be discharged; provided always that the work or labor for which such person is informed against was done and performed in his or her dwelling-house or work-shop, or on his or her premises or plantation, and that such work or labor has not disturbed other persons in the observance of the first day of the week as the Sabbath: and provided also that nothing in this section contained shall be construed to allow any such person to openly expose to sale any goods, wares, merchandise, or other article or thing whatsoever, in the line of his or her business or occupation." (C. S. 5723, §§ 33, 34. But see P. 

L. 1933, Chap. 115, making sale of newspapers and recreations lawful).

Some decisions respecting Sunday Sunday begins at midnight of Saturday and continues twentyfour hours. 

Goods sold on Sunday cannot be recovered for by suit; drugs and articles considered to be strictly "of necessity and mercy" would undoubtedly be excepted. 

The exercise of one's worldly calling on Sunday is usually held to constitute a single offense. 

A master is not liable for the violation of the Sunday law by his servant, unless it was done with his consent or direction. 

A loan of money made, or a note given for money lent, on 

Sunday is illegal. 

Any contract made on Sunday will be void in New Jersey; although if a subsequent express promise on a secular day be made, it may enable one to maintain a suit on the ground of a contract than newly made. (See Reeves v. Butcher, 2 Vr. 224).

But no parol agreement on Sunday to extend or alter a legal contract is lawful. [See further under general title "Vice and Immorality," where are Forms].

TENEMENT-HOUSES 

465 Tenement-Houses 

Violation of Act—procedure

The very extensive Act of 1904 concerning tenement houses, comprised 209 sections being much amended since; the subject is now very complicated as to what is or is not lawful. 

The procedure to punish for violation is as follows:

Every District Court in any city or judicial district, every Justice of the Peace in any county, and any Police Justice or Recorder in any city, has jurisdiction. (Act as am. by P. L. 1921, p. 

944; N. J. Cum. Supp. 2622).

The proceedings are, in the main, summary, and therefore if before a Justice of the Peace, is to be before him as a magistrate. 

The action is to be in the name of the State Board of Tenement House Supervision as plaintiff. On a verified complaint the magistrate is to issue a summons, returnable in from one to ten days, or a warrant (but see below), returnable forthwith. The process must state what paragraph of the Act and the particular part or parts thereof are alleged to be violated. On the return, or at an adjourned date, the testimony is to be heard (without pleadings) and summarily, and judgment as to the guilt or nonguilt of the defendant determined, no jury being allowed. 

Execution is to be against the goods, chattels and person of defendant; that is, if defendant does not pay the judgment he may be committed to the county jail for not over 90 days.

On a second conviction, besides the money penalty, defendant may be imprisoned in the county jail or workhouse, with or without hard labor, any number of days not exceeding one for each dollar of penalty.

In the case of a freeholder no warrant is to issue against him unless affidavit is first made that he is about to abscond from the State.

The summons may be served five days before the return day; and the posting of a copy of the summons in a conspicuous place in the tenement house and mailing of a copy to each person owning or controlling the property (when such names are filed with the State Board) are to be considered as sufficient service. (C. 

S. 5353, §§ 188, 196).

In case of oath that a building is being used contrary to the Act, the magistrate may issue a search warrant to an officer or employé of the State Board to enter and search, examine and inspect the building. 

Fines are to paid over to the State Treasurer.

The form of conviction is statutory and must be followed. [Act of 1904]. It appears below.

Timber 

Proceedings before a Justice of the Peace

By the Timber Act any person who cuts, etc., timber on land to which he has no right and title, without leave of the owner, shall forfeit for each tree, sapling or pole the sum of eight dollars, one-half to the landowner and one-half to the person prosecuting. But such prosecution must be brought within eighteen months. (C. S. 5396, §§ 1, 6). 

The Justice is given jurisdiction whenever the penalty shall not exceed one hundred dollars; and he is to ignore any claim the defendant may offer to make to the land, and is to adjudge and to issue execution for the judgment, unless the defendant shall not only plead title, but enter into bond with freehold surety in double the amount demanded, besides costs of suit, conditioned for his appearance at the next Court where the same may be cognizable; in which case the Justice must dismiss the action. To plead title and not to give bond will, therefore, be ineffective to void the Justice's jurisdiction.

The demand should state the number of trees and the other

TIMBER 

467 requisites in the Act, and the judgment should designate the penalty or penalties. The place, time and circumstances must be specifically set out, and that the defendant has neither right nor permission to cut the trees. (Walker v. Pierson, 1 Penn. 454; 

Clark v. Collin, 3 Gr. 473; Miller v. Stoy, 2 South. 476). The form of action is "in Debt," as per Court decisions. 

The action is cognizable in  (For proceedings for penalties, see under general subject, "Penalties and Fines."

Such action, however, must not be confounded with an ordinary action in Tort, which will lie for damages to the owner, independent of this action for a penalty or for penalties. 

It is also a criminal offense, unless done by mistake or without intention to injure or defraud the owner. (C. S. 1788, § 138).

The plea of title Title to Land, Plea of 

As the jurisdiction of a Justice of the Peace in The Small Cause Court does not extend to civil actions wherein the title to land shall come in question, it follows that to take advantage of this want of jurisdiction the defendant shall file a plea of title, which he must do in writing. (S. C. A., §§ 26, 27).

The plea is not only to be in writing but signed by the defendant and delivered to the Justice. The latter must countersign it and deliver it to the plaintiff (if defendant first tenders the bond named below). The object of this is that, if the plaintiff thereupon commences suit in the higher Court, which he may do, this plea may be offered in evidence to rebut any allegation that the suit, being for a claim in Tort under $200, should have been begun in The Small Cause Court, or that it was not brought there and discontinued because of such plea; and it will enable plaintiff in such higher Court to carry costs. 

The mere tender of the plea is not sufficient to cause the Justice to dismiss the action before trial. Before acting on it the 

Justice shall require and receive from the defendant the bond, such as is specified in the Act (see Form below. Also see Forms 

345 and 346 in Timber Act).

Without such plea and such bond tendered, the Justice will proceed as if no plea had been made, but then if he finds, upon hearing the proofs offered, that the question of title is involved, he should, himself, dismiss the case for want of jurisdiction.

The plea and bond may be tendered on the return day of the summons, or, if the cause is adjourned, upon the first ad-

TITLE TO LANd, Plea of 

469 journed day. But it cannot be filed later. (Shannon v. Flood, 1 

Gr. 301).

Where a defendant is surprised at the demand, and is unable to file both his plea and bond upon the return day, he should ask for an adjournment, which the Justice should grant.

The bond ought to be free of interlineations and erasures, with dates and amounts written out in words at length and not in figures merely; such a bond, in fact, as does not hazard the rights of the plaintiff if he is compelled to prosecute upon it. (Greacen v. Beam, 3 Gr. 460).

The form of the action, whether in Tort or in Debt (it would be rare for a plea of title to be pertinent in an action on Contract), will not preclude defendant from tendering the plea. The statute says if "in any action" title be pleaded, the defendant shall, etc.; and while the Justice may believe the plea does not apply to the facts of the case, or is only for delay, it is his duty, if properly filed, and with the accompanying bond, to accept it. He has no option.

A right of way is a hereditament, and a plea of title may properly be made if the action should concern it. Nor is such a plea confined to a freehold title, but may be of a possessory or leasehold right, or any right to enter and have possession. (Randolph v. Montfort, 1 Harr. 226; Chambers v. Wambough, 4 

Dutch. 531; Campfield v. Johnson, 1 Zab. 83). 

Who pays costs

Each party is to pay to the Justice his own costs, when defendant pleads title to an action and gives bond. Otherwise the costs take the usual course.

Ordinances with penalties 

Any township committee may, by ordinance, prescribe penalties for the violation of an ordinance or any section thereof by fine not exceeding $100, or imprisonment in the township lockup or county jail not exceeding ninety days and until costs are paid, or by both fine and imprisonment, enforceable before any 

Justice of the Peace of the county. (C. S. 5580, §§ 22, 23). 

Procedure to enforce ordinances 

Any constable, or any officer of the township police department (where such exists), may arrest, without warrant, any person who, within his view, shall violate any ordinance or section thereof of the township, and take the offender before any Justice of the Peace within the township. Thereupon the officer shall forthwith subscribe to a complaint in writing and make oath thereto, setting forth what ordinance or section is violated. 

When there is not arrest on view, any person may complain, on oath, before any Justice of the county, that a person or corporation has violated a township ordinance, or section whereupon he is to issue a process, either summons or warrant (at his discretion) against the offender; but, if the offender is a corporation, a summons only. Warrants will be returnable forthwith; summons in not less than five nor more than fifteen days. The process must state the ordinance, or if it has sections, the section of the ordinance, violated. The Justice may issue subpoenas for witnesses as in usual cases. Any constable of the county or police officer of the township may execute the process. And the fees to Justice and constable will be the same as in usual cases in The 

Small Cause Court. (§§ 23, 24). 

Persons so arrested shall, on their appearance before the Jus- 4744

TRESPASS ON LANDS 

471 tice, be entitled to demand an immediate hearing. If not demanded, or the process be a summons, the Justice may adjourn the hearing to a convenient day. In case of adjournment, and the person is under arrest, the Justice may commit him to the township lock-up or county jail unless he shall enter into bond to the township in a sum not exceeding $100, with satisfactory security, conditioned to appear at the adjourned date. (§ 25).

At the hearing the Justice shall hear testimony and adjudge the case without the filing of pleadings. If the judgment be a fine only, execution shall issue forthwith; if imprisonment only, an order of commitment forthwith, and if both fine and imprisonment the order of commitment shall be until the fine be paid with costs, or until he be otherwise discharged according to law. If the judgment be for imprisonment only the Justice, or a Common Pleas Judge, may, at any time after the expiration of the term of imprisonment, order defendant's discharge, notwithstanding the costs are unpaid, on being satisfied of his inability to pay; and if for fine and commitment until fine and costs are paid, the same course may be followed as to the discharge from imprisonment. (§ 26).

Proceedings are summary and are to be before the Justice as a magistrate.

Where a police department is established in a township and a police force appointed, the township committee may appoint one of the Justices of the Peace of the township to hear and dispose of complaints for violation of ordinances, and fix his compensation; in such case the usual fees will go to the township. (§ 58). 

Trespass on Lands

The offense of hunting and fishing by trespasser While this offense has been noticed before (see under general head "Fish and Game"), it may be well to state the features of the statute passed in 1912 (as amend. in 1923) more fully. 

It is unlawful for any person to trespass upon the occupied lands of another "for the purpose of hunting with a gun or fishing, killing or catching any game or fish enumerated in the statutes, after public notice on the part of the owner, occupant, lessee or licensee thereof, forbidding such trespass, such notice bearing the name of said owner, occupant, lessee or licensee being posted conspicuously on the corners of said property and along the roads or highways abutting said property, and on all boundary lines bordering on adjoining lands, and at each point where a stream enters upon or leaves said property." (P. L. 1923, p. 313; N. J.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Cum. Supp. 1354). The penalty is a fine not exceeding $20 and costs.

By another section the same matter is made unlawful if the offender has been "forbidden so to trespass by the owner, occupier, lessee or licensee," which means by word of mouth or otherwise, so the offender knows it is forbidden. The penalty then is the same.

Jurisdiction is given to enforce the_Act_to "every Justice of the Peace, Police Court or Recorder." The Justice in such a case acts as a magistrate.

An arrest may be made without warrant by such owner, occupant, lessee or licensee or any officer of the law, and the offender taken before the magistrate or Court, and if, on a hearing, he is convicted, the judgment of conviction is to pay the fine stated, or, on failure to pay it, the offender may be committed to the county jail until the fine is paid. In prosecutions, the failure of the defendant to produce a written permit to hunt and fish on the lands trespassed upon, signed by the owner, occupant, lessee or licensee shall be prima facie proof that he was forbidden so to trespass. (Ibid).

Where one while on another's property destroys crops, orchards, fences, etc., the owner, etc., may arrest him without warrant, and, on conviction, the fine may be $500, or imprisonment six months or less. (Ibid).

Fines so recovered are to be paid to the Board of Fish and 

Game Commissioners of the State. (P. L. 1923, p. 314; N. J. 

Cum. Supp. 1355).

It is a crime for any person to run hounds and horses upon the lands of another without the consent of the owner or person in the possession. The Act makes it a misdemeanor.
