Trial of Cause

I. BY JUSTICE, WITHOUT JURY 

Trial before Justice in absence of one party

The Small Cause Court Act clearly states what the Justice is to do on the return day, or an adjourned day, in the absence of one of the parties: "Except where the defendant consents that the trial be had at once on the return of a warrant, the day mentioned in the summons or in the bond or recognizance, for the appearance of the

defendant, or when no bond or recognizance is given, the day set by the Justice for the trial shall be the first trial day of the action, and on said day at the time and place specified the cause shall be tried, unless an adjournment is granted; if the defendant shall not appear at said time and place or at the time and place to which the cause is adjourned, and no sufficient reason shall be assigned why he does not appear, the Justice may proceed to hear the cause in his absence; if the plaintiff shall not appear at said time and place or at the time and place to which the cause is adjourned, and no sufficient reason shall be assigned why he does not appear, the Justice shall grant the defendant a nonsuit, but if the defendant is entitled to move the trial on a demand filed against the plaintiff, the Justice may proceed to hear the cause in the absence of the plaintiff." (S. C. A., § 28).

But "to hear the cause" in the absence of either plaintiff or defendant means on sworn proof, for no judgment can be given by default only. 

Practice in "collection" cases

What are usually called "collection" cases are those in which the plaintiff is reasonably certain the defendant will make no defense, having none, because the simple book account, note, etc., sued upon is certainly due and unpaid. 

In such cases, where the action is on a book account, it is customary for the plaintiff to hand or send to the Justice an affidavit of the correctness of the itemized account at the time the state of demand is filed. If the state of demand is served with the summons, a copy of such affidavit may accompany it. The affidavit must set forth that the copy of the book account “is a true copy of the original entries, and that all the credits and allowances to which the defendant is entitled appear on such statement; or setting forth that the defendant is not entitled to any credits or allowances, and that the sum of money or balance claimed by the plaintiff is justly due and owing to him." (S. C. 

A., § 37). This being done, in the absence of the defendant on the return day, the Justice may consider the affidavit as sufficient evidence for the plaintiff and enter up a judgment on the strength of such evidence. He may also do this if the defendant does appear but makes no demand to see the original books of account. 

If, however, defendant appears and demands to see the original books, the cause should not be heard without their production, and, if necessary, the cause should be adjourned that they may be produced.

In the case of suits on promissory notes, checks and other written contracts, sealed or unsealed, while the affidavit of plaintiff may also be used as in the case of book accounts, yet it is re- J-30

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

quired that the actual note, or other contract be produced at the hearing, whether defendant asks for it or not. The reason for this seems to be that the Justice should see the note, etc., to be sure the defendant signed and entered into the obligation. The affidavit can be taken as evidence, but it must be corroborated by the production of the original paper-writing. 

The sections of the Small Cause Act referring to proof by affidavit are §§ 37-39, to which the Justice is referred. On reading it he will note that in the affidavit of plaintiff (or his agent, or attorney, etc.), it must appear that "the affiant has competent knowledge of the fact or facts sworn to." A bookkeeper may properly make affidavit to a book account, but some outside person who merely copies from the books would hardly be competent to swear to the correctness of the account, much less to its being still due and unpaid. The Justice must satisfy himself that an account is due and is unpaid. Even when original books are produced, while the entries on it are evidence, still plaintiff must put in evidence, by himself, or a bookkeeper, or treasurer or some competent person that the charges are not only correct but unpaid. 

Justice cannot act as agent of plaintiff in hearing a cause The Justice cannot act as an attorney or agent of the plaintiff in attending to his suit; the interest he then has in the event of the action serves to disqualify him. (S. C. A., § 10). Merely to adjourn a cause when plaintiff is not present on the return day is not acting as plaintiff's agent, but, as he must be indifferent between the parties, he must always protect equally the rights of both parties. Even to seem to be a "plaintiff's Justice" is as repugnant to true equity as to grasp at technicalities to defeat a just claim of plaintiff. 

Evidence, etc., in an uncontested cause

The inquiry is sometimes made whether the Justice has a right in hearing a cause not contested, to reject the plaintiff's evidence because he is not satisfied of its truth, although it stands uncontradicted. The answer is clear. If the evidence is legal, the Justice must accept it as true, and adjudge accordingly. It is the defendant's business and duty to appear and defend himself, or controvert the plaintiff's testimony, and, in his absence, the 

Justice cannot act as his counsel, or assume any contradictory facts to plaintiff's testimony to be true. He may even have a personal knowledge of certain facts, but he cannot found a judgment upon such knowledge. He must act entirely upon the sworn evidence before him.

And the admission of plaintiff's evidence is to be governed by the same rules as if the defendant were present. In other

words, although nobody objects, evidence clearly incompetent, whether oral or in writing, should not be received or considered by the Justice. If he hears it, he should reject it from his mind; because the Justice is sworn to discharge his duty impartially and justly, and is governed by the same rules of law and evidence when the defendant is not present, as when he is. There must be sufficient legal evidence to support the demand. (White v. 

Cranmer, 2 Penn. 549). 

All proceedings to be regular

The proceedings must also be regular in form. It must appear by the constable's return to the process that it was legally served. The Justice should always examine the process and its return before hearing the cause, as a defect in either would deprive him of jurisdiction, and subsequent proceedings would be fatal upon certiorari or appeal. 

Challenge to a Justice

Before proceeding to trial a challenge may be made to the Justice for any of the reasons stated previously. If not made at this time it will be too late to make it, unless such challenge goes to his jurisdiction, which, if void, cannot be otherwise than void whether he is challenged or not. 

Evidence, etc., in contested cause

This matter will be spoken of under the next division of this general subject, "Trial by Jury," as, whether the trial be with or without a jury, the subject of contested evidence comes under the same legal rules as to presentation of proofs, cross-examination, etc.

Trial if first process is a civil warrant If the first process is a civil warrant, and no jury is asked for, the hearing before the Justice will take place precisely as if it had been commenced by summons. There may be a difference as to the time fixed for the hearing, but none as to the methods adopted by the Justice in the final investigation of the cause to enable him to arrive at a true judgment. (See elsewhere under general title "Warrant, Civil"). 

Rendering judgment

The Justice may make up his judgment at once, upon considering the plaintiff's proofs, and after hearing plaintiff or his counsel, and defendant or his counsel, if present; or he may publicly adjourn his determination to a subsequent hour or day for

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

that purpose. When the hearing is completed, and the judgment is actually rendered there can be no re-opening of the cause, unless by consent of parties.

Neither the plaintiff or defendant, nor counsel, need be present when judgment is rendered. It may be determined and entered by the Justice in their absence as well as in their presence. 

But the plaintiff, or his attorney, must have been notified of the time, if it be an adjourned date, and the defendant also, if the defendant appeared at the hearing. (Day v. Hall, 7 Hal. 203).

Judgment of nonsuit on defendant's motion It frequently happens that a defendant appears at the hearing on the return day, or the adjourned day, and, by counsel, moves to "nonsuit" the plaintiff. This is to "put the plaintiff out of 

Court," as the expression often is; it is asking that the action be dismissed. It is an oral motion; need not be in writing. If granted it simply dismisses the cause ends it as to the particular action. It is not a final judgment of the Court on the merits of the cause; therefore it cannot be appealed from to the Common 

Pleas, though it may be reviewed by the Supreme Court on certiorari; but it is final so far as pursuing the cause further in the same Court is concerned, except by a new action. 

It is proper for the Justice to grant defendant's motion to nonsuit- 1. When defendant appears but plaintiff does not appear on the return day or at the time fixed for trial, to press his suit, and no sufficient reason is assigned why he does not appear. 

The Justice must wait a reasonable length of time for the plaintiff to appear and move his cause, and then, if the defendant is present and makes the motion, a judgment of nonsuit should be given, or, if the demand is filed and defendant files a set-off, the defendant, instead of asking for a nonsuit, may proceed and prove his claim. (S. C. A., § 28).

In ordinary "collection cases," where plaintiff has filed in advance, or sends on the return day an affidavit to his claim, it is customary to adjourn the cause if to be contested and not to nonsuit. 

2. Where plaintiff shall not, on or before the return of the summons (or civil warrant), file a state of demand. (S. C. A., § 24). 

3. When there is a defect in the process or its service, or in the demand. Thus the summons may be illegally drawn, or misserved; or the demand may not set forth a cause of action. In the latter case the plaintiff may offer to amend, and this the Justice must allow, if it comes within his statutory power. A summons illegally drawn, or mis-served, could not be amended as to

form of service, against the objections of the defendant, because the defect is radical; the statute has not been pursued and the 

Justice then has no jurisdiction. But the demand may be amended, although, if it does not then present a cause of action, the motion to nonsuit must prevail. After proper amendment the cause will proceed, or, if the defendant is surprised, he can ask for an adjournment and it should be granted. 

4. Where there is non-joinder of necessary parties in the action. (Craft v. Smith, 6 Vr. 304). 

5. When, after the plaintiff's side of the cause is heard by the Justice (without a jury) the plaintiff has not made out a case. 

It can even be made after the defendant enters upon his defense, it being a matter then, as before, discretionary with the Court. (Romaine v. Norris, 3 Hal. 82).

There are other causes which may operate to require the Justice to dismiss the cause (which is equivalent to a nonsuit) even without any motion by the defendant. Such are: 

6. Where the Justice finds himself without the necessary jurisdiction. 

7. Where it appears that the plaintiff has altered the papers in the proceedings, without motion or permission, in order to gain an undue advantage, or from any other unlawful motive. (Blackwell v. Leslie, 1 South. 113). 

Costs of nonsuit

In judgments of nonsuit, the costs of the action fall upon the plaintiff, unless he sues in the capacity of executor or adminis trator. (S. C. A., § 47). 

If defendant moves action on his set-off

When the plaintiff does not appear, but the defendant does, and files a set-off, the defendant's account, if sworn to as the law directs, is placed on precisely the same footing as the demand of the plaintiff, and if his account be the greater he may take judgment against the plaintiff and have costs. Or if plaintiff is present but refuses or neglects to move his cause, the defendant may move action on his set-off and the burden of proof will then be upon him. His witnesses must be examined, and his proof be as clear and competent as is required of a plaintiff when supporting his demand. The position of the parties will be exactly reversed. And the plaintiff, if present, may cross-examine witnesses, precisely as in other cases. Should the defendant fail to sustain his account and judgment is rendered dismissing the cause, each party will pay the costs he has incurred before the 

Justice. (See under general title "Set-off and Recoupment").

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Usual method to begin trial When there is a contest, but no jury has been asked for, the trial will proceed at the time appointed before the Justice, without a jury. It is the practice in such instance for the plaintiff, or his counsel, to say, “I move this cause," and then, if the defendant desires to postpone, or to ask for a nonsuit, to do so at once. If his motion is not granted the Justice at once hears the matter at issue.

After a hearing has been begun and the plaintiff's case rested, the Justice cannot adjourn the further hearing without defendant's consent. (Stretch v. Forsyth, 2 Penn. 713; State v. Mercantile Co., 34 Vr. 505).

When an action has been once begun before a Justice, he may proceed to its final determination, notwithstanding his term has expired or he has resigned. (S. C. A., § 7).

Other matters, many equally applicable to a trial before a Justice alone or before a jury will be found under the head below, entitled, "III. Some General Matters about Trials," etc. 

Demand for jury

II. TRIAL BY JURY 

Either party to a civil suit at law in The Small Cause Court may demand a trial by jury. This demand may be made at any time between the appearance of the defendant and the trial; and may be made by one party in the absence of the other. It cannot be made after the Justice begins to hear the cause. (S. C. A., § 33).

It cannot be made before the appearance of the defendant (Ibid; see Kean v. Scull, 2 Penn. 544), but it may issue in defendant's absence after his appearance. (Lummis v. Stratton, 1 

Penn. 245).

A jury trial cannot be denied because the party asking it refuses prepayment of jury fees (MacKensie v. Gilbert, 40 Vr. 

184), unless some statute other than the Small Cause Act so directs; as, for example, in bastardy cases, where fees for the jury must be paid in advance.

It is not usual for a plaintiff to demand a jury, although he has an equal right to do so as the defendant. Whoever demands it, defendant or plaintiff, the Justice cannot deny the demand, even if made but one minute before the intended time for hearing, unless not in good faith.

But if the party who demands a jury prevents it from being summoned by his own conduct, the Justice may try the cause, and he cannot complain.

The demand may be made orally, and by an attorney; it need not be in writing.

Number of jurymen 

The venire, which is the writ to call the jury, will issue for "six men, if the demand or matter in dispute do not exceed the sum of fifty dollars; or a jury of twelve men, if the demand or matter in dispute exceed that sum." (S. C. A., § 33).

Thus, if the demand is general for two hundred dollars, but only fifty or less is claimed in the body of the demand, six men are sufficient. If the plaintiff's claim is for less than fifty dollars, but the defendant's set-off is for more than that sum, twelve men must be called. (Jones v. Oliver, 2 Hal. 123).

The verdict on a claim of over fifty dollars may be for less than that sum, but that will only affect the payment of costs of the large jury, and not void the proceeding. All the Justice can do in issuing his venire is to take the amount claimed in the demand, or set-off, and from it judge of the number of jurymen to be selected. 

More than a six, or twelve-men jury, cannot be permitted, even by consent. (M'Cormick v. Bloomfield, 1 South. 72). So a less number will not be lawful, even if both parties agree to it, or if the agreement be that six jurymen shall be put for twelve. (Mitten v. Smock, 2 Penn. 911). 

The venire

When a jury is properly demanded the Justice must issue a venire. The venire must be in writing, directed to a constable. 

The Justice cannot depute a person not a constable to serve a venire. (Robins v. Martin, 15 Vr. 368).

The venire must be sealed with the Justice's official seal, if the action be in The Small Cause Court (otherwise by the usual wafer seal or scroll), and signed by him.

The constable shall, at the time designated in it for its return, annex thereto a panel containing the names of the jurors whom he has summoned; and the statute then says: "If, on the return of the venire, it shall appear that one or more of the jurors are disqualified to serve, or do not appear, then the constable who served the same shall by order of the Court, immediately summon others who shall serve in their stead." (S. C. A., § 33).

After the constable receives the venire he can demand of any qualified person that he act as juror and be at the place of hearing at the appointed time, under the penalty of the law; but he should always show his authority, (which is the venire itself). 

That the constable should not merely see that the jurors are lawfully qualified to serve, but indifferent to the parties, as far as possible, is generally understood to be his duty. And the constable himself should be indifferent and free of bias. "The Justice should be very careful on this head, and see that the constable to whom he directs the venire stands indifferent between the

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

parties, not only as it respects objections which constitute legal challenges to the array, but to all favor, or suspicion thereof; and in this case listen to the reasonable suggestions of either party on the subject made in the presence of the other." (Penn. Treatise, p. 153). 

Qualification of jurors

It is required that the jury shall have each of four qualifications, viz.: (S. C. A., § 33, as amend. by P. L. 1921, p. 68). 

1. Be citizens. An alien cannot serve, but if he is sworn without challenge it is too late to object. Women are now eligible, but mothers of minor children are exempt from service. (P. L. 

1925, p. 311). 

2. Be above twenty-one and under sixty-five years of age.

If a mistake is made, and a juror is sixty-five or over, and neither of the parties knows it and so does not object, it will not make the judgment void. 

3. Be not of kin to the parties. When the relationship has extended to the ninth degree the English law has excluded a juror, and our Courts have held to the same rule. 

4. Be not interested in the event of the suit.

It is the business of the constable to ascertain the qualifications of those whom he selects. He is sworn to faithfully perform his duty, and it is his duty to follow the law. 

Return of venire

The venire may be returnable the same day it is issued, if the parties make no objection, and are ready for trial, and if it is made so returnable in the venire. This is frequently done, and there is often less objection to it than to postpone the selection of jurors and the trial to another day, because it gives less opportunity for "packing" a jury, or influencing it before they are sworn.

After the return of the venire the constable cannot change the panel he has returned by substituting a name, unless by consent of the parties, or to replace a juror who has been excused, by challenge or otherwise. He may, before the return, however, but should not do it at the suggestion of either party. (Lyon v. 

Tharp, 2 Penn. 463; Boyles v. McEowen, 2 Penn. 677). In fact the constable should not allow either party to see or know the names of the jurors before the return is made. 

The constable cannot take money or reward to summon, or excuse a juryman; and, if he summons any person who has applied to him to become a juror he will forfeit $150, one-half to go to any person who shall prosecute. (C. S. 2965, § 5). 

Nor can the Justice call a juryman, nor swear one not called

TRIAL OF CAuse 

481 by the constable, it being solely the business of the latter to summon the jury. (Robson v. Archer, 1 Penn. 107).

The Justice may direct the constable to immediately summon other jurors to act in the stead of any disqualified, or not appearing (S. C. A., § 33), and the constable should then supplement his return, state the fact of the order, and who is summoned, in place of whom, and the Justice enter it in his docket. 

An irregular form of return to a venire will be cured by a trial without objection and a verdict. (Halsey v. Nutman, 1 

Penn. 329).

The Justice must enter the names of the jurors in his docket, and, of course, he must enter any order he may give for substitutions. (Lindsley v. Boyle, 1 Penn. 207).

If, at the return of a venire called by a defendant, and the hour for trial, the defendant does not appear, the Justice should dismiss the jury and try the cause himself, unless plaintiff objects. 

Fines upon jurors for non-attendance Jurors, who do not attend when summoned, unless for good reasons, or who refuse to serve, shall forfeit a fine for refusal, not exceeding twenty dollars not less than one dollar, as the Justice shall think proper to impose; and the Justice is authorized and required to issue an execution, directed to any constable of the county, to levy the fine of the goods and chattels of the offender. The fine, when recovered, shall be paid by the Justice to the county collector, for the use of the county. (S. C. A., $35).

This fine should be imposed by the Justice regardless of whether either party to the cause demands it or not. Whenever a juror defaults in his appearance, and no cause appears, the Justice should, after trial, summon him to show cause, at a certain day, why he should not be fined, pursuant to the Act. But he must have notice, or the fine will be illegal, as no man is to be condemned unheard, or without opportunity for defense.

The time allowed for the juror to appear, when so summoned, should be reasonable. Then, if the juror does not appear, or if he does, and makes no good excuse for disobeying the call of the constable, the Justice should enter up a fine in his docket, and issue execution against his goods and chattels. It cannot issue against the body. (State v. Hollingshead, 1 Harr. 539).

The fine must not be made a part of the record in the civil suit in which the jurors were summoned, but entered in the docket as a separate proceeding. (Ibid).

A joint conviction of two or more jurors is illegal. Each case is to be considered separately.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Common law challenges to the jury

When the jury are in Court the time to challenge has arrived, and it must be before the juror challenged is actually sworn. (P. 

L. 1911, p. 220; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1651).

Formerly, challenges "to the polls" were tried by triors. 

Under that law most of the decisions are based. It is now directed, however, that "all challenges to the array, or to individual jurors, for any cause whatever, shall be triable by the Court." (C. 

S. 2978, § 43). Consequently the Justice tries the qualifications of any individual jurors as well as of the whole jury. 

Challenges, by the common law, are of two kinds: First, to the array, or whole jury; second, to the polls, or single jurors. 

I. To the Array: This is an exception to the whole panel and is subdivided into principal challenges and to the favor. A principal challenge is grounded on such manifest presumption of partiality that, if found true, it unquestionably sets aside the array or jury. A challenge to the favor is for causes not manifest and conclusive in themselves, but such circumstances as raise suspicion from which it may be concluded that the constable is not indifferent, although no special legal objection can be raised against him. Among the principal causes of challenge to the array are: 

1. That the constable is of kindred, either by blood or marriage, with either party. If of kindred, it extends to the ninth degree. If by marriage, however, the kindred must continue.

For instance, if the wife is dead, and there are children living by the marriage, the kindred continues. (Vanauken v. Beemer, 1 

South. 364). 

2. That the jurors are returned on the nomination, suggestion, persuasion, or command of either party, however indirectly. 

Indeed, any interference with or directions about the selection by a party to the suit is illegal. (McDonald v. Shaw, Coxe 6). 

3. That the constable is partial. For instance, if it can be proved that he had declared his wishes or opinion as to the result of the suit, or had taken money or other valuable thing. 

4. That the constable has malice. If he has had a law suit with one of the parties, which gave rise to displeasure or hatred, it is a cause of challenge to the array. 

5. That the constable has been the adviser of one of the parties, or in his employ. 

6. That the constable is interested in the event of the dispute. But it is not an objection to the array or polls that the township or city in which a constable or juror lives is interested in the event of the suit. (C. S. 2977, § 39). 

7. That the constable is not legally holding his office.

Challenges to the array for favor comprise many things which

cannot well be enumerated, but which operate to disqualify the constable. For instance, if there is no relation between him and one of the parties, yet if his son is related by marriage to the son of the party, it is a proper subject for the consideration of a Justice whether the constable stands indifferent or not. Favor of any kind excludes. 

II. To the Polls: That is, to individual jurors. Such challenges are also principal, and to the favor. They are to be made as the juror is asked to be sworn. Those which are principal causes may be thus enumerated : 

1. Defect of statutory qualifications; as if he is under twenty-one, or over sixty-five years of age. This defect, it is sometimes thought, can be waived by the parties. But this view is erroneous, as over-age disqualifies, unless it is unknown to the Court and parties and is unobjected to. (Sutton v. Petty, 2 South. 504). 

2. Related by blood. The law presumes that one kinsman will favor another before a stranger; and, however remote the relationship may be, it is a good challenge. (Van Nuys v. Givens, 3 Zab. 201). 

3. Of kindred by affinity, or marriage. This latter is equivalent to that of blood. If the plaintiff or defendant marries the daughter or cousin of the juror, or vice versa, and the same continues, or issue be had, and be living, it is a good challenge. A challenge for relationship must show how related. (Hinchman v. 

Clark, Coxe 446). 

4. When the juror has rendered a verdict before in the same 

This does not extend to a similar cause between different parties, or to a different cause between the same parties. cause. 

5. When the juror has acted as referee, or arbitrator before, in the same cause, although he may not have signed a report or award. 

6. If he has been counsel for, or given advice to either party. 

But his being related to one of the counsel will not of itself disqualify. 

7. If there was a law suit between the juror and either party of a nature to awaken malice. 

8. If either party has tampered with a juror, by bribery, or by explaining his cause to him in private with a view to influence him. 

9. If he is an alien, idiot, lunatic, or atheist, or cannot understand the English language. Atheism is a proper cause for a principal challenge, because the credibility of witnesses rests more or less upon the sanctity of the oath, and a man who has no belief in a God would not be likely as a juror to regard the obligations of the oath of another, or of his own oath. The law, therefore,

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

properly excludes from the jury box those who have no belief in God, or in future rewards and punishments. Alienage has always been a good ground for challenge. 

10. If he is interested in the event of the cause. Thus if he has commenced an action before the same Justice involving the same controversy, he should be excluded. (Gardiner v. Lanning, 2 Penn. 651). The mere fact that he is "a neighbor" is not cause for challenge. 

11. Conviction of some crime which affects his credit, as treason, felony, perjury, cheating, etc.

Challenges to the polls for favor may be made as to anything which, in the judgment of the challenger, would disqualify a juror's judgment from being fair and impartial in making a decision upon sworn evidence. 

Trial of foregoing challenges to jurors

The Justice is to be the judge of the legality of the jury, or the qualifications of the jurors. The evidence is to be given before him, immediately after the challenge is made, and he will thereupon decide. The juryman himself (whose examination is called examination on voir dire), the party challenging, or outside witnesses, may be sworn to support the truth of the challenge. If there seems to be ground for suspicion that an individual juror is not free from bias, he should be promptly discharged, as if he were otherwise disqualified. The juror may even swear positively he is not biased, but it is the mind of the Court, and not the juror's mind, which must be satisfied of that fact. 

Jurors may not challenge themselves, ordinarily, but can claim exemption by reason of age, etc. However, if any of the causes which might afford a ground for the common law challenge of one of the parties exist, the juror ought to make it known, that either party may take advantage of it, and that there be afterward not even the suspicion of partiality. 

Peremptory challenges to jurors

Besides the common law challenges above described there are six peremptory challenges permitted in the trial of civil causes in all the Courts of law in this State. The statute says they may be made, "as their names are drawn from the box." But as the names are not "drawn from the box" in the Justice's Court, the jurors should be challenged as they are called out by name, by the constable, though at any time before being actually sworn they may be challenged. It is too late afterward. And such challenge, when once made, cannot be withdrawn after the juror has been set aside, and the next juror called. (P. L. 1911, p. 220; C.

S. 1651; Furman v. Applegate, 3 Zab. 28; Leary v. N. J. St. Ry. 

Co., 26 N. J. L. J. 153).

A peremptory challenge is one for which no reason need be given, and the party challenged is bound at once to step aside. 

The six challenges are allowed to each side and may be made as to any juror, notwithstanding a previous challenge of the same juror "for cause" has not been sustained. Before challenging the juror may be questioned by either party, or his attorney, so as to elicit information for determining whether or not to interpose such peremptory challenge. (P. L. 1911, p. 220; N. J. Cum. Supp. 

1651, § 43d).

When the array of jurors unchallenged or challenged and accepted, falls short of the required number, the constable is obliged to summon others in their stead, and may do so from bystanders, or go out in the vicinity and secure them. 

Exemptions from jury duty

While a juror may not challenge himself he may claim exemption under the law, if entitled to exemption from jury service. Thus decrepitude, sickness, deafness and similar disability will exempt. Counselors and attorneys-at-law, officers of the 

Courts, clergymen and physicians, policemen, school teachers (if required to act during school session) and dentists are privileged by necessity or custom from service on juries and may be discharged upon application. So also firemen, telegraph superintendents, managers, line men and operators, and officers and attendants in asylums. Most of these are exempt by statute. But, if summoned, the exemption need not be claimed. 

Members of the National Guard of New Jersey are exempt after one year of service, and when honorably discharged are exempt for life. (P. L. 1918, p. 811; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1953). 

The oath to the jurors

When the jurymen are ready to hear the cause, they must be placed together, and the oath administered by the Justice. They should stand while taking the oath, as it is more reverent. The custom is to have the constable hold a Bible before three or four of the jurors, who will each place his right hand upon it. The 

Justice then utters the words of the oath, and each juror will answer "I do." (Formerly it was necessary to kiss the Bible on taking an oath, but this necessity is now dispensed with. C. S. 

3775, § 39). The next three or four jurors are then sworn in the same manner, until all are sworn. If there are several Bibles all may be sworn at the same time. The oath to be administered is statutory (S. C. A., § 34), and is given in the succeeding Forms.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

The affirmation of jurors The Small Cause Act does not permit jurors merely to "declare." They must swear or affirm. (S. C. A., § 34). If a juror affirms, it must be at his request. The Justice should then ask him if he has conscientious scruples against taking an oath, because if he has not he should swear, this being more approved by the law. If he answers that he has, the ceremony of touching his hand to the Bible will be dispensed with, and, in lieu thereof, he will hold up his right hand, and the Justice will repeat the words of the oath, but beginning, "You, A. B., do solemnly, sincerely and truly declare and affirm," etc., to which the juror should assent by repeating the words: "I do so affirm." 

III. SOME GENERAL MATTERS ABOUT TRIALS BEFORE OR WITHOUT A JURY 

Stenographer for testimony

It is of rare occurrence for stenographic notes to be taken of a hearing or trial before a Justice, but an Act of 1914 (P. L., p. 

256; N. J. Cum. Supp. 826) requires that "in all trials or proceedings had before any Court, official, tribunal, board or governing body of this State, where not otherwise provided for by law, such Court, etc., shall, upon request of either party to such trial or proceeding, at the expense of the party so requesting, designate a competent stenographic reporter, who shall be duly sworn to report verbatim any such trial or proceeding, excepting the arguments of respective counsels." Independently of this statute, as all Courts are open and public, a stenographer may privately take down proceedings. 

Opening the cause

To prevent confusion and make the profession of the law as dignified as it intrinsically is, every Justice should require a regular procedure. The first thing to be done, therefore, after the jury is sworn, and after hearing any motions which either counsel may make, looking to an adjournment, amendment, or nonsuit, is for the counsel of the plaintiff to state to the Court and jury the facts upon which he expects to recover a judgment. He should read the demand, or state its substance. Then follows the calling of witnesses or presentation of proofs.

Plaintiff or defendant may try his own cause The plaintiff or defendant may try his own cause, but, if he appears by attorney, the latter must be a licensed attorney-at-law. (C. S. 4055, §§ 16, 17).

The trial and proofs 

If at the hour for trial the plaintiff or defendant does not promptly appear, the Justice, in fairness, should wait a brief time. before beginning to hear the cause or to entertain a motion to dismiss the action. If a jury has been summoned and defendant does not appear, the Justice must dismiss it, and hear the cause alone, for no jury is required where no issues of fact are raised by the defendant.

The plaintiff has the burden upon him of making out, under his oath or that of one or more other witnesses, the truth and justness of his claim, (unless defendant appears and admits the demand).

It is no compliance with the rule requiring proof for a Justice to call a witness or two, who know nothing about the case, and to swear them so as to enter their names as witnesses upon the docket. Such a practice was severely censured by Chief Justice Hornblower in Crane v. Brundage, 2 Green 603, and it was intimated that it might be a cause for the impeachment of the Justice.

If the action is brought upon a note, or book account, the signature to the note, or correctness of the account, must be legally proven.

The proof of consideration of a note, or of the delivery of the goods sold need not be made, as it will be presumed, where the fact is not disputed by the defendant. 

Should the defendant be present and not plaintiff, and defendant has no set-off to be legally proved, the Justice cannot proceed to try the cause for the plaintiff, and defendant should move to nonsuit. (Cavalier v. Dougherty, 1 Hal. 227).

In each instance a witness must be first sworn or, if conscientiously scrupulous of taking an oath, affirmed. The oath is to be administered by the Justice (not by one of the parties, or counsel), and is in the words given in Form, below, which is the form required in  (S. C. A., § 34). 

In taking the oath, the witness puts his right hand upon the Bible. If he affirms he does not touch the Bible, but raises his right hand, and to the Justice responds, "I do so affirm." 

An objection to the witness as incompetent may be made before or after he is sworn, and sometimes after he has given his evidence, when, if the objection is sustained, his evidence will be excluded.

The party whose witness is being examined must question the witness first. This is the direct examination. In this inquiry the rule is not to put a leading question, or one suggesting the answer to the witness. Questions which are not relevant to the issue may be objected to, and if impertinent need not be answered.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

The witness can at any time, in this matter, put himself upon the protection of the Court. A witness may also use memoranda, if it is simply to refresh his recollection. But it must first appear that he made it himself, or another in his presence. 

Any question put may be objected to by opposing counsel, and the Justice must then rule upon it, saying "It is allowed," or "objection sustained." But it is too late to object to a question after it is answered, though a motion may be made to strike out the answer if it ought not to enter into consideration of the case. 

The usual exception where sworn proof is not required before judgment in The Small Cause Court, is where the defendant appears and confesses judgment. But it has been held that if defendant procures an adjournment on the express condition that if he did not appear on the adjourned day judgment should be rendered against him for the demand, and does not appear, it amounts to a confession and there need be no proofs. (Baldwin v. Brown, 2 Penn. 533).

The Justice may himself put any question to the witness which he deems proper to elicit the truth; but it should be a legal one. 

Of the direct evidence

The evidence should be presented in logical order; that for plaintiff first unless defendant admits the claim and his defense is set-off, or recoupment, when his witnesses will logically come first. The usual form of direct evidence is by means of witnesses put upon the stand for examination in the presence of the jury, although it may be, when a written contract, or obligation, is being sued upon, that it should be presented first and proved, and then any proper testimony may follow. 

The cross-examination

After a witness has been examined by his counsel, the next succeeding step is the cross-examination by the opposite counsel, or party, if he acts as his own counsel. This may be upon all points covered by the direct examination, but not outside of it; although, if the witness is one of the parties to the suit, he may be questioned upon anything relating to the suit, whether outside of the direct examination or not. If the witness is not a party to the suit, and the cross-examiner wishes to prove extraneous matter by him, he must make the witness his witness afterward. 

The re-direct and re-cross-examination A re-direct examination by the first party is permissible, to throw any new light upon the witness' previous evidence, or, perhaps, may be allowed to prove a point forgotten in the direct ex-

TRIAL OF CAuse 

489 amination. Then a re-cross is allowed. But the Justice, in his discretion, must not permit this to go far. Our Courts condemn any loose practice in this regard, and say that a long second or re-direct examination is usually unwise and unnecessary, and, therefore, wasteful of time. 

One counsel to examine

Questions to the witnesses should always be put by counsel when present, and the rule is not to permit two counsel upon the same side to interrogate the same witness. The same counsel who conducts the direct examination must re-examine. This rule is almost inflexible in Courts which practice strictly according to legal methods. 

Defense to be stated

When the plaintiff has finished submitting his proofs, the defendant's counsel should state, in brief, the defense to be made to the action, and what proof will be offered to sustain it. He is not obliged to do so, but the same reasons are in its favor that make it proper for plaintiff's counsel to open his side of the cause. 

Burden of proof

As before stated, if the defendant admits the plaintiff's de mand, and waives all proof of it, yet contests judgment, his witnesses are to be first sworn, and then those of the plaintiff in rebuttal. In this case the burden of proof is thrown on the defendant, and he opens the cause. But the natural and usual course is for the plaintiff's witnesses to be called first, as the burden of proof is upon him; then those for the defendant; then any the plaintiff may desire to have examined in rebuttal; and the defendant's in surrebuttal.

It is not customary to go farther; nor should the Justice allow new witnesses to be called to prove points already clear, after the party's side is presented. This, however, is entirely at the discretion of the Justice, and he must use it to facilitate proceedings and to guard the legal rights of both parties. 

No exceptions allowed; objections to be noted 

There cannot be exceptions taken to the admission of evidence, as in the higher Courts, since the cause is not reviewable in that form. But the party who objects to any written evidence may request the Justice to note such objection in his docket. 

Sometimes certain facts are admitted by the opposite party in the course of the trial; if they are important, to give jurisdiction upon which to base a verdict, they should be also noted in the docket; but the latter is not to be lumbered up by unimportant statements. J-31

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

No nonsuit after evidence submitted In cases of trial by jury, there may be no judgment of nonsuit or discontinuance after the merits of the cause on either side are submitted to the jury, unless by consent of both parties. The proper time to make a motion for such judgment is, therefore, before witnesses are called, or before the case of plaintiff is closed. (S. C. A., § 49). 

Summing up the cause

After the evidence is laid before the jury (when one is called), including all documents admitted as testimony, the rule is for the parties, or their counsel if they have any, to "sum up the cause." The party having the affirmative of the issue, or the burden of proof, whether plaintiff or defendant, has the closing argument. Usually this is the plaintiff. But where plaintiff's claim has been admitted, without evidence, the defendant having the burden of proof, his counsel should close the argument. Where there are two counsel upon a side and both wish to speak, the rule is for one counsel on the affirmative to make an address, the two counsel in opposition to follow, and the other counsel on the affirmative to close.

Arguments must be confined to the evidence; if they wander from it the Justice should ask counsel to confine himself to the facts in the cause.

Counsel's time may also be limited by the Court to a reasonable extent.

As to admitting the reading of any authorities, it is held that it is within the discretion of the Court. As in this State the jury are to judge of the facts only and the Court to instruct them as to the law, there is rarely any occasion for counsel to quote from authorities in summing up to the jury. He should address his remarks as to the law to the Justice and read him authorities, if he will hear them; but no unnecessary consumption of time is allowable even then. 

The Justice's charge to a jury

The Justice must charge the jury upon matters of law when requested so to do. This does not consist in haranguing them on questions of fact, but simply stating the law involved in the controversy, in a manner and spirit entirely impartial to the parties. 

It is usually better, because safer, not to ask the Justice to do this, and few Justices will volunteer to do this, unless requested. To merely read the statute under such circumstances is no charge. It is his duty to declare the law upon any point fairly and plainly involved in the cause, if requested.

If there is no question of law in dispute then it is no error

to refuse to charge. Nor need he charge upon a specific proposition submitted by counsel, unless it is made clearly to appear that the proposition was warranted by the evidence and involved in the verdict to be rendered. Nor upon points on which he is not asked to charge. Nor need he take up several points on which he is requested to charge and express a separate opinion upon each, if he so generally instructs them as to give the parties the benefit of all the principles and rules of law contained in his several points. (Westcott v. Danzenbaker, 1 Hal. 132; Davison v. 

Schooley, 5 Hal. 145; Youngs v. Sunderland, 3 Gr. 32).

If the jury, after retiring, return into Court and request to be informed upon a point of law the Justice must charge them then, whether he has done so before or not. When the jury ask for instructions, he cannot refuse; but he may and must refuse to argue the facts with them, or even to state facts as proved. 

They are to be the sole judges of the facts. 

The oath to the constable to attend a jury The constable must be sworn to attend the jury, after which he conducts them to a private room and locks the door, so that they may deliberate undisturbed, and without separation. The oath to him is to be administered by the Justice, as the Small 

Cause Act requires. (See Form below). 

The constable should be sworn, and not affirmed, unless he states that he is conscientiously scrupulous of taking an oath. 

That this oath was administered should appear upon the docket. 

Considering the verdict

It may happen that the jury will be ready to give their verdict without moving from their seats, but only in exceptional cases should this be done. They may take out with them any bonds, notes, deeds, books of account, or other written documents admitted in evidence, but no others.

While they are deliberating the constable must not suffer either party, or strangers, to get access to them, nor have any kind of communication with them. He must not, himself, speak to them, except by order of the Court, "unless it be to ask them whether they have agreed upon their verdict." He may not write or make signs to them. In short, the jury must not see, or have communication with anybody but themselves until they come to a determination, unless they ask for more instructions covering the law, in which case the constable must bring them before the Justice, who must publicly charge them upon the law as requested, and they must again retire.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE The verdict 

The jury should come to a verdict upon the facts presented to them. They cannot act upon their personal knowledge of facts, unless one or more of them has been sworn as witnesses. 

They are to act solely according to evidence produced at the trial. 

When the verdict is determined, and made unanimous, the jury will return into Court, and the Justice will call their names, the constable at the same time counting them aloud. (The usual formula is as stated in a Form below). 

If no one dissents to the verdict as stated by the foreman this must be considered the verdict of the whole jury in the cause. 

Neither party may require that the jury, after they return with a verdict, be polled in a civil cause. 

Form of the verdict

In cases of actions on Contract, the finding of the jury, if for plaintiff, should be, "We find for plaintiff- dollars." If the verdict is that nothing is due the plaintiff, the proper finding is, "No cause of action.' If there is something found due the defendant, he having filed a set-off as directed by the statute, the verdict will be, "We find for defendant- 

-dollars."

In cases of Tort, the finding of the jury must be for the plaintiff a certain sum in damages; or if for defendant, that they find "No cause of action."

In actions to recover penalties for violation of some statute or ordinance, "Guilty of the offense charged" or "Not guilty," is the proper verdict.

If the jury find a verdict clearly unlawful, as for the defendant a certain sum when he has not filed or claimed a set-off, the Justice should send them back to deliberate again. But if they then insist on their verdict he can only discharge them and record it.

The verdict must be openly pronounced by the jury through its foreman, and cannot be written and handed in to the Justice. 

It should not be rendered for more than the plaintiff's demand; but if it is, the plaintiff may consent to remit the surplus and take judgment for the residue. Neither can it be simply for the plaintiff for costs, as the statute directs in what case costs may may be given; nor that "a note set up by defendant be delivered nor that the damages of the plaintiff are assessed so much, and the defendant ordered to restore the goods. 

Where in one suit there are several distinct causes of action, it is proper to direct the jury to find and assess for each matter separately.

The parties to the action need not be present when the verdict is taken; but if they are near at hand the Justice should send

the constable after them, and wait a few minutes for them to arrive. 

A special verdict

Special verdicts by juries are not countenanced as a rule in  Nevertheless, it has been held that the section of the general Practice Act relating to higher Courts, that "no jury shall in any case be compelled to give a general verdict, so that they find a special verdict and show the truth of the fact and require the aid of the Court; but if of their own will they give a general verdict, the same shall be received," (P. L. 1903, p. 

580, § 159; C. S. 4103) applies to juries in The Small Cause 

Court. (Springer v. Reeves, 1 South. 207).

It has also been held that a Court may, when proper, recommend the jury to find a special verdict against the consent of either or both the parties. (Walkins v. Tintard, Coxe 378).

Exemplary damages 

A jury may sometimes render a verdict for exemplary damages, as they are called; damages in excess of the real injury shown, as a punishment for committing the injury at all. It is only allowed in actions in Tort and where there was clearly malice on the part of the defendant. 

A verdict on Sunday

A verdict may be rendered on Sunday if the jury fail to agree until that day. But the Justice should simply note the verdict, and not enter up judgment in his docket until Monday and of the date of Monday. As he can do no official act on Sunday (except in criminal and certain semi-criminal matters) a judgment entered upon that day would be void. (Van Riper v. Van 

Riper, 1 South. 156). 

Struck jury; jury of view

The statutes of this State relating to struck juries and juries of view do not apply to The Small Cause Court. 

Disagreement of the jury

When the jury are not of one mind, and are unable to become so after a full interchange of views, they will so report to the Justice, who, if he is satisfied they cannot agree, and it will be fruitless to keep them longer together, will discharge them.

The rule as to the period when this may be done is thus declared in this State by Chief Justice Hornblower: "The jury ought to be kept together until the confinement and privations they have

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

endured are such as to satisfy the Court that their disagreement is not the result of mere trick or obstinacy in some of the jurors, but a conscientious difference of opinions, honestly and intelligently adhered to, and which compels them rather to suffer the inconveniences and privations of a jury room than to yield up to their associates." (Gulick v. Van Tillburgh, 1 Harr. 417).

They are entitled after their discharge to be paid the same fees as if they had agreed upon a verdict. 

Upon a disagreement of the jury a new jury may be called, and it is usual to fix a subsequent day for the trial, by adjournment. But none of the former jurymen are competent to serve upon such new jury. 

Should a second jury disagree, a third may be called, etc.

The statute fixes no limit to the number of successive juries which may be summoned, except by the words, "until a verdict is obtained."

If a jury do not disagree, however, but give a verdict which is not a verdict, and cannot be amended, the jurisdiction of the Justice ceases; the plaintiff must bring his suit anew. 

Entry of judgment upon verdict (See general title, "Judgment").

You do swear in the presence of Almighty God [or do affirm, if he declares he is conscientiously scrupulous of taking an oath] that you will, to the utmost of your ability, keep every person sworn [or affirmed] on this jury together in some private and convenient place, without meat or drink, water excepted; that you will not suffer any person to speak to them, nor speak to them yourself, except by order of the Court, unless it be to ask them whether they have agreed on their verdict, until they have agreed on their verdict. 

355. Procedure on return of jury 

The Justice should say: "Gentlemen of the jury, have you agreed upon your verdict?" The answer being in the affirmative, the Justice will continue: "Who shall say for you?" To which it is usual for one or more of the jury to answer: "The foreman." The Justice then inquires: "Who do you find for?" when the foreman will orally deliver the verdict, and the Justice record it. Then the Justice will say, "Gentlemen of the jury, listen to your verdict, as the Court has recorded it. You say that you find" [stating the verdict to them, in the same words in which it was given, adding afterwards]: "and so say you all," to which they usually nod assent. If none state they object it means assent.

Some general remarks Vagrancy

Vagrancy is often classed in the statutes with disorderly conduct, and proceeded against under the Disorderly Persons Act. (See under that general subject). But it, like disorderly conduct, may also be proceeded against under other enactments, and this is usually done when the offender is a child under a certain age. 

Adult vagrants should be proceeded against under the Disorderly Persons Act, but not children, the intent of the law being to be less severe with children than adults.

Truants from school may be considered as vagrants and treated as disorderly persons, or as juvenile deliquents, but are no longer to be proceeded against before a Justice of the Peace (see P. L. 1914, p. 464, §§ 14, 15; N. J. Cum. Supp. 3217), although a Justice may take a complaint against them in first-class counties, and transfer it immediately to the Juvenile Court. (P. 

L. 1912, p. 608, § 10; N. J. Cum. Supp. 916).

Attention should also be paid to the formation and jurisdiction of "Juvenile and Relations" Courts. (P. L. 1929, p. 274), now established in each county which gives exclusive jurisdiction to that Court as to the misconduct of children under sixteen.

Vessels, Licensing Masters, Etc. 

Registration, licensing, etc.

By an Act of 1919 no person may operate a power vessel of any kind upon the waters of this State without being licensed; the vessels to be first registered with the Board of Commerce and Navigation, and with other provisions to be consulted. (P. L. 

1919, p. 563). Penalties run from $50 to $100, to be recovered in a civil action of Debt before a District Court or Justice of the 

Peace having jurisdiction.

But a supplement to the Act (P. L. 1920, p. 292) provides for a summary proceeding before "any magistrate of the county, or Recorder, or Police Magistrate," and provides for a complaint, summons or warrant, appeal, etc., and the penalty for violation of the Act of 1919 is a fine not exceeding $100, or imprisonment not exceeding ten days, or double such penalty for a second offense. 

The supplement of 1920 needs to be carefully consulted in any such summary proceeding.

As there is no repealer in the supplement, we judge the civil proceeding mentioned in the former paragraph may be had, or the summary proceeding, according to the complainant's desire. 

Vice and Immorality

I. THE "SUNDAY" LAWS AND THE 1933 RESERVATIONS 

Offenses against the Sabbath

The offenses against the Christian Sabbath have until recently been the following, and prosecutions are to be begun within thirty days after the commission of the offense. The fact that many of the provisions named are termed by some "The Blue Laws of New Jersey," and that some are enforced and others not, does not alter the fact that they are existing statutes and intended to be obeyed. The Act concerning matters under this general head of "Vice and Immorality" is known as "The Vice and Immorality 

Act" (Revision of 1877; C. S. 5712) and, before amendments, forbade on Sunday:

All worldly employment or business, ordinary or servile labor or work, either upon land or water (works of necessity and charity excepted), shooting, fishing (if with seine or net, see below), sporting, hunting, racing or frequenting tippling houses, or any interludes or plays, dancing, singing, fiddling, or other music for the sake of merriment; and all playing at football, fives, nine pins,

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

bowls, long bullets or quoits, and any other kind of playing sports, pastimes or diversions; but the forfeiture ($1 for the use of the township poor) is limited to offenders of fourteen years or upwards. (C. S. 5712, § 1).

But it is not an offense to walk, ride or drive for recreation; nor to print, publish and sell newspapers; nor to sell and deliver milk; nor to hire conveyances for driving unless made so by the governing body of municipalities or incorporated camp meeting associations; nor in case of a person going to or from a place of worship within the distance of twenty miles, or going to call a physician, surgeon or midwife, or carrying a mail to or from any post office, or "going express" by order of any public officer. Hotels may also dress victuals for travellers, or boarders. It is also made lawful for railroad companies to run one passenger train each way over their road. (Ibid, §§ 1, 1a).

It is further provided, that if any person is found fishing, sporting, playing, dancing, fiddling, shooting, hunting, gunning, traveling, or going to or returning from any market, or landing, with carts, wagons, or seeds, or behaving in a disorderly manner on the Sabbath, any constable or citizen may stop such person at once, and detain him until the next day, when he may be taken before a Justice of the Peace. (Ibid, § 1).

To expose for sale any wares, fruit, meat, fish, or chattels, etc., on Sunday is to occasion a forfeiture of $2. (Ibid).

To cast, draw, or make use of any seine or net for the purpose of catching fish in any pond, lake, stream or river, or to aid or assist therein is punishable with a forfeiture of $14 for every offense. (§ 2).

Driving a stage, unless in cases of necessity or mercy or to carry a mail, is punishable by a fine of eight dollars for every offense. The Act directs that every Justice of the Peace seeing or knowing any such stage to be driven, shall stop and detain the same until the next day, and then inflict the penalties. (§ 3). 

All wagoners, carters, draymen, drovers, butchers or their servants, traveling with wagons, to load or unload merchandise, or driving animals, are subject to a penalty of $2 for every offense. If cattle, sheep or hogs are being driven to market, they may be stopped by the Justice until the next day. (§ 4). 

To serve any writ, process, warrant, order, judgment or decree (except in criminal cases, or breach of the peace) will not only make it void in the service, but the party upon whom it is served may have damages upon him who serves it the same as if there had been service without writ or process. (§ 5). Subsequent statutes have made exceptions; for example, the Motor Vehicle, Fish and Game, Bastardy, etc., Acts.

To wilfully disquiet or disturb any assembly met for relig-

ious worship, either by making a noise, or rude or indecent behavior, or profane talk, whether in the meeting or out of it, is punishable by a fine of $10. Any citizen or freeholder may at once apprehend such person if it be on Sunday that he disturbs the meeting, and detain him until the next day. This Act is not limited to Sundays however, as on any other day it is unlawful to disturb such meeting. (§§ 9, 17).

All transportation of freight, excepting milk, on any highway, railroad or canal on the Sabbath, is forbidden. Every Justice seeing or knowing of the passage of such freight, must stop and detain the same until the next day and then enforce the pen alty. (§§ 13, 31). The penalty is $20. (§§ 29-32 of the "Vice and Immorality" Acts are misplaced, and relate to § 13). 

In 1927 (P. L., p. 218) barbers were forbidden to shave on

Sunday under a penalty of $25 fine or 30 days imprisonment, and for a second offense double the same. 

Exemption of certain persons

Persons who religiously observe Saturday as the Sabbath (as Seventh-day Baptists or Hebrews) cannot, usually, be convicted of having labored or worked on Sunday; but the burden of proof will be upon them to show that they uniformly keep the seventh day as the Sabbath, and habitually abstain from following any business on that day, or recreation, and devote it exclusively to exercise and religious worship. But even in this case the work must not disturb other people in the observance of the Sabbath, nor may any articles of merchandise be openly exposed for sale. 

Reservations in 1933 Act

Reservations, by amendment, to the general Act, were made in 1933 (P. L., Chapter 115) declaring it not to be unlawful to print, sell, etc., newspapers, sell and deliver milk, walk, ride or drive for recreation, hire horses and carriages on Sunday, unless disturbing those observing the day, but permitting municipalities and Camp Meeting Associations to regulate these matters. How ever, the Act is inoperative until adopted by the legal voters of any city, borough, town, township or village in manner as set forth. (It is not very clear why this amending Act was passed as it scarcely changes the previous statutes).

II. PROFANITY AND DRUNKENNESS 

Punishing profanity and drunkenness 

All persons who profanely swear and curse are liable to a

HONEYMAN'S Justice fine of fifty cents for each offense, and all persons becoming intoxicated (tramps excepted, who are punished by the Tramp Act) are liable to a fine of one dollar for each offense for the use of the township poor. (C. S. 5714, §§ 6, 7). 

In the former case every Justice is required to convict without other proof, if the swearing or cursing is in his presence, or hearing; otherwise the usual complaint must be made. There may be a conviction for each oath uttered during a single day, and without separate complaints or convictions; they may all be embraced in one information and conviction. (Johnson v. Barclay, 1 Harr. 1). 

If on conviction of profane swearing the offender does not at once pay the forfeit, or give security for its payment within six days, then, if he be over fourteen years of age, he shall be committed to the jail of the county, city or town corporate for a time not exceeding four days. If he be not above fourteen years of age, distress and sale to pay the same will issue against the goods and chattels of his parents or masters. (§§ 14, 15). 

In the case of intoxication conviction may be upon the view of the Justice, the confession of the party, or testimony of witnesses. Of course a complaint is necessary unless the Justice views the offense. In case of conviction the offender must pay down the fine and costs at once, or give security for their payment within three days, or the offender must be committed to jail for a space of time not exceeding four days. (§ 7).

All prosecutions must be within thirty days from the commission of the offense. (Ibid, § 23).

III. PUBLIC SHOWS 

Plays, etc., to be licensed 

All interludes, farces, or plays, games, tricks, jugglery, sleight of hand, bear-beating, or bull-baiting, of any kind, exhibited for gain or reward on any public stage, or any public place, without a license in writing first obtained under the hand of three Justices of the Peace of the county, city, or town corporate, are contrary to law, and the offenders are liable to a fine of sixteen dollars. (Ibid, § 8. City charters and borough and town ordinances usually supersede this provision).

As the Crimes Act makes the cruelly beating or torturing of any animal a misdemeanor, it is clear that bear-beating and bullbaiting could not lawfully be licensed. (See C. S. 1792, § 155).

The Act does not prevent the exhibition of any natural curiosity, or any invention or improvement in mechanics or arts.

IV.

PROCEDURE IN GENERAL 

Arrests made by whom

Where not otherwise specified above, the arrests are to be in the usual way, by a regular constable, either upon his view or upon a warrant regularly issued.

It, is, however, lawful for any persons who own and reside on lands "situated beyond and within one mile of the corporate limits of any city" to designate, in writing, one or more special constables, for any term not exceeding one year, who may apprehend offenders under this Act and detain them until next day, when they are to be taken before a magistrate, unless they enter into bond to appear at a day he may designate to answer the charge, when he may discharge them from custody. (C. S. 5722, 32b). 

Jurisdiction of Justice of the Peace

In all cities jurisdiction under the Vice and Immorality Act is given to the Recorder or Police Justice, who are to have exclusive jurisdiction, unless the Recorder is a member of the governing body. But if there is neither, a Justice of the Peace has jurisdiction. (§§ 26a, 26b). In other places the complaints are to be made only before a Justice of the Peace, unless some statute, or ordinance permitted under some statute relating to some other class of municipalities, directs that other magistrates may have jurisdiction.

It is to be remembered that the "Vice and Immorality” Act is not a Crimes Act. Hence, while various Recorders, etc., may be authorized to take cognizance of "all criminal cases," that means only cases designated as crimes in the Crimes Act, or some other Act making an offense a misdemeanor. To secure jurisdiction under the Vice and Immorality Act some statute must express the fact that such jurisdiction is given. 

Complaint and conviction

The proceedings under the Vice and Immorality Act before a Justice of the Peace are not in The Small Cause Court, but before the Justice as magistrate. (Handlin ads. State, 1 Harr. 96).

The complaint must be made within thirty days from the time of the commission of the offense. (C. S. 5720, § 23). In drawing it the language of the statute should be closely studied. 

No "state of demand" is necessary; the complaint is sufficient. But if the conviction is on view, or confession, it must be so stated in the conviction.

The offender may be convicted of the offense either upon the personal view of the Justice without a complaint, or the confes-

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

sion of the party offending, or proof by any witness or witnesses; but in the latter case written complaint must be made in the usual manner and a process served personally. (Handlin ads. State, supra). 

If he chooses, the offender may pay the forfeiture and charges to the Justice before conviction, in which case that ends the matter, except that the Justice must pay over the forfeiture to the overseer of the poor to whom it belongs. 

One complaint and a joint conviction of two or more persons for offenses individually separate and distinct are illegal; there must be separate proceedings.

The conviction must be in writing, signed by the Justice, and according to the Form prescribed in the statute (which is given in the Forms below). It should state fully the witnesses, if any, and the particular offense, showing it comes within the statute. 

The conviction is to be written on a sheet of paper and kept by the Justice, unless in case of appeal; it is not to be written out in the Justice's civil docket, as the proceedings are not in The Small Cause Court, nor in the Complaint Docket, which is only for criminal, or semi-criminal matters.

After conviction, and in cases where distress is allowed, a warrant must issue to the constable, commanding him to make distress of the goods and chattels of the offender, and to pay therefrom the penalty to the overseer of the township. 

In default of such distress, a commitment will issue to have the offender placed in jail for a term, at the discretion of the Justice, not exceeding ten days. (§ 1). But this is not applicable to all the offenses under the Vice and Immorality Act. It is appliccable to the offenses against the Sabbath, although in a conviction of fishing by seine or net on Sunday the term in jail is not limited to ten days, but is to be until the forfeiture is paid, or the offender is "delivered by due course of law." (§ 2). In the case of disturbing religious meetings it is applicable. (§ 9). In the case of drunkenness if the fine is not paid or security given for payment within three days, the offender is to be committed not exceeding four days. (§ 7). In the case of profane swearing, the forfeit is to be paid down at once, or security given to pay within six days, or the offender is to be sent to jail not exceeding four days; but if he is not above fourteen years of age, the warrant of distress and sale is to be against his parent or master. (§ 15). 

Sale by distress

In all cases where a Justice is empowered to issue a warrant of distress for the levying of a penalty or fine, and no mode for the disposal of the distress is pointed out, the Justice may, in such warrant, order a sale within a certain time, not less than four nor

more than ten days distant unless the penalty be sooner paid. (C. 

S. 1946, § 23). 

Trial by jury

In the trial of offenses under the Vice and Immorality Act, every offender may have a jury upon demand, except where under the Act the Justice is authorized to convict on his own view or personal knowledge. The jury must consist of six men. A venire will issue to a constable to summon them, and the issue will be whether the person is guilty or not guilty of the offense charged against him. The trial will proceed as in other cases of trial by jury. The costs, however, of the Justice and constable upon the venire, the jury, and swearing and attending the same, must in all cases be paid by the person demanding the jury. (C. S. 5720, § 25). 

Where committed

No person shall be committed to the county jail of any city or town corporate for an offense not committed within such city or town corporate. In other words, when the offense is committed outside of a city or town corporate, the commitment must be to the county jail; but otherwise to the lockup, or jail, of such city or town corporate, unless there is none, and then to the county jail. The imprisonment must be in the municipality where the offense is committed when practicable. (Ibid, § 27). Appeals

No conviction under the Vice and Immorality Act can be removed into the Supreme Court by certiorari, but the defendant may appeal to the next Quarter Sessions, which will hear and determine it in a summary way. But before appealing the appellant must pay to the Justice the penalty and costs of prosecution, which will be returned to the appellant if the judgment is reversed. (§ 19). 

Fees and costs

Same now as in usual criminal cases. (See under general title, "Fees and Costs").
