Warrant (Civil) 

What a civil warrant is

A civil warrant, used as a first process in an action, whereby the body of the defendant is to brought into Court to answer to such action, is what is termed in law a capias ad respondendum. 

It means "that you take to respond." It is to be used in place of a summons only under circumstances to be named below, or when the law permits it.

There is also the capias ad satisfaciendum, which means "that you take to satisfy," but this is a combination of execution and warrant, and is used only as the final process in an action. (See under general title "Execution").

When the capias ad respondendum to be used There are many cases where the civil warrant (capias as it is shortly termed) is employed in actions to recover penalties, or in other proceedings, but in such case its basis must be found in the special statute itself, regulating such actions or proceedings. 

There it is more in the nature of a criminal process. 

In ordinary civil actions on Contract à capias can be used only when the defendant is guilty of some fraud connected with the contract; or is about to practice a fraud upon the plaintiff by way of prevention of the collection of his debt. Formerly there were statutes permitting imprisonment in actions for debt in cer-

WARRANT (CIVIL) 

507 tain cases, but their abolition was finally accomplished in New 

Jersey in 1840.

The following are the provisions of the statute which now permit a capias to be used as the first process in an action on Contract: "A warrant shall be issued only in actions on contract and upon proof by affidavit or otherwise to the satisfaction of the Justice, that there is a debt or demand founded upon contract, express or implied, due the plaintiff from the defendant, specifying the nature and particulars of said debt or demand, and establishing one or more of the following particulars: "I. That the defendant fraudulently contracted the debt or incurred the obligation respecting which suit is brought; or, "II. That the defendant is about to remove any of his property out of the State with intent to defraud his creditors; or, "III. That the defendant has assigned, removed or disposed of, or is about to assign, remove or dispose of, any of his property with intent to defraud his creditors." (S. C. A., § 13). 

It will be noticed that two matters must appear "to the satisfaction of the Justice" before there may be an order for the warrant: First, That there is a "a debt or demand founded upon contract, express or implied, due the plaintiff from the defendant," which is to be specified in the affidavit, or proof. Second, That there was fraud in the incurring of the obligation; or that there is about to be such a disposition of the property by defendant as shows an "intent to defraud his creditors." Proof of one or the other alone will not do. If the debt is shown but not the fraud, or a fraud is shown and not the debt, no warrant can issue. 

The language of the statute that the proof is to be "by affidavit or otherwise" does not mean that it may be oral proof. It must be by affidavit, or something in writing that may be "filed by said Justice." (§ 14).

An agent, or other third party, having a competent legal knowledge of the facts to which he swears, may make the affidavit, but he must aver knowledge of his own. (Bowne v. Titus, 1 Vr. 344).

Too great importance cannot be attached to the affidavit. It is the foundation of the right of the Justice to issue the capias, and should it not contain facts which are even colorably fraudulent, the capias will be set aside on the summary review which the Act authorizes a Supreme Court Justice, or other Judge, to make. 

It will not be sufficient for the affidavit to follow the language of the statute, and declare "that the defendant fraudulently contracted the debt or incurred the obligation respecting which suit is brought," or use a mere sentence in the statute. Such facts must be set out as will "establish one or more" of the particulars

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

specified in the statute and such facts as sworn to and standing alone would establish a case of fraud before a jury. (Kipp v. 

Chamberlain, Spen. 658; Bowne v. Titus, 1 Vr. 343). These decisions relate to a capias ad satisfaciendum (an execution-warrant), but embrace the same principles as those under consideration.

Fraud in inception of the debt Fraud in the inception of the debt means clear dishonesty. "Fraud," one definition says, "in its general acceptation may be defined as the misrepresentation or concealment of a material fact." It is "any cunning, deception, or artifice used to circumvent, cheat or deceive another." Fraud in contracting the debt, in the nature of things, means some fraudulent conduct at the time of the contract whereby the other party was deceived. 

Fraud subsequent to the contracting of the debt Fraud subsequent to the contracting of the debt is usually to be judged by circumstances rather than words. For example, the debtor may be arranging to remove at night instead of by day, out of the county. Or he may be arranging to go out of the State with his property, which may be ample to satisfy his debt, but without being willing to do anything whatever toward settling the debt.

To merely state that a man refused to apply certain funds to the payment of his debt would be insufficient; he might have a good reason; but if the circumstances of his refusal are, for example, that he denies the existence of such funds, and hides them from reach; or if he declares he will get away and thus "do" the plaintiff, he is guilty of fraudulent intent. 

There cannot be counter affidavits presented to the Justice, nor can the original proof filed be amended. The defendant is not to be sent for, first, and permitted to rebut plaintiff's statement upon his oath, or that of any parties on his behalf; nor, after he appears, can he be heard in defense on the merits, until the matter comes up for trial. 

Order, filing and docket entry

The Justice is to file the affidavit (and other written proofs, if any) and then, if satisfied a warrant should issue, he must prepare an order that a warrant issue, and file such order with the proof. (S. C. A., § 14). At the same time he must make an entry in his docket of the filing of the affidavit and order, under the general provisions of the statute requiring him to keep full proceedings in actions before him in his docket. 

The order should recite the facts and be to the effect that a

WARRANT (CIVIL) 

509 warrant shall issue against the defendant for an amount to be specified.

The capias and its service The capias must be legally drawn, or the constable will have no right to act upon it.

It must be tested the day it is issued, be signed by the Justice and sealed with his official seal, when (as is usual) the proceedings are in The Small Cause Court (S. C. A., § 11), otherwise with the usual scroll seal.

It is to be returnable "forthwith," which means as soon as the constable can arrest the defendant and convey him to the place designated in the process, to be before the Justice who issued it. 

The statement of the names of the plaintiff and defendant, the nature of the action, the place where the defendant is to be brought, the amount demanded, the order for the arrest, the signature and official seal of the Justice and the indorsement, must all receive the same attention, as in the case of any other first process. The sum demanded must be indorsed on the warrant, with costs, in order that if the defendant deems proper to pay the same without further proceedings he may do so.

Any irregularity in the issuing and form of the warrant is waived by the defendant appearing and entering into recognizance, without objection. "The rule is that a general appearance of the defendant is a waiver of all objections to the form of the process and the manner of its service." (Clifford v. Overseer of 

Frankford, 8 Vr. 154; Murat v. Hutchinson, 1 Harr. 467).

If a month intervenes before the arrest can be made, still the warrant is good. Being returnable at no fixed time, but "forthwith," that means forthwith after the officer has apprehended the defendant.

The arrest cannot be made on Sunday. (C. S. 5715, § 5). 

As the constable can only serve a summons within the county, so a civil warrant stands on the same footing. The Justice has no jurisdiction beyond the county; hence the constable must find the defendant within that territory, and cannot proceed to hunt for him outside (unless per some special statute).

The return of the constable to the warrant, if defective, may be amended by him before the trial of the cause, provided he has served the warrant in accordance with the law and it is only the "return" that is incorrect. (S. C. A., § 107). 

Proceedings subsequent to the arrest

Upon the arrest of the defendant there are six courses open to him: 

1. He may pay to the constable the sum due, with costs, as

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

indorsed on the warrant. The constable's receipt will be a full discharge to the defendant from the plaintiff's demand. (S. C. 

A., § 18). 

2. He may, instead of going before the Justice, give to the constable a bond to the plaintiff in the manner described in the 

Act. (Ibid, § 20).

Of the sufficiency of the one or more sureties who may execute the bond, the constable must judge. As he would be liable for negligence if he took an insufficient bond, he is to observe the utmost caution respecting it, yet not an arbitrarily oppressive one. 

The debt should be prospectively secured; no "straw bond" will comply with the statute.

The bond must be an obligation to the plaintiff (by name), not to the constable, or Justice. 

3. When taken before the Justice, or at any time before trial, he may enter into recognizance as stated in the Small Cause 

Act. (S. C. A., § 21). 

It should be noted that both the constable by whom the defendant is arrested and the Justice, if the defendant is brought before him under the warrant, should be reasonable and not arbitrary in their conduct in the matter of giving defendant time to prepare his bond, and obtain the surety, provided the defendant goes immediately about it. In the eye of the law the object of the warrant and arrest is, not to punish the defendant, but to secure the debt due to the plaintiff, which latter is best made sure by having the defendant give bond with freehold surety. While the defendant goes to see his bail, if near at hand, the constable must accompany him; or the bail may be sent for, in which case the officer (or the Justice, if defendant is before him) should await a proper time for the arrival of the bail before further steps are taken. 

4. If the Justice chooses to commit the defendant to the constable's care until the time fixed for the trial, such commitment must be in writing, the same as a commitment to jail. (§ 19). 

Otherwise, if constable permits defendant to go away, and he does not subsequently appear at the time to which the hearing is adjourned, the defendant will be discharged from arrest. (Dunham v. Solomon, 1 Harr. 50).

During such committal to the constable the latter may confine him in a proper room and take all needful precautions that he shall not escape. If necessary, he may summon to his aid any men of the county to prevent his escape.

If the plaintiff discharges the defendant from arrest upon his verbal promise to appear before the Justice, it is, practically, a discharge to that action, and if he does not appear the plaintiff can go no further in that suit. (Anonymous, 2 Hal. 120).

WARRANT (CIVIL) 

511 5. He may go to jail to await the hearing, which must be "not exceeding three days from the time of the warrant." 

A., § 19). (S. C. 

The "command to the constable to convey the defendant to the jail" means a written commitment in due form. 

6. Before the trial of the cause, the defendant may make application to one of the Judges of the Supreme, Circuit or Common Pleas Court, or a Supreme Court Commissioner, to set aside the order for arrest. Of course he will have given, in the meantime, a bond, either to the constable or Justice, or allow himself to have been committed, as the constable cannot delay service of the capias to await a review of the order. The application to the higher authority is to have the order set aside, before the trial. (§ 15).

The Justice, Judge or Commissioner above named will not take further proofs on the hearing before him, but consider only the facts set forth in the original affidavit, or proof. (Painter v. 

Houston, 4 Dutch. 121).

If such Judge, etc., holds that the proof was sufficient to warrant the arrest, the application will be dismissed, and the Justice of the Peace will go on with the trial at the time set, as if no such application to a higher authority had been made. If, however, such Judge, etc., holds the proof insufficient to warrant an arrest, he will make an order, directing that the order of arrest be set aside, which, when filed with the Justice, will conclude the suit, and the bond given will become void. In such case, the plaintiff may begin a new action by summons in the usual manner, but cannot have process against the defendant's body. (S. C. A., § 15). 

Persons privileged from arrest

The distinction made by the statute between those liable and those not liable to arrest under a civil warrant is incomplete, as certain persons are privileged from arrest by special statutes, or by the common law. For example: 

1. While usually executors, administrators and heirs cannot be held to bail, they may if they have wasted or converted to their own use the estate of the testator, or intestate. (C. S. 2261, § 6). 

2. An infant cannot be held to bail, when the plea of infancy would be a bar to the action. 

3. In actions on bail bonds, recognizances of bail, and replevin bonds, the defendant cannot be held to bail. 

4. Nor can members of a corporation, sued in their corporate capacity. 

5. Nor ambassadors of foreign nations.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

6. Witnesses in a suit while going to, attending upon, and returning from Court, allowing one day for every 30 miles from their residence; also the officers of the Court, are privileged from arrest while attending to Court duties. The witnesses, however, must be regularly subpoenaed witnesses. (C. S. 2224, § 14). 

7. Senators and representatives in Congress, while going to, attending, or returning from their respective Houses. (Const. 

U. S., Art. I, § 6). 

8. The Executive of a State or of the United States. 

9. Members of the State Legislature, while the Legislature is sitting, or in going to and returning from it. (Const. of N. J. 

Art. 14, Sec. 4, par. 8). 

10. A legal voter on the day of election. 

11. Every person belonging to the National Guard of the 

State, going to, returning from or remaining at any place at which he is required to attend for military duty. (P. L. 1917, p. 177, § 59; N. J. Cum. Supp. 1953). 

12. Idiots and lunatics, during the time of their idiocy or lunacy. (C. S. 2794, § 20). 

13. Women are exempt. (S. C. A., § 11). 

Trial before the Justice

On the day set for the trial, the proceedings before the Justice are to be the same as if the action were begun by summons. 

If the defendant has not entered into recognizance it must be speedy ("not exceeding three days," unless defendant consents to a longer time); but otherwise there may be one or more adjournments for reasonable cause, a jury trial, if required by either party, and all the proceedings are to be in usual form. (See under general title "Trial of Cause").

But after judgment rendered for plaintiff, the execution may be against the body, when the capias first issued is in force, or if certain facts are then shown by affidavit, (as to which, see under general title "Execution"). 

Proceedings on forfeiture of defendant's bond 

The statute says: "If the recognizance" [given by defendant when action is begun by capias] "shall become forfeited, the Justice may, on five days' notice to the surety, to be served as a summons should be, enter up a judgment against the surety in favor of the plaintiff for the amount of the judgment against the defendant in the original action, with interest and costs, and issue execution thereon as in other cases." (S. C. A., § 22).

This, however, can only be after the judgment is forfeited by breach of all its conditions. It will not be forfeited simply because defendant does not appear on the day of trial, for in his

WARRANT (CIVIL) 

513 absence the Justice will, on motion of plaintiff, proceed and determine the case, and, if judgment be recovered against the defendant, defendant will comply with the conditions of the bond if he surrenders himself to the constable on the execution to be issued, or if he pays the judgment, or if his surety pays the judgment. 

The proper proceeding, therefore, on the part of the plaintiff, after the bond is given, is, first, to secure judgment; second, to issue execution; third, if the execution should be returned unsatisfied, the Justice may then give five days' notice to the surety to be served as a summons by a constable, and, on the return day, he may give judgment of forfeiture of the recognizance for the amount of the judgment, with interest and costs, whereupon execution will issue against the surety.

What a will is

What is usually known as a will, generally called in law a "last will and testament," is a formal instrument in writing properly signed, sealed and witnessed, by which a person may dispose of his property to take effect after his death. 

Besides written wills, however, there are what are called nuncupative wills, which are wills, not in writing, made during the last sickness of the deceased, being such as the testator may have been unable to duly execute. Such consist of a verbal declaration by the testator of his wishes as to disposal of his property, made in the presence of witnesses called upon by him to bear witness that such is his will. The proofs have to be circumstantial and positive to make such a will stand a test.

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE 

Requisites of written will The following are the requisites to the execution of a lawful will (not nuncupative), and are given here because a Justice of the Peace may have to prepare a will, although it should always be drawn by a careful lawyer, familiar with the effect of all its provisions: 

1. The will must be in writing, signed by the testator, who must be twenty-one years of age or over, and of sound mind, memory and understanding. 

2. It must be declared by him to be his last will, in the hearing of at least two witnesses. 

3. The witnesses must be present at the same time, and must either see the testator make his signature, or hear him acknowledge the making thereof. 

4. The witnesses must thereupon subscribe their names to the will as witnesses thereto in the presence of the testator, and at his request.

If all these requirements are not strictly observed, the will will be void.

It is not necessary that the witnesses shall know the contents of the will; nor is any seal necessary, though it is usual to affix a seal, actual or by scroll, after the testator's signature.

No person interested under the will, as executor, legatee, or otherwise, should be a witness.

If there has been a preceding will it should be expressly revoked by the new will. (For statutes as to wills, see C. S. 5861 et seq.). Miscellaneous

A married woman above the age of twenty-one may devise her real or personal property by will the same as if she were an unmarried woman, but not any estate to which her husband would be, at her death, entitled in law. (C. S. 3235, § 9).

An executor of a will need not give bonds, unless required by the will.

A codicil to a will requires all the formalities of an original will to make it effective, and so to do all written revocations of wills.

A will can be cancelled in no other way than by being burned, torn or obliterated by the testator himself, or in his presence, and by his direction and consent, or by revocation in writing, executed in the same manner as wills are required to be executed. (Munday v. Munday, 2 McCart, 294).

HONEYMAN'S JUSTICE Woodchucks 

Destruction and premium 

By an Act of 1912 (P. L., p. 587; N. J. Cum. Supp. 83) provisions are made for the destruction of woodchucks (usually known as groundhogs). A premium of fifty cents for each one killed is to be paid by the board of chosen freeholders of the county (but see exception below). If one wilfully and fraudulently collects such premium, or assists in the same, he will be guilty of a misdemeanor. 

Proceedings before Justice

When a person has slain such animal and desires to obtain the premium, he may produce it before any Justice of the Peace of the county in which it was killed, and make affidavit before him of the time and place of killing; or he may produce the pelt alone, if entire from the tip of the nose. Upon such production the Justice, in the presence of such person and one qualified voter of the county, is required to cut off the ears of the animal, and, in the presence of such persons, burn the same. A certificate is then to be given to the person producing the animal, or pelt, directed to the board of chosen freeholders, containing these facts: "The kind of animal, and when, where and by whom killed, and the date, by whom and in the presence of what qualified voter the ears of such animal were destroyed, and the residences of the person killing the said animal and of said voter." 

The affdavit is to be filed by the Justice, or he is to "cause the same to be filed," in the office of the county collector. 

In order that the Act may not be effective in any county the board of chosen freeholders must pass a resolution by a twothirds vote of all its members that the Act "is not for the best interest of the people of the county they represent."
